text:
MINNEAPOLIS — In its travel advisor­ies, the U.S. State Depart­ment warns Amer­ic­ans not to visit Hon­duras’ Gra­cias a Dios region, alert­ing them to viol­ent crime, armed rob­bery, murder and act­ive ter­ror­ist groups.

But for Hon­dur­ans, the mes­sage is less stark. “Over­all, Gra­cias a Dios is a low­crime, func­tion­ing depart­ment,” says a State Depart­ment back­ground report obtained by the Asso­ci­ated Press.

The report, and sim­ilar doc­u­ments about Guatem­ala, Mex­ico and El Sal­vador, were pre­pared for use in immig­ra­tion courts, where asylum denial rates have soared to 94% dur­ing Pres­id­ent Trump’s second term.

The reports use cherry­picked data, care­ful phras­ing and in some cases facts that don’t stand up to scru­tiny to cre­ate mis­lead­ing depic­tions of coun­tries that are in fact often plagued by viol­ence, gov­ern­ment cor­rup­tion and police inac­tion.

They appear designed to make it easier for judges to deny asylum to people from those nations f lee­ing domestic viol­ence and crim­inal gangs, paint­ing pic­tures of life in their home coun­tries that often clash with real­ity.

The reports have been “reverse-engin­eered,” said Elliot Young, a pro­fessor at Lewis & Clark Col­lege who ana­lyzed the doc­u­ments for the col­lege’s Migra­tion and Asylum Lab.

“They’re try­ing to hit the most fre­quent kinds of [asylum] cases that come up and provide counterevid­ence to the over­whelm­ing evid­ence that these are dan­ger­ous places,” said Young, a scholar of Latin Amer­ica and asylum law who has test­i­fied as an expert wit­ness in more than 700 asylum cases.

In a state­ment, the State Depart­ment said that in line with U.S. laws and reg­u­la­tions it “may provide inform­a­tion about con­di­tions in for­eign coun­tries” to immig­ra­tion courts and U.S. Cit­izen­ship and Immig­ra­tion Ser­vices. The Justice Depart­ment, which over­sees immig­ra­tion courts, did not respond to a request for com­ment on what role the reports play in influ­en­cing asylum decisions.

Cut­ting back on asylum has been a center­piece of Trump’s immig­ra­tion crack­down dat­ing to his first term, when he dis­missed migrants wait­ing in Mex­ico to get into the U.S. as “not legit­im­ate asylum-seekers.”

Most asylum seekers, the Repub­lican pres­id­ent said, were flee­ing poverty.

“Asylum is a very spe­cial pro­tec­tion inten­ded only for those flee­ing gov­ern­ment per­se­cu­tion based on race, reli­gion and other pro­tec­ted status,” he said in a 2018 White House appear­ance.

Trump was years out of date.

Although asylum was largely seen after World War II as a way to pro­tect people flee­ing polit­ical per­se­cu­tion, the defin­i­tion was expan­ded long ago, includ­ing to encom­pass some people flee­ing domestic and crim­inal viol­ence.

But he had a point about poverty.

Legal and illegal migra­tion, par­tic­u­larly from Latin Amer­ica, has soared over the last two dec­ades as people have sought more eco­nomic oppor­tun­ity, with increas­ing asylum claims based on safety fears from domestic part­ners and crim­inal gangs.

Even dur­ing Pres­id­ent Biden’s years, most asylum claims were rejec­ted.

But deni­als have jumped from roughly 72% at the end of that Demo­cratic admin­is­tra­tion to 94% in June under Trump, accord­ing to the data research non­profit Trans­ac­tional Records Access Clear­ing­house.

Trump was elec­ted to a second term in part by focus­ing on frus­trated voters who had seen illegal immig­ra­tion soar under Biden, with bor­der arrests from Mex­ico reach­ing a record 250,000 in Decem­ber 2023.

The asylum sys­tem, mean­while, faced a back­log of mil­lions of cases.

The Trump admin­is­tra­tion has reshaped immig­ra­tion courts as part of its push to increase deport­a­tions, organ­iz­ing mass hear­ings, author­iz­ing mil­it­ary law­yers as immig­ra­tion judges and giv­ing judges more lee­way to sum­mar­ily dis­miss claims.

Immig­ra­tion judges must weigh whether people seek­ing asylum based on domestic viol­ence or crim­inal threats have a reas­on­able fear of per­se­cu­tion because of their race, reli­gion, nation­al­ity, polit­ical views or an often-debated catch-all cat­egory, “mem­ber­ship in a par­tic­u­lar social group.” They also have to show that their gov­ern­ment can’t or won’t pro­tect them and that they can’t move else­where in their home coun­try to escape per­se­cu­tion.

The reports offer what can some­times seem like travel bro­chure descrip­tions of life in these coun­tries.

They men­tion good schools, low crime, qual­ity hos­pit­als and con­sti­tu­tions that pro­tect indi­vidual rights, with brief notes that “the avail­ab­il­ity of ser­vices” can vary across each coun­try.

Take El Sal­vador, where the gov­ern­ment of Pres­id­ent Nayib Bukele has long faced accus­a­tions of wide­spread human rights abuses, includ­ing tor­ture.

The State Depart­ment report takes a far more gen­er­ous view of the situ­ation, not­ing the gov­ern­ment approach to rights abuses “is no dif­fer­ent than that of developed coun­tries in Europe and North Amer­ica, includ­ing the United States itself,” and high­light­ing a hand­ful of pro­sec­u­tions tied to the civil war, which ended in 1992.

“In any coun­try, a rogue offi­cial can mis­treat those under their power,” it says.

For Hon­duras’ Gra­cias a Dios province, viol­ent crime rates “com­pare favor­ably with rates of viol­ent crime in many parts of the United States,” the report says.

Former offi­cials and advoc­ates say the six-page reports pale in com­par­ison to tra­di­tional State Depart­ment human rights reports, lengthy dis­sec­tions of more than 100 nations around the world, which under the second Trump admin­is­tra­tion have been trun­cated and delayed.

“These shorter reports clearly don’t address the full range of human rights issues that the coun­try reports have tra­di­tion­ally addressed,” said Scott Busby, former deputy assist­ant sec­ret­ary in the Bur­eau of Demo­cracy, Human Rights and Labor at the State Depart­ment and now a senior adviser at the group Human Rights First.

They are “espe­cially prob­lem­atic given that the coun­try reports them­selves for last year have yet to be issued,” he said.

In many ways, the reports appear aimed most dir­ectly at asylum reg­u­la­tions around a per­son’s abil­ity to escape per­se­cu­tion by simply mov­ing.

Those reg­u­la­tions are key for any­one seek­ing asylum based on domestic or crim­inal viol­ence.

The reports high­light spe­cific parts of each coun­try, men­tion­ing places like an off-the-beaten track tour­ist des­tin­a­tion in Guatem­ala and a province in El Sal­vador that has low crime and 24-hour emer­gency med­ical care.

But those men­tions tell only part of the story.

“The fact that there may be pock­ets of a coun­try that are rel­at­ively safe for some people doesn’t mean that every­body can just move to that part of the coun­try,” said Neela Chakrav­ar­tula, an asylum attor­ney with the Cen­ter for Gender & Refugee Stud­ies at UC Law San Fran­cisco.

If that were the case, Chakrav­ar­tula said, “We’d all be liv­ing in Malibu.”

text:
SANTA FE, N.M. —

The Archdiocese of Santa Fe says local Catholics are free to skip Sunday Mass because of fears related to Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

According to Archbishop John C. Wester, attendance is already down because many people fear ICE will tear their families apart.

In a letter, the archbishop wrote that he doesn’t want Catholics to feel they have sinned by staying home. He encouraged them to set aside time each Sunday to pray, read Scripture or join a televised Mass.

Wester said parishes have reported a drop in attendance as some Catholics weigh the risk of arrest against their obligation to attend Sunday Mass. He said those who stay home may struggle spiritually and feel they have sinned by missing worship.

“I do this with great sadness: sadness that some feel unable to worship freely in ‘the land of the free,’” he wrote.

The dispensation will remain in effect until he or his successor rescinds it.

title: Wrongfully deported Maine residents sue ICE for refusing to return confiscated property
description:
Two Maine residents detained by immigration agents earlier this year, including one who was deported under the wrong name, have joined a federal lawsuit seeking to have the government return personal property to people after their release.
The two men joined five other plaintiffs as part of a class action lawsuit against Immigration and Customs Enforcement filed in Washington, D.C., last month.
The complaint accuses the agency of repeatedly failing to return personal property to detainees even after they were released from ICE custody.
ICE did not immediately return a request for comment on Friday afternoon.

text:
Francesca Albanese, the United Nations special rapporteur on the Israeli-occupied Palestinian territory, has left Costa Rica’s Santamaria airport after being denied entry to the country and spending a second night held up there.

Costa Rica’s move on Thursday to hold Albanese at the airport put the small Central American country’s increasingly close alignment with the United States and Israel on security and foreign policy into the spotlight.

“I’m outside the airport. Finally. Thank you to everyone who helped me,” Albanese said on X at about 07:00 GMT on Saturday, after sending a series of posts from the airport serving the capital city, San Jose.

She wrote earlier, at about 04:00 GMT, that the Constitutional Court of the country ordered her to “be let out to go to a hotel and rest and the immigration police does not let me”, adding: “Am I detained? HELP?”

She also said Air France staff were “actively ignoring” the Constitutional Court ruling with excuses, adding that she had been awake for more than 50 hours.

UN human rights chief Volker Turk said on Friday he was “deeply concerned” by Costa Rica’s decision to bar Albanese from entering the country and urged authorities to reconsider after she was stopped at Juan Santamaria airport.

The UN Human Rights Office said on X that Albanese was denied entry on “claimed national security grounds”.

Albanese, in another post on X, lamented the uncomfortable conditions in the airport, adding that she was “counting the hours till my flight tomorrow”, without specifying the destination.

But the Constitutional Chamber of Costa Rica’s Supreme Court confirmed late on Friday that her destination would be Mexico when it issued a second interim order, directing that she be transferred to a hotel, according to the AFP news agency.

She had previously told local media that she intended to travel on to Mexico, but that immigration authorities told her she needed to return to France, to which she objected.

Albanese also said authorities took her passport and that she was offered a detention room to sleep.

The US-aligned government of Costa Rica asserted that Albanese was the subject of an “international alert over links to terrorist acts”.

Italian embassy assisting Albanese

The Italian Embassy in Costa Rica is providing consular assistance to Albanese after Costa Rican authorities denied her entry, the Italian Ministry of Foreign Affairs said on Friday.

The ministry said the Italian ambassador contacted Albanese and sent a consular official to the airport to help.

Italian officials have repeatedly urged Costa Rican authorities to allow her entry, but Albanese remains in the airport’s international transit area and has not formally entered the country, it added.

Albanese had travelled to Costa Rica to receive an honorary doctorate from the state-run University of Costa Rica.

A UN special rapporteur is an independent expert appointed by the UN Human Rights Council to investigate and report on rights abuses in a specific country.

Albanese, who has been sanctioned by the US under measures related to the International Criminal Court, said she hoped Costa Rica would reverse the decision and rejected what she described as efforts to link her to “terrorism”.

text:
Francesca Albanese, the UN special rapporteur on human rights in the Palestinian territories, has been stranded in an airport terminal after being denied entry to Costa Rica.

Albanese posted a photo on X showing a suitcase beside a row of empty seats, with the caption: “This is where I will spend my first night in Costa Rica.”

She is awaiting a court decision on whether she can enter the country or must leave.

Costa Rican immigration authorities blocked her entry on November 26, saying she was the subject of an international “alert” over alleged ties to terrorism and that her presence posed a national security risk.

Albanese is a high-profile independent investigator scrutinising human rights abuses in the Palestinian territories. She is among a group of experts appointed by the 47-member UN Human Rights Council in Geneva to monitor and report on human rights conditions in individual countries and the observance of specific rights worldwide.

She was sanctioned by the United States in July 2025 over her work and sharp criticism of US and Israeli policies during the war in Gaza. Secretary of State Marco Rubio described her actions as a “campaign of political and economic warfare against the United States and Israel.”

Albanese had travelled to Costa Rica at the invitation of the University of Costa Rica, which was scheduled to award her an honorary doctorate.

After she was denied entry, a habeas corpus petition was filed on her behalf with the Supreme Court’s Constitutional Chamber. The court issued an interim order allowing her to remain in the country and gave immigration authorities 24 hours to explain why they had denied her entry.

While the petition is pending, Albanese remains in a room at the airport. From there, she joined the university’s honorary doctorate ceremony by video call. One of her assistants, who was allowed into the country, accepted the degree on her behalf.

In her speech, Albanese said the decision to deny her entry could be related to the sanctions.

“I am deeply outraged that the Costa Rican government has spread false information linking me to terrorism. Defending human rights is not terrorism, and the government will answer for these insinuations, as it should in a country governed by the rule of law,” Albanese said.

Costa Rica's right-wing government is among a number of governments in the region that have sought to cosy up to the Trump administration, accepting third-country deportees from the US in a move that provoked heavy criticism, and has built a Bukele-style mega-prison as part of its vow to crack down on crime.

Albanese criticised what she described as the Costa Rican government’s complicity in Israeli policies of oppression against Palestinians, citing its signing of a free-trade agreement with Israel that awaits legislative ratification.

Costa Rican President Laura Fernández has not commented on the issue, but her minister of the presidency, former President Rodrigo Chaves, addressed the court’s intervention on social media.

“Yet another usurpation by an increasingly arbitrary judiciary, one that usurps the powers of the other two branches of government and now protects foreigners flagged by international alerts for ties to TERRORIST ACTS!” Chaves wrote about the habeas corpus petition that halted Albanese’s expulsion.

text:
Francesca Albanese, United Nations Special Rapporteur on the situation of human rights in Palestinian

Costa Rica has denied entry to Francesca Albanese, the United Nations special rapporteur on human rights in the Palestinian territories, over alleged links to terrorism. The move drew criticism from UN human rights chief Volker Turk, who urged the government to reconsider its decision. Albanese, an Italian national, was stopped at Juan Santamaria International Airport, which serves the capital San Jose, on Thursday. She had travelled to Costa Rica to receive an honorary doctorate from the state-run University of Costa Rica. The UN human rights office said Albanese was denied entry on “claimed national security grounds”. Costa Rica’s immigration authorities said she was the subject of an international “alert” over alleged links to terrorist acts and that the decision was consistent with national security measures. Turk said he was “deeply concerned” by the move and called on Costa Rican authorities to reconsider the ban. Albanese, speaking from the airport, rejected the allegations and warned that the government would be held accountable for linking her to terrorism. “I am deeply indignant that the government of Costa Rica has spread false information that links me to terrorism,” she said in an address to the university ceremony, which she attended virtually. Her assistant, who was allowed into the country, accepted the honorary degree on her behalf. “Defending human rights is not terrorism and the government must answer for these insinuations, as should be the case under the rule of law,” she added. According to news agency reuters, in an interview with journalist Ahmed Shihab-Eldin, Albanese said authorities had taken her passport and threatened to forcibly put her on a flight out of the country. “I was almost forced to board the plane to be shipped back to Paris. I said no, and I opposed it... and they threatened to put me on the plane by force,” she said. A habeas corpus petition was filed on her behalf before Costa Rica’s Supreme Court Constitutional Chamber. The court issued an interim order allowing her to remain in the country and directed immigration authorities to explain their decision within 24 hours, according to the Associated Press. Costa Rica’s ombudsman criticised immigration authorities for “automatically” denying her entry without assessing her case, official status or immunity as a UN rapporteur. However, former president and minister of the presidency Rodrigo Chaves criticised the court’s intervention, calling it “yet another usurpation by an increasingly arbitrary judiciary”.

Albanese, appointed in 2022, has faced criticism from Israel and its allies over her statements on the war in Gaza. The United States sanctioned her in July 2025. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio accused her of conducting a “campaign of political and economic warfare against the United States and Israel”. Israeli UN ambassador Danny Danon praised Costa Rica’s decision. Costa Rican authorities later allowed Albanese to spend the night at a hotel near the airport. She is expected to leave for Mexico on Saturday, while the legal challenge to the entry denial remains a point of contention.

text:
The Port of Seattle now acknowledges that federal officials gave staff limited notice of immigration enforcement activity at Sea-Tac Airport, after US Rep. Pramila Jayapal said ICE had notified the airport a day before agents arrested a father and daughter at an Alaska Airlines jet bridge.

Jayapal said in a letter that Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told her TSA sent DHS a list of passengers on the flight who had outstanding warrants.

According to Jayapal, Mullin said Ricardo Larrando Mendoza's name was flagged because of an alleged final deportation order and ICE notified the airport the day before the arrest.

It still doesn't explain why Larrando Mendoza was allowed to get past a TSA checkpoint before he was detained on the jetway, along with his daughter Sofia Hernandez-Mejia.

The Port’s account confirms that TSA officials provided limited notice of enforcement operations to federal and Port personnel.

The Port said the notices did not include identifying information about individuals and were one-way communications for situational awareness.

Port staff took no action in response and complied with the Keep Washington Working Act and Port Commission policy, the statement said.

Port Commissioners say they have called for an independent investigation with access to relevant records, communications and personnel, supported by outside legal counsel. The Port is also conducting an internal review.

Jayapal said Alaska Airlines told her office that it received notice of the arrest only on the day it happened.

She questioned whether DHS followed a standard procedure that she said calls for airlines to receive advance notice and said she would press Mullin for answers and request ICE body camera footage.

The arrests, captured on video and widely reported, prompted renewed scrutiny of federal enforcement at the airport.

The Port Commission said ICE enforcement “does not belong in our airports,” citing disruption, fear among travelers and workers, and the difficult position it can place local law enforcement in.

text:
Around Thanksgiving, a claim (archived) circulated online that staff at Dilley Immigration Processing Center in Texas served a Thanksgiving dinner in front of detained parents and children before packing the food away, claiming it was only for employees.

Immigration and Customs Enforcement detains non-U.S. citizens at immigration processing centers like Dilley while resolving their immigration cases to "secure their presence for immigration proceedings or removal from the U.S." The Texas Tribune reported in August that Dilley Immigration Processing Center was the only detention center for families in the U.S.

Aaron Parnas, who shares news headlines on social media, posted a video about the claim on TikTok with the caption, "NEWS: CHILDREN IN DETENTION CENTER WERE SHOWN THANKSGIVING MEAL, FORCED TO WATCH AS GUARDS PACKED IT AWAY."

Claims also circulated on Facebook and X (archived, archived). Snopes readers contacted us about the claim.

The claim came from an NBC report from February that featured an account from a Russian couple held at Dilley Immigration Processing Center in Texas with their three children. According to the children's mother, named only as Oksana, families held at the center gathered for what they thought was "a Thanksgiving celebration" in November 2025 to find "turkey, sandwiches, pastries and pies" set out on tables.

However, Oksana said that when a parent asked when the celebration would start, staff told the people gathered that the food was only for staff and packed it away.

At the time of this writing, Snopes had no primary evidence, such as video surveillance from inside the processing center, to prove Oksana's claim to NBC. However, we also had no primary evidence that the incident Oksana described did not take place. Therefore, we leave this claim unrated.

In an emailed statement to Snopes, a Department of Homeland Security spokesperson wrote:

These claims are absolutely FALSE. Detained illegal aliens receive holiday meals in the dining halls with menus tailored to the occasion. Any staff potlucks occur in areas inaccessible to residents.

A spokesperson for CoreCivic, which manages Dilley Immigration Processing Center as part of a contract with ICE, called the claim "patently false." The spokesperson also said that staff offered people detained at Dilley holiday meals and activities, and that any separate staff meal would have happened in a separate area inaccessible to detainees.

We also contacted Elora Mukherjee, the director of the Immigrants' Rights Clinic at Columbia Law School who NBC reported represented Oksana and her partner Nikita in seeking release from Dilley, to ask whether she had heard other accounts from families held at Dilley that corroborated Oksana's account and await a reply.

Mukherjee repeated (time code 48:27) what appeared to be Oksana's account of Thanksgiving 2025 at the center during a forum hosted by the Senate Judiciary Committee's Democrats in March, the month after NBC's report. We await replies to our queries.

Declarations from Dilley paint damaging picture of child detainment

Lawyers who sought to make the U.S. government adhere to the Flores Settlement, which sets minimum standards for the detainment of children, submitted dozens of sworn declarations from detained parents and children at Dilley to a federal judge starting in June 2025, three months after the Tribune reported the Trump administration would reopen the center.

The Flores Settlement said children must be not be held for long periods of time in immigration prisons or detention facilities and should generally be released as quickly as possible. Courts have previously interpreted the legal limit for detention of a child under the Flores Settlement to be 20 days.

Oksana and Nikita's three children had reportedly been detained at Dilley for more than 120 days in February. Using data the government filed as part of its fight to end the Flores Settlement, the Tribune said in an August report that in February, when NBC reported on Oksana and Nikita's family's detention at Dilley, the average length of a child's stay at the center was 47.5 days.

We reviewed 21 declarations submitted on Dec. 8, 2025, shortly after the alleged Thanksgiving dinner at Dilley. However, the declarations were all dated before Thanksgiving 2025, which was on Nov. 27. We reviewed four declarations (N.V.S.M, C.R.G, N.G. and D.C.R.R.) given in November but before Thanksgiving in case the alleged employee-only dinner happened before actual Thanksgiving. None of the declarations we reviewed corroborated Oksana's account.

Lawyers filed more declarations in March 2026. We reviewed 33 declarations given between October 2025 and March. None mentioned Thanksgiving.

The declarations we reviewed attested to the damaging physical and psychological effects of children's detention at Dilley. Speaking to NBC, Oksana and Nikita complained of a lack of activities and education for their children and difficulties accessing basic needs like medicine or fresh food. The Texas Tribune also cited declarations that echoed these concerns.

In February, after NBC published its report, the DHS refuted what Deputy Assistant Secretary Lauren Bis called "false claims about the ICE Dilley facility including that children are denied medical care and don't have educational resources."

It was unclear at the time of this writing whether Oksana, Nikita and their children remained in Dilley or another immigration processing center or whether U.S. authorities had deported or released them.

text:
The Trump administration has been rejecting droves of applicants to the immigration program that helped first lady Melania Trump stay in the U.S.

According to reporting by The Washington Post on Friday, approvals for the EB-1A visa program reserved for people of "extraordinary ability" have been cratering under the Trump administration. Melania Trump obtained permanent residency in 2001 as a working model through the EB-1 program, a step that eventually led to her securing U.S. citizenship.

According to federal immigration data cited by the Post, the share of approved EB-1A petitions fell from 75 percent in the last months of former President Joe Biden's term to 32 percent by mid-2026. U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services approved roughly 5,200 people for the visa over the first three quarters of fiscal year 2026, which is down from close to 8,900 during the same stretch of fiscal year 2024.

"It's a huge, huge drop," Kate Angustia, a former immigration officer now working as counsel at the American Immigration Lawyers Association, told the Post. "It's strange because the Trump administration has repeatedly said they want the best and the brightest."

Attorneys who spoke to the Post said that officers increasingly seem to be denying applicants based on their own judgment of who qualifies and that some firms are no longer bothering to handle the petitions altogether. "It's become so much more subjective," Rachel Baskin, a Long Island immigration attorney, said.

Memphis attorney James Hollis said a tech entrepreneur who had raised more than $60 million in venture capital was found to meet none of the program's criteria.

"They're killing AI entrepreneurs," Hollis told the Post. "They're absolutely annihilating them."

The Department of Homeland Security defended the trend and insisted that USCIS "will never sacrifice quality and screening for speed."

The first lady's office did not respond to the Post's request for comment.

text:
Peninsula school districts are preparing for potential immigration enforcement raids on their campuses amid an uptick in area enforcement.

In October, the San Mateo County Office of Education notified all 23 public school district superintendents of confirmed immigration enforcement activity in East Palo Alto and Redwood City, according to a written statement from SMCOE Superintendent Marco Chávez.

The notice was meant to give district leaders a “shared, confirmed understanding of the situation” so they could make their own decisions, Chávez said.

Under California law, school staff should verbally decline to let ICE officers into a nonpublic area of a school, such as classrooms and offices, without a valid judicial warrant or court order.

ICE has denied that it targets schools. Yet, at least four instances of immigration enforcement near or at schools have been documented in California since Jan. 2025. ICE has not responded to repeated requests for written comment.

One main part of guidance schools gave to staff was to recognize the difference between an ICE administrative warrant and a judicial court warrant. ICE officers can only enter public school campuses with a judicial warrant.

County-wide rise in arrests

The warnings came before a sharp rise in arrests. San Mateo County’s rapid response network has confirmed 43 ICE arrests in November alone. That activity comes amid a major 45-day ICE operation underway in the state, according to the Washington Examiner.

Immigration arrests in San Mateo County have climbed since the summer, according to Martha Ruch, a senior attorney in the immigration program at Community Legal Services in East Palo Alto, which is part of the county’s rapid response network.

“There used to be maybe one or two arrests every month, and now there are multiple arrests every week, sometimes multiple arrests in a day,” Ruch said.

Schools preparing for enforcement

School letters from Ravenswood, Sequoia Union High School and Palo Alto Unified District advised families to create an emergency plan in case of enforcement, but to keep children enrolled in school.

In addition to emailing families and students about this issue, many schools have implemented formal processes in case ICE comes to campuses for enforcement.

Palo Alto Unified District has trained all administrative staff including front-office workers to immediately report if ICE agents approach a school campus to the superintendent’s office for guidance, according to Assistant Superintendent Yolanda Conaway.

“We’re of the stance that if we don’t have to provide access, we are not going to provide access… The ICE warrant itself is a reason for us to ask questions. It is not a reason for us to respond,” said Conaway.

Courtney Carlomagno, principal of Greene Middle School in Palo Alto, explained that if ICE comes to the front office, staff are trained to immediately shut down their computers, ask agents for identification and review any paperwork or warrants.

Noor Hussein, a 10th and 11th grade teacher at San Jose High School, is concerned that California law is not enforced against ICE agents.

“It’s scary to think how they act with impunity. I’m like a mama bear with my students, I really am. I genuinely could see myself using my body in between them and a student if I feel like they are putting their hands on a student,” Hussein said.

Ravenswood has trained all administrative staff on protocols if ICE comes to campus, while teachers are briefed but not formally trained. “We don’t anticipate that anything would happen directly in classrooms,” said Rob Granados, director of strategy and academic operations at Ravenswood City School District.

Absences at schools

Granados explained that absences occur surrounding warnings the district sent to families.

“We recognize that whenever there are reports or even rumors of immigration enforcement activity, that can create fear and uncertainty for families. So this may affect students’ ability to attend school consistently. I think there is an impact,” Granados said.

Ravenswood and Palo Alto districts say they generally excuse absences that are due to fear of ICE enforcement.

Hussein said she noticed increased absences surrounding ICE enforcement activity in San Jose. Many of her students are directly impacted by the raids.

“Events that happen around the community will impact attendance… there will be students that stay home or parents that opt to have their students stay home. And so, we’re just living in this era of just uncertainty,” Hussein said.

In San Mateo County, arrests appear to be aimed at specific individuals, Ruch said. Most of the detainees she works with have prior removal orders, suggesting the local arrests are targeted at people who ICE already has files on.

For those clients, legal options are limited by the time they reach her. The hardest part of working with families, Ruch said, is having to be the bearer of bad news while they seek support.

“If rapid response is the first time you’ve had a consultation with an attorney, it’s often too late… My biggest pointer is to urge people to request consultations now or as soon as they can so that they’re armed with information and don’t end up in an obscure emergency situation.”

Amina Wase is a master’s candidate in the graduate journalism program at Stanford University

text:
Claim:

One day before a federal court's deadline to comply with a subpoena to provide the names of residents in the Bruckner migrant shelter in the Bronx to Immigration and Customs Enforcement, the city of New York notified the court that all the residents had moved out and the shelter was empty.

In November 2026, a claim (archived) circulated online that, instead of obeying a government subpoena to provide names of residents in a New York City migrant shelter to Immigration and Customs Enforcement, Mayor Zohran Mamdani moved the shelter residents out and told the government the shelter was empty.

For example, one Threads user who shared the claim wrote:

A federal judge ordered NYC to turn over the names of all the residents at the emergency migrant shelter by Nov 20. Instead of appealing the decision, Mamdani moved everyone who was at the migrant shelter to city ran shelters and responded on the 19th with "no residents are in the migrant shelter". A CLASS ACT. He just doesn't stop! 💙

The claim also circulated on Facebook, X, Instagram (archived, archived). Snopes readers contacted us about the claim.

The claim is true. The Mamdani administration and the previous Eric Adams administration have refused since at least October 2025 to comply with an ICE subpoena to provide the names and dates of birth of noncitizen residents at the Bruckner migrant shelter at 825 East 141st St. in the Bronx, a borough of New York City.

A federal judge had ordered New York and the federal government to submit proposals for a "special master" who would pass the names of noncitizen residents with certain serious criminal histories from the city to ICE by Nov. 20.

However, on Nov. 19, lawyers for the city wrote in a letter to the judge that the city had moved all the residents at Bruckner out of the shelter and sought to close it, which they argued rendered the case moot.

At the time of this writing, ICE had not responded to New York's Nov. 19 filing, though the filing suggests ICE disagreed that moving residents out of Bruckner meant the court could not enforce the subpoena.

We contacted New York City Hall and ICE for comment on the next steps of the case and await replies.

Last-minute filing could change direction of year-long case

The U.S. government initially submitted a petition in a New York district court in October 2025, asking it to order New York City to comply with an August subpoena that asked for the names and dates of birth of any residents at "the shelter located at 825 East 141st Street, Bronx, NY" who were not U.S. citizens and had criminal histories that involved "murder, manslaughter, rape, robbery, assault, grand larceny, burglary, or assault of a law enforcement officer."

In January 2026, the day after Mamdani took the oath of office, lawyers for the city wrote in a court filing that ICE's petition amounted to an "improper fishing expedition" (Page 5) where agents cast a wide net looking for people who committed offenses under U.S. Title 8, which governs immigration, citizenship, visas and deportation.

According to the city, ICE had issued the subpoena for the names of the shelter residents "in the hopes of finding evidence of law-breaking later" (Page 4), which the city's lawyers called an "unreasonable and unlawful use of the administrative subpoena power" ( Page 5) .

However, the court disagreed. On Nov. 6, Judge Lewis A. Kaplan wrote that the court had "no choice" but to order the city to comply with the subpoena because it had not shown that doing so would be "unduly burdensome" (Page 1).

In the meantime, Kaplan wrote that ICE had agreed to "the appointment of a special master who will identify residents of the facility with certain serious criminal histories and provide only those names to the agency" (Page 2). Kaplan wrote that New York and ICE should confer and submit a proposal for how to appoint and pay the "special master" by Nov. 20.

Lawyers for the city wrote in a letter to the judge the day before the Nov. 20 deadline that the city had moved the remaining residents (172 people as of Nov. 6) out of Bruckner. The lawyers for the city wrote, "In light of Bruckner's closure today, there are zero current residents of Bruckner. Accordingly, there are no current Bruckner residents to identify, which makes this matter moot" (Page 2).

The city's lawyers wrote in the same letter that, "Counsel for the City is aware that the United States disagrees that the matter is moot and intends to submit an opposition to this letter" (Page 2).

Bruckner's closure 'unrelated' to subpoena litigation

There is no evidence that Bruckner's closure was in direct response to Kaplan's decision to enforce the ICE subpoena for residents' names.

The Threads post that spread the claim about Mamdani's involvement in Bruckner's closure appeared to suggest that Mamdani or his administration closed the site to circumvent or outsmart ICE's subpoena. That appears to be speculation.

Lawyers for the City of New York wrote on Nov. 19 that Bruckner "has long been scheduled to be closed by the end of this year" (Page 1) in accordance with an executive order from February 2026. In an attached declaration, Rudy S. Giuliani, the Executive Director of NYC Mayor's Office of Housing Recovery, wrote, "The closure of Bruckner is unrelated to this litigation; it is pursuant to the Mayor of New York's Emergency Executive Order 2" (Page 4).

That executive order said the city would transition residents from Bruckner, the city's last remaining "Humanitarian Emergency Response and Relief Center" into "standard Department of Social Services/Department of Homeless Services facilities" by the end of 2026 (Page 4).

Gothamist, a New York City news and culture website, reported on Nov. 19, citing city officials, that some Bruckner residents "had left and found housing or were staying with friends. Others were relocated within the city's municipal shelter system." That appeared to support the Threads post's claim that the city moved people living in Bruckner to "city ran" shelters. Snopes contacted New York City Hall to confirm this statement and await a reply.

text:
WASHINGTON -- The Trump administration is abusing the grand jury process in an effort to unmask social media users anonymously criticizing its immigration enforcement tactics, civil rights attorneys claim in a federal court filing Friday.

A federal class action, backed by the American Civil Liberties Union, seeks a court order enjoining the Justice Department and Department of Homeland Security from conducting a “bad-faith investigation” that violates the anonymous individuals' First Amendment free speech rights.

The scope of the investigation remains a mystery, but the ACLU says government lawyers have issued dozens of grand jury subpoenas seeking to identify critics and provide their personal information to U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement investigators.

ACLU attorneys sued on behalf of four unnamed social media users, asking the district court in Washington to block subpoenas seeking account information for users of social media companies, including Meta, Bluesky and X, formerly known as Twitter. Chief Judge James Boasberg ordered the ACLU case's unsealing on Wednesday.

Boasberg scheduled a Jan. 6 hearing for arguments on the ACLU’s request for a preliminary injunction against the government. The administration has until Dec. 14 to respond in writing to the ACLU’s allegations.

Spokespeople for DHS and U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro's office in Washington didn't immediately respond to requests for comment. Pirro, Attorney General Todd Blanche and DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin are named as defendants in the ACLU's lawsuit.

ACLU lawyers say Pirro's office has used the term “Investigation 18” to describe efforts to identify and obtain the personal information.

"The investigation," the ACLU says, “is a bad-faith fishing expedition initiated to gather intrusive intelligence and facilitate retaliation against dissenters.”

The ACLU says its lawsuit in Washington is the “first systemic civil challenge, and the first case that will be litigated in public view, to the Trump administration’s abuse of grand jury unmasking subpoenas.”

“The government is weaponizing the grand jury process to retaliate against people for expressing their political views online,” ACLU attorney Laura Moraff said in a statement.

The ACLU argues that the subpoenas to social media platforms are part of a broader pattern of intimidation. DHS has sent hundreds of administrative subpoenas to tech companies in the past year to seek information about online ICE critics, the ACLU says.

The civil rights organization says the Trump administration has shifted to using grand jury subpoenas — a more secretive process — after encountering pushback to the administrative subpoenas from users and tech companies.

The ACLU lawsuit's plaintiffs include a Bluesky user who wrote about an ICE-related shooting in New York by posting: “Burn ICE to the ground. Burn DHS to the ground. Salt the earth.” Another plaintiff is a college student whose posts on X included an expletive directed at DHS, ICE and Trump.

“Defendants’ rampant use of subpoenas to unmask critics of the federal government is occurring against the backdrop of repeated suggestions that Defendants are building a database of dissenters,” ACLU lawyers wrote.

text:
ANN ARBOR — Activists braved chilly, drizzly weather on Nov. 27 to promote awareness of escalating federal immigration detainee flights out of local airports and call on the Wayne County Airport Authority to increase transparency about the operations.

The demonstrators set up a 40-foot banner reading "End ICE flights at Willow Run" on the Stone School Road overpass on Interstate 94 in Ann Arbor. The effort was part of a nationwide push to oppose U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) deportation and detainee transfer flights, which have increased sharply this year.

"We're not asking (WCAA) to prohibit ICE flights, because they can't do that, but we would like them to cooperate with us and allow us on airport grounds," said Kris Olsen, 63, of Ann Arbor, a member of the Coalition to Shut the Camps, which aims to pressure ICE to shut down detention centers. "They're not even allowing us on the airport grounds to make these observations."

An ICE Flight Monitor tracked 7,722 immigration-enforcement flights in 2024, a figure that increased more than 80% to 13,962 in 2025. There have been 17,640 such flights in 2026, through October, according to figures compiled by Human Rights First, an organization that monitors immigration enforcement and detention practices.

The increases are reflected locally, especially at Willow Run Airport in Ypsilanti. There were no ICE flights at Willow Run during 2024, according to Human Rights First. In 2025, there were 88 such flights at Willow Run while there have been 165 this year, through October.

"ICE is real active in Ypsilanti, so we're trying to make people aware of that," said Jim Eng, 75, of Ann Arbor, one of about a dozen protesters who gathered on the bridge over I-94 on Friday.

He and others with local activist organizations protest each Friday on the bridge, shining a spotlight on a different issue each week.

Olsen said this week, they were calling on the airport authority to increase transparency regarding ICE flights out of both Willow Run Airport and Detroit Metropolitan Airport in Romulus, which has seen three ICE flights so far this year. Both airports are operated by the authority.

The airport authority declined to comment directly on the protesters' demands and directed The Detroit News to a resolution passed Feb. 18, affirming that the authority does not participate in federal immigration enforcement or assist with deportations.

Olsen said the authority should do more. She pointed to policies that have been in place for years at King County International Airport, near Seattle, as a blueprint for how the authority can help keep civilians informed about detainee movement by ICE.

Under a 2023 executive order, the King County airport limits the services it provides for ICE flights and documents their activity in an online log. The airport also provides livestreamed cameras of its airfield and, more recently, passenger counts and flight notifications.

Olsen said she is part of a nationwide network that tracks ICE operations at airports. When notified that an ICE detainee is being flown out of Willow Run, she and others drive there and park about a half-mile away so they can photograph the aircraft and its passengers using high-powered camera lenses.

"Our goal is to get these pictures up on the internet, on the socials, so in case anybody recognizes (detainees), they can try to find their family members because (ICE agents) take them on the planes and they don't tell anybody," she said.

Federal officials have defended the administration's deportation operations, saying ICE will continue using contracted service providers that work with multiple airlines to carry out removals, according to Reutersreports.

The U.S. Department of Homeland Security has also maintained that its immigration enforcement efforts are lawful and intended to advance the administration's deportation agenda.

WASHINGTON (AP) — The Trump administration is abusing the grand jury process in an effort to unmask social media users anonymously criticizing its immigration enforcement tactics, civil rights attorneys claim in a federal court filing Friday .

A federal class action, backed by the American Civil Liberties Union, seeks a court order enjoining the Justice Department and Department of Homeland Security from conducting a “bad-faith investigation” that violates the anonymous individuals' First Amendment free speech rights.

The scope of the investigation remains a mystery, but the ACLU says government lawyers have issued dozens of grand jury subpoenas seeking to identify critics and provide their personal information to U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement investigators.

ACLU attorneys sued on behalf of four unnamed social media users, asking the district court in Washington to block subpoenas seeking account information for users of social media companies, including Meta, Bluesky and X, formerly known as Twitter. Chief Judge James Boasberg ordered the ACLU case's unsealing on Wednesday.

Boasberg scheduled a Jan. 6 hearing for arguments on the ACLU’s request for a preliminary injunction against the government. The administration has until Dec. 14 to respond in writing to the ACLU’s allegations.

Spokespeople for DHS and U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro's office in Washington didn't immediately respond to requests for comment. Pirro, Attorney General Todd Blanche and DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin are named as defendants in the ACLU's lawsuit.

ACLU lawyers say Pirro's office has used the term “Investigation 18” to describe efforts to identify and obtain the personal information.

"The investigation," the ACLU says, “is a bad-faith fishing expedition initiated to gather intrusive intelligence and facilitate retaliation against dissenters.”

The ACLU says its lawsuit in Washington is the “first systemic civil challenge, and the first case that will be litigated in public view, to the Trump administration’s abuse of grand jury unmasking subpoenas.”

“The government is weaponizing the grand jury process to retaliate against people for expressing their political views online,” ACLU attorney Laura Moraff said in a statement .

The ACLU argues that the subpoenas to social media platforms are part of a broader pattern of intimidation. DHS has sent hundreds of administrative subpoenas to tech companies in the past year to seek information about online ICE critics, the ACLU says.

The civil rights organization says the Trump administration has shifted to using grand jury subpoenas — a more secretive process — after encountering pushback to the administrative subpoenas from users and tech companies.

The ACLU lawsuit's plaintiffs include a Bluesky user who wrote about an ICE-related shooting in New York by posting: “Burn ICE to the ground. Burn DHS to the ground. Salt the earth.” Another plaintiff is a college student whose posts on X included an expletive directed at DHS, ICE and Trump.

“Defendants’ rampant use of subpoenas to unmask critics of the federal government is occurring against the backdrop of repeated suggestions that Defendants are building a database of dissenters,” ACLU lawyers wrote.

text:
ALBUQUERQUE, N.M. —

A man was arrested after fatally stabbing his female coworker at the gas station they both worked at on Thanksgiving.

Fabian Miguel Morales, 42, is accused of the fatal stabbing of Cindy Lou Preston, 45, inside the Shell gas-station store in the 3000 block of North Main Street at the corner of North Main and Vista Parkway.

A 911 call was made shortly after 1 p.m. Thursday, Nov. 26, by a man who was outside the gas-station store when the stabbing took place. When the man went inside the store, he found Preston lying on the floor bleeding and saw Morales flee from the store.

When officers arrived, they found Preston deceased.

Roswell Police Department investigators believe Morales intentionally cut his own hand with a knife shortly before attacking and stabbing Preston. Information gathered in the investigation indicated Morales and Preston may have been in a romantic relationship at the time or in the past.

A medical investigator’s initial examination of Preston at the gas station determined she had been stabbed multiple times in the neck.

Police arrived at the hospital where Morales was being treated for the laceration on his hand and arrested him on an outstanding warrant unrelated to the stabbing. He was later arrested for the stabbing and charged with first-degree murder.

title: Federal court orders authorities to stop making warrantless immigration arrests - Yahoo
description:
A U.S. District Court judge ordered federal authorities to stop making warrantless immigration arrests in Montana.
Upper Seven said it has secured the release of 71 individuals in wrongful immigration arrests since it started such work.

description: Francesca Albanese, the U.N. special rapporteur on human rights in the occupied Palestinian territories, is stranded at Costa Rica’s main airport awaiting for a court to decide whether she could
text:
FILE - Francesca Albanese, the U.N. special rapporteur for the West Bank and Gaza, speaks during the 5th World Conference on Creative Economy in Jakarta, Indonesia, Oct. 22, 2026.

SAN JOSÉ, Costa Rica (AP) — Francesca Albanese , the U.N. special rapporteur on human rights in the Palestinian territories, was stranded in an airport terminal on Friday after being denied entry to Costa Rica .

Albanese posted a photo on X showing a suitcase beside a row of empty seats, with the caption: “This is where I will spend my first night in Costa Rica.”

She is awaiting a court decision on whether she can enter the country or must leave.

Costa Rican immigration authorities blocked her entry on Thursday, saying she was the subject of an international “alert” over alleged ties to terrorism and that her presence posed a national security risk.

Albanese is a high-profile independent investigator scrutinizing human rights abuses in the Palestinian territories. She is among a group of experts appointed by the 47-member U.N. Human Rights Council in Geneva to monitor and report on human rights conditions in individual countries and the observance of specific rights worldwide.

She was sanctioned by the United States in July 2025 over her work and sharp criticism of U.S. and Israeli policies during the war in Gaza. Secretary of State Marco Rubio described her actions as a “campaign of political and economic warfare against the United States and Israel.”

Albanese had traveled to Costa Rica at the invitation of the University of Costa Rica, which was scheduled to award her an honorary doctorate.

After she was denied entry, a habeas corpus petition was filed on her behalf with the Supreme Court’s Constitutional Chamber. The court issued an interim order allowing her to remain in the country and gave immigration authorities 24 hours to explain why they had denied her entry.

While the petition is pending, Albanese remains in a room at the airport. From there, she joined the university’s honorary doctorate ceremony by video call. One of her assistants, who was allowed into the country, accepted the degree on her behalf.

In her speech, Albanese said the decision to deny her entry could be related to the sanctions.

“I am deeply outraged that the Costa Rican government has spread false information linking me to terrorism. Defending human rights is not terrorism, and the government will answer for these insinuations, as it should in a country governed by the rule of law,” Albanese said.

Costa Rica's right-wing government is among a number of governments in the region that have sought to cozy up to the Trump administration, accepting third-country deportees from the U.S. in a move that provoked heavy criticism, and has built a Bukele-style mega-prison as part of its vow to crack down on crime.

Albanese criticized what she described as the Costa Rican government’s complicity in Israeli policies of oppression against Palestinians, citing its signing of a free-trade agreement with Israel that awaits legislative ratification.

Costa Rican President Laura Fernández has not commented on the issue, but her minister of the presidency, former President Rodrigo Chaves , addressed the court’s intervention on social media.

“Yet another usurpation by an increasingly arbitrary judiciary, one that usurps the powers of the other two branches of government and now protects foreigners flagged by international alerts for ties to TERRORIST ACTS!” Chaves wrote about the habeas corpus petition that halted Albanese’s expulsion.

Costa Rica’s ombudsman’s office criticized immigration authorities for “automatically” denying Albanese entry without assessing her case, her official status or her immunity as a U.N. rapporteur.

U.N. High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Türk also said he was “deeply concerned” by Costa Rica’s decision to deny her entry.

text:
The American Civil Liberties Union filed a lawsuit in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Georgia challenging a Department of Homeland Security policy that allows immigrants previously released from custody to be taken back into detention. The complaint asks courts to block the policy, as a federal judge in California did last year.

Why it matters

The lawsuit argues the re-detention policy violates the Fourth Amendment, and the policy reverses a decades-old practice that generally protected released immigrants from re-detention absent a change in circumstances. The outcome could affect immigrants across the United States who remain under release conditions.

The complaint covers immigrants in Georgia, North Carolina and South Carolina under ICE's Atlanta Field office, with two Georgia men at the center of the lawsuit. Whether the court will grant the requested block has not yet been determined.

The players

Department of Homeland Security

The federal department responsible for immigration enforcement, including U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, whose policy reversal is challenged in the lawsuit.

American Civil Liberties Union

A nonprofit civil rights organization that litigates constitutional issues, including Fourth Amendment challenges to government detention practices.

The details

Under the policy DHS adopted in May 2025, officials can take previously released immigrants into custody without assessing whether their circumstances have changed. The ACLU's complaint calls on courts to block the policy, as a federal judge in California did last year.

Timeline

May 2025: DHS reversed its decades-old re-detention policy.

Last year (2025): A federal judge in California blocked a similar policy.

Earlier in November 2026: The ACLU filed the lawsuit in the Northern District of Georgia.

Legal Context

The lawsuit tests whether re-detaining released immigrants without a changed-circumstances review satisfies Fourth Amendment limits on seizures. It follows a federal judge in California blocking a similar policy last year, and the Georgia court's ruling will show whether that approach holds elsewhere.

Immigrants who have been released under supervision may face re-detention without a review of whether their circumstances have changed. Those with pending release conditions in Georgia, North Carolina and South Carolina are the most directly affected under the Atlanta Field office's jurisdiction.

The takeaway

Policy changes that alter detention rules can take effect quickly, so immigrants on release conditions should understand their current obligations and seek legal advice when facing new custody. Depositphotos

A lawsuit raises new questions

Dayanne Figueroa, a U.S. citizen, was driving to work after dropping her son off at school when she encountered federal immigration officers in Chicago. Her subsequent arrest is now the subject of a $1 million lawsuit against the federal government.

Her case is drawing attention to ICE enforcement practices under President Donald Trump. It could also open the door to more legal challenges over how immigration officers conduct arrests across the country.

thenews2.com/Depositphotos

Trump's immigration crackdown

President Donald Trump returned to the White House in 2025 with plans to carry out a major immigration crackdown. His administration expanded immigration enforcement efforts, supported by additional funding provided through the One Big Beautiful Bill Act.

The increased funding supported broader enforcement operations. However, these operations have drawn criticism from communities, civil rights organizations, and lawmakers. Some enforcement practices have also become the subject of legal challenges.

thenews2.com/Depositphotos

ICE operations face scrutiny

Immigration and Customs Enforcement, commonly known as ICE, has faced increased scrutiny over its enforcement activities. Operations in several communities have raised concerns about how officers identify people, carry out arrests, and handle encounters with the public.

Operation Metro Surge in Minnesota drew national attention following the fatal shootings of two U.S. citizens by federal immigration officers in January 2026. The incidents intensified public attention on ICE and its methods. They also added to concerns about accountability when federal enforcement actions lead to serious consequences.

Depositphotos

A Chicago arrest sparks legal action

The lawsuit centers on Dayanne Figueroa, a US citizen who was arrested in Chicago in October 2025. Her arrest happened during Operation Midway Blitz, an immigration enforcement campaign carried out in the city.

According to the lawsuit, Figueroa had just dropped her son off at school when officers approached her vehicle. The incident has since become an important example in the debate over ICE enforcement. Her legal team argues that the officers' actions went beyond what was legally acceptable.

Depositphotos

What happened during the arrest

Video of the October encounter reportedly shows officers driving into Figueroa's vehicle before pulling her out by her legs. The incident took place in front of multiple witnesses, according to reporting by Axios.

Figueroa was also recovering from kidney surgery at the time. Her physical condition has become an important part of the allegations against the officers. The lawsuit alleges that officers used excessive force and failed to provide timely medical attention. Figueroa was eventually taken to a hospital after experiencing medical complications while in custody.

Depositphotos

Why she wants $1 million

Figueroa's legal team filed the lawsuit under the Federal Tort Claims Act, a federal law that allows people to seek damages from the US government in certain circumstances involving wrongful acts by federal employees.

The complaint alleges false arrest, false imprisonment, assault, battery, negligence, and intentional infliction of emotional distress. It also raises concerns about her medical treatment while in custody and seeks up to $1 million in damages.

The case is not simply about financial compensation. It also aims to bring attention to the decisions made during the operation and establish accountability for the treatment she says she experienced.

Little-known fact: The Federal Tort Claims Act includes a special provision allowing certain claims involving assault, battery, and false arrest by federal law enforcement officers.

Depositphotos

The fight for accountability

Figueroa has already taken several steps to challenge what happened to her. She testified before Congress and filed both a police report and an administrative complaint following the arrest.

After receiving no response to her administrative claim, Figueroa pursued legal action against the federal government. She has emphasized the importance of accountability for her treatment during the operation. She also explained that she hopes sharing her experience will help bring meaningful changes to how immigration enforcement is carried out.

Depositphotos

More lawsuits could follow

Figueroa's case may be only the beginning of a much larger legal battle. Attorneys at Democracy Forward, the organization representing her, say they know of other administrative claims that could eventually become lawsuits.

Jeff Dubner, the organization's lead attorney, described the case as the beginning of this type of legal challenge. Some of these pending claims could develop into federal lawsuits if the necessary legal requirements are met. However, the number of cases that will ultimately reach court remains uncertain.

Little-known fact: Under federal law, an agency's failure to decide an FTCA claim within six months can allow the claimant to treat it as denied and proceed to court.

jjbooma/Depositphotos

Minnesota cases add pressure

The legal challenges are not limited to Chicago. Minnesota has also become a major focus following Operation Metro Surge, which attracted national attention because of deadly encounters involving federal immigration officers.

According to the Minnesota Reformer, activists and immigrants have filed claims under the Federal Tort Claims Act over alleged misconduct during the operation. Although the circumstances vary, these claims raise questions about how federal officers can be held accountable when their enforcement actions allegedly cause harm.

Depositphotos

Renee Good's family files two lawsuits

One of the most closely watched legal cases involves the family of Renee Good, who was killed by an ICE agent in Minneapolis. On October 1, 2026, her family filed a lawsuit against the federal government under the Federal Tort Claims Act, seeking compensation for her death.

The family also filed a separate lawsuit that personally named the agent who shot her, along with Stephen Miller, Kristi Noem, and former Border Patrol Commander Gregory Bovino. These legal actions add another layer to the growing scrutiny of federal immigration enforcement and the people responsible for overseeing it.

Ale_Mi/Depositphotos

How the government may respond

Figueroa's attorneys anticipate that the federal government may seek to dismiss the lawsuit. They believe the government could invoke the FTCA's discretionary function exception, which protects certain government decisions and actions from liability.

The Justice Department stated that federal immigration officers may have legal protections for their official actions. It also emphasized that the FTCA contains specific requirements and exceptions and that filing a lawsuit does not establish the validity of its allegations.

thenews2.com/Depositphotos

Do officers have immunity?

A central legal question is whether the federal government can be held liable for the officers' alleged misconduct. The FTCA permits certain lawsuits against the United States, although statutory exceptions and legal defenses may limit which claims can proceed.

Democracy Forward's Jeff Dubner argued that federal law enforcement officers do not have blanket immunity for immigration arrests or other enforcement activities. However, the legal arguments still need to be examined through the court process. The lawsuit's outcome could help clarify important legal boundaries.

Depositphotos

A bigger legal battle ahead

Figueroa's lawsuit arrives as immigration enforcement faces growing legal and political scrutiny. With additional claims reportedly waiting to move forward, the administration could face several challenges involving arrests and other actions taken during its enforcement operations.

For Figueroa, the case is about more than the $1 million she is seeking. She wants her experience to lead to meaningful change and greater accountability. Whether her lawsuit succeeds remains to be seen, but it has placed important questions about federal enforcement practices before the courts.

Demonstrators from the immigration advocacy organization CASA chant “Up up with liberation, down down with deportation” outside of the U.S. Supreme Court on Thursday, May 15, 2025, as justices heard oral arguments on the Trump administration’s legal challenge to birthright citizenship.

A federal judge in the District of Columbia Wednesday issued a classwide injunction to prevent the Trump administration from implementing its second attempt at redefining the constitutional right to birthright citizenship.

The order from Judge Christopher Reid Cooper will remain in effect while litigation continues. A classwide injunction blocks action affecting a defined group of individuals, as opposed to a nationwide injunction.

In a memorandum opinion , Cooper noted the Supreme Court earlier this year denied President Donald Trump’s executive order that would deny citizenship to babies born from immigrants either in the country unlawfully or on a temporary basis, in the case Barbara v. Trump.

“Yet Barbara’s ink had scarcely dried when the President issued a second executive order—Executive Order 14418, at issue here—directing federal agencies to withhold recognition of citizenship from additional categories of U.S.-born children with noncitizen parents,” he wrote. “As the Supreme Court has made clear, however, the President cannot carve out new exceptions to birthright citizenship for children born within the United States and subject to its laws.”

The American Civil Liberties Union, which led the first challenge against the Trump administration’s birthright citizenship order and is leading the second, welcomed the ruling.

“Enough is enough,” Cody Wofsy, deputy director of the ACLU’s Immigrants’ Rights Project, said in a statement. “The Supreme Court has twice rejected efforts to gut birthright citizenship, in 1898 and again earlier this year. Third time is not the charm, and the President needs to accept that birthright citizenship is the law of the land.”

The Department of Justice did not respond to States Newsroom’s request for comment.

Earlier this month, Cooper seemed skeptical of the legality of the Trump administration’s second attempt to redefine the constitutional right to birthright citizenship.

The president’s recent executive orders would deny citizenship to babies born in the United States to parents deemed part of a designated terrorist organization and to parents who purposefully came to the United States to gain citizenship in what critics call “birth tourism.”

The executive order also aimed to deny citizenship to children born to foreign diplomatic staff and children born in U.S. territories where Congress has not passed a law granting citizenship.

There is already a small carve out for birthright citizenship, extended to children born to foreign diplomats.

The Source: Information in this story came from official statements released by U.S. Rep. Pramila Jayapal, the Port of Seattle Commission and Alaska Airlines, and original reporting by FOX 13 Seattle.
text:
The Port of Seattle Commission is moving toward an independent investigation into how airport staff handled advance federal notice before U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents arrested a father and daughter at an Alaska Airlines boarding gate last weekend.

The Nov. 21 arrests at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport drew widespread scrutiny after passenger video of the incident circulated online. U.S. Rep. Pramila Jayapal, D-Wash., said Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin informed her that federal officials notified the airport one day before the operation, contradicting initial accounts from Port officials that they received no advance warning.

What we know:

ICE agents detained two passengers, Sofia Hernandez Mejia and her father, Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza, on Saturday, Nov. 21, as they boarded Alaska Airlines Flight 1306.

According to Jayapal's account of her conversation with Mullin, the Transportation Security Administration sent the Department of Homeland Security a pre-flagged passenger manifest listing travelers with outstanding warrants, flagging Ricardo for an alleged final order of deportation.

Port leadership confirmed to the Port of Seattle Commission on Nov. 25 that TSA officials had provided "limited notice" of enforcement operations to

Port and federal personnel, characterizing the messages as one-way alerts for situational awareness that did not include passengers' identifying information.

Meanwhile, Alaska Airlines stated it was not given appropriate advance notice and only learned of the operation at the gate on the day of the flight.

What we don't know:

Port commissioners stated they were not informed of the TSA notifications, how frequently such alerts occur or what details they contained prior to Jayapal's inquiry. Additionally, Jayapal said DHS is supposed to follow a standard operating procedure requiring advance notice to airlines, which does not appear to have been followed, prompting both Jayapal and Alaska Airlines to investigate whether federal agents violated established protocols. Mullin also told Jayapal that ICE body-camera video from the incident is part of an ongoing internal investigation and has not yet been released publicly or to Congress.

What they're saying:

Jayapal criticized federal officials' transparency and vowed legislative action once Democrats assume the House majority in January. "Far too often, what ICE claims to have happened is contradicted by the actual evidence," Jayapal said. "ICE should not be operating in our airports, and I intend to push to include this restriction as well as to ban masks and require judicial warrants to break the incarceration pipeline as soon as we take control of Congress."

The Port of Seattle Commission emphasized its commitment to scrutinizing its own operations alongside federal agencies. "Being a welcoming Port is more than a policy on paper. It must be reflected in our operations, decisions, and actions," the commission said in a statement. "We will hold our own institution accountable while continuing to demand accountability from federal agencies."

Alaska Airlines noted that while it must comply with federal law enforcement, it does not direct immigration operations. "The events of Nov. 21 at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport deeply impacted our employees, guests and community," the airline said. "Decisions about the timing, location and manner of federal law enforcement operations rest with the responsible agencies."

Featured

Local perspective:

Port leadership told commissioners that staff took no action in response to the TSA alerts and complied with both commission policy and the Keep Washington Working Act, a state law restricting local agencies from assisting with federal civil immigration enforcement. Still, Port Commissioner Hamdi Mohamed requested an external review to verify whether any Port personnel violated local policies or improperly facilitated access to the secured jet bridge, where access credentials are issued by the Port.

What's next:

The Port of Seattle Commission is drafting a formal order to retain outside legal counsel and launch an independent investigation with full access to internal records, communications and staff. Port leadership is also scheduled to provide an update on its internal review at the commission's next public meeting.

At the federal level, Jayapal said she will continue pressing Mullin to release the ICE officers' body-camera footage and clarify whether DHS still follows airline notification rules. When the new Congress convenes in January, Jayapal plans to introduce legislation banning ICE operations at airports, prohibiting agents from wearing masks during arrests and requiring judicial warrants for immigration detainers.

text:
SAN JOSÉ, Costa Rica — Francesca Albanese, the U.N. special rapporteur on human rights in the Palestinian territories, was stranded in an airport terminal on Friday after being denied entry to Costa Rica.

Albanese posted a photo on X showing a suitcase beside a row of empty seats, with the caption: “This is where I will spend my first night in Costa Rica.”

She is awaiting a court decision on whether she can enter the country or must leave.

Costa Rican immigration authorities blocked her entry on Thursday, saying she was the subject of an international “alert” over alleged ties to terrorism and that her presence posed a national security risk.

Albanese is a high-profile independent investigator scrutinizing human rights abuses in the Palestinian territories. She is among a group of experts appointed by the 47-member U.N. Human Rights Council in Geneva to monitor and report on human rights conditions in individual countries and the observance of specific rights worldwide.

By clicking Sign up, you agree to our privacy policy.

She was sanctioned by the United States in July 2025 over her work and sharp criticism of U.S. and Israeli policies during the war in Gaza. Secretary of State Marco Rubio described her actions as a “campaign of political and economic warfare against the United States and Israel.”

Albanese had traveled to Costa Rica at the invitation of the University of Costa Rica, which was scheduled to award her an honorary doctorate.

After she was denied entry, a habeas corpus petition was filed on her behalf with the Supreme Court’s Constitutional Chamber. The court issued an interim order allowing her to remain in the country and gave immigration authorities 24 hours to explain why they had denied her entry.

While the petition is pending, Albanese remains in a room at the airport. From there, she joined the university’s honorary doctorate ceremony by video call. One of her assistants, who was allowed into the country, accepted the degree on her behalf.

In her speech, Albanese said the decision to deny her entry could be related to the sanctions.

“I am deeply outraged that the Costa Rican government has spread false information linking me to terrorism. Defending human rights is not terrorism, and the government will answer for these insinuations, as it should in a country governed by the rule of law,” Albanese said.

Costa Rica's right-wing government is among a number of governments in the region that have sought to cozy up to the Trump administration, accepting third-country deportees from the U.S. in a move that provoked heavy criticism, and has built a Bukele-style mega-prison as part of its vow to crack down on crime.

Albanese criticized what she described as the Costa Rican government’s complicity in Israeli policies of oppression against Palestinians, citing its signing of a free-trade agreement with Israel that awaits legislative ratification.

Costa Rican President Laura Fernández has not commented on the issue, but her minister of the presidency, former President Rodrigo Chaves, addressed the court’s intervention on social media.

“Yet another usurpation by an increasingly arbitrary judiciary, one that usurps the powers of the other two branches of government and now protects foreigners flagged by international alerts for ties to TERRORIST ACTS!” Chaves wrote about the habeas corpus petition that halted Albanese’s expulsion.

Costa Rica’s ombudsman’s office criticized immigration authorities for “automatically” denying Albanese entry without assessing her case, her official status or her immunity as a U.N. rapporteur.

U.N. High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Türk also said he was “deeply concerned” by Costa Rica’s decision to deny her entry.
