description:
UN Human Rights chief Volker Turk said on Thursday he hopes to visit the United States to address domestic and international human rights concerns with high-ranking officials, weeks after Washington boycotted a meeting in Geneva over its record.
While raising domestic and international human rights concerns with senior officials, Turk did not say what issues he wanted to raise but he called this year for an independent probe into the deaths of people in US immigration custody.
Earlier, Washington abstained from a UN meeting where its rights under Donald Trump were due to be examined, marking the second year in a row it has done so in prompting backlash from campaign groups including Human Rights Watch.
US officials accused UN human rights bodies of anti-American discourse while upholding their performance including on expulsions which they state are enforced under US immigration law.
Furthermore, the Department of Homeland Security stated it is mandated to provide a safe, secure and humane environment in detention.
text:
UN Human Rights chief Volker Turk said on Thursday he hopes to visit the United States to address domestic and international human rights concerns with high-ranking officials, weeks after Washington boycotted a meeting in Geneva over its record.

While raising domestic and international human rights concerns with senior officials, Turk did not say what issues he wanted to raise but he called this year for an independent probe into the deaths of people in US immigration custody.

The US mission in Geneva is closed for the Thanksgiving holiday and did not immediately address inquiries on the planned trip and whether US officials would meet with Turk.

Earlier, Washington abstained from a UN meeting where its rights under Donald Trump were due to be examined, marking the second year in a row it has done so in prompting backlash from campaign groups including Human Rights Watch.

It is crucial to note that Washington along with North Korea, Israel and Russia was among a minority of states voting against Turk’s renewal for the role in July underscoring a widening clash between the Trump administration and the UN.

US officials accused UN human rights bodies of anti-American discourse while upholding their performance including on expulsions which they state are enforced under US immigration law. Furthermore, the Department of Homeland Security stated it is mandated to provide a safe, secure and humane environment in detention.

text:
By Andrew Rice | The Center Square

The U.S. Supreme Court will hear arguments in a case that could determine the future of immigrant asylum laws.

On Nov. 30, justices on the high court will hear arguments in Wassily v. Blanche, a case over whether noncitizens whose asylum in the United States was later terminated because of criminal convictions are eligible to become lawful permanent residents. The case focuses on Tamer Wassily and Byron Velasquez Arreaga, migrants from Egypt and Guatemala, respectively, who were convicted of crimes that led to the government moving to revoke both men’s asylum status.

The two men sought to become lawful permanent residents in the United States, citing fear of persecution in their home countries to prevent their return. An immigration judge granted Wassily’s request to become a lawful permanent resident, but the Board of Immigration Appeals said he was ineligible because of his criminal conviction.

Matthew O’Brien, deputy director of the Federation for American Immigration Reform, said immigration law allows for migrants who committed crimes to have their asylum status terminated.

“The U.S. is not under any domestic statutory obligation, or international legal obligation to accept any alien for asylum or continue to shelter any alien who has already been granted asylum,” O’Brien wrote in an email to The Center Square.

O’Brien said the case boils down to protecting American citizens and national sovereignty over the interests of immigrants who could be harmed in foreign countries.

“Actions have consequences, and if [Wassily and Velasquez] were genuinely concerned about being returned to their countries of origin, then they should have refrained from engaging in criminal behavior in the state that had granted them protection,” O’Brien said.

Lawyers for Wassily and Velasquez urged the justices to reject the lower court’s decision to terminate asylum and prevent the two from obtaining lawful permanent residence status.

“It will harm all those who, but for termination, would have been worthy of waivers for humanitarian, family-unity, or public-interest reasons,” lawyers for Wassily and Velasquez wrote in a petition to the high court.

O’Brien said only green card holders with exceptionally good civic, social and economic success in the United States who are convicted of minor violations should be allowed to remain in the country.

“Illegal aliens who have been convicted of any kind of crime should not be allowed to remain in the U.S. under any circumstances,” O’Brien wrote. “Doing so simply rewards them for serial violations of America’s laws.”

However, lawyers for the two migrants said the decision to terminate their asylum will also have ripple effects on immediate family members. When a principal applicant for asylum commits a “particularly serious crime,” the derivative status that applicant’s spouse or children can also be terminated, according to U.S. immigration law.

Wassily was convicted of third-degree stalking and child endangerment, according to a court filing. Velasquez was convicted of driving while intoxicated. Both convictions were deemed particularly serious crimes by an immigration judge.

In 2023, nearly 5,000 individuals received derivative asylum in the United States, according to court records.

“If the decision below stands, these innocent spouses and children – through no fault of their own – will be precluded from adjusting to [Lawful Permanent Resident] status and will face removal themselves,” lawyers for Wassily and Velasquez wrote.

The rule of lenity, a principal of criminal law, requires courts to interpret a statute as narrowly as possible when it is unclear about whether specific criminal activity is prohibited. However, the rule does not apply to civil cases, including immigration, the area issue before the court.

O’Brien said he expects the justices to pay attention to this aspect of the case and settle whether the rule can apply to immigration issues.

“This seems like a settled issue. The Second Circuit, which has never been accused of being conservative, definitively found that none of the arguments advanced by the petitioners in this matter had any merit,” O’Brien wrote. “I would expect that the Supreme Court’s opinion will be focused primarily on the rule of lenity and its inapplicability in the civil, immigration context”

title: Dignity Act Lame-Duck Push: Bacon Says It Can Pass This Congress - Immigration Analytics
description:
Where does Don Bacon stand on the Dignity Act?
As this site’s Dignity Act explainer describes, applicants would pass background checks, pay restitution and stay current on taxes in exchange for protection from removal and work authorization.
Can the Dignity Act really pass before January?
No dignity status exists, no application form has been published, and no one can file for the program today.
Anyone charging fees to “register” for the Dignity Act is selling something the law does not provide.
text:
A group of House Republicans now wants the Dignity Act passed in the lame-duck session, before Democrats take over Congress, but nothing has been scheduled and the bill still faces long procedural odds.

Rep. Don Bacon (R-Neb.), who is retiring when his term ends in January, told Fox News Digital in an interview published Nov. 25 that immigration reform built on the Dignity Act would pass in the current Congress. “It’s going to happen under this Congress,” he said. His argument was strategic: if Republicans wait, he warned, the Democratic majorities arriving in January would likely push a broader bill that looks more like an amnesty. Rep. Marlin Stutzman (R-Ind.) made a similar case for passing a Republican-led plan before January, and the bill’s sponsor, Rep. María Elvira Salazar (R-Fla.), called the current moment a favorable window, citing President Trump’s stated openness to working with Democrats on immigration.

The new element is the call for lame-duck action itself. When the bill’s cosponsor list grew to 56 on Nov. 16, most of the momentum came from Democrats, and the bill’s Democratic co-lead, Rep. Veronica Escobar of Texas, was reported to be planning a reintroduction in 2027. Bacon, Stutzman and Salazar are now arguing for the opposite timeline. The White House did not respond to Fox News’s request for comment, and no floor vote, committee markup or discharge petition on the bill had been announced as of Nov. 26.

Where does Don Bacon stand on the Dignity Act?

Bacon, who represents Nebraska’s Omaha-based 2nd District, announced in June 2025 that he would not seek reelection in 2026, so he leaves the House when the 119th Congress ends on Jan. 3, 2027. He has backed the Dignity Act publicly for months. In an August interview with Newsweek, he said the administration had overreached on deportations, put the main responsibility on Congress to fix the law, and named the Dignity Act as his preferred vehicle. He also said people with Temporary Protected Status who have clean records and jobs should have a route to permanent residence.

His latest comments add urgency rather than new policy. As a departing member, Bacon is free of reelection pressure, and his pitch is aimed at fellow Republicans: act now on a bill drafted by a Republican, or negotiate later on terms set by Democratic leaders.

What would the Dignity Act actually do?

The bill, H.R. 4393 in this Congress, pairs border and enforcement spending with a renewable legal status for some long-term undocumented immigrants. As this site’s Dignity Act explainer describes, applicants would pass background checks, pay restitution and stay current on taxes in exchange for protection from removal and work authorization. It does not create a direct path to citizenship, and the status differs from a green card in important ways, as covered in this comparison of dignity status and lawful permanent residence.

Can the Dignity Act really pass before January?

It is possible on paper but unlikely in practice. Several obstacles stand in the way:

House floor access: The bill has not cleared committee. Without support from House leadership, supporters would need a discharge petition with 218 signatures, and House rules attach waiting periods measured in legislative days before such a petition can reach the floor.

Senate votes: Even if the House acted, most bills need 60 votes to end debate in the Senate. Sen. Ruben Gallego (D-Ariz.) told Fox News he is willing to work with Salazar, but no Senate companion vote has been scheduled.

Competing deadlines: The current stopgap funding law expires Dec. 11, and DHS funding and E-Verify are part of that fight, leaving little floor time for a major immigration bill.

The White House: President Trump said Nov. 20 that he could make deals with Democrats but would veto bills that do not meet his terms, and administration officials have repeatedly rejected anything they consider amnesty, as reported earlier.

If the bill does not pass by Jan. 3, it expires and must be reintroduced in the 120th Congress, where Democrats are expected to control both chambers. Democratic leaders have signaled they will start with the American Dream and Promise Act, which offers permanent residence to narrower groups, rather than the Dignity Act’s renewable status.

What this means for undocumented immigrants and employers now

Nothing has changed in the law. No dignity status exists, no application form has been published, and no one can file for the program today. Anyone charging fees to “register” for the Dignity Act is selling something the law does not provide. Employers should continue to follow existing Form I-9 rules, and individuals in removal proceedings should rely on the defenses available under current law.

Quick answers

What did Don Bacon say about immigration reform? In a Nov. 25 Fox News Digital report, Bacon said reform would pass in the current Congress and warned that waiting for the Democratic majorities in January could produce a broader bill.

Is the Dignity Act law? No. It is a pending House bill, H.R. 4393, that has not passed either chamber or cleared committee.

Has a vote on the Dignity Act been scheduled? No floor vote, markup or discharge petition had been announced as of Nov. 26.

Does the Dignity Act give a green card or citizenship? No. It offers a renewable legal status with work authorization, not permanent residence or a direct path to citizenship.

What happens to the bill on Jan. 3, 2027? If it has not passed, it expires with the 119th Congress and would have to be reintroduced.

title: Wave-Through Admission: Ninth Circuit Puts Entry Proof on Immigrants
description:
A permanent resident who claims a wave-through admission at the border carries the burden of proving it, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit ruled in a published opinion filed Nov. 17.
The Department of Homeland Security treated the 2015 adjustment as his admission, which put the 2017 offense inside the five-year window.
After this ruling, one element of that charge, the date of admission, can rest on a fact the respondent must establish.
Sources U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit, Elizondo Urzua v. Blanche, No.
§ 1361, burden of proof upon alien 8 U.S.C.
text:
A divided Ninth Circuit panel held that a green card holder who says he was waved through the border decades ago must prove that entry himself, and the answer can decide whether an old conviction makes him deportable.

A permanent resident who claims a wave-through admission at the border carries the burden of proving it, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit ruled in a published opinion filed Nov. 17. In Elizondo Urzua v. Blanche, No. 25-604, the court read 8 U.S.C. § 1361 to put that burden on the immigrant even in a case where the government is the side charging deportability, a reading that now binds immigration courts across the nine western states the circuit covers.

For a green card holder, the date of “admission” starts the clock for one of the most frequently charged deportation grounds: a crime involving moral turpitude committed within five years after admission, under 8 U.S.C. § 1227(a)(2)(A)(i). Under Matter of Quilantan, 25 I&N Dec. 285 (BIA 2010), a wave-through counts as an admission because the law asks whether the entry was procedurally regular, not whether the traveler had lawful status. Many long-term residents first crossed that way, some as children in a car an inspector waved on.

A 1994 crossing against a 2015 green card

The petitioner, a citizen of Mexico, said he entered in 1994 at age 13, asleep in a friend’s car that was waved through. He became a permanent resident in 2015 through adjustment under 8 U.S.C. § 1255(i). On that Form I-485, the opinion notes, he said at least three times that he had entered without inspection. In 2023 he pleaded no contest to rape of an unconscious person, an offense committed in 2017, and was sentenced to three years.

The Department of Homeland Security treated the 2015 adjustment as his admission, which put the 2017 offense inside the five-year window. If the 1994 crossing counted instead, the charge failed. That turn follows from the Board of Immigration Appeals’ framework in Matter of Alyazji, 25 I&N Dec. 397 (BIA 2011), under which adjustment serves as the admission only for someone with no earlier one. The immigration judge rejected the 1994 claim without an adverse credibility finding, and the Board dismissed his appeal, holding under Quilantan that he had to prove lawful inspection by clear and convincing evidence, while acknowledging that DHS bears the burden on every element of deportability.

What the majority and the dissent fought over

Section 1361 says that in any removal proceeding “the burden of proof shall be upon such person to show the time, place, and manner of his entry into the United States.” The obstacle was Iran v. INS, 656 F.2d 469 (9th Cir. 1981), which said the provision applies only in proceedings involving illegal entry. Writing for the majority, Judge Lawrence VanDyke called that line dicta: “this broad, unreasoned dicta does not require us to reject the plain meaning of § 1361 in this case.” “Therefore, Elizondo Urzua bore the burden of proving that his 1994 entry was procedurally regular,” the court held, and his own adjustment filings gave the Board substantial evidence to find he had not.

Judge Ronald Gould dissented. “Because I disagree that Iran‘s interpretation of § 1361 is dicta, I respectfully dissent,” he wrote, insisting that “that reasoned decision binds us.” He would have sent the case back to decide whether the government met its own burden of proving removability.

The practical effect. Section 1229a(c)(3) requires DHS to prove an admitted person deportable by clear and convincing evidence. After this ruling, one element of that charge, the date of admission, can rest on a fact the respondent must establish. That is likely to make an applicant’s earlier answers on Form I-485 close to decisive years later. The majority did not separately address whether the Board was right to demand clear and convincing proof, so the standard a respondent must meet remains an open question.

The reasoning may also travel. Wave-through claims matter for cancellation of removal for permanent residents, which requires seven years of continuous residence after admission “in any status” under 8 U.S.C. § 1229b(a)(2). The applicant already bears the burden there, but the opinion’s broad reading of § 1361 gives government lawyers another argument in any dispute over how and when someone entered. For long-term residents, the lesson tracks other recent cases on when a green card holder’s status ends: old filings and a later wave-through account need to match.

What comes next

A dissent built on the claim that the majority ignored binding circuit precedent is the classic setup for a petition for rehearing en banc, which in a case where the United States is a party is generally due within 45 days of judgment under Federal Rule of Appellate Procedure 40. The ruling lands as appellate timelines are tightening on the agency side too, with the BIA’s 10-day appeal deadline rule taking effect Dec. 17 and the Board’s end of equitable tolling for late appeals.

This article is for general information and is not legal advice.

Sources

8 U.S.C. § 1227(a)(2)(A)(i), crimes involving moral turpitude

8 U.S.C. § 1229a(c), burdens of proof in removal proceedings

Matter of Quilantan, 25 I&N Dec. 285 (BIA 2010); Matter of Alyazji, 25 I&N Dec. 397 (BIA 2011)

title: Warrantless ICE Arrests Barred in Montana Without Escape-Risk Finding
description:
According to Newsweek, the court found a high likelihood that DHS was engaging in a pattern and practice of unlawful warrantless arrests in Montana.
It counted at least 50 likely unlawful arrests since July 31 and noted that most DHS arrests in the state since late July were made without warrants.
The court reasoned that the request is simple: document the flight-risk assessment and do not make unlawful warrantless arrests (order at 24–26).
How it fits the national picture Montana is the latest of several districts to limit warrantless immigration arrests.
Under the reported Montana order, DHS must provide the documentation to plaintiffs’ counsel within 72 hours.
text:
A Montana federal judge has ordered DHS to stop warrantless civil immigration arrests in the state unless agents first find, person by person, that the individual is likely to escape before a warrant can be obtained.

Chief U.S. District Judge Brian Morris of the District of Montana on Nov. 25, 2026, granted interim relief in Verde Hernandez v. Department of Homeland Security, No. CV-26-301-GF-BMM (Great Falls Division). The 35-page order bars federal immigration agents from making warrantless civil arrests anywhere in the District of Montana without a prior, individualized determination that the person is likely to escape before a warrant can be obtained, the standard in 8 U.S.C. § 1357(a)(2). It also requires documentation of each warrantless arrest to be given to plaintiffs’ counsel within 72 hours and bars moving anyone arrested without a warrant out of the district for seven days.

The ruling matters beyond Montana because of how it handles the government’s threshold defenses. Judge Morris rejected arguments that the INA’s jurisdiction-channeling provisions bar the suit, held that an unwritten enforcement practice can be reviewed under the Administrative Procedure Act, and found that people already released remain at realistic risk of re-arrest. Those are the same arguments DHS is raising in warrantless-arrest cases in Colorado, Oregon, California and New York.

What the court ordered

The plaintiffs sued on behalf of themselves and others similarly situated and asked for a temporary restraining order, a preliminary injunction and a stay under 5 U.S.C. § 705 (order at 9). The order does not certify a class. Newsweek, which first reported the ruling on Nov. 27, described it as an interlocutory ruling and not a final judgment. As reported by Newsweek and reflected in the order’s closing section, the relief:

bars DHS from warrantless civil immigration arrests in the District of Montana unless agents first make an individualized finding that the person is likely to escape before a warrant can be obtained;

requires DHS to send the order promptly to the officers, agents and contractors involved;

requires DHS to give plaintiffs’ counsel documentation of each warrantless arrest within 72 hours; and

bars transferring anyone arrested without a warrant out of the district for seven days.

According to Newsweek, the court found a high likelihood that DHS was engaging in a pattern and practice of unlawful warrantless arrests in Montana. It counted at least 50 likely unlawful arrests since July 31 and noted that most DHS arrests in the state since late July were made without warrants. The plaintiffs are represented by Upper Seven Law.

The legal framework

Immigration officers usually arrest on an administrative warrant under 8 U.S.C. § 1226(a). Section 1357(a)(2) allows a warrantless arrest only when an officer has reason to believe the person is in the United States unlawfully and “is likely to escape before a warrant can be obtained.” The court also pointed to 8 C.F.R. § 287.8(c)(2)(ii), DHS’s own warrant rule, and to the 48-hour custody-determination requirement in 8 C.F.R. § 287.3(d) (order at 5–6).

How the court got past DHS’s threshold defenses

Standing. DHS argued that any future injury was speculative. The court found a policy and practice of unlawful arrests in Montana, drawing in part on rulings from other districts, and a realistic threat of re-arrest under the Lyons and Melendres line of cases (order at 9–16). Earlier release orders did not moot the claims, because those orders bar re-detention but do not protect against a new unlawful arrest. “Nothing categorically exempts Plaintiffs from Defendants’ unlawful policy,” the court wrote (order at 16).

Jurisdiction-stripping. The court rejected DHS’s reliance on 8 U.S.C. § 1252(a)(5), (b)(9) and (g) (order at 16–19). The plaintiffs challenge an arrest policy, not a removal order. Their claims are collateral to removal proceedings. And § 1252(g) is read narrowly under Ninth Circuit precedent. The court also called DHS’s reading of the Jennings v. Rodriguez “detain in the first place” passage an overgenerous use of dicta. The portions of the order reviewed for this article do not address 8 U.S.C. § 1252(f)(1), the limit on classwide injunctions against the operation of certain INA provisions. That is a likely issue on any appeal.

Final agency action. DHS argued there was no reviewable policy. The court disagreed, writing that “both logic and law require unwritten policy to be reviewable” (order at 21). It held that the practice marks the end of agency decision-making and has direct legal consequences, because the arrests and detentions are concrete (order at 19–24).

An “obey the law” injunction. The court rejected the argument that the requested injunction was too vague because it only told agents to follow the statute. The court reasoned that the request is simple: document the flight-risk assessment and do not make unlawful warrantless arrests (order at 24–26).

The order then found the plaintiffs likely to succeed on their APA and § 1357(a)(2) claims and found the remaining injunction factors in their favor. This article’s account of those later sections is based on Newsweek’s report and a summary review of the order, not a line-by-line reading.

How it fits the national picture

Montana is the latest of several districts to limit warrantless immigration arrests. The order cites a related District of Montana case, Hernandez v. Crosson, No. 4:26-cv-280 (D. Mont. Aug. 31, 2026), in which a class was certified. In September, that litigation produced an order releasing 24 people held in Cascade County, the Daily Montanan reported. Newsweek also linked to parallel litigation in Colorado, Oregon, California and New York. Immigration Analytics has covered individual warrantless-arrest rulings, including the Maine SIJ teen case, and a home-raid suit dismissed on standing in which the warrant question was left open. The Montana order is broader: it applies to every warrantless civil arrest in the district.

What it means for practice

Removal defense and habeas counsel in Montana should ask whether a client was arrested without a warrant after Nov. 25 and request the escape-risk documentation and Form I-213. A missing or boilerplate justification may support habeas relief or a compliance motion.

Escape-risk documentation is the written record of why an officer believed a particular person was likely to escape before an administrative arrest warrant could be obtained. The officer must make that assessment before the arrest, based on facts known at the time. The record should explain what the officer observed or learned, when, and how those facts supported the decision to arrest immediately. Suspected unlawful presence alone is insufficient. During a roadside stop, for example, the mere possibility that the driver could leave when the stop ends does not establish escape risk. A reliable address where officers reasonably expect to find the person weighs against such a finding. Specific facts indicating that the person will soon move on and be difficult to locate before a warrant can be obtained may support it. The officer can record the reasoning in the Form I-213 narrative or a separate arrest report. Under the reported Montana order, DHS must provide the documentation to plaintiffs’ counsel within 72 hours.

The seven-day transfer bar gives families and lawyers a short window to file in Montana before a detainee is moved to another circuit.

Practitioners elsewhere can cite the order’s standing, § 1252 and final-agency-action analysis. It does not bind other courts, and it rests on the court’s factual findings about Montana.

Interim relief only. The order is not a final judgment. Expect an appeal and stay request to the Ninth Circuit, where § 1252(f)(1) is likely to be contested.

Any DHS notice of appeal or motion for a stay pending appeal in the Ninth Circuit.

Class certification and further proceedings in No. CV-26-301-GF-BMM.

The first 72-hour documentation reports to plaintiffs’ counsel, and any compliance disputes.

This article is for general information and is not legal advice.

name: Litigation
title: Lawsuit Alleges Sprawling Federal Grand Jury Investigation into Anonymous ICE Critics Online
description:
Plaintiffs’ case is the first systemic civil challenge, and the first case that will be litigated in public view, to the Trump administration’s abuse of grand jury unmasking subpoenas.
“The government is weaponizing the grand jury process to retaliate against people for expressing their political views online,” said Laura Moraff, staff attorney with the ACLU’s Speech, Privacy, and Technology Project.
Despite their name, grand jury subpoenas are rarely requested by grand jurors themselves; they are typically requested by prosecutors, with no oversight from the judge.
“Using grand jury subpoenas to unmask and intimidate critics of ICE is an alarming abuse of power,” said Laura Follansbee, staff attorney with the ACLU of DC.
After the court ordered the case unsealed on Wednesday, Plaintiffs filed public versions of the complaint and other documents today.
text:
Four social media users who have posted content critical of the Trump administration are pushing back against secretive subpoenas aimed at unmasking their identities

November 27, 2026 12:00 am

WASHINGTON — Four social media users filed a class action lawsuit last week challenging grand jury subpoenas sent by the federal government to tech companies seeking their identifying information. The lawsuit alleges the subpoenas were issued as part of an abusive investigation (“Investigation 18”) that probes users who anonymously post content on social media that is critical of the Trump administration’s immigration enforcement tactics. The secretive “unmasking” subpoenas for these four users were sent to Bluesky, X (formerly known as Twitter), and Meta. Plaintiffs’ case is the first systemic civil challenge, and the first case that will be litigated in public view, to the Trump administration’s abuse of grand jury unmasking subpoenas. After the case was initially filed under seal, newly unsealed court filings were filed on the public docket today.

“The government is weaponizing the grand jury process to retaliate against people for expressing their political views online,” said Laura Moraff, staff attorney with the ACLU’s Speech, Privacy, and Technology Project. “The First Amendment guarantees our right to criticize the government, including anonymously, and no one should fear being investigated for disagreeing with the president. This crackdown on dissent is antithetical to our nation’s core values.”

The grand jury subpoenas were sent to tech companies as part of a campaign to target users who criticize the U.S. government online. While the plaintiffs’ initial filings point to 35 subpoenas related to Investigation 18, they suggest the true number is likely far higher. Despite their name, grand jury subpoenas are rarely requested by grand jurors themselves; they are typically requested by prosecutors, with no oversight from the judge.

“Using grand jury subpoenas to unmask and intimidate critics of ICE is an alarming abuse of power,” said Laura Follansbee, staff attorney with the ACLU of DC. “The use of subpoenas to punish social media users for their speech is chilling not only for our clients but for others who fear being targeted because of their political beliefs. Our democracy cannot function if citizens are too afraid to speak up.”

In the last year, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) has sent hundreds of administrative subpoenas to tech companies seeking information about people who criticize ICE online. The ACLU and its affiliates have filed multiple motions to quash these subpoenas, which are issued by federal agents without approval by a judge. Facing pushback from users and tech companies, the government began shifting to grand jury subpoenas, which are subject to secrecy rules and are generally more difficult to challenge.

“We filed this case because the Trump administration is illegally and secretly targeting online critics just because it doesn’t like what they’re posting,” said Jake Snow, senior staff attorney at the ACLU of Northern California. “That sets a dangerous and terrifying precedent that threatens all of our fundamental rights.”

The four plaintiffs are filing suit pseudonymously to protect their anonymity. The suit argues that Investigation 18 violates the First and Fourth Amendments because it was initiated in a bad faith effort to gather intelligence on dissenters and to retaliate against people for protected political speech. Plaintiffs are seeking a preliminary injunction to halt the investigation and prevent the government from forcing companies to hand over people’s information to the government.

Investigation 18’s pattern of seeking to unmask anonymous critics fits into the administration’s broader pattern of retaliation against people criticizing and protesting the federal government’s immigration enforcement practices. People across the country have faced brutal retaliation by immigration enforcement, ranging from surveillance to destruction of property to arrest for filming ICE activity in public spaces, and federal agents have cracked down on protests near detention facilities and enforcement actions.

The suit was filed as a class action — meaning plaintiffs seek to vindicate their own interests as well as others whose identity information has been or will be requested by grand jury subpoenas as part of Investigation 18 — in the United States District Court for the District of Columbia on Monday, Nov. 16. After the court ordered the case unsealed on Wednesday, Plaintiffs filed public versions of the complaint and other documents today. The plaintiffs are represented by the ACLU, the ACLU of DC, and the ACLU of Northern California.

description: (The Center Square) – The U.S. Supreme Court will hear arguments in a case that could determine the future of immigrant asylum laws.
text:
Stocks are rising as Wall Street closes out an erratic week …

The Iran-backed Houthi rebels say that an airstrike in south…



The U.S. Supreme Court in Washington, D.C. Photo: massmatt / Flickr / CC BY 2.0 / Cropped from Original

(The Center Square) – The U.S. Supreme Court will hear arguments in a case that could determine the future of immigrant asylum laws.

On Nov. 30, justices on the high court will hear arguments in Wassily v. Blanche, a case over whether noncitizens whose asylum in the United States was later terminated because of criminal convictions are eligible to become lawful permanent residents. The case focuses on Tamer Wassily and Byron Velasquez Arreaga, migrants from Egypt and Guatemala, respectively, who were convicted of crimes that led to the government moving to revoke both men’s asylum status.

The two men sought to become lawful permanent residents in the United States, citing fear of persecution in their home countries to prevent their return. An immigration judge granted Wassily’s request to become a lawful permanent resident, but the Board of Immigration Appeals said he was ineligible because of his criminal conviction.

Matthew O’Brien, deputy director of the Federation for American Immigration Reform, said immigration law allows for migrants who committed crimes to have their asylum status terminated.

“The U.S. is not under any domestic statutory obligation, or international legal obligation to accept any alien for asylum or continue to shelter any alien who has already been granted asylum,” O’Brien wrote in an email to The Center Square.

O’Brien said the case boils down to protecting American citizens and national sovereignty over the interests of immigrants who could be harmed in foreign countries.

“Actions have consequences, and if [Wassily and Velasquez] were genuinely concerned about being returned to their countries of origin, then they should have refrained from engaging in criminal behavior in the state that had granted them protection,” O’Brien said.

Lawyers for Wassily and Velasquez urged the justices to reject the lower court’s decision to terminate asylum and prevent the two from obtaining lawful permanent residence status.

“It will harm all those who, but for termination, would have been worthy of waivers for humanitarian, family-unity, or public-interest reasons,” lawyers for Wassily and Velasquez wrote in a petition to the high court.

O’Brien said only green card holders with exceptionally good civic, social and economic success in the United States who are convicted of minor violations should be allowed to remain in the country.

“Illegal aliens who have been convicted of any kind of crime should not be allowed to remain in the U.S. under any circumstances,” O’Brien wrote. “Doing so simply rewards them for serial violations of America's laws.”

However, lawyers for the two migrants said the decision to terminate their asylum will also have ripple effects on immediate family members. When a principal applicant for asylum commits a “particularly serious crime,” the derivative status that applicant's spouse or children can also be terminated, according to U.S. immigration law.

Wassily was convicted of third-degree stalking and child endangerment, according to a court filing. Velasquez was convicted of driving while intoxicated. Both convictions were deemed particularly serious crimes by an immigration judge.

In 2023, nearly 5,000 individuals received derivative asylum in the United States, according to court records.

“If the decision below stands, these innocent spouses and children – through no fault of their own – will be precluded from adjusting to [Lawful Permanent Resident] status and will face removal themselves,” lawyers for Wassily and Velasquez wrote.

The rule of lenity, a principal of criminal law, requires courts to interpret a statute as narrowly as possible when it is unclear about whether specific criminal activity is prohibited. However, the rule does not apply to civil cases, including immigration, the area issue before the court.

O’Brien said he expects the justices to pay attention to this aspect of the case and settle whether the rule can apply to immigration issues.

“This seems like a settled issue. The Second Circuit, which has never been accused of being conservative, definitively found that none of the arguments advanced by the petitioners in this matter had any merit,” O’Brien wrote. “I would expect that the Supreme Court's opinion will be focused primarily on the rule of lenity and its inapplicability in the civil, immigration context”

title: Trump said he was 'too tough' on immigration. PolitiFact reviews his campaign promises
authors: Maria Briceño and Amy Sherman, PolitiFact reporters, Maria Briceño, Amy Sherman, PolitiFact reporters
description:
Trump, who said he had been “too tough” on immigration, said he would work out an immigration “deal” with Democrats but provided no details.
On Nov. 9, Trump told reporters “we’re not going to have amnesty or anything” for immigrants illegally in the country.
Here’s a look at where Trump’s immigration promises stand.
During his first term, Trump used executive orders to impose travel bans on people from seven countries, suspending their visas for 90 days.
The Trump administration has not appealed this decision.
text:
In his first sit-down interview after the midterm elections where his party resoundingly lost control of both chambers of Congress, President Donald Trump both acknowledged that his immigration agenda might have turned away some voters and praised it.

CBS News’ “60 Minutes” correspondent Ross Douthat asked Trump if his immigration crackdown hurt Republicans in the elections.

“I think it both helped and hurt,” Trump said in the interview that aired Nov. 8. “I think I got an A+ for closing up the border. I get very high marks for getting the bad ones out.”

But the administration also removed “people that had good jobs” in landscaping or hotels, in some cases people who paid taxes, he said, and that hurt the party.

Trump, who said he had been “too tough” on immigration, said he would work out an immigration “deal” with Democrats but provided no details.

After the Nov. 3 election, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin floated the idea of working with Congress on a legal pathway for immigrants who came to the U.S. illegally as children and who are protected from deportation under the Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals program, or DACA.

On Nov. 9, Trump told reporters “we’re not going to have amnesty or anything” for immigrants illegally in the country.

Trump has promoted Stephen Miller, his former deputy chief of staff, as his new chief of staff. Miller led Trump’s first-term hard-line immigration agenda, supporting policies that separated families arriving at the border and that banned the entry of people from several Muslim-majority countries.

During Trump’s second term, Miller has been a leading architect of Trump’s immigration strategy and has pushed the administration to arrest at least 3,000 immigrants a day.

Immigration experts doubt that Trump will cool down on enforcement as Miller embraces his new role.

“Promoting Stephen Miller hardly signals a retreat from the administration’s mass deportation agenda,” said Tom K. Wong, director of the U.S. Immigration Policy Center at the University of California, San Diego. “Until we see actual changes in enforcement priorities, the president’s remarks seem more like a change in political messaging than a change in policy.”

PolitiFact has tracked Trump’s progress on immigration campaign promises on our MAGA-Meter. Here’s a look at where Trump’s immigration promises stand.

Promise: Carry out the largest domestic deportation operation in American history

This is In the Works.

The Department of Homeland Security said that as of October, the administration had deported about 1.2 million immigrants during Trump’s second term. Immigration experts say it’s hard to independently verify the scale of deportations, because the administration isn’t releasing monthly or comprehensive data.

The Migration Policy Institute, a nonpartisan think tank, analyzed DHS data and estimated that from January 2025 to July 31, the administration deported about 980,000 people. The institute said that on an annual basis, while the total deportations are up from the Biden and first Trump administrations, they remain below the levels from the early 2000s.

The Deportation Data Project at the University of California, Los Angeles, and the University of California, Berkeley, obtained data from ICE showing the agency arrested and detained about 42,000 people in July, a monthly record during this term.

A substantial proportion of those arrested within the country are people who lived in the U.S. for more than a decade, said Elizabeth Cohen, a Boston University political science professor.

“Trump‘s immigration agenda has dramatically expanded an already costly interior enforcement apparatus,” Cohen said, although most deportations continue to originate at the border, and border encounters have fallen sharply from Biden administration levels.

Promise: Finish the border wall

This is In the Works.

DHS reported Nov. 3 that from the beginning of Trump’s second term in late January 2025 through Oct. 30, U.S. Customs and Border Protection completed approximately 330 miles of new border barriers. This includes 139.5 miles of primary walls that face Mexico; 73.9 miles of waterborne barriers, which are usually floating infrastructure placed in bodies of water along the southern border; and 116.2 miles of secondary walls, which are barriers behind the already existing primary walls.

On Nov. 9, the Supreme Court ruled the Trump administration can continue with border wall construction along the southern border in the Big Bend region of Southwest Texas, which environmentalists say could harm wildlife and the area’s residents. It lifted a district judge’s order from October that halted construction.

Since Trump signed the One Big Beautiful Bill Act on July 4, 2025, which included funding to build the border wall, CBP has awarded 11 contracts to build segments of new wall and detection technology.

CBP says the money awarded in part is for building a “smart wall,” which is a mixture of steel walls, roads, detection technology, cameras and lighting.

CBP has designated $34.6 billion of the law’s funding for the border wall.

Promise: Revoke the temporary legal status of Haitians

This is In the Works.

In a 6-3 vote in June, the Supreme Court paved the way for the administration to revoke Haiti’s Temporary Protected Status designation, which protected hundreds of thousands of Haitians from deportation.

In recent months, about 1,000 of the 350,000 people with TPS have been deported to Haiti, according to Human Rights Watch, which cited Haiti’s National Migration Office. Haitians were also deported to Mexico in 2025 and 2026.

Trump made this promise in 2024 as he and running mate JD Vance spread the lie that Haitian immigrants in Springfield, Ohio, were stealing and eating people’s pets.

Promise: Restore and expand the travel ban

This is a Promise Kept.

During his first term, Trump used executive orders to impose travel bans on people from seven countries, suspending their visas for 90 days. After a legal battle, the Supreme Court ruled that the president can issue a travel ban under certain circumstances.

President Joe Biden revoked the ban; Trump resurrected it in his second term and expanded it to 19 countries.

Promise: Restore Remain in Mexico program

This is a Promise Broken.

In 2021, Biden terminated Trump’s first-term Migrant Protection Protocol, aka Remain in Mexico program. In January 2025, at the start of his second term, Trump signed an executive order to reinstate the program, which sent certain migrants seeking asylum to Mexico to await their U.S. immigration court proceedings.

On Oct. 7, a federal court ruled the program’s implementation is unlawful. The Trump administration has not appealed this decision.

Promise: Require proof of citizenship at the polls

This is a Promise Broken.

Trump lobbied for the passage of the SAVE America Act. The legislation would require people to provide documentary proof of citizenship, such as a passport or birth certificate, when registering to vote. It passed the House in February but stalled in the Senate. It’s unlikely that the incoming Democratic-controlled Congress will pass this legislation.

Federal law already says only U.S. citizens can vote in elections for Congress and president. When applying to register to vote, people sign a form attesting that they are U.S. citizens.

text:
A federal judge in the District of Columbia Wednesday issued a classwide injunction to prevent the Trump administration from implementing its second attempt at redefining the constitutional right to birthright citizenship.

The order from Judge Christopher Reid Cooper will remain in effect while litigation continues. A classwide injunction blocks action affecting a defined group of individuals, as opposed to a nationwide injunction.

In a memorandum opinion, Cooper noted the Supreme Court earlier this year denied President Donald Trump’s executive order that would deny citizenship to babies born from immigrants either in the country unlawfully or on a temporary basis, in the case Barbara v. Trump.

“Yet Barbara’s ink had scarcely dried when the President issued a second executive order—Executive Order 14418, at issue here—directing federal agencies to withhold recognition of citizenship from additional categories of U.S.-born children with noncitizen parents,” he wrote. “As the Supreme Court has made clear, however, the President cannot carve out new exceptions to birthright citizenship for children born within the United States and subject to its laws.”

The American Civil Liberties Union, which led the first challenge against the Trump administration’s birthright citizenship order and is leading the second, welcomed the ruling.

“Enough is enough,” Cody Wofsy, deputy director of the ACLU’s Immigrants’ Rights Project, said in a statement. “The Supreme Court has twice rejected efforts to gut birthright citizenship, in 1898 and again earlier this year. Third time is not the charm, and the President needs to accept that birthright citizenship is the law of the land.”

The Department of Justice did not respond to States Newsroom’s request for comment.

Earlier this month, Cooper seemed skeptical of the legality of the Trump administration’s second attempt to redefine the constitutional right to birthright citizenship.

The president’s recent executive orders would deny citizenship to babies born in the United States to parents deemed part of a designated terrorist organization and to parents who purposefully came to the United States to gain citizenship in what critics call “birth tourism.”

The executive order also aimed to deny citizenship to children born to foreign diplomatic staff and children born in U.S. territories where Congress has not passed a law granting citizenship.

There is already a small carve out for birthright citizenship, extended to children born to foreign diplomats.

text:
Scott Brocato:

All right, Bob, let's start with the story of Michell Germán and her family. They're back in El Paso after being released from ICE custody last Friday.

Bob Moore:

Yeah, we've talked about this case previously. So Michell is a senior at El Paso High School, very popular student. About a month ago, she, her little sister who's a student at Lamar Elementary, and their parents were arrested by ICE in what ICE has said is a "targeted operation" without explaining why this particular family was targeted and they were taken to a facility known as Dilley outside of Austin, which is the only place that ICE has to hold families in detention. And they were there for more than 20 days, which is a significant number because ICE has rules that it can't detain children for more than 20 days. And so Michell and her sister clearly exceeded that threshold.

So their lawyers kind of put pressure on them. There's a lot of public pressure because of the media coverage. And so earlier this week, or I guess at the end of last week, ICE decided to free them. The parents are wearing ankle monitors known as "alternative to detention." The family still has an immigration process to go through. They're seeking asylum. We know from history that only a relatively small percentage of people seeking asylum, especially in this age, receive it.

So their future is still very much uncertain, but it now looks at least like Michell will be able to graduate with her classmates at El Paso High this year and be back with her friends. It was a very emotional time for the students at the school having to deal with this. And Michell and her family said that support from them really helped them get through a difficult time.

Scott Brocato:

The next story: amid continuing enrollment declines, the Socorro ISD becomes the largest school district in El Paso County.

Bob Moore:

So literally forever in El Paso history, the largest school district has been the El Paso Independent School District, which is pretty much the historic core of the city. El Paso ISD's population has been in decline for more than a decade. Socorro, which is out on the eastern fringe, had seen pretty rapid growth until the last four years or so, and its population started to decline. And so now this year, because Socorro is declining a little bit less than El Paso, it surpassed El Paso ISD as the largest district, which is both a historic moment, but also a continuing warning sign of significant issues we have going forward in El Paso. We continue to see declining enrollment for all three of our largest districts: El Paso, Socorro, and Isleta, their rates of decline steepened this year.

So the challenge is getting worse. They're losing about 4% of their student population every year. It's starting out at the elementary level, but it's gonna start rippling through middle school and then high school. And it's gonna present a lot of challenges for the school districts, for taxpayers, and for the community in general as to how we manage these changes we're facing.

El Paso is not alone in this. Schools across the country, including in New Mexico, are facing the same challenges, largely driven by declining birth rates. Although in El Paso, immigration enforcement is probably adding to the challenges. I just mentioned one story of a family that was put in ICE detention. Other families have been deported or chosen to leave. That's also putting some pressure on enrollment too.

Scott Brocato:

And finally, Meta pledges $53 million to help El Paso Electric customers pay bills and lower energy costs.

Bob Moore:

So we've talked multiple times in the last few months about complaints about higher energy costs in El Paso, largely as a result of climate change. It's getting hotter, people are running their coolers longer. It's probably one of the biggest affordability challenges El Paso has.

So this week, Meta, which is building a massive data center here in El Paso that's politically proven to be very, very unpopular, announced that they'll make a donation to this fund that's managed by the El Paso Community Foundation to help El Paso Electric customers who are having difficulty paying their bills. The initial payment is about $15 million to pay down energy bills for people who can't afford it. But then there's also $2 million a year for the next 19 years in there that's meant to help weatherize homes and also deal with some affordability issues.

I suspect this is the first of a number of announcements Meta is going to make about investments it's making in the nonprofit sector in El Paso. Obviously, they are trying to get over some the political pressure that's being brought and you're seeing some of the similar things playing out with Project Jupiter and Doña Ana County, where they had offered to essentially reduce some bills for electric rate payers there although the county commissioners have been very resistant to that for a variety of reasons that we explain in our story.

Scott Brocato:

And where can folks find that story and more?

Bob Moore:

text:
By Emma Farge

GENEVA, Nov 27 (Reuters) – UN Human Rights chief Volker Turk said he hoped to visit the United States to discuss rights issues there and abroad with senior officials, weeks after Washington spurned a meeting in Geneva over its record.

Turk did not say what issues he wanted to raise, but has called this year for independent investigations into deaths of people in US immigration custody.

The US mission in Geneva, which is closed for the Thanksgiving holiday, did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the planned trip and whether US officials would meet with Turk.

Earlier this month, Washington stayed away from a UN meeting where its rights record under President Donald Trump was due to be examined – the second year in a row it has done so – drawing criticism from campaign groups including Human Rights Watch.

Washington disengaged from the Geneva-based UN Human Rights Council last year, citing an anti-Israel bias. It has cut and withheld funding from a number of agencies, demanding reforms.

“I intend to visit next year. I would seek to engage with the authorities, as well as on the Hill and with civil society,” Turk told Reuters on Thursday.

He said he planned to be in Washington and was aiming for April.

Washington, along with North Korea, Israel and Russia, was among a minority of states opposing Turk’s reappointment to the post in a vote in July that highlighted a deepening confrontation between the Trump administration and the UN.

US officials have previously accused UN human rights bodies of “anti-American” rhetoric while defending their own record, including on deportations which they say are carried out in accordance with US immigration law.

The Department of Homeland Security has said it is committed to ensuring a “safe, secure and humane” environment in detention.

(Reporting by Emma Farge; Editing by Andrew Heavens)

text:
Why It Matters

Federal appeals courts issued October decisions that opened or deepened disagreements among circuits on criminal, immigration and Indian law questions, according to a new Congressional Research Service (CRS) report. Where circuits disagree, federal law is applied unevenly to similarly situated litigants. ​

The report notes that relatively few appellate decisions are reviewed by the Supreme Court, so the circuit courts are often the last word on consequential legal questions. For congressional staff and advocates, the cases show where the same federal statute can produce different results depending on where a case is heard.

The Big Picture

The report covers selected cases relevant to Congress, and only those in which the controlling opinion itself recognizes a split among the circuits.

In criminal law, a divided Ninth Circuit affirmed a conviction in United States v. So, which concerns 18 U.S.C. § 3292. The majority held that the inquiry into a foreign government's "final action" is objective, aligning with the Eleventh Circuit and splitting with the Fifth Circuit, which looks to the foreign government's subjective belief.

In immigration law, the Sixth Circuit held in Castro-Fuentes v. Blanche on Oct. 27 that it lacked jurisdiction to review denials of protection from removal when the petitioner did not challenge the reinstated removal order. It overruled its own earlier decision. The court aligned with the Eighth, Ninth and Eleventh Circuits and split from the Fourth and Seventh Circuits.

A divided Tenth Circuit panel in Mukantagara v. Mullin allowed a mother and son to challenge the termination of the mother's refugee status. The majority described itself as splitting with the Fourth, Eighth and Ninth Circuits. It reaffirmed an earlier decision that had been vacated for reconsideration in light of Mullin v. Doe.

Advertisement

In tribal law, the Tenth Circuit, sitting en banc, overturned an earlier en banc decision in United States v. Hebert on Oct. 14. A defendant who raises the defense that the General Crimes Act does not apply because he or she is Indian must prove it by a preponderance of the evidence. The Fifth and Ninth Circuits place that burden on the government.

The First Circuit's decision in In re MCP 191 largely dismissed or denied challenges to a 2024 Federal Communications Commission rule on communications services for incarcerated individuals. The court held it lacked jurisdiction over the states' claim about commissioner term limits because the states had not first presented it to the commission. A 2025 rule superseded the 2024 rule during litigation, and some challenges were held in abeyance.

The Bottom Line

The Tenth Circuit remanded the Hebert cases for further proceedings, including possible retrials. The Mukantagara case went back to the district court for further proceedings.

In each of the four decided splits, the court's chosen rule governs only within its own circuit, so the burden of proof in Indian country prosecutions and the reach of review in immigration cases depend on the circuit where a case is filed.

By Emma Farge

GENEVA, Nov 27 (Reuters) – UN Human Rights chief Volker Turk said he hoped to visit the United States to discuss rights issues there and abroad ​with senior officials, weeks after Washington spurned a meeting ‌in Geneva over its record.

Turk did not say what issues he wanted to raise, but has called this year for independent investigations into deaths of people in US immigration custody.

The US mission in Geneva, which is ‌closed ​for the Thanksgiving holiday, did not immediately ⁠respond to a request ⁠for comment on the planned trip and whether US officials would meet with Turk.

Earlier this month, Washington stayed away from a UN meeting where its rights record under President Donald ​Trump was due to be examined — the second year in a row it has done so — drawing criticism from campaign ⁠groups including Human Rights Watch.

Washington disengaged ⁠from the Geneva-based UN Human Rights Council last ​year, citing an anti-Israel bias. It has cut and withheld funding ​from a number of agencies, demanding reforms.

“I intend to ‌visit next year. I would seek to engage with the authorities, as well as on the Hill and with civil society,” Turk told Reuters on Thursday.

He said he planned to be ⁠in Washington and was aiming for April.

Washington, along with North Korea, Israel and Russia, was among a minority of states opposing Turk’s reappointment ⁠to the post ‌in a vote in July that highlighted ⁠a deepening confrontation between the Trump administration and ​the ‌UN.

US officials have previously accused UN human rights ​bodies of “anti-American” ⁠rhetoric while defending their own record, including on deportations which they say are carried out in accordance with US immigration law.

The Department of Homeland Security has said it is committed to ensuring a “safe, secure and humane” environment in detention.

(Reporting by Emma Farge; Editing ​by Andrew Heavens)

text:
The immigration judge who ordered the deportation of former Columbia University student and anti-Israel activist Mahmoud Khalil has been promoted for the second time in roughly a week, emerging as a key figure in the Justice Department’s efforts to carry out President Donald Trump’s deportation agenda.

Jamee Comans was named acting director of the Executive Office for Immigration Review on Tuesday, according to an updated personnel biography on the DOJ’s website. Her appointment, first reported by Bloomberg Law, comes just days after Attorney General Todd Blanche tapped her to serve as chief immigration judge, overseeing the nation’s immigration courts.

Recommended Stories

▶

The rapid succession of promotions underscores a broader personnel realignment underway at the DOJ as the Trump administration seeks to accelerate deportation proceedings while confronting an unprecedented volume of litigation challenging its immigration enforcement policies.

Notably, Blanche on Tuesday directed attorneys from across the department to reinforce U.S. attorneys’ offices inundated with lawsuits from immigration detainees. As the Washington Examiner previously reported, more than 97,000 habeas corpus petitions have been filed by immigration detainees since Trump returned to office, including roughly 10,000 since October alone.

While Blanche’s directive addresses challenges to immigration detention in federal courts, Comans will oversee the administrative court system responsible for adjudicating removal proceedings and immigration appeals.

Comans replaces Sirce Owen, who had returned to the acting director position over the summer and presided over a significant expansion of the immigration judiciary.

Just five days before Comans’s latest promotion, Owen welcomed her to the chief immigration judge position during a Thursday investiture ceremony at the DOJ’s headquarters in Washington, where Comans administered the oath of office to 32 new permanent and temporary immigration judges.

“Her appointment takes place at a time of historic growth,” Owen said in a statement.

According to the DOJ, the latest round of appointments brought the number of immigration judges nationwide to more than 800, an all-time high for the agency. The department also said it had reduced the immigration court backlog by more than 678,000 cases since January 2025.

Comans gained national attention last year while presiding over the removal proceedings of Khalil, a legal permanent resident who became one of the first high-profile targets of the Trump administration’s crackdown on noncitizens involved in anti-Israel campus demonstrations.

In April 2025, Comans found Khalil removable after Secretary of State Marco Rubio invoked a rarely used provision of federal immigration law allowing for the removal of noncitizens whose presence could have serious adverse foreign policy consequences.

Comans subsequently ordered Khalil’s deportation to Algeria or Syria in September 2025 on a separate statutory ground, finding that he had deliberately omitted material information from his application for permanent residency, including his involvement with the United Nations Relief and Works Agency for Palestine Refugees and Columbia University Apartheid Divest, a coalition of anti-Israel campus activist groups.

Rubio has described UNRWA as “a subsidiary of Hamas,” a U.S.-designated terrorist organization. As of August, federal investigators had referred more than 100 current or former UNRWA employees to the State Department for potential suspension or debarment over suspected affiliations with Hamas or participation in the Oct. 7, 2023, terrorist attacks against Israel. UNRWA has disputed allegations of institutional ties to Hamas, and Khalil has denied wrongdoing and accused the administration of targeting him for his political speech.

The Board of Immigration Appeals, which also operates under the Executive Office for Immigration Review, rejected Khalil’s appeal in April. Khalil is now challenging his removal order before the 5th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals and separately petitioned the Supreme Court last month to review a ruling that opened the door to his rearrest.

In a filing Friday, Solicitor General D. John Sauer urged the justices to take up Khalil’s case to resolve a split among federal appeals courts over the authority of district judges to entertain habeas corpus challenges arising from immigration removal proceedings. The DOJ maintains that the lower appeals court ruled correctly in Khalil’s case.

Khalil remains out of immigration custody while the Supreme Court weighs whether to hear his case.

Comans also brings nearly a decade of experience prosecuting immigration cases on behalf of the federal government. Before joining the immigration bench in 2021, she spent nine years as an attorney for Immigration and Customs Enforcement, including three years as a deputy chief counsel in Louisiana.

She became an assistant chief immigration judge in 2023, overseeing courts in Maryland and Louisiana, before moving into a senior policy role in December 2025.

A graduate of Mississippi College School of Law, Comans also served in the Navy Reserve from 2001 to 2022, including as a naval intelligence officer supporting Operation Enduring Freedom in Afghanistan.

Unlike federal judges appointed under Article III of the Constitution, immigration judges operate within the executive branch under the authority of the attorney general. Comans’s latest appointment puts her in charge of the agency encompassing both the immigration trial courts and the Board of Immigration Appeals, giving her a central administrative role in implementing the department’s immigration adjudication priorities.

text:
A top City Hall staffer who spent five months in a federal immigration lockup kept pulling his $125,000 salary while behind bars — and insiders said officials had no choice but to keep signing checks.

Rafael Rubio Bohorquez, 53, a Venezuelan national, was picked up by ICE agents on Jan. 12 on charges that he lied on a federal application for asylum and temporary protected status in the US.

The wrinkle came after President Trump eliminated a Biden-era policy regarding work visas for immigrants from Venezuela, Haiti and other nations.

Bohorquez, who joined the council staff last year, remained in custody until a judge ordered him released from the Delaney Hall detention facility in Newark, New Jersey in June — with his taxpayer-funded salary intact, The Post has learned.

According to former council staffers, the city had to keep drawing the paychecks.

“They would have had to pay that at the time, or when he was released,” one source said, citing city policy and union contracts. “He was entitled to that.”

Federal immigration agents busted Bohorquez in Bethpage, Long Island, in January, alleging that the Venezuelan national lied about his criminal record. He had been busted in 2023 in Queens on a third-degree assault rap after allegedly slugging his roommate.

The record was later wiped clean, but ICE officials said he had to be held accountable for lying.

However, he was granted asylum on May 27, and Judge Ann Donnelly released him on June 19 on a $5,000 bond, with the US Department of Justice filing an appeal three days later, which is still pending.

“Rafael was detained by ICE at a routine appointment,” City Council General Counsel Nwamaka Ejebe said this week. “As the judge found, he was wrongly detained. The City Council followed all applicable rules and laws to place him on administrative leave.”

Bohorquez, who still works for the council, could not be reached for comment.

text:
UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Turk on Friday urged Costa Rica to reconsider its decision to deny entry to Francesca Albanese, the UN special rapporteur on the occupied Palestinian territory.

"I am deeply concerned by the denial of entry to Francesca Albanese ... on claimed national security grounds," Turk said in a statement on US social media platform X.

He said the decision was difficult to reconcile with Costa Rica's longstanding commitment to human rights and called on authorities to allow Albanese to enter the country.

Costa Rican immigration authorities said Albanese had been denied entry on national security grounds, citing an alleged international alert linking her to terrorist acts.

Immigration Director Omer Badilla did not identify the authority behind the alert or provide evidence supporting the allegations.

Albanese, an Italian legal expert appointed by the UN Human Rights Council in 2022, had been invited by the University of Costa Rica to receive an honorary doctorate.

She rejected the allegations and called on Costa Rican authorities to provide evidence or retract them.

Costa Rica's Constitutional Court issued an interim order preventing authorities from forcibly removing Albanese while it considers a habeas corpus petition filed on her behalf, according to local media reports.

The US imposed sanctions on Albanese in July 2025 over her work related to the International Criminal Court's actions concerning US and Israeli officials.

Turk previously urged Washington to reverse the sanctions, saying UN experts should be able to carry out their mandates without punitive measures.

text:
At the crack of dawn on October 12, 2026, just three weeks before the midterm election, federal agents were pounding on the door of Democratic Minnesota Representative Ilhan Omar’s home in Washington, D.C.

Agents were armed and supported by a search warrant and conducted a raid on the Minnesota Democrat’s home, despite her protests and assertion of legislative privilege.

Classic Intimidation Tactics

“You don’t show up to somebody’s house that early in the morning unless you’re trying to freak them out. And you know it obviously did freak all of us out,” Omar said, recounting the incident in an interview.

The Minnesota representative blames President Donald Trump. “He’s got everything to do with it,” she said. Omar, who represents Minnesota’s 5th congressional district, pointed to past statements from the Trump administration alluding to the possibility that something might happen to her.

“Ultimately, their goal is to intimidate and scare people from wanting to participate and vote,” she posited. “I think it’s doing the opposite,” the Minnesota Democrat added.

While Omar says that she will continue to pursue accountability for Trump’s alleged misdeeds, she says that the raid did cause her significant concern. Now that her address is public, the congresswoman, who also has three children, said she would look for a new place to live.

Bizarre Haul

Omar also recounted the oddity of the items federal agents seized from her home.

“To walk away with 17 items of, like, 10 that were just notebooks and like old phones was such a bizarre, bizarre thing,” said the Minnesota rep.

More than a dozen subpoenas from a grand jury have also been issued to Omar’s family and relatives. According to prosecutors and investigators, Omar allegedly supplied false birth information to immigration officers, which eventually led to her becoming a US citizen in 2000. Omar immigrated to the US from Somalia in 1995.

According to the congresswoman, as many as 25 agents combed through her belongings the day of the raid and spent around four to five hours searching her home. Prosecutors applied for the warrant on October 2, 2026, with a judge signing off on the action a week later.

Same Old Charges

This is not the first time the Trump administration has targeted the Minnesota Democrat, one of Trump’s harshest critics. A similar inquiry was conducted against Omar in 2019, during Trump’s first term, but found insufficient evidence to charge the congresswoman with any wrongdoing. The administration of former President Joe Biden waved off the charges and declined to pursue further investigation.

Minnesota prosecutors also investigated Omar over claims that her ex-husband was her brother. The investigation was eventually dropped when prosecutors decided that the deadline to charge the congresswoman had passed. When asked whether her ex-husband is her brother, Omar replied, “Not to my knowledge.”

Trump supporters have also taken a dim view of the Minnesota representative, chanting “Send her back!” at a Trump rally. A few weeks ago, a man who sprayed Omar with vinegar at a town hall meeting was sentenced to 14 months in prison.

As of press time, Omar has also not been formally charged with any crime. However, if prosecutors prove their claims, Omar’s naturalization could be revoked.

A federal judge recently ordered the release of 169 pages of court records related to the execution of the search warrant.

Trump Washes His Hands of the Incident

For his part, the president says that he has had no hand whatsoever in the investigation against Omar.

“I’ve always found her to be totally crooked personally, but that has nothing to do with me,” Trump said.

However, the president also said that Omar may be deported or go to jail if any irregularities are discovered.

While not accusing President Trump directly, former President Obama said that the raid against Omar — who also happens to be a former staffer of his — was obviously a “transparent effort to intimidate someone.”

The Department of Justice recently submitted court filings saying that there was an “inadvertent” misunderstanding over whether Matthew Berry, the House’s general counsel, agreed with the Trump administration’s position on the Constitution’s Speech or Debate Clause, which in turn shields legislators from any government action related to the performance of their official legislative duties.
