text:
Four immigrants who were detained by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) filed a federal lawsuit on Monday alleging sexual abuse, harassment, forced labor, and negligence against the private company that manages the facility where they were held and against two of its employees.

The victims were detained between 2023 and 2025 at the ICE Southern Louisiana Immigration Processing Center (SLIPC), which is administered by the GEO Group, the largest prison operator in the United States, which manages some 23 immigration centers across the country.

This is the largest detention center for migrant women in the country, which also houses transgender men and people who identify as non-binary. This center had previously been reported for similar abuses and other management deficiencies, including inadequate medical care, insufficient or poor-quality food, and denial of legal and translation services.

The four immigrants identify the center’s then-deputy director, Emmanuel Reyes, and former detention officer David Courvelle as the main perpetrators. Courvelle had already pleaded guilty to sexual abuse in June of this year and is currently serving a three-year prison sentence in Louisiana.

The Department of Homeland Security (DHS), which oversees ICE, has distanced itself from any connection to the defendants. “Neither David Courvelle nor Emmanuel Reyes were employed by ICE. Both were contractors working for a private company [...] ICE cooperated fully with the investigation; currently, neither Reyes nor Courvelle has any connection to the center,” the department replied to EL PAÍS via email.

Among the plaintiffs are two transgender men of Mexican nationality who currently reside in Mexico: Luis Rentería González, 38, who was detained at this center for 32 months; and Mario García Valenzuela, 43, who spent 22 months in detention. The third victim is Kenia Campos-Flores, a woman of Salvadoran origin who spent 15 months in detention; and the fourth has kept her identity confidential for fear of further reprisals and is referred to in the lawsuit under the pseudonym Jane Doe.

“[The plaintiffs’] gender identity is a key factor in the treatment they suffered,” said attorney Stephanie Alvarez Jones of the National Immigration Project — one of the five organizations that filed the lawsuit — during a telephone interview with EL PAÍS. “Deputy Director Reyes targeted and specifically punished detainees who were transgender or non-binary — those who did not directly identify as women. We saw that in the program he implemented and in the way he spoke to our plaintiffs.”

According to the lawsuit, Reyes used his position of authority to subject detainees to ongoing abuse and force them to perform heavy physical labor at night, outside the regular volunteer work program typically offered at these detention centers.

For this night work program, Reyes recruited transgender men or gay people, such as the plaintiffs. The center’s deputy director threatened them with interfering in their immigration cases and expediting their deportation, as well as with harming their close family members, sending them to solitary confinement, and even killing them. “If you think you’re a man, I’m going to treat you like a man,” recalls Mario García Valenzuela, quoting what Reyes told him in one of the testimonies cited in the lawsuit.

The document also details two incidents in which Reyes sexually assaulted Luis Rentería González while he was performing cleaning duties at night, between December 2023 and early 2024. Rentería González reported the abuse in April 2024 and sought ICE’s intervention: he filed multiple complaints through the Department of Homeland Security’s Office of the Inspector General (OIG) hotline and sent a written complaint to ICE, detailing the sexual abuse he had suffered.

However, Rentería González’s complaints were dismissed in August 2024, and in the same month he reported the abuse, he was placed in solitary confinement for 14 days on Reyes’s orders. In August and September 2024, FBI and ICE agents interviewed Rentería González and other detainees, and he reiterated his allegations but received no response. On the contrary, he suffered retaliation from other GEO Group employees working at the center.

Mario García Valenzuela also claims that he was sexually assaulted on at least three occasions by Officer David Courvelle and that he was subjected to retaliation when he reported what had happened. On one occasion, he was placed in solitary confinement for 43 consecutive days without any documentation of the reasons for his isolation.

The plaintiff identified as Jane Doe also claims to have suffered systematic sexual assaults between February and May 2024 at the hands of Reyes, who threatened to kill her and harm her family. “I know where you are, I know where your family is. You have no one to protect you,” Reyes would tell her, according to her statement in the lawsuit. She also suffers from epilepsy, and her seizures became more frequent at the detention center, where she was denied access to medication and care from a neurologist until she was deported to her country of origin on January 6, 2025.

text:
The United States Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) have denied claims that children were shown a Thanksgiving feast in a detention center before being told it was for staff only.

ICE's denial relates to claims that in 2025, staff members at an immigration detention center in Texas showed detained children a Thanksgiving spread before telling them the food was for employees, took away treats given to children at Christmas, and prevented children from hugging a staff member dressed as Santa.

Read More on News

The claims were made by Elora Mukherjee, director of the Immigrants’ Rights Clinic at Columbia Law School.

She represents multiple families detained at the Dilley Detention Center and described the incidents during the March 17, 2026, Senate Judiciary Committee Democrats spotlight forum hosted by Dick Durbin.

The Dilley detention center—officially the Dilley Immigration Processing Center—is a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detention facility in Dilley, Texas, used to detain migrant families with children.

Mukherjee told the Senate forum that children were presented with food including turkey, sandwiches, pies and pastries before being told it was for employees.

“Then the staff covered each tray of food and told the children that the food was for the employees only, and children were left in tears,” Mukherjee said.

A separate allegation concerning children being pushed away from Santa reportedly appeared in a detained parent’s sworn declaration.

The claims about behavior at the detention center once again gained attention this week as The Bulwark published details of the March forum. During another Thanksgiving week, the outlet cautioned: “But the alarm is still ringing. And there are still kids in Dilley, heading into another Thanksgiving with little hope—not even the fleeting variety—in sight.”

The Tennessee Holler similarly re-shared Mukherjee’s testimony on Thanksgiving, adding: “Trump’s goons are taunting imprisoned immigrant kids in (for-profit) detention centers with Thanksgiving feasts and Christmas treats they don’t let them actually eat. Sadistic.”

ICE Responds to Thanksgiving Claims

As the article once again shone a spotlight on Dilley, ICE hit back in a post on X, where they firmly denied all of the claims.

“These claims are absolutely FALSE. Detained illegal aliens receive holiday meals in the dining halls with menus tailored to the occasion. Any staff potlucks occur in areas inaccessible to residents. Treats given to children remain theirs; there is no practice of collecting them afterward. Resident welfare funds cover these items,” ICE wrote on X.

They clarified that last Christmas, Santa did visit the center and take photos with the children, adding that “the sole restriction was that children could not sit on his lap.”

ICE went on: “ICE standards expressly permit schedule adjustments for religious and civic holidays so long as nutritional requirements are met, and facilities are required to facilitate observances, including dietary needs, worship, and work restrictions, while preserving security and order. “Detention is a choice. Illegal aliens can take control of their departure through the CBP Home App and receive $3,000 plus a free flight to self-deport now, preserving the option to return legally. Those who refuse will be arrested and deported.”

In response to ICE's denial, Mukherjee told Newsweek, "The facts speak for themselves. Multiple families have bravely spoken up about both the Thanksgiving and Christmas incidents, including in sworn testimony filed in federal court."

Earlier this week, YouTube children’s star Rachel Accurso, better known as Ms. Rachel, joined Texas Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa at the Dilley detention center in a push to end family detention at the location.

Accurso cited the position of the American Academy of Pediatrics, which has warned about the impact detention can have on children. She described child detention as harmful and praised Hinojosa's efforts to end the practice.

"We don't want to be people who abuse and hurt children, and we don't want to support people making money off the abuse of children," Accurso said. "This is a violation on the human rights of kids."

Newsweek reached out to ICE via email for comment.

Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Rebecca Flood and Cristina Diciu.

title: Jorge Linares ICE Release Ends 10 Days in El Paso, Case Unclear - Immigration Analytics
description:
Jorge Linares is out of ICE custody.
World Boxing Association president Gilberto Mendoza announced on Nov. 25 that Linares was “back with his family,” Telemundo reported.
On Thanksgiving Day, Linares posted an Instagram story with his wife that read “De vuelta a casa!
Telemundo said the terms of his release have not been disclosed, and EFE reported that DHS did not detail the case.
ICE can also decline to pursue the case, or an immigration judge can terminate it.
text:
Jorge Linares is out of ICE custody. The Venezuelan former three-division world champion was released after roughly 10 days at the El Paso Processing Center, ending the Jorge Linares ICE detention that began at El Paso International Airport on Nov. 15, but nothing made public so far says whether the government’s removal case against him has ended, paused or simply moved off the detained docket.

World Boxing Association president Gilberto Mendoza announced on Nov. 25 that Linares was “back with his family,” Telemundo reported. On Thanksgiving Day, Linares posted an Instagram story with his wife that read “De vuelta a casa!!” (“Back home!!”) and called coming home on the holiday the best gift he could receive, according to the Spanish news agency EFE. Telemundo said the terms of his release have not been disclosed, and EFE reported that DHS did not detail the case.

A release is not a ruling

The positions the two sides staked out in the first week have not changed on the record. ICE said Linares entered the United States on Oct. 26, 2023, with permission to stay temporarily and remained past that period, and an ICE spokesperson said he would stay in custody “pending removal proceedings,” AFP reported. His lawyers said he is authorized to be in the country and has cooperated fully, and after the release they declined to say more “out of respect for his privacy and the legal process,” EFE reported. As the earlier coverage of the Linares overstay dispute explained, both statements can be partly true when a pending application stops unlawful presence from accruing without restoring status.

That matters because ICE has several ways to let someone go, and they lead to very different places. A person ICE treats as admitted and then out of status is ordinarily held under 8 U.S.C. 1226(a), the discretionary detention provision, which allows release on a bond of at least $1,500 or on conditional parole while removal proceedings continue. ICE can also decline to pursue the case, or an immigration judge can terminate it. The first two leave the overstay charge alive; the last two end it. Until his lawyers or DHS say which path applied, the accurate description is that Linares is free, not that he has won.

His route also differs from the one facing many recent detainees. The administration’s mandatory detention position has targeted people who entered without inspection, treating them as applicants for admission with no right to a bond hearing. ICE’s own account says Linares was admitted, which is likely why the bond and parole tools under section 1226 were available to him at all.

What a non-detained case looks like now

If ICE filed a Notice to Appear, the case now sits on the non-detained docket, which historically moves far more slowly than detained cases. The pace may not be as slow as it once was. Under EOIR’s Nov. 23 Policy Memorandum 27-02, a represented respondent whose lawyer files a Form EOIR-28 at least 15 days before a master calendar hearing gets a scheduling order instead, with 10 days to file pleadings and merits hearings targeted within 90 days, as covered in the site’s report on PM 27-02 filing deadlines.

Release terms can also carry their own risk. People freed from ICE custody are often required to report for check-ins, and those appointments have themselves become arrest points, an issue a federal court addressed in the San Diego check-in re-detention case. Linares’s case also joins a run of widely reported detentions this month that ended in release, including an Argentine acrobat freed on bond and a Maryland jockey who held a valid work permit.

The open questions are concrete: whether an immigration court case exists and when its first hearing is set, whether he was released on bond, parole or recognizance with reporting conditions, and what application his lawyers say keeps him authorized. Any of those would tell readers more than the release itself.

This article is for general information and is not legal advice.

President Donald Trump's asylum ban is headed to the Supreme Court, and it's burdened by a legal weakness that even the court's conservative majority may struggle to look past.

The justices will soon decide whether Trump can bypass Congress and existing federal immigration law to cut off access to asylum on his own, reported NPR.

Trump imposed the ban within hours of returning to the White House, and his administration has since canceled thousands of pending asylum applications and fired more than 100 immigration judges. Critics argue that together, those moves have all but closed a pathway Congress built for people fleeing persecution.

Asylum protections are written into federal law, and two lower federal courts have already rejected Trump's case for overriding them, but the ban has stayed largely in effect because the case remains tied up in litigation, which leaves the 6-3 conservative majority being asked to decide whether a president can set aside a law Congress passed.

"The president does not have the right to unilaterally override the protections Congress has afforded those fleeing danger," said Lee Gelernt, the ACLU attorney leading the challenge to a ban he calls an "unprecedented power grab that would put countless lives in danger."

The administration defends the proclamation as a necessary shield against an "invasion" at the southern border and against abuse by what Trump calls "fake" asylum seekers. Border Patrol apprehensions have since plunged to fewer than 99,000 at the southwest border in fiscal 2026, a 95 percent drop from Biden-era levels, according to federal data.

Simon Hankinson of the Heritage Foundation warned that striking down the ban "would be disastrous," and he argued that most people arriving at the border "want to get a job" and don't qualify for asylum.

But critics say the shutdown has come at a steep cost, as asylum denial rates hit 94 percent in June, up from about 50 percent denial rates in 2024, according to Syracuse University's TRAC.

Los Angeles attorney Madhavi Narayanan described an Ethiopian client who survived torture and once would have had a "slam dunk" case, but instead he was ordered deported to Uganda, a country he had never set foot in.

The judge, she recalled, told her, "I'm not allowed to consider this."

In December, the court will also examine the administration's practice of deporting asylum seekers to third countries, while a separate challenge targets its push to indefinitely hold thousands of people facing deportation.

Advocates say wins could finally loosen Trump's grip on asylum approvals, which have sunk to their lowest point in decades.

text:
The news last week that four provisions of a law intended to regulate U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement action in Connecticut were blocked by a federal judge was “not a surprise” to some immigration advocates. But, they argued, it didn’t erase the impact of state officials’ willingness to take action in the face of President Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown.

“I think it underlines our state, and especially our legislators’ willingness to still pass policies that could be challenged because they were the right thing to do, and send a message to residents — immigrant and non-immigrant — that is is where Connecticut stands,” said Constanza Segovia, organizing director for Connecticut For All and co-founder of Hartford Deportation Defense.

She said when the laws were passed, including the provision that aimed to stop agents from wearing masks or other facial coverings when they interface with the public, advocates were aware there would be pushback.

But Segovia, other advocates and some lawmakers said they are exploring the ways in which the state’s existing laws and new proposals that might come up in the 2027 legislative session can offer residents protection in response to safety concerns related to federal immigration enforcement actions.

In the meantime, though, Carolina Bortolleto, an organizer with Greater Danbury Unites for Immigrants, said the ruling still “leaves Connecticut less safe” because “no one wants masked agents running around neighborhoods.”

Senate Bill 397 was passed in 2026 and quickly was challenged by the U.S. Justice Department. The federal government called the law “blatantly unconstitutional,” saying that the state has no authority to tell federal agents what they can and cannot do. The government also argued that the law goes against the Supremacy Clause of the U.S. Constitution, which says that when state and federal laws clash, federal laws override those of the states. Judge Vernon Oliver agreed.

The state law, Oliver wrote, “plainly imposes conditions on how federal officers must conduct and present themselves during the course of their federal duties, and it subjects them to criminal and civil penalties if they do not abide by those state-imposed conditions.”

“But the Supremacy Clause ensures that federal operations are not chilled by state prosecution and that federal officers are immune from state prosecution when acting within the scope of their federal authority,” he added.

ICE officials did not return a request for comment.

Yet even in the wake of the decision, some immigrant rights advocates like Bortolleto were sounding a note of optimism. A provision of the bill that requires ICE agents to have a warrant in locations like schools, hospitals and places of worship remains in effect.

“I think that’s really important because I think that section of the bill is what goes the longest way to making immigrant folks feel safer,” she said. Bortolleto said that she hoped that during the legislative 2027 session that begins in January, doctors’ offices could be added to the list of protected areas.

Advocates also say that agents have frequently been observed wearing masks in the state even when that portion of the law was in effect.

Miguel Castro, a member of the Meriden Middletown Immigration Alliance and second vice chair of the Connecticut Hispanic Democratic Caucus, noted the injunction is temporary and he still has hope that Connecticut will ultimately succeed.

“Our state still has an opportunity to go back to the court process and challenge this as it is sits today,” he said. “It is a responsibility of the state under the 10th Amendment of the Constitution, using the sovereignty of our state, that it is our duty and fiduciary responsibility to protect the members of our community, and that’s what we intend to do.”

Dealing with masked agents presents a variety of concerns, advocates say.

“It’s a traumatic experience to see someone or a group of people with masks on, and they are carrying weapons, and you are by yourself and you have nothing to defend yourself with,” said Juan Fonseca Tapia, a co-founder of Greater Danbury Unites for Immigrants. “All you’ve got is a phone.” That phone can be used to record agents and provide evidence of abuses, but when those agents are masked, advocates say it can complicate accountability. The bill also sought to make officers wear identification, a provision that was blocked by Friday’s ruling.

Segovia said it would be a priority in 2027 to look for regulatory loopholes that disenfranchise immigrants and people of color, and make sure they are closed.

Supporting working-class immigrants means “supporting expansive healthcare policies that include everybody, regardless of immigration status,” Segovia said. Lawmakers should “make sure that nobody can touch our kids’ ability to go to public schools and public universities, regardless of their immigration status,” along with other key rights like renter protections.

Segovia’s group is among those pressing the Lamont administration to put $10 million toward legal aid and emergency cash assistance for immigrants impacted by ICE enforcement.

House Speaker Matt Ritter, D-Hartford said that he is interested in having that discussion in the new year. Ritter said the attempt to regulate ICE activity was worth pursuing, but ultimately there are “just limits to what the states can do.” He said it’s time for the Democratic majority in Washington to step up.

“It’s not me throwing my hands up in the air saying, ‘we’re going to give up.’ We’re going to do everything we can to be helpful,” he added. “But there’s 259 Democrats in the House and 56 in the Senate, and if they need help learning how to pass bills I’m glad to go down there and try to help them.”

Rep. Steven Stafstrom, D-Bridgeport, a key backer of Connecticut’s law as co-chair of the legislature’s Judiciary Committee, said he was disappointed with the ruling. But “we’re not backing down,” he said.

Stafstrom said there are still legal remedies to holding agents accountable for abuse of use of force.

“One of the things that was blocked was having the inspector general do investigations into abuse of use of force, but just because that piece was inexplicably blocked, doesn’t mean Connecticut won’t continue to enforce state laws, it will just fall to individual states attorneys for the judicial districts to do that,” he said.

title: Trump effectively ended asylum. Advocates look to the Supreme Court to restore it - NPR
description:

text:
For nearly two years, the Trump administration has prohibited asylum claims at the U.S.-Mexico border, canceled thousands of pending asylum applications and overhauled the immigration court system with mass firings. Critics say that combined, these moves have effectively shut down a once vital pathway for those fleeing persecution or danger.

The U.S. Supreme Court will soon consider whether the president can circumvent Congress and existing federal immigration law and unilaterally suspend access to asylum protections.

The legal challenge to the president's ban, which went into effect within hours of President Trump retaking office, is the latest legal case against the administration's seismic immigration policy changes that will be taken up by the high court. Those policy changes, critics say, have robbed asylum seekers of basic due process rights and have transformed the immigration court system into a deportation arm of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

In legal filings, the Trump administration has insisted the proclamation is a necessary protection against "invasion" along the southern border and what the president and conservative critics have long said is abuse of the system by "fake" asylum seekers. Since it has been in place, the chaotic crush of people crossing into the U.S. has plummeted. U.S. Border Patrol apprehensions dropped to their lowest level in agency history this year. The agency recorded fewer than 99,000 Southwest border apprehensions in fiscal year 2026 — a 95% decline compared with more than 1.8 million per year under President Biden, according to U.S. Customs and Border Protection data.

"The difference between an average month under Trump and an average month under Biden is just staggering," Simon Hankinson, a senior research fellow with the Border Security and Immigration Center at the Heritage Foundation, a conservative think tank closely aligned with Trump, told NPR. And should the Supreme Court reverse the ban, "it would be disastrous," he added.

Hankinson contends that most people arriving at the southern border don't qualify for asylum. "And even if they did, they've already passed through Mexico, which is a safe third country where they could claim asylum, especially if they're coming from Venezuela or Afghanistan. So you have a population that overwhelmingly will not qualify under U.S. law for asylum. They're here because they want to get a job," he said.

But, critics say, taken together the administration's moves have gutted access to asylum.

Despite newly restored quiet along the southern border, the president's argument for the asylum ban has been rejected by two lower federal courts. It has, however, remained largely in place as the case is tied up in court battles.

In December, the Supreme Court will review the administration's strategy of deporting immigrants to third countries that have agreed to adjudicate asylum claims, even as some of those countries face human rights abuse allegations and cannot guarantee that the person seeking asylum won't be returned to their home nation.

The administration faces a third legal battle that could end its attempt to indefinitely detain thousands of people in deportation proceedings.

If the majority-conservative court rules in favor of immigrant advocates in the lawsuits, advocates say, the decisions could finally break the choke hold that the Trump administration has had on asylum approvals, which are at their lowest in decades. National asylum denial rates soared to 94% in June, up from about 50% in 2024 — the last full year of the Biden administration. That's according to TRAC, a research project at Syracuse University that tracks data about immigration judges.

"The president does not have the right to unilaterally override the protections Congress has afforded those fleeing danger," said Lee Gelernt, lead counsel and deputy director of the Immigrants' Rights Project at the American Civil Liberties Union, one of the groups behind the challenge to the asylum ban. "The courts are right to reject this unprecedented power grab that would put countless lives in danger. We look forward to making our case before the Supreme Court."

Lawyers for migrants seeking asylum are hoping for wins at the high court. For several of Madhavi Narayanan's clients, this could be lifesaving. A Los Angeles-based immigration attorney with Human Rights First, she is currently representing immigrants who, prior to Trump's second term, would have had what she calls "slam dunk" asylum petitions.

One of them is a 30-something Ethiopian man called ZG, who arrived in the U.S. through Mexico in February 2025 after enduring extensive torture in his native country. Narayanan requested that NPR use only ZG because he fears retribution from the Ethiopian government. Upon turning himself in at the southern border, ZG was placed into detention and immediately filed an asylum petition.

Narayanan said ZG is a member of an Indigenous group in Ethiopia that's part of an ongoing armed conflict in that nation, which human rights organizations report is at risk of committing more atrocities against civilians. And, Narayanan, who has been working on the case for nine months, said she has produced documents and letters to support his claims of torture.

"Any other time, it would have been a really straightforward case," she said, adding that "there's a wide, wide range of human rights reports explaining that folks in this exact position would be at high risk" of violence and death if they were to return to Ethiopia.

But instead of an immigration hearing, ZG was given a deportation order this month to Uganda, a country he has never set foot in and one that does not recognize the military violence in Ethiopia as a war.

In an effort to curb asylum applications and alleviate a crushing backlog of cases for U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services, the Trump administration is urging ICE attorneys to terminate asylum claims by convincing immigration judges that an application is incomplete or that a person can't substantiate their claims. Or the administration could argue what it did in ZG's case: that he could apply for asylum in a third country.

It has proved to be a highly successful strategy for the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), which has so far canceled thousands of pending cases.

Narayanan said experiences like ZG's reflect how Trump's changes to immigration courts have all but eliminated due process rights, including evidentiary hearings, clearing the way for summary removals. They also show how new guidelines are designed to limit a judge's autonomy. Recounting the events of the motion to end ZG's claim, Narayanan said the immigration judge told the court that his hands were tied.

"He was basically like, 'OK, I hear everything that you said, but I read this case and I'm not allowed to consider this,'" Narayanan recalled.

According to the Executive Office for Immigration Review, nearly 60 policy memorandums have been issued so far during the second Trump administration — a sharp increase when compared with the 30 immigration-court-related memorandums issued during Biden's four-year term.

The administration has also been aggressive in its pursuit to remake the immigration court bench, purging more than a hundred experienced immigration judges. Jennifer Peyton, a former assistant chief immigration judge in Chicago, told NPR that immigration courts across the country have become unrecognizable.

"Everything is different now," said Peyton, who was fired via email in July 2025 after more than nine years on the bench.

During Trump's first year back in office, nearly 40% of immigration judges were fired or resigned. Nearly all of them have been replaced with what the administration calls "deportation judges," who critics say are ideologically aligned with the president's immigration agenda and keen to rubber-stamp asylum denials and expedited removal orders. That shift, plus Trump's previous appointees, has overhauled the immigration bench. Now more than half of immigration judges are Trump appointees.

Of those new immigration judges, very few have experience working on behalf of migrants. About two-thirds of them come from a homeland security or military legal background, according to an essay in The Yale Law Journal by Geoffrey Heeren, an immigration law and policy professor at the University of Idaho. He wrote that "only about eleven of the new [immigration judges] have clear prior immigrant-defense experience, and of those, only one does not also have DHS or military legal experience."

In her previous role, Peyton was part of the immigration-judge hiring-and-training team with the Justice Department. She now practices immigration law representing asylum seekers and appears before the same judges she helped train. In those instances, Peyton said, she feels a bit more at ease because she knows the quality of the training they received. But when she argues cases in front of unfamiliar hires, she said, she's often dismayed.

"There is no doubt in my mind, when I have the misfortune to appear before them, that they don't know the immigration law so much and they don't care that they lack the training that we so rigorously put them through when I was on that team," Peyton said.

She added: "The vast majority have not been taught the process of evaluating a case, but rather the shortcuts to make sure that these procedural roadblocks come up, to make sure that the noncitizens are stripped of their due process."

title: Precarious care and medical neglect in Greek immigration detention - Oxford Law Blogs
description:
Stergios is a researcher who focuses on issues of immigration detention, everyday life in displacement and informal support.
These are important concerns, and ones I have encountered repeatedly in my research on immigration detention in Greece.
These shortages are serious, but they do not fully explain the medical neglect documented in Greek detention facilities.
Beyond the promise of better healthcare Medical neglect in Greek detention centres is often discussed as a failure of implementation: insufficient funding, poor management or inadequate staffing.
After more than a decade researching immigration detention in Greece, I find it increasingly difficult to see medical neglect as an exceptional failure of the system.
text:
Post by Andriani Fili and Stergios Magkriotis. Andriani is a Wellcome Trust Postdoctoral Research Fellow at the Centre for Criminology, University of Oxford, and co-director of Border Criminologies. Stergios is a researcher who focuses on issues of immigration detention, everyday life in displacement and informal support. He holds a PhD in Sociology from the University of Edinbrugh. Andriani and Stergios are collaborating under the project 'Medicalising Immigration Detention'. This post is part of a thematic series on healthcare and detention.

When discussing healthcare in immigration detention, we usually focus on what happens to the people detained. We consider the lack of medical treatment, deteriorating physical and mental health, and, in some cases, preventable deaths. These are important concerns, and ones I have encountered repeatedly in my research on immigration detention in Greece. But understanding how medical neglect persists also requires looking at how healthcare is organised, who provides it, and the institutional conditions under which medical decisions are made.

Having researched immigration detention in Greece since 2011, including through my work as an NGO practitioner providing support to detained people, I have seen how the promise of healthcare often bears little resemblance to what happens in practice. More recently, through interviews with healthcare professionals working in pre-removal detention centres, I have become increasingly interested in how their working conditions shape the care that detained people receive. What emerges is not simply a story of insufficient resources or overworked professionals. Rather, it is a picture of a healthcare system operating within, and often accommodating, an institution whose primary purpose is confinement and removal.

When healthcare becomes part of detention

The relationship between public health and immigration control in Greece is well established. As I have explored previously, migrants have long been portrayed as threats to public health, their bodies associated with disease and contamination. In 2012, for example, political rhetoric about migrants as a "public health bomb" helped justify police operations, compulsory medical examinations and detention. The contradiction is difficult to ignore. While migrants have been presented as threats to the health of the wider population, they are confined in institutions where their own health is systematically undermined.

Overcrowding, inadequate sanitation, limited access to doctors and serious medical neglect are widely documented. The European Committee for the Prevention of Torture has repeatedly raised concerns about healthcare in Greek detention facilities. Its 2024 report described appalling conditions, including an outbreak of tuberculosis in the Corinth pre-removal detention centre. These are not isolated incidents. Through Detention Landscapes, a project documenting human rights violations in Greek detention facilities, we have recorded numerous accounts of people being denied medical assistance. One person described repeatedly asking for medical attention, only to receive paracetamol. Another reported being beaten after asking to be taken to hospital.

These experiences reveal something important: access to healthcare is not simply a question of whether a doctor is available. It is also about who decides whether someone can see that doctor, whether their suffering is believed, and whether their health is considered a priority at all.

The organisation of medical neglect

In Greece, healthcare and psychosocial services in pre-removal detention centres (PRDC) are provided through AEMY, a state-owned company operating under private law rules. On paper, this arrangement ensures the presence of doctors, nurses, psychologists, social workers and interpreters. In practice, however, services have been characterised by chronic understaffing, temporary contracts and fragmented responsibility. At the end of June 2026, only seven doctors and six psychologists were deployed by AEMY in the six mainland PRDCs. In Amygdaleza, where 704 people were detained, only two doctors were deployed, while in Corinth, which holds 385 detainees, there was no doctor or psychologist. These shortages are serious, but they do not fully explain the medical neglect documented in Greek detention facilities.

In interviews conducted with healthcare workers, many described entering detention work almost by accident, often because they needed employment or professional experience. Some had little knowledge of the institutions in which they would be working. Once inside, they encountered unclear responsibilities, limited supervision, inadequate equipment and frequent interference by police. In some cases, police officers effectively determined whether detained people could access medical services. Their descriptions suggest an institutional environment in which medical decisions are frequently shaped by police authority.

One psychologist explained how officers could decide whether someone needed to see a doctor or psychologist, or simply refuse to open a cell. The consequences of these arrangements fall most directly on detained people, whose access to treatment becomes dependent on the discretion of those responsible for their confinement. The problem, then, is not simply that healthcare professionals cannot always do their jobs. It is that medical care is organised through the same structures of power that govern detention.

Healthcare professionals occupy a complicated position within these institutions. Their work can alleviate suffering, but it can also contribute to the normalisation and administration of detention. One psychiatrist interviewed for our research described the expectations placed on staff in particularly stark terms: "The only thing that concerns us [AEMY] is for you to be there from 8 to 4 and for no one to die." This account raises questions about what healthcare is expected to achieve in detention. Is its purpose to respond meaningfully to people's health needs, or to maintain a minimum level of medical provision that allows detention to continue?

Our interviews also revealed differences in how professionals negotiated their roles. Some challenged police decisions, questioned discriminatory treatment and attempted to secure medical assistance for detained people. Others developed close working relationships with police officers or accepted institutional practices that restricted access to care. These differences matter. Healthcare workers are not a homogeneous group, and working within a coercive institution does not necessarily mean that every professional reproduces its violence in the same way.

The key here is how these different practices are shaped by the institutional arrangements governing healthcare. Temporary employment, limited supervision, unclear responsibilities and police interference can restrict professional independence while allowing harmful practices to become routine. In this sense, examining healthcare labour is not about shifting attention away from detained people. It is about understanding the mechanisms through which their suffering is produced and sustained.

Beyond the promise of better healthcare

Medical neglect in Greek detention centres is often discussed as a failure of implementation: insufficient funding, poor management or inadequate staffing. These problems are real, and addressing them can make an immediate difference to detained people's lives. But I think we need to ask a more difficult question: what happens when healthcare is organised within institutions whose primary purpose is not care, but control? In my research, I have argued that medical neglect should not be understood simply as an absence of healthcare. Medical services may formally exist, while access remains restricted, treatment is delayed and the health problems caused by detention itself remain unaddressed.

Healthcare can therefore become part of what sustains detention. Its presence helps present confinement as regulated and humane, even when it does little to prevent the harm produced by confinement. These tensions were also central to discussions at our recent Health, Care, and Control workshop in Bologna, which brought together researchers, practitioners and activists working on immigration detention in Greece and Italy.

One important question remains: if we challenge detention because healthcare is inadequate, do we risk suggesting that detention would become acceptable if healthcare improved? Better staffing, independent medical provision and meaningful accountability are necessary. But they cannot resolve the fundamental contradiction of providing care within institutions that systematically undermine people's health. After more than a decade researching immigration detention in Greece, I find it increasingly difficult to see medical neglect as an exceptional failure of the system. It is deeply connected to how detention operates, alongside the uncertainty, isolation and violence experienced by those confined.

Understanding the organisation of healthcare, including the roles and practices of those who provide it, helps expose these processes. Ultimately, the question is not only how to improve healthcare inside detention, but how to challenge a system that – by its very design – produces ill health in the first place.

text:
When Dinah* arrived in the UK, she was so traumatised that she could not speak.

Her husband, a political activist in their home country, which openDemocracy is not naming for their safety, had fled ahead of her. Dinah was then abducted by men determined to find out where he was, who gang-raped her repeatedly for a month.

By the time she sought asylum in the UK, Dinah was “completely disassociated,” said Laura, a psychologist working with the NGO Freedom From Torture, whose surname we cannot publish for security reasons. “She was hospitalised following a suicide attempt and was not able to respond or talk. It’s the rape, it’s the humiliation, that can have hugely damaging effects psychologically, physically, on self-worth and in relationships.”

Now, changes proposed in the government’s Immigration and Asylum Bill risk limiting survivors like Dinah’s chances of securing protection in the UK by stating that those appealing a rejected asylum claim must have raised all relevant matters at the start of the process.

The new system will not only “disincentivise late disclosure” of new information, but penalise it. “If an appellant provides late evidence during the course of an appeal, this should be taken into account as damaging to the appellant’s credibility,” the proposed legislation states. Decision-makers will be able to consider whether there are “good reasons” to explain the late disclosure.

This proposal is at odds with recent warnings by experts and politicians over the need to avoid perpetuating harmful “rape myths” about how survivors should behave. The trial of rapist Russell Brand has led to criticism – including in the House of Lords last week – of arguments made in court that rape victims would not delay reporting their abusers.

In reality, there are many reasons why an individual may not come forward in the aftermath of an attack, including that sexual violence trauma can impact the ability to share painful experiences. This has led experts across the migrant rights sector to warn the government that the proposed legislation risks harming the most vulnerable asylum claimants.

“We know even in other circumstances, not only in conflict, that even if the person who experienced violence is now in a safe place, they are not ready to talk, sometimes for years,” said Kateryna Shukh, a Ukrainian psychologist from Mariupol who lives in Norway. These are people “who still don’t have the feeling of safety”.

The proposed law change comes as the government’s latest immigration statistics show that in the year ending September 2026, only 38% of asylum-seeking people were granted protection on their first try, with thousands more having to appeal an initial rejection. Experts told openDemocracy that the plans would penalise women for not feeling ready to talk about their abuse.

Under the plans, people going through a “late claims process” – who raise reasons for their asylum claim after detention or a removal notice – will see their appeals fast-tracked, making it harder to have new evidence heard.

“An asylum and appeal system that fails to recognise the realities of trauma risks denying survivors meaningful access to sanctuary and justice, compounding the harm they have already endured and potentially sending them back into the hands of their torturers,” said Nadine Tunasi, the head of survivor activism at Freedom from Torture.

“Access to protection must not depend on a survivor’s ability to disclose traumatic experiences within an arbitrary time frame. Survivors must be given the time, support and fair opportunity to tell their stories and to access justice without fear that the effects of their trauma will be used against them.”

“Particularly with sexual trauma there is an increased likelihood of delayed disclosure as there are often high levels of shame,” said Laura. “That is very hard to verbalise at any point.”

Trauma in the system

The nature of asylum interviews can compound trauma, making it even more difficult for survivors to disclose in a timely manner.

“Often, it may be the state officials in their country of origin who have that have actually tortured them,” Laura said. “They feel very unsafe at the point that they're being interviewed by members of authority in the UK. They're often very long interviews in rooms that may be reminiscent of a cell.

“They're being interviewed or interrogated by members of authority that they don't know, so there's often high levels of mistrust, which is very common with people surviving post-traumatic stress disorder.”

Laura finds that this means sexual violence is often not disclosed until much later in the asylum process, including during a medico-legal report, a clinical document produced by an independent clinical psychologist that assesses evidence of torture, serious harm, or health conditions relevant to an asylum or human rights claim.

The asylum system, says Laura, needs “to have some acknowledgement that in this environment you may not get all the information at that point, because asylum seekers are often terrified, and that's not conducive to being able to open up about experiences of someone's trauma,” not least because of the “high levels of shame that they don't want to disclose.”

Accommodation can also impact trauma, with women who have experienced rape housed alongside men, or in hotels and barracks with male security guards. Men who have been raped and sexually abused can end up sharing rooms with strangers.

“There are lots of safeguarding concerns with asylum accommodation and Freedom from Torture advocates that vulnerable people shouldn’t be placed in large hotels often with other vulnerable people or be sharing bathrooms, bedrooms, and women and children shouldn’t be placed in accommodation with men,” said Laura.

An epidemic of violence

Dinah is one of millions of women worldwide who have experienced sexual violence in conflict zones. The United Nations documented 9,788 cases of conflict-related sexual violence across countries including Ukraine, Sudan, Myanmar, Haiti, Afghanistan and the Central African Republic last year. The figures represent a “sharp” increase from 2024.

But the documented incidents are a tiny fraction of the overall abuse, said UN special representative Pramila Patten. They “should be understood not as the full picture, but as an indication of a much broader pattern of violations that remain largely unseen and underreported.”

In the Darfur region of Sudan, the charity Médecins Sans Frontières treated nearly 4,000 survivors of sexual violence between January 2024 and November 2025, in what they described as “systematic attacks.” Across the border in Ethiopia’s Tigray region, tens of thousands of women have reported suffering sexual abuse since the 2020 conflict with the government began.

The UN has recorded 1,000 cases of “widespread and abhorrent” sexual violence against prisoners of war in the Russian-occupied territories of Ukraine since the start of the full-scale invasion in 2022, while the NGO Save Ukraine found that one in ten children rescued from the occupied territories had experienced sexual abuse.

Shukh, a co-founder of Bereginia – Mariupol's Women Association, has worked with women experiencing gender-based violence since Russia’s invasion that began in 2014. Speaking to openDemocracy, she is clear that supporting survivors starts “with creating a safe space”.

It can take a long time for a survivor to disclose violence, and they may discuss other issues and experiences before feeling safe to do so, she explained. “Sometimes it's not a question of talking directly on this experience, but about creating this safety and to help them to continue normal life with that experience.”

A Home Office spokesperson said: “The Bill will continue to safeguard survivors of sexual violence, while cracking down on wider exploitation of the system.

“The credibility considerations are well-balanced and contain appropriate safeguards, including taking circumstances such as trauma into account. This will enhance the robustness of all decision-making and ensure survivors are protected.”

As for Dinah, she slowly started to recover. Laura vividly remembers how, after months of being non-verbal, one day Dinah laughed.

“It was very gradual, and the first conversations were very much about trying to talk about things that she actually enjoyed or gave her pleasure, and that was really the starting point,” Laura explained. “It was being able to connect on a more positive memory and connect through art that she started speaking, and then we moved onto trauma-focused therapy to help process her experiences of rape.”

title: Ontario Court Ruling Offers New Hope To 2600 Skilled Trades Immigration Applicants
description:
The decision offers renewed hope to approximately 2,600 foreign workers whose applications Ontario returned in November 2025 following concerns about widespread fraud and misrepresentation.
Why Ontario Returned 2,600 Skilled Trades Applications Ontario suspended its Express Entry Skilled Trades Stream on November 14, 2025, following a review that identified systemic concerns about fraud and misrepresentation.
Will All 2,600 Ontario Skilled Trades Applicants Benefit?
What The Ruling Could Mean For Canadian Immigration Programs The significance of the Ontario court decision extends beyond the Skilled Trades Stream.
What Affected Ontario Skilled Trades Workers Should Do Next Workers whose applications Ontario returned in November 2025 should retain their original application documents, correspondence confirming completeness, fee receipts and application return notices.
text:
On this page you will find:

What the Ontario immigration court ruling means

Why Ontario returned 2,600 skilled trades applications

Why the court ruled in favour of applicants

Whether all affected applicants could benefit

What the ruling means for other Canadian immigration programs

What skilled trades applicants should do next

Frequently asked questions

Hundreds of skilled trades workers have won a major legal victory against the Ontario government over its decision to return thousands of immigration applications without assessing them individually.

The Divisional Court of the Ontario Superior Court of Justice ruled on November 16, 2026, that the Ontario Immigrant Nominee Program (OINP) could not apply new regulatory powers retroactively to applications that officials had already confirmed were complete.

The decision offers renewed hope to approximately 2,600 foreign workers whose applications Ontario returned in November 2025 following concerns about widespread fraud and misrepresentation.

CityNews reported that 204 applicants will have their applications reviewed following the ruling. Thousands of other affected workers could potentially benefit from the legal precedent, although the judgment does not automatically reinstate their applications.

The case also raises important questions about how Canadian immigration authorities apply regulatory changes to applications already in their processing inventories.

Why Ontario Returned 2,600 Skilled Trades Applications

Ontario suspended its Express Entry Skilled Trades Stream on November 14, 2025, following a review that identified systemic concerns about fraud and misrepresentation.

The stream operated through Canada’s Express Entry immigration system and provided a pathway to permanent residence for foreign nationals with qualifying skilled trades work experience in Ontario.

Successful applicants received a provincial nomination worth an additional 600 Comprehensive Ranking System (CRS) points, significantly improving their chances of receiving a federal invitation to apply for permanent residence.

Ontario returned approximately 2,600 outstanding applications and refunded application fees when it suspended the stream.

The province relied on regulatory changes introduced on June 30, 2025, which expanded the OINP director’s authority to return applications without making a decision.

The changes allowed Ontario to consider factors including immediate labour market requirements and systemic concerns about compliance and enforcement.

However, many affected workers had submitted their applications in 2024, well before Ontario introduced the new regulations. Provincial immigration officials had already confirmed that their applications were complete.

Some applicants had waited considerably longer than the original estimated processing times before Ontario returned their files.

What Did The Ontario Court Decide?

The court ruled in favour of the applicants by a two-to-one majority in Singh v. The Minister of Labour, Immigration, Training and Skills Development (2026 ONSC 6441).

Borders Law Firm and Rathod Law Firm, which both represented affected applicants, published accounts of the judgment following the decision.

The court directed Ontario to assess the applications involved in the legal challenge individually using the regulatory framework that existed before June 30, 2025.

Under those rules, the OINP director had an obligation to make a decision once officials confirmed that an application was complete.

The court majority concluded that Ontario could not remove that entitlement by applying a subsequent regulatory amendment retroactively.

The judges acknowledged the province’s legitimate concerns about immigration fraud. Ontario retains the authority to investigate individual applications and refuse candidates who fail to meet program requirements.

However, the majority found that general concerns about program integrity did not justify using the new regulatory power to return previously completed applications.

The court also ordered the minister to pay $20,000 in agreed legal costs.

Why The Timing Of The Regulatory Change Matters

A central issue in the case was the legal principle against retroactive legislation.

Governments generally need to express a clear intention when introducing legislation or regulations that affect rights established under previous rules.

Ontario’s June 2025 amendment contained no explicit provision extending the new return powers to applications that officials had already accepted as complete.

According to the lawyers involved, the court majority concluded that applicants had acquired a legal entitlement to an individual decision under the previous regulations.

The dissenting judge took a different view, arguing that the entitlement to a decision represented a procedural step towards obtaining a provincial nomination rather than an established substantive right.

The divided judgment leaves open the possibility that Ontario could seek permission to appeal to the Court of Appeal for Ontario.

What Happens To The Affected Applications?

Ontario must reconsider the applications covered by the court order under the previous regulatory framework.

If provincial immigration officials intend to refuse an application, they must provide written notice explaining their concerns and give the applicant 30 days to respond.

Applicants may therefore have an opportunity to provide additional documentation addressing questions about their employment history, qualifications or eligibility.

Relevant evidence could include:

Employment reference letters detailing duties and responsibilities

Pay statements and payroll records

Employment contracts

Records of employment

Canadian income tax documents

Trade certification or apprenticeship records, where applicable

Applicants should ensure that their documents accurately reflect their employment circumstances.

The ruling does not guarantee a provincial nomination or permanent residence. Ontario can still refuse individual applications on appropriate grounds.

Will All 2,600 Ontario Skilled Trades Applicants Benefit?

The immediate legal remedy applies to the applicants who participated in the judicial review proceedings.

The remaining workers could benefit from the legal precedent, particularly if Ontario confirmed their applications were complete before June 30, 2025.

However, the judgment does not automatically require Ontario to reopen every returned application.

The province could voluntarily extend its approach to other affected applicants in similar circumstances. Alternatively, workers outside the original proceedings may need to explore their own legal options.

Individual circumstances, application dates and legal deadlines could influence the remedies available.

Affected workers should seek professional legal advice rather than assume Ontario will contact them or resume processing their applications automatically.

Does The Ruling Reopen Ontario’s Skilled Trades Stream?

Ontario’s former Express Entry Skilled Trades Stream remains closed to new applications.

The province introduced a major restructuring of its immigration program in June 2026, replacing eight former immigration streams with the Ontario Workforce Priority Stream.

The new expression of interest system opened on August 4, 2026.

The court ruling addresses Ontario’s handling of applications under the former Skilled Trades Stream. It does not require the province to resume accepting new applications through that pathway.

Workers seeking an Ontario nomination should review the eligibility requirements of the current program or explore alternative Provincial Nominee Programs (PNPs) and federal immigration pathways.

What The Ruling Could Mean For Canadian Immigration Programs

The significance of the Ontario court decision extends beyond the Skilled Trades Stream.

Canadian immigration authorities regularly change eligibility criteria, suspend application intake and restructure immigration programs in response to economic conditions, government priorities and processing pressures.

The Ontario judgment highlights the importance of distinguishing between rules governing future applications and those affecting applications already in processing inventories.

Immigration candidates often spend years accumulating work experience, obtaining qualifications and meeting program requirements before submitting an application.

Changes introduced during processing can have significant financial and personal consequences, particularly for temporary residents approaching the expiry of their work permits.

The judgment could provide a useful precedent in future disputes involving regulatory changes and outstanding immigration applications.

However, its application to other provincial or federal immigration programs will depend on the legislation governing those programs and the circumstances of each case.

Governments retain considerable authority to restructure immigration programs, including introducing legislative provisions that explicitly address outstanding applications.

What Affected Ontario Skilled Trades Workers Should Do Next

Workers whose applications Ontario returned in November 2025 should retain their original application documents, correspondence confirming completeness, fee receipts and application return notices.

They should also maintain up-to-date evidence of their employment history and immigration status.

The court ruling does not automatically restore expired work permits, extend temporary resident status or authorize employment in Canada.

Affected workers should continue to monitor their Canadian work permit expiry dates and explore any available options to maintain lawful status.

For those who invested years in establishing themselves in Ontario, the court ruling provides a potentially important opportunity to revive their pathway to permanent residence.

Much will depend on Ontario’s implementation of the judgment and whether the province extends its response beyond the applicants directly involved in the litigation.

text:
Migrant support groups expressed hope Friday that the Constitutional Court’s landmark ruling against a blanket ban on foreign residents’ political activities will give residents greater freedom to speak out on issues that directly affect their lives.

In a 6-3 decision Thursday, the court found the Immigration Act provision unconstitutional, 49 years after it was introduced. The court said the ban violated the principle of proportionality by restricting foreign residents’ freedom of expression more than necessary.

For years, the broad restriction on political activities has left foreign nationals uncertain about where the line falls between legitimate advocacy and prohibited activity, according to Udaya Rai, head of the Migrants' Trade Union.

"Immigration authorities have interpreted the provision too broadly. We have long feared visa-related disadvantages because even speaking at a rally organized by a political party or taking part in a public forum could be interpreted as political activity," Rai said.

For the Seoul Branch of the Native Language Teachers Union (KGLU NTU), the ruling affirms foreign residents' right to have a say in the policies that shape their everyday lives.

"This ruling affirms our basic human and democratic rights to engage with the government, speak out about our living and working conditions and advocate for our rights without fear of reprisal," said the KGLU NTU chair, surnamed Day. "We believe this ruling provides clarity on how foreigners living in Korea can participate fully in society. This is a significant step forward for human rights, and we fully support it."

Introduced in 1977, the provision broadly prohibited foreign nationals residing in Korea from engaging in political activities. A 2005 amendment added an exception for activities permitted under other laws, but it did little to narrow the scope of the ban.

Although violations are not subject to criminal punishment, foreign residents can face administrative measures, including orders to leave the country.

The case began in 2021, when two Mongolian students in Korea sought to learn about presidential candidates' policies toward foreign residents so they could urge them to address discrimination and provide broader protection for their basic rights.

After learning of the ban, they filed a constitutional complaint on July 2, 2021, arguing that the restriction could discourage them from expressing their views.

Five years and five months later, the court issued a ruling of constitutional nonconformity. It allowed the provision to remain in force until Dec. 31, 2028, giving lawmakers time to revise it.

The decision does not give foreign nationals an unrestricted right to engage in political activities. Restrictions under separate laws, including bans on joining political parties and making political donations, remain in place.

“The decision confirms that foreigners’ political expression is also protected under freedom of expression, which is a fundamental human right,” said Kim Kwang-jae, an attorney at Shin & Kim who represented the petitioners.

Kim said the court took into account that the vague provision could discourage foreign residents from expressing even ordinary opinions or calling for better treatment.

"The court recognized the chilling effect caused by unclear rules and the difficulty of seeking remedies as key grounds for its decision. This ruling could also serve as a standard for reviewing other regulations affecting foreigners in the future," he explained.

The ruling is also likely to prompt scrutiny of current administrative practices that may discourage foreign residents from speaking out, including immigration authorities' requirements that some international students on scholarships pledge to refrain from political activities.

"The ball is now in the National Assembly's court," said Kim Seon-taek, a professor of law at Korea University. "The Constitutional Court said that political activities threatening the national interest, security or public order can still be restricted. But what exactly counts as such activity? The law needs to spell that out."

The professor said lawmakers should adopt a framework in which political activities are generally permitted, with specific exceptions clearly laid out.

"The Assembly should consult migrant groups, legal experts and civic organizations when drawing up the revisions," he added.

text:
UN Special Rapporteur Francesca Albanese condemned Costa Rica's decision to deny her entry into the country, rejecting allegations of links to terrorism and demanding that authorities substantiate their claims or apologize.

Albanese, the UN special rapporteur on the situation of human rights in the occupied Palestinian territories, arrived at Juan Santamaria International Airport at the invitation of the University of Costa Rica, which was scheduled to award her an honorary doctorate on Friday.

Costa Rica's immigration director, Omer Badilla, said in a video statement that authorities denied Albanese entry on national security grounds, citing an alleged international alert over links to terrorist acts.

Badilla neither identified the authority that issued the alert nor provided evidence supporting the allegations.

Speaking to Costa Rican news outlet Delfino.cr from the airport, Albanese categorically rejected the accusations.

“They have to prove it or retract and apologize,” she said, stressing that governments have the right to regulate entry into their territory but not to defame individuals.

“It is ridiculous. Not even the United States went that far,” she added.

Albanese also accused Costa Rican authorities of attempting to send her back to France against her will.

In a statement, the University of Costa Rica urged immigration authorities and the Foreign Ministry to clarify the legal grounds for their decision and ensure that Albanese receives appropriate treatment as a UN expert on mission, as well as guarantees of due process.

The university described the denial of entry as a matter of serious concern requiring a public explanation, highlighting Costa Rica's longstanding commitment to international law and freedom of thought.

Meanwhile, Costa Rica's Constitutional Court issued an interim order preventing authorities from forcibly removing Albanese from the country pending a ruling on a habeas corpus petition filed on her behalf, according to local media reports.

The court also ordered immigration officials to submit a sworn report explaining their actions within 24 hours.

Albanese, an Italian legal expert appointed by the UN Human Rights Council in 2022, has been an outspoken critic of Israel's genocide in Gaza and its treatment of Palestinians in the occupied West Bank.

The US imposed sanctions on Albanese in July 2025 over her cooperation with the International Criminal Court (ICC), drawing criticism from the president of the UN Human Rights Council.

Costa Rica denied entry to UN special rapporteur Francesca Albanese on Thursday after she arrived at an airport near San José. Immigration chief Omer Badilla said authorities acted on an international alert over alleged links to terrorist acts.

He did not say who issued the alert or what acts it referred to.

text:
Mayor Michelle Wu announced that the City of Boston, the Boston Housing Authority, and a coalition of 17 major cities and public housing authorities across the country have filed a lawsuit against the Trump Administration to protect federal housing assistance for Boston families and children. The lawsuit challenges the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development’s (HUD) November 2026 rule that would largely prohibit households with mixed immigration statuses from receiving federal housing assistance, unlawfully evicting U.S. citizens and other qualifying residents from their homes, including thousands of children.

“Under this cruel and illegal rule, hundreds of children and families in Boston could lose their housing,” said Mayor Michelle Wu. “Today, the City and the Boston Housing Authority are joining cities nationwide to halt this unlawful plan and keep families together. While we challenge these federal actions, residents should consult our local housing and legal aid partners to fully know their rights and protect their housing.”

For decades, families with mixed immigration statuses have been allowed to live together in federally assisted housing, receiving financial support only for family members with qualifying immigration statuses. The new HUD rule would end this long-standing practice that keeps families together and housed. In doing so, HUD would defy Congress’s specific intent in pursuit of the Administration’s cruel immigration agenda.

“Almost every family we house at the Boston Housing Authority has previously suffered through a period of homelessness,” said Kenzie Bok, Administrator of the Boston Housing Authority. “It is wrong to suddenly change program rules and plunge hundreds of children into that nightmare a second time. These are Boston kids, they are eligible for federal housing in their own right, and they deserve to stay safely in their homes.”

The Trump Administration’s rule would be devastating for families across the country. In Boston alone, more than 500 families—including almost 900 children, nearly all of them American citizens—would lose housing assistance. The rule would also, for the first time, impose citizenship verification checks on individuals 62 years or older, jeopardizing access to housing for additional vulnerable Bostonians and subjecting thousands of eligible seniors to onerous paperwork requirements.

“This rule tears at the very fabric of family unity and housing stability in our communities. For decades, we’ve had a system that ensured families have access to programs that could keep them safely housed. Now, the Trump Administration is forcing them to make an impossible choice: stay together and become unhoused, or separate to keep a roof over their heads,” said Courtney White, Interim Executive Director of the Mayor’s Office for Immigrant Advancement. “Boston is a home for everyone, regardless of where you come from. With this lawsuit, we will continue to push back against this administration’s continued targeted attacks on Boston’s immigrant communities and fight to ensure that everyone has access to safe, dignified housing.”

This lawsuit was filed in federal court in the District of Massachusetts and alleges that HUD’s new rule violates federal law and undoes decades of established policy without adequate explanation. The City of Boston and Boston Housing Authority are joined as plaintiffs by the City and County of San Francisco, City of Chicago, City of Los Angeles, County of Los Angeles, City of New York, Martin Luther King, Jr. County, City of Providence, City of San Diego, County of Santa Clara, City of Seattle, Housing Authority of the City and County of San Francisco, Housing Authority of the City of Fresno, Housing Authority of Fresno County, Housing Authority of the City of Los Angeles, Los Angeles County Development Authority, San Diego Housing Commission, and the Housing Authority of the City of Santa Barbara. Parallel cases have been filed by the Commonwealth of Massachusetts, alongside 21 other states and the District of Columbia, and a coalition of leading housing organizations, including Massachusetts Union of Public Housing Tenants, Fall River Housing Joint Tenant Council, Border Workers United, and Alfred E. Smith Resident Association represented by the National Housing Law Project, The Legal Aid Society, LatinoJustice PRLDEF, Winston Taylor, Greater Boston Legal Services and Massachusetts Law Reform Institute.

Families who may be affected are encouraged to reach out to the Mass Union of Public Housing Tenants at info@massunion.org or 617-825-9750, and to look out for future communications from the Boston Housing Authority about their due process and appeal rights.

The U.S. Department of Homeland Security (DHS) accused Washington Gov. Bob Ferguson on Wednesday of spreading "vile and hateful lies" about Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents.

"Governor Bob Ferguson and his fellow sanctuary politicians are spreading the most vile and hateful lies about the brave men and women of @ICEgov, " the agency said in a post on X.

The DHS post did not cite any specific comments Ferguson has made about ICE or its agents. It came four days after ICE agents arrested a father and daughter at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport (SEA) as they boarded a flight to Los Angeles. Ferguson criticized the arrests that day.

Ferguson criticizes ICE arrests at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport

"ICE is completely and totally out of control," Ferguson wrote on X Saturday afternoon. "Like many Americans, I'm outraged by masked agents, who do not identify themselves, dragging people off jetways as they board a flight, creating chaos in our communities.

"Today's actions at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport are just the latest example of ICE's deeply un-American tactics," he continued.

In a statement on X Saturday evening, ICE said the woman arrested hurled hot coffee at officers as they arrested a man from Mexico who had overstayed his visa. The agency identified the woman as a Mexican citizen who had also overstayed her visa. She was arrested and will be charged with assaulting a federal officer, according to ICE.

"Assaulting and obstructing law enforcement is a crime and a felony," ICE stated Saturday. "Secretary Mullin has been clear: anyone who assaults or obstructs law enforcement will be prosecuted to the fullest extent of the fullest extent of the law."

DHS accuses Ferguson of obstructing ICE, details Washington arrests

DHS also accused Ferguson of obstructing ICE in its Wednesday post.

"ICE is arresting dangerous illegal aliens every single day, including in the state of Washington. In the last few months, ICE has arrested illegals convicted of murder, child rape, and drug trafficking in the Evergreen State," DHS stated in its post Wednesday. "Governor Ferguson and his cronies may continue to obstruct us and put illegal aliens over the safety of the American people, but the Trump Administration will always put America first by arresting and removing illegal aliens like these."

Ferguson defends Washington's ICE license plate restrictions

Ferguson posted his own statement hours after DHS issued its online statement.

"My administration has taken numerous actions to protect Washingtonians from President Trump's cruel immigration agenda," Ferguson wrote on X. "One example: We shut down the ability of ICE and CBP to renew confidential and undercover license plates. We believe we were the first state to do this, and that other states have since followed our example."

"In response, the Trump Administration sued me," Ferguson continued. "In their lawsuit, they allege that among states who have opposed President Trump's agenda, 'Washington has been one of the worst offenders.'"

Ferguson's post refers to lawsuits announced this past May. The Justice Department claimed Maine, Massachusetts, Oregon and Washington state are imposing unconstitutional restrictions that impede law enforcement and threaten agents' safety.

"By denying undercover license plates to DHS components, including ICE, while issuing them to their own state agencies, these governors are pursuing discriminatory and obstructionist policies against federal law enforcement," acting Attorney General Todd Blanche said in a statement at the time.

State officials pushed back. Some argued their policies are intended to make citizens safer by not facilitating aggressive tactics by unidentified agents carrying out Trump's mass deportation agenda.

Ferguson said Wednesday that Washington state is "proudly and vigorously defending that lawsuit."
