text:
PHOENIX (AZFamily) — Two Arizona acrobats who were detained by ICE agents earlier this month have reunited for the first time and are describing their experiences.

Agustin Baccega and Gustavo Romanello were released Wednesday in time to spend the holiday together. The couple is originally from Argentina and spent years with Arizona Circus Center in Tempe.

They spoke to Arizona’s Family within an hour of their arrival in Phoenix on Wednesday night. They had been held in two different facilities in Florence and Eloy. Baccega was still wearing the clothes he had on when he was released.

A photo shows Baccega and Romanello hugging in tears outside the gates of the Florence facility.

Reunion after nearly a month

After nearly a month apart, the couple was back together.

“At least we’re together. It was hard being apart from each other, for now it’s a relief to be out and thankful,” Baccega said.

Detention by ICE agents

On Nov. 7, the circus performers were traveling to Phoenix when ICE agents approached them at Sky Harbor Airport, despite their valid work permits. They were coming back to attend a memorial for a fellow circus trainer.

They described the experience as terrifying.

“I felt like I was about to faint; you can’t argue with these people [ICE agents]. We’ve seen on the news what they do when someone shows resistance, like I either go, or they shoot me here or I don’t know, that was my thought,” Baccega said.

Different detention experiences

Baccega was held at a detention center in Eloy. Romanello was held in Florence. The two described different experiences.

“They gave me two sets of clothes. People have extra food and breakfast, and we could be outside,” Baccega said. He said he also had access to a library.

Romanello said his experience in Florence was the opposite of his husband’s.

“We didn’t really get time to go outside. I was given one shirt, one pair of shorts, one pair of shoes and underwear, so I had to wash my stuff in the sink,” Romanello said.

Their loved ones fought for their release, and the couple was able to send letters to each other.

“Every night I held it close, I took my letter everywhere with me. I knew that we have all the papers to present, all the papers to show we were never illegal in the country, so I had faith,” Baccega said.

Immigration case continues

Romanello was ordered to wear an ankle monitor. The couple has more court dates. They said they need to heal mentally.

“Wherever I go I’m going to feel like I have to hide for something I did not do,” Baccega said.

The couple lives in Florida. They said it is unclear when they can return or what will happen next.

In a statement, ICE officials said work permits do not prevent agents from making arrests.

text:
Overview

Stories continue to be shared that those trying to visit the U.S. B visa visitors are being subjected to a long lookback into their history of entries to the U.S. when a son or daughter was born in the U.S. U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) officers are rumored to be asking questions of parents presenting B visitor visas for admission to the U.S. about previous visitor entries resulting in the birth of a child in the U.S. based on the enforcement of Executive Order 14419 ending Birth Tourism (EO 14419).1

EO 14419 is dated August 6, 2026, and was published in the Federal Register on August 11, 2026. In some cases, the result of such inquiries is the cancellation of the visa for fraud. Of course, the EO also applies to those foreign nationals applying for nonimmigrant visas at U.S. consular posts abroad. In addition, the EO may facilitate actions against entities, organizations, or individuals within or outside the U.S. that facilitate or enable birth tourism.

The EO defines the term “birth tourism” as, “ (a) the entry of any foreign national into the United States via a nonimmigrant visa for the purpose of giving birth on American soil; or (b) any effort by any foreign national to facilitate the entry of any foreign national into the United States via a nonimmigrant visa for the purpose of giving birth on American soil.”

The EO applies retroactively and prospectively to those who engage(d) in birth tourism with no limit to the scope of the retroactive review. It does not withhold recognition of citizenship already acquired via birth in the U.S. Exemptions are available for foreign nationals whose actions are taken due to humanitarian grounds or when their entry is in the national interest of the U.S.

Examples of Enforcement

On August 12, 2026, the Department of State (DOS) (Office of the Spokesperson) announced it established a “Birth Tourism Prevention Task Force” to carry out EO 14419, working with the Department of Homeland Security (DHS). In its published Fact Sheet regarding the Task Force, it notes that the Task Force, “reviews the activities of visa holders worldwide to identify instances of birth tourism, take action to revoke visas of those who engage in or facilitate it, and dismantle the networks that profit from this abuse.”2 It announced that Task Force had already revoked 600 visas of foreign nationals related to birth tourism abuse pursuant to the EO.

The examples provided of birth tourism fraud in the Fact Sheet are:

Foreigners who willfully misrepresent the purpose of their travel or entry into the United States may be permanently ineligible for a U.S. visa or entry to the United States.

The Department has uncovered patterns that illustrate the lengths some applicants will go to circumvent our laws in order to secure U.S. citizenship for their children – and potentially for themselves in the future.

One couple used a conference and a vacation trip to go shopping as cover stories to give birth to two children in the United States, lying about their travel purpose in two separate visa applications. On the second occasion, the couple concealed that they had a child. The visas have been revoked.

In another case, a foreign government official requested a visa to travel on behalf of her government for just one week but instead stayed three months and gave birth in the United States before departing. The Department revoked the visa.

Another traveler applied for a visa to go on vacation in Orlando and instead traveled to Los Angeles and gave birth five days after arrival. The Department revoked the visa.

Some of the news related to enforcement efforts include:

In Europe, a U.S. embassy identified more than four hundred suspected birth tourism cases since 2024. Investigators traced them to at least six companies that coached applicants on what to say in their visa interview, arranged U.S. housing, and set up delivery plans.

One U.S. embassy in North Africa revoked over one hundred visas for “birth tourist” parents who came to the United States primarily to give birth so their children would get U.S. citizenship.3

At the state level, Texas Gov. Abbott also signed an Executive Order authorizing state agencies to investigate birth tourism schemes within Texas’ healthcare industry and to take enforcement actions against any licensed or regulated individual or entity advertising, soliciting, assisting, or providing unlawful birth tourism schemes.4

Chinese nationals no longer will be allowed to travel to the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands (CNMI) visa-free due to concerns in part related to birth tourism.5

Historical Points

Before the EO, the Department of State (DOS) published a revised provision of the Foreign Affairs Manual (FAM) in April of 2024 regarding the assessment of a B visitor visa applicant related to birth tourism. 9 FAM 402.2-4(A)(8) states:

“Visiting temporarily for pleasure does not include travel for the primary purpose of obtaining U.S. citizenship for a child by giving birth in the United States. Any B NIV applicant who you have reason to believe will give birth during their stay in the United States is presumed to be traveling for the primary purpose of obtaining U.S. citizenship for the child.”

This section contains the following important points of note:

Rebuttable presumption. The applicant “can overcome this presumption” by establishing “a different and permissible primary purpose of travel” — e.g., a “medically complicated pregnancy” needing “specialized medical care … not available in or near” the home country or visiting “a dying family member.”

What does not rebut it? “The fact that an applicant has an arranged birth plan with a doctor or medical facility in the United States or simply expresses a preference to give birth in the United States … is not sufficient to rebut the presumption;” a key factor is “whether the applicant has access to reasonable medical care in or near the country where the applicant resides.”

Citizenship carve-out. “If a child would acquire U.S. citizenship at birth if born outside the United States, the presumption does not apply.”

Consular safeguards. Officers “must not ask a visa applicant whether they are pregnant unless [they] have a specific articulable reason,” “must not, as a matter of course, ask all female applicants … whether they are pregnant,” “may not require B NIV applicants to provide evidence that they are not pregnant,” and must assess “only the applicant’s current purpose of travel,” not a future possibility of pregnancy.

Accompanying applicants. A companion whose “primary purpose of travel is to assist or accompany another visa applicant” who does not qualify may face “doubt on their credibility,” cross-referencing INA 214(b).

What about the assessment of intent at entry by CBP officers at ports of entry regarding birth tourism?

In the past, CBP would follow a similar approach to the one outlined in the FAM provision noted. Recently, in a national liaison meeting with representatives of the American Immigration Lawyers Association (AILA) on October 23, 2026, CBP officials confirmed that they have received no new guidance related to the implementation of EO 14419. They noted that they would continue to review the issue when presented via an assessment of the “totality of the circumstances, including economic solvency and need for specialized medical care.” In addition, they confirmed that they were aware of DOS revoking issued visas based on their internal review.

How to prepare for admission to the U.S. in the future as a nonimmigrant?

For those planning to enter the U.S. under nonimmigrant categories other than as a B visitor, it is not clear that the EO only applies to B nonimmigrant visas. So, preparing to address questions regarding your primary purpose of entry to the U.S. is still relevant and important, especially while pregnant in particular in addition as to prior admissions to the U.S. after which a child was born in the U.S.

Based on experiences reported to date and the guidance noted in the FAM, consider the following preparatory actions:

Be prepared to explain as to a current and prior requests for admission the primary purpose for the request(s). Note to expect the possibility of such questions from CBP when obviously pregnant or traveling with your U.S. citizen child.

Be able to address special medical needs regarding gynecological or obstetric care in the U.S.

As for most nonimmigrant visitors, be able to document your residence, employment, and ties to your home country to prove your nonimmigrant intent.

If seeking specialized medical care, be able to document insurance coverage and/or payment arrangements for medical care.

If seeking or used specialized medical care in the U.S. in the past, be able to document such care via sworn statements from the medical provider, invoices, and/or medical care information from the provider.

Footnotes

1. Kocherga, Angela, Trump administration’s new visa task force worries families in border cities, (October 26, 2026) NPR. “In a statement to NPR the State Department said it has revoked thousands of visas including those of border parents. But the agency did not give a specific overall number, or say how many were on the border, or whether there is now a policy to question Mexican visitors about why their children were born in the United States.”

2. See. State Department Establishes Task Force to End Birth Tourism Fact Sheet (August 12, 2026) https://www.state.gov/releases/office-of-the-spokesman/2026/08/state-department-establishes-task-force-to-end-birth-tourism .

3. See Trump Administration Dismantles Global Birth Tourism Networks published by U.S. Mission China on June 12, 2026, https://china.usembassy-china.org.cn/trump-administration-dismantles-global-birth-tourism-ne. tworks/ before the issuance of EO 14419.

4. See Executive Order No. GA-57 relating to unlawful birth tourism schemes in Texas. The EO references investigations as to Texas hospitals offering “birth packages” as well as a Houton-area facility that claims to have facilitated birth tourism for 1,000 plus foreign national and to have coached customers to mislead or deceive federal immigration officials as to the purpose of their visits to the U.S. The Governor’s order requires the Texas Department of State Health Services, Health and Human Services Commission, Office of the Inspector General, Texas Medical Board, Texas Board of Nursing, and the Texas Department of Licensing and Regulation to investigate claims of birth tourism schemes in Texas’ healthcare industry with the authority to revoke operational state licenses and deny state benefits/contractshttps://gov.texas.gov/news/post/governor-abbott-issues-executive-order-cracking-down-on-birth-tourism-schemes .

text:
ELECTORAL POLITICS| GOVERNMENT POLICY

10 November: Essex Reform councillor Carl Johnson compares a 78-year-old retired woman teaching English to asylum seekers at Wethersfield camp to a ‘Nazi collaborator’ and claims that she facilitated ‘an invasion’ and ‘their being able to sexually abuse women and children’, leaving her ‘sick, angry and shaky’. (ITV News, 10 November 2026)

10 November: Bicester West Reform councillor Michael Wilson defends his attendance, alongside Patriotic Alternative members, of a protest in Bicester on 7 November against plans to house up to 1,250 male asylum seekers on a former MOD site. (Oxford Mail, 10 November 2026)

11 November: In Belgium, 3,000 people form a human chain around the Palace of Justice in Brussels and demonstrations are held in 60 municipalities against the ‘human raids law’ that allows police officers to enter private properties to arrest and deport foreign nationals. (European Correspondent, 11 November 2026)

11 November: Reform partially boycotts the Senedd after its member Joe Martin is banned from speaking until he apologises for remarks claiming that white people are being ‘replaced’. (BBC News, 11 November 2026)

16 November: Research by IRR finds that mainstream political parties have created a permissive environment for intimidatory far-right flagging campaigns to develop, and that, in the absence of effective government action, it has been left to local communities to defend their neighbourhoods. (IRR, 16 November 2026)

17 November: The Danish Red-Green alliance criticises Social Democrat prime minister Mette Fredriksen for invoking the language of ‘population replacement’. Her remarks, made to the media in the context of the ‘Rwanda plan’, are welcomed by the Danish People’s Party and the far-right Stram Kurs. (Nordiskpost, 19 November 2026)

17 November: Disabled People Against the Cuts and the National Survivor User Network criticise the Milburn review into young people not in work, education or training for proposing to cut young people’s sickness and disability benefits and potentially roll back protections in the Employment Rights Act. (Guardian, 17 November 2026; Morning Star, 18 November 2026)

18 November: The home secretary says that a new ‘impartiality standard’ to ensure all members of the public receive equal treatment from the police is needed to tackle the ‘corrosive and growing’ perception of ‘two-tier policing’. (Guardian, 18 November 2026)

18 November: A High Court judge grants Birmingham City Council an interim injunction against seven flag activists, including Raise the Colours co-founder Ryan Bridge, and ‘persons unknown’, banning the unauthorised placing of all flags on council-owned street furniture. Conservative and Reform leaders condemn the decision, which is welcomed by Brummies United Against Racism. (Guardian, 18 November 2026)

19 November: Southwark council passes a harm reduction motion calling on the government to review the Misuse of Drugs Act 1971 to ‘assess its effectiveness in protecting public health and safety’ as well as to respond to drug deaths by establishing safer drug consumption facilities in England and Wales. (Politics Home, 19 November 2026).

21 November: Just over half of 500 residents of the Suffolk village of Barnham vote in a referendum to ‘leave the UK’ after plans are approved to house 931 single male asylum seekers at RAF Barnham. (BBC News, 21 November 2026)

23 November: A government-commissioned review of the personal independence payment system, co-led by Stephen Timms and with input from people with lived experience of disability, recommends an overhaul of the Pip system but, in contradiction to Milburn’s review, suggests retaining it for all ages. (Guardian, 22 November 2026)

ANTI-FASCISM AND THE FAR RIGHT

11 November: Tens of thousands of right-wing activists, led by nationalist president Karol Nawrocki, march for Independence Day in Warsaw, Poland, under the slogan ‘Poles are masters of their own land’, amid political tension over a mass shooting in Krakow that killed six people. (Reuters, 11 November 2026)

13 November: A judge in Gijón, Spain, suspends all activities of the far-right group Núcleo Nacional over alleged hate crimes and illegal association after 14 members are arrested on suspicion of inciting hatred against vulnerable groups and police seize over 20 firearms in searches, including of the group’s Madrid headquarters. (Al Jazeera, 13 November 2026)

14 November: According to Searchlight, an anti-immigrant protest held outside the Crowne Plaza hotel in Basingstoke was coordinated by a coalition of far-right Patriot groups from across southern England. (Facebook [Basingstoke Gazette], 14 November 2026; Searchlight, 13 November 2026

14 November: Around 40 anti-racists confront a ‘Stop the Boats’ march in Oxford by the far-right Oxfordshire Patriots. (Oxford Student, 14 November 2026)

15 November: 24-year-old Isabel Peralta, spokesman for Núcleo Nacional, is arrested in Spain after police intercept a phone call in which she says she regrets that a work shift kept her from carrying out a mass shooting on protestors in Paris, saying ‘I’d kill 60 of them’. Police find a large cache of weapons at her home, including some decorated with swastikas. (Telegraph, 15 November 2026)

15 November: A Free Party conference on ‘remigration’ takes place in Prague, Czech Republic, featuring speakers from Germany’s AfD, Slovakia’s Republika and Hungary’s Mi Hazánk, with attendees invited to sign the ‘Save Europe Act’. Meanwhile, over 1,000 anti-fascists blockade the event. (Romea, 12 November 2026; Searchlight, 15 November 2026)

15 November: Czech police charge 18 people, including seven minors, over a premeditated attack by masked neo-Nazis armed with metal batons on an anti-fascist march in Frýdek-Místek in September 2025, where two protesters were hospitalised with broken jaws, cheekbones and noses. (Searchlight, 15 November 2026)

16 November: Three teenagers (aged 16 and 17) with links to a neo-Nazi network are detained in Poland on suspicion of preparing a terrorist attack after officers seize chemicals that could be used to make explosives. The arrests come days after a far-right mass shooting in Krakow that killed six people. (Independent, 16 November 2026)

17 November: An estimated 20,000 anti-fascists fill the streets of Parma, Italy, to confront a 1,000-strong national ‘remigration’ march organised by a coalition of neo-fascist groups, including CasaPound, who chant in praise of Mussolini. (Searchlight, 17 November 2026)

20 November: 24-year-old white supremacist Mikka Anderson is found guilty at Newcastle Crown Court of preparing an act of terrorism after he planned to firebomb a migrant hotel in Hull and made Molotov cocktails. (LBC, 20 November 2026)

22 November: A group called British Security UK, a so-called volunteer-led security group which does not require volunteers to have any security qualifications or training, is named as part of a worrying rise in intimidating street vigilantes surrounding far-right figures like Tommy Robinson and Paul Golding. (Guardian, 22 November 2026)

22 November: A planned Britain First rally in Coventry is called off after the coach company says it can no longer transport the group. Around 60 supporters gather outside Coventry train station alongside roughly 200 counter-protesters. (Coventry Live, 22 November 2026)

ANTI-TERRORISM AND NATIONAL SECURITY

19 November: The UN Human Rights Committee criticises misuse of ‘vaguely worded’ national security and anti-terrorism laws in its first comprehensive guidance on freedom of association, ‘spurred’ by events in countries including the UK, North Korea, Russia, China and Israel. (Guardian, 19 November 2026)

19 November: Following PSNI property searches in Bangor and Belfast, four men are arrested as part of an ‘extensive and ongoing investigation into extreme right-wing terrorism’. (Irish News, 20 November 2026)

POLICING| PRISONS| CRIMINAL JUSTICE SYSTEM

10 November: It is revealed that Dame Cressida Dick, who led the 2005 operation in which Jean Charles de Menezes was fatally shot and, as Met Commissioner, rolled out live facial recognition (despite an 81 percent false-positive rate) and more than doubled stop-and-searches, has worked since September 2025 as a paid adviser to US tech firm Palantir, which recently won a contract worth £10m with three English police forces. (Byline Times, 10 November 2026)

12 November: The Prisons and Probation Ombudsman calls for the formation of an independent investigator to hold prison staff to account, stating that some prison officers are getting away with bullying and assaulting inmates. (Independent, 12 November 2026)

12 November: A report by HM Inspectorate of Constabulary finds bias in the algorithm used in retrospective facial recognition, which is more likely to falsely flag ethnic minority people as suspects, increasing risk of wrongful arrest. (Guardian, 12 November 2026)

15 November: Internal FOI figures released by South Wales police reveal that 24 percent of people selected for facial recognition checks were from ethnic minorities, despite this group making up only 7 percent of the area’s population. (Guardian, 15 November 2026)

15 November: West Yorkshire police refer themselves to the IOPC after two people, aged 22 and 23, die in Leeds after their car is hit by a car being pursued by police. The driver and three passengers of the pursued car are arrested. (Guardian, 15 November 2026)

19 November: A Cambridgeshire teenager who wrote a neo-Nazi inspired manifesto describing his desire to kill people before taking his own life, pleads guilty to collecting information useful in preparing an act of terrorism. The judge says it is not in the youth’s ‘best interests’ to jail him and issues a three-year youth rehabilitation order and a criminal behaviour order. (BBC News, 19 November 2026)

20 November: A Paris court sentences three French police officers to between one and two years’ prison for an assault, captured on video six years ago, on Black music producer Michel Zecler, whom they punched, hit with truncheons and tear-gassed while hurling racist abuse, then falsely accused of having assaulted them. Zecler’s lawyer hails the ruling as historic. (Le Monde, 21 November 2026; Morning Star, 22 November 2026)

20 November: Patriot Platform founder Daniel Thomas (aka Danny Tommo) is sentenced to 15 months in prison after being found guilty of criminal damage for slashing a dinghy used by migrants crossing the English Channel with a knife while a French rescue worker was on board. (Guardian, 20 November 2026)

23 November: Martha Goddard is sentenced to ten years’ prison for causing criminal damage to McDonald’s and Starbucks stores and a BBC building in Norwich by setting light to improvised incendiary devices. Posters were left at the scene calling for the bombing of Gaza to stop and criticising BBC coverage. (BBC News, 23 November 2026)

ASYLUM | MIGRATION| BORDERS|CITIZENSHIP

Asylum and migrant rights

12 November: The Home Office refuses settlement to a blind Nigerian pensioner who has lived in the UK for 26 years, telling her to ‘go back to India’, where she has never been in her life. (Guardian, 14 November 2026)

18 November: Data reveal that between May and October 2026, roughly 80 pe cent of international student visas were refused on credibility grounds, with 90 percent of applications from India, Sri Lanka and Nepal, 84 percent from Nigeria, and 79 percent from Bangladesh refused. (The PIE, 18 November 2026)

20 November: Research by Refugee and Migrant Justice warns that proposed asylum and settlement reforms could leave some refugees facing decades of uncertainty over their immigration status, affecting their ability to establish secure lives in the UK (Electronic Immigration Network, 20 November 2026)

Borders and internal controls

10 November: The EU and Nigeria sign a migration management agreement committing Nigeria to tightening its borders to prevent transit of refugees and migrants, making it the 24th country with which the EU has return or readmission agreements, 18 of which are legally binding. (EU News, 11 November 2026)

12 November: EU cooperation with Egypt on migration is strengthened as the Egyptian interior ministry agrees to a working arrangement with the EU’s police training agency CEPOL, adding to its cooperation with Europol and Frontex against undocumented migration. (DNE Africa, 15 November 2026)

14 November: The body of a young man in his 20s is found on a beach near Le Touquet, France, the morning after a French patrol stopped an attempted nighttime boarding of a ‘makeshift vessel’ preparing to cross the Channel. (BBC News, 14 November 2026)

Reception and detention

10 November: As the Home Office approves plans to house six asylum seekers in the village of Tillingham, Essex, residents and the leader of Maldon District Council write to the home secretary to raise concerns. (Colchester Gazette, 10 November 2026)

10 November: Researchers from Oxford University claim that since 2000, 112 foreign nationals have died in Greek police stations or migrant centres with inadequate healthcare provision, including 44 suicides and 34 deaths which were never officially registered. (Reuters, 10 November 2026)

12 November: Communities secretary Angela Rayner approves plans to redevelop and refurbish MoD Bicester, Oxfordshire, to house 1,256 asylum seekers, with final approval yet to be made as residents of nearby Piddington seek a legal challenge to oppose the plans. (Guardian, 12 November 2026)

13 November: Refugee Support Aegean reports that over 3,000 people seeking asylum have been arrested for illegal entry or stay in Greece in the first half of 2026, and of the nearly 1,200 prosecutions, over 1,000 have resulted in conviction, with children separated from parents and grandparents who are sent to prison. (Ekathimerini, 13 November 2026)

14 November: An undercover reporter for an ITV documentary at the Crowborough immigration centre, Inside the Asylum Camp, finds survivors of torture unlawfully held there and exposes inadequate welfare checks, suggesting that Clearsprings Ready Homes is failing in its duty of care. Following the screening, the Helen Bamber Foundation reports on the continuing harm caused to vulnerable people by their placement in military sites. (Guardian, 14 November 2026; HBF, 16 November 2026)

15 November: Thames Water warns that the proposed extended accommodation blocks at Campsfield House Immigration Removal Centre, Oxfordshire, will sit just 20 metres from a sewage pumping station, meaning detainees will face ‘odour, noise, vibration, lighting associated with maintenance activities, insects and flies’. (Guardian, 15 November 2026)

text:
A coalition of human rights and immigrant advocacy organizations has sued the Trump administration, accusing Immigration and Customs Enforcement of abandoning its own protections for pregnant, postpartum, and nursing immigrants and subjecting vulnerable women to prolonged detention and GPS shackles, OK! can reveal.

According to court documents obtained by OK!, the lawsuit was filed November 24 in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia against the Department of Homeland Security, ICE, DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin, and acting ICE Director David Venturella.

ICE Accused of Abandoning Protections

The six plaintiff organizations claim ICE has stopped following a 2021 directive that generally prohibits detaining pregnant, postpartum, or nursing individuals unless required by law or exceptional circumstances exist.

The July 1, 2021, directive defines exceptional circumstances as national security concerns or an imminent risk of death, violence, or physical harm. It also requires senior ICE officials to approve covered detentions, consult medical personnel, and review continued custody at least once a week.

The complaint alleges ICE disregarded those requirements without formally withdrawing the directive.

Hundreds of Expectant Mothers Held Behind Bars

According to the filing, internal ICE data obtained through a Freedom of Information Act request showed the number of pregnant women in detention increased by 1,320% between January 2025 and March 2026.

The plaintiffs also allege the average monthly length of detention increased 390% when comparing periods in which ICE followed the directive with February 2025 through January 2026.

The lawsuit claims more than 557 pregnant women have been detained since 2025 for an average of 43 days, with nearly 14% held for at least 90 days. One woman was allegedly detained for 219 days, nearly seven months of her pregnancy.

Miscarriages and Mothers Separated From Babies

The complaint details several cases that plaintiffs say illustrate the consequences. A pregnant woman held in Kentucky reportedly sent an emergency request saying she had been bleeding. The next day, she allegedly miscarried while shackled to a hospital bed.

Another woman, who was in the third trimester of a high-risk pregnancy, allegedly was told by officers that ICE would take her baby after birth. The filing claims she signed away her right to appear before an immigration judge and was deported while eight months pregnant.

The plaintiffs also describe nursing mothers separated from their infants and allegedly denied breast pumps. One woman who was breastfeeding reportedly remained in detention without a pump, while another pregnant woman said a GPS ankle monitor caused pain and worsened her high blood pressure.

Trump Administration Faces Legal Battle

The complaint cites records from multiple detention facilities nationwide. The organizations argue the administration violated the Administrative Procedure Act and the Accardi doctrine, which requires agencies to follow their own binding rules.

They are asking the court to declare the alleged abandonment unlawful, set aside the challenged policy, pause its enforcement while the case proceeds and order ICE to comply with the 2021 directive.

The lawsuit does not challenge the government's general authority to carry out deportations or seek to overturn individual removal orders.

The case, Robert & Ethel Kennedy Human Rights Center et al. v. Department of Homeland Security, is pending. No ruling has been issued on the allegations.

text:
PHOENIX (AZFamily) — A new Government Accountability Office report says U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement potentially overpaid for warehouses it bought with immigration detention funding and pays millions for empty beds at some facilities.

The Government Accountability Office examined how ICE is using $45 billion in detention funding at the request of Congress. The money was provided under the One Big Beautiful Bill, which passed in July 2025, and is available through 2029. The report found ICE has committed about $9 billion so far.

Warehouse purchases

The report found ICE spent more than $1 billion on 11 warehouses, including one in Surprise. Prices ranged from $35 million to $145 million.

For nine of the warehouses, ICE paid at least 50% more than the local tax assessment. Auditors said that means ICE potentially overpaid, but noted assessments are not always a reliable measure of value.

ICE plans to sell seven of the warehouses. Auditors warned the sales could result in losses.

ICE has continued to buy facilities. In July and August, it bought four existing detention facilities for more than $2 billion.

Empty beds

The report estimates ICE pays about $13 million a month for empty beds at five facilities.

Reaction from lawmakers

Sen. Ruben Gallego wants to look further into the financials.

“We have to figure out if there’s any level of corruption in this. This is American taxpayer dollars. I don’t think it should be used to buy these massive detention beds,” Gallego said.

“They should stop buying them like now and sell off what they can,” he said.

U.S. Rep. Greg Stanton also commented.

“Needs to be fully investigated. I mean, it raises incredible questions,” Stanton said.

“How the hell were we spending so much additional money for excess space for detention facilities when we don’t even need those additional beds?” he said.

Recommendations

Auditors made two recommendations: that ICE update its spending plans on time and develop life-cycle cost estimates and evaluate alternatives before making new investments.

The Department of Homeland Security, which oversees ICE, agreed with both recommendations. In its response, DHS wrote that it “remains committed to ICE strengthening the necessary processes.”

text:
BALTIMORE —

Kilmar Abrego Garcia, a Maryland man who was mistakenly deported to a maximum-security prison in El Salvador, has left the United States for Spain after a federal judge dismissed his immigration case and the Department of Homeland Security allowed him to travel to any country that would accept him.

Abrego Garcia was arrested in Baltimore last spring while on his way to pick up his 5-year-old son from his grandmother's house. He was accused by DHS and Trump administration officials of being a gang member, a claim he has consistently denied and that has not been proven in court.

DHS defied a judge's order and deported him to El Salvador, later attributing the mistake to an administrative error.

"I'm happy this time because this time I'm leaving with my freedom, not like before when they took me out inhumanely," Abrego Garcia said.

Cameras captured his arrival in Spain, where he landed on a commercial flight with his wife and legal team. He remained silent when reporters questioned him at the airport, asking about his plans in Spain.

Hours later, Abrego Garcia said, "The government did not decide where my story continues. My family and I decide."

Maryland U.S. Sen. Chris Van Hollen, who met with Abrego Garcia in El Salvador one month after his deportation, described the outcome as significant.

"They wanted to leave him to rot there, to rot there for the rest of his life. Instead, what we have is our judicial system, working with the good legal team and we have this outcome where Garcia is able to essentially chart his own future and destiny,” Van Hollen said.

Abrego Garcia was held at CECOT, a maximum-security prison in El Salvador known for harsh conditions and torturing prisoners. He was told he would never leave.

He was later brought back to the United States before the Trump administration made another attempt to deport him, this time to Africa.

A federal judge signed an order on Friday allowing Abrego Garcia to leave the country without restrictions by Dec. 24. He was removed from the no-fly list, and his ankle monitor was taken off.

"I keep believing that I'm victorious, and I've always said this, because the United States is a country that follows the laws and justice has been served," Abrego Garcia said.

His attorney, Simon Sandoval-Moshenberg, said the departure is temporary but acknowledged the challenges of returning under the current administration.

"He's the husband of a U.S. citizen. He's the father of a severely disabled, very young U.S. citizen child. He is eligible to return to the United States as a lawful permanent resident," Sandoval-Moshenberg said.

Abrego Garcia is currently in Spain on a tourist visa, with his lawyers stating he has received formal invitations from countries around the world.

"There's lots of options for my future. We haven't decided what's next for my family," Abrego Garcia said.

While Abrego Garcia's wife traveled with him to Spain, she plans to return to the United States to care for their children. His attorney said he has a long future in Maryland.

DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin commented on Abrego Garcia's departure, saying, "We are delighted to announce that Kilmar Abrego Garcia has self-deported from the United States to Spain."

text:
A federal judge in California has ordered a halt to the Immigration and Customs Enforcement's (ICE) practice of re-arresting immigrants during their routine check-ins. This decision, while not directly affecting Cubans in Florida, sets a significant legal precedent against such tactics.

Simultaneously, a class-action lawsuit filed in Georgia is progressing within the same federal circuit that includes Florida. If successful, it could compel ICE to modify its approach in that state as well.

Judge Dana M. Sabraw of the Southern District of California certified the case Fanfan et al. v. Noem et al. as a class action, instructing ICE to refrain from re-arresting individuals already released with ongoing court cases during check-ins, unless a significant change in circumstances is individually assessed.

The ruling is currently applicable only in San Diego and Imperial counties.

This case was initiated by the Center for Human Rights and Constitutional Law alongside UCLA's School of Law. "ICE was drawing these individuals to check-ins or ICE appointments and re-detaining them without justification," stated Monika Langarica, the legal director of the organization.

The implications of ICE's re-arrest practices during check-ins for Cubans in Florida are part of a continually evolving immigration landscape. Stay updated on the latest developments in our U.S. Immigration section.

This is not the first such order; in December 2025, Judge Sabraw had previously issued a temporary restraining order in the case, while a San Francisco court blocked the same practice for Northern California.

Georgia Lawsuit: Its Significance for Florida

The most critical judicial front for Cubans in Florida began on November 12 in the Northern District of Georgia. The ACLU from Georgia, North Carolina, and South Carolina, along with the Foley Hoag law firm, filed a class-action lawsuit against the Department of Homeland Security, Secretary Markwayne Mullin, ICE Acting Director David Venturella, and Kristen Sullivan, the acting director of ICE's Atlanta office.

The lawsuit challenges the "redetention policy" that DHS adopted around May 2025, abandoning the "change of circumstances policy" that the Atlanta ICE office had followed for over four decades.

Under the previous policy, ICE could not re-arrest someone previously released without first determining that their circumstances had materially changed. "Our clients have adhered to the rules imposed by the government. They have attended court hearings, ICE check-ins, and complied with the conditions of their release," said Corina Scott, an attorney with the ACLU of North Carolina.

Georgia's link to the 11th Circuit, which also covers Florida and Alabama, is key. If the lawsuit succeeds and reaches appeal, a ruling from that court would be binding across the circuit.

As of this edition, the court has not yet ruled on the motions for stay and class certification filed on November 17.

Implications for Cubans in Miramar

Thousands of Cubans with Form I-220A regularly visit the ICE office in Miramar, South Florida, where arrests during these appointments and alleged abuses have led to a federal complaint filed by the SPLC and Americans for Immigrant Justice.

Currently, the judicial decisions from California and Georgia do not directly impact Florida. However, the legal framework they establish—requiring individual assessments before re-arrest—is already being used by attorneys in habeas corpus petitions in the Southern District of Florida, where over 97,000 detainees have resorted to this since Trump's return.

The legal outlook for Cubans with I-220A is mixed: Last May, the 11th Circuit recognized the right to bond hearings for detainees within the country, but on November 17, the same court ruled that the I-220A does not equate to the parole required by the Cuban Adjustment Act, blocking a path to residency for many.

While courts determine the extent of these protections, experts advise continuing to attend appointments in Miramar, as failing to do so increases the risk of detention. It's recommended to always have an immigration attorney accessible before any ICE appointment.

text:
A dramatic video of federal immigration officers making arrests at a Seattle airport has become the new focal point for criticism of the Trump administration’s mass deportation campaign.

The footage shows chaos as masked Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers in plain clothes whisk two individuals away from the jet bridge as passengers were boarding an Alaska Airlines flight on Saturday.

The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) said it targeted Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza of Mexico after he overstayed his visa. ICE officers also arrested Larrondo Mendoza’s daughter, Sofia Hernandez Mejia, after she allegedly “hurled hot coffee” at one of the agents and charged her with assaulting a federal officer.

Advertisement

The family’s attorney told KUOW that Hernandez Mejia did not intentionally throw the coffee at the officers.

“When somebody’s charging at you, you’re going to drop a cup of coffee,” she said.

The family entered the United States in 2015 on tourist visas before Larrondo Mendoza submitted an application for asylum, which remains pending, that same year, as required by asylum rules, his attorney said. Their visas expired after six months, according to KUOW.

Advertisement

His daughter is pursuing citizenship through her marriage to an American citizen.

Washington Governor Bob Ferguson (D) expressed “outrage” over the arrest, accusing ICE of being “completely and totally out of control.”

“Like many Americans, I’m outraged by masked agents, who do not identify themselves, dragging people off jetways as they board a flight, creating chaos in our communities,” he said at the time. “Today’s actions at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport are just the latest example of ICE’s deeply un-American tactics.”

For months, ICE has been making arrests at airports across the country, often at gates and ticket counters, targeting foreigners who have overstayed their visas. ICE earlier reached an agreement with the Transportation Security Administration (TSA), allowing the airport security agency to provide information to federal immigration agents, ABC News reported in July.

Advertisement

Scott Mechkowski, former ICE deputy field office director in New York, said that a pending asylum claim does not mean someone has legal status.

“A pending asylum claim isn’t legal status, and it’s not a free pass,” Mechkowski said. “Congress gave ICE the authority to arrest and detain while the case plays out.”

“If he had complied, agents would have walked him off that plane quietly,” he said of the Seattle case. “The drama on that jetway was self-inflicted.”

Matthew Kolken, a New York-based immigration lawyer who represents such clients, echoed that neither a pending asylum application that has yet to face a decision nor a work permit serves as legal status. He said ICE can justify its arrest solely based on a visa overstay.

A pending asylum application generally gives an applicant authorization to remain in the United States and stops the accrual of unlawful presence, but is not considered lawful immigration status.

“When you file that asylum application, that stops the accrual of unlawful presence,” Kolken said. “That doesn’t mean that you’re in the United States legally.”

An asylum officer with U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services typically handles applications filed by foreigners already in the country who are not in deportation proceedings, which is the case with Larrondo Mendoza. ICE can choose to open deportation proceedings in the interim and take someone into custody based on the overstaying of a visa.

“It just means that you are going to be allowed to remain in the United States without accruing any additional time that would trigger a bar if you have to leave the U.S. So, yes, the individual is entitled to an adjudication of their asylum application, they’re afforded that due process, but ICE is not precluded from starting deportation against you because you violated the United States immigration law for overstaying your visa,” he added.

In April 2025, the Trump administration issued a memo instructing immigration judges to “pretermit,” or deny without a hearing, asylum applications that lack any legal basis. The memo cited the roughly 4 million pending cases in immigration courts, saying that judges “should take … all appropriate action to immediately resolve cases on their dockets that do not have viable legal paths for relief or protection from removal.”

“I’ve had asylum applications pending for 25 years. So there’s a major asylum office backlog and one of the things that ICE is doing now by encountering individuals who are are traveling … within the boundaries of the United States is they’re instituting removal proceedings, and that, therefore, it takes their asylum application away from the asylum office and into the hands of an immigration judge,” Kolken said.

text:
Senate investigators will now examine the size of the prison giants’ windfalls as part of their ongoing probe into DHS spending, Sen. Maggie Hassan’s office told us. The New Hampshire Democrat is in line to chair the powerful Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee when her party takes control of the chamber in January.

CoreCivic landed the biggest payday, selling four facilities in California, Kansas and Minnesota to Markwayne Mullin’s department for $2.21 billion in July and August.

Its latest quarterly filing records a gain of $1.77 billion after the costs of completing the deals, and $1.29 billion after tax—more than 11 times CoreCivic’s $116.5 million profit from its entire business last year alone.

GEO Group reported a $560 million post-tax gain after selling its three-facility Adelanto complex in California to DHS for $950 million on Oct. 2.

It’s estimated to retain $340 million from its $453 million sale of the Northwest ICE Processing Center in Tacoma, Washington, on Nov. 17, after taxes and expenses.

The profits alone do not establish that taxpayers overpaid. But the DHS buying spree is helping finance $1 billion in share-buyback initiatives designed to reward CoreCivic and GEO Group’s investors—which may include Trump.

The 80-year-old’s brokers have repeatedly bought and sold the firms’ shares since he returned to office, as PunchUp revealed on Wednesday. His organization has said outside investment managers control those transactions, and did not comment when asked whether he still holds stock in either company.

“The Department of Homeland Security appears to have entered into a number of deals that wasted taxpayer resources while enriching President Trump, and these deals all came as there are serious concerns about pay-to-play and corruption at DHS,” Hassan told PunchUp.

CoreCivic has previously said it held no discussions about Trump’s investments and had no advance knowledge of who traded its shares.

Selling the buildings to DHS has not ended the companies’ earnings potential.

CoreCivic continues to run all four properties under ICE agreements, while GEO also retained its Adelanto operating contract and secured a new 10-year deal covering Tacoma.

At Appleton, Minnesota, alone, CoreCivic expects annual revenue of around $75 million once the prison is fully operational.

The company has already used $500 million from its property-sale proceeds to fund a stock repurchase agreement. GEO plans another $500 million buyback partly using its Tacoma profits.

This reduces the number of available shares, increasing current investors’ stakes in future earnings.

CoreCivic has also used the sales to repay more than $700 million in debt, strengthening its finances as ICE continues to grow its detention network.

And GEO Group’s sell-off is not over. The company is negotiating with ICE over up to three more facilities, dependent on agreeing a price and ongoing management contracts.

Announcing the Tacoma deal, GEO Group chief George Zoley made clear whose interests the company was pursuing. “We remain focused on allocating capital to enhance long-term value for shareholders, including through accelerated share repurchases,” he said.

The spending has drawn Democratic scrutiny on Capitol Hill, with Hassan opening an investigation into Appleton, and Reps. Bennie Thompson and Betty McCollum demanding answers from Mullin about its cost and conditions.

The prison had stood empty for 16 years before reopening this month, and House Democrats have questioned whether its rushed reopening has made it suitable for detainees sent there.

PunchUp previously revealed that Minnesota’s corrections commissioner, Paul Schnell, said a sale for roughly $3 million had been discussed. CoreCivic described that account as “categorically false.”

Minnesota Rep. Betty McCollum, a senior member of the House Appropriations Committee, said those findings raised serious questions about the administration’s dealings with the prison giants.

“These two corporations happen to have deep donor ties to Trump’s political machine, raising significant questions about impropriety,” she told PunchUp. “The Democratic-led 120th Congress will investigate and hold the administration accountable, even as Republicans have refused to act.”

CoreCivic has defended the federal purchase price, saying independent appraisers hired by the government assessed replacement costs, depreciation, land, and renovations, and that officials conducted a separate review.

DHS has defended the acquisitions as a way to rapidly increase detention capacity for Trump’s mass-deportation campaign without waiting for new construction.

PunchUp has approached the White House, DHS, GEO Group and CoreCivic for comment.

text:
A federal judge in California blocked the Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) from re-arresting immigrants during their routine check-in appointments, in a decision that does not directly protect Cubans in Florida but marks a growing legal stance against that tactic.

In parallel, a class action lawsuit filed in Georgia is progressing within the same federal circuit that covers Florida and could, if successful, compel ICE to change its behavior in that state as well.

Judge Dana M. Sabraw of the Southern District of California certified the class action suit Fanfan et al. v. Noem et al. and ordered that ICE cannot re-detain individuals who have already been released with open court cases during their check-in appointments without first conducting an individual assessment that demonstrates a significant change in circumstances.

The order applies only to San Diego and Imperial counties.

The case was brought forward by the Center for Human Rights and Constitutional Law and the UCLA School of Law.

"ICE was drawing those people in for check-ins or ICE appointments and detaining them without reason," said Monika Langarica, legal director of that organization.

Las redetenciones de ICE en citas de control y sus implicaciones legales para cubanos en Florida forman parte de un panorama migratorio en constante cambio. Sigue los últimos desarrollos en nuestra sección de

This is not the first order of its kind: in December 2025, Judge Sabraw had already granted a temporary restriction in the case, and a court in San Francisco blocked the same practice for Northern California.

Georgia's Lawsuit: Why It Matters to Florida

The most significant legal front for Cubans in Florida opened on November 12 in the Northern District of Georgia.

The ACLU of Georgia, North Carolina, and South Carolina, along with the law firm Foley Hoag, filed a class action lawsuit against the Department of Homeland Security, Secretary Markwayne Mullin, Acting ICE Director David Venturella, and the Acting ICE Office Director in Atlanta, Kristen Sullivan.

The lawsuit challenges the "re-detention policy" that DHS adopted around May 2025, when it abandoned the "change of circumstances policy" that the ICE office in Atlanta had followed for over four decades.

Under that previous policy, ICE could not arrest someone who had been released again without first determining that their circumstances had materially changed.

"Our clients have complied with the rules imposed by the government. They have appeared at court hearings, attended check-in appointments, and adhered to the conditions of their release," said Corina Scott, attorney for the ACLU of North Carolina.

The key for Florida is that Georgia is part of the 11th Circuit, the same one that covers Florida and Alabama. If the lawsuit succeeds and goes to appeal, a ruling from that court would be binding throughout the circuit.

At the close of this edition, the court has not yet issued a decision on the suspension and class certification motions filed on November 17.

What changes —and what doesn't— for Cubans in Miramar

Thousands of Cubans with the I-220A form periodically visit the ICE office in Miramar, in South Florida, where arrests have been documented during these appointments and alleged abuses that led to a federal complaint filed by the SPLC and Americans for Immigrant Justice.

None of the judicial decisions from California or Georgia have any direct effect in Florida today.

However, the legal line they outline—requiring individual evaluation before re-detaining—is already being used by lawyers in habeas corpus petitions in the Southern District of Florida, where more than 97,000 detainees have resorted to this route since Trump’s return.

The legal landscape for Cubans with I-220A is mixed: last May, the 11th Circuit recognized the right to bail hearings for detainees within the country, but on November 17, that same court ruled that the I-220A is not equivalent to the parole required by the Cuban Adjustment Act, closing that path to residency for many.

While the courts determine the extent of these protections, experts advise continuing to attend appointments in Miramar: failing to appear increases the risk of detention. It is recommended to always have an immigration lawyer readily available before any appointment with ICE.

title: Green Card Update: USCIS Tightens Rules for Abused Migrant Children - Newsweek
description:
The first policy focuses on who qualifies for SIJ protection, giving USCIS officers more scope to examine the circumstances behind a juvenile court order.
The second focuses on the green card process, including when USCIS can review or revoke an earlier SIJ approval and potentially begin removal proceedings.
Read More on News Those with approved SIJ petitions may ultimately be eligible to apply for lawful permanent residence, commonly known as a green card.
The two USCIS policy updates were issued on November 20, took effect immediately, and apply to pending and future cases.
Under PA-2026-17, USCIS said immigration officers will independently determine whether an applicant qualifies for SIJ classification and whether the request is bona fide.
text:
The Trump administration has tightened rules for some young immigrants seeking green cards after experiencing parental abuse, neglect, or abandonment, according to two new policy updates from U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS).

The changes affect the Special Immigrant Juvenile (SIJ) program, which provides immigration protection to certain unmarried immigrants under 21 who have been subject to state juvenile court proceedings related to parental abuse, neglect, abandonment, or a similar basis under state law.

The first policy focuses on who qualifies for SIJ protection, giving USCIS officers more scope to examine the circumstances behind a juvenile court order. The second focuses on the green card process, including when USCIS can review or revoke an earlier SIJ approval and potentially begin removal proceedings.

Read More on News

Those with approved SIJ petitions may ultimately be eligible to apply for lawful permanent residence, commonly known as a green card.

Newsweek has contacted USCIS for comment via email outside working hours.

USCIS primarily administers immigration benefits, including green cards, asylum, work authorization, and citizenship, but has taken a more active role in immigration enforcement under the Trump administration. In October, the agency said it had taken enforcement actions affecting about 2.2 million people since President Donald Trump returned to office.

The two USCIS policy updates were issued on November 20, took effect immediately, and apply to pending and future cases.

Under PA-2026-17, USCIS said immigration officers will independently determine whether an applicant qualifies for SIJ classification and whether the request is bona fide. Officers can interview applicants, seek additional evidence about the factual basis for juvenile court findings, and consider information from government databases.

The same policy directs officers to give additional scrutiny to certain cases involving claims that one parent abandoned the applicant. USCIS said officers should assess whether a primary purpose for seeking the juvenile court order was protection from parental maltreatment rather than obtaining an immigration benefit.

The second policy, PA-2026-18, applies when people with SIJ classification seek green cards. USCIS said applicants must meet the legal requirements for permanent residence and merit a favorable exercise of discretion.

Under the policy, USCIS may revoke an approved SIJ petition for "good and sufficient cause" if it later finds the petition was not bona fide, involved fraud or willful misrepresentation, or was approved in error.

USCIS may also place applicants in deportation proceedings if their green card application is denied or their SIJ petition is revoked.

USCIS said the changes are intended to address fraud, national security, and public safety concerns in the SIJ program.

In a July 2025 report, the agency analyzed more than 300,000 SIJ petitions filed from the beginning of fiscal 2013 through February 2025. It identified 853 known or suspected gang members who had filed SIJ petitions and said most of those petitions were approved. The agency said more than 600 known or suspected MS-13 members had filed SIJ petitions and more than 500 had been approved.

The report also said nearly 19,000 SIJ petitioners had criminal arrests, including at least 120 arrested for murder. The figures have not been independently verified by Newsweek.

"The Special Immigrant Juvenile visa program is infected with fraud and abuse," James Percival, DHS general counsel, wrote in a post on X.

SIJ filings increased from 18,711 in fiscal 2020 to 78,156 in fiscal 2025, a 317 percent increase. USCIS said the growth contributed to a visa backlog that has left applicants waiting about five years after SIJ approval for a visa to become available.

The National Immigration Project and End SIJS Backlog Coalition have criticized the changes, saying they could make it harder for young people who have experienced abuse, neglect, or abandonment to secure permanent protection. The groups said they are considering possible legal action.

"The law Congress wrote hasn't changed. USCIS changed the rules anyway, in the middle of young people’s cases, and told its officers to treat a child who survived neglect, abuse, and abandonment like a suspect," Rebecca Scholtz, supervising attorney at the National Immigration Project and a member of the steering committee of the End SIJS Backlog Coalition, said in a statement.

"Singling out children Congress chose to shield, who lack the power to fight back, is cruelty by design. We will keep fighting to protect the rights of SIJS youth, alongside the young people these dangerous policies target."

Aaron Reichlin-Melnick, senior fellow at the American Immigration Council, wrote in a post on X, "The Trump admin’s war on migrant children continues; under this very major change in policy, the government is likely going to begin mass rejecting applications for Special Immigrant Juvenile Status and moving to deport as many migrant teens and young adults as they can."

title: Federal Tort Claims Act Suit Tests Chicago Border Patrol Arrest - Immigration Analytics
description:
A U.S. citizen pulled from her car by federal agents during Chicago’s Operation Midway Blitz has filed a Federal Tort Claims Act lawsuit against the United States, seeking up to $1 million.
A tort claim against the government cannot reach court until the agency has had six months to answer an administrative claim, and the operation’s first arrests are now past that mark.
The suit pleads false arrest and imprisonment, battery, intentional infliction of emotional distress and negligent denial of medical care.

text:
A U.S. citizen pulled from her car by federal agents during Chicago’s Operation Midway Blitz has filed a Federal Tort Claims Act lawsuit against the United States, seeking up to $1 million. Dayanne Figueroa, 31, a paralegal, sued on Nov. 23 in federal court in Chicago over her Oct. 10, 2025, arrest in the West Town neighborhood, Newsweek reported, and the case is an early test of what damages law still offers people hurt in immigration operations.

A tort claim against the government cannot reach court until the agency has had six months to answer an administrative claim, and the operation’s first arrests are now past that mark. More suits like this one are likely to follow.

Two accounts of one traffic lane

According to the complaint as described by Newsweek, Figueroa had just dropped her son at school when an unmarked SUV driven by a Customs and Border Protection agent moved into her lane and struck her car. Agents pulled her out by the legs, handcuffed her and held her for hours without a warrant or probable cause, first at the Broadview processing facility and then at a site in Lombard, the filing says. Recovering from kidney-related surgery, she was initially refused medical help and later taken to a hospital by ambulance, according to the complaint, which lists internal bleeding, a torn muscle and a broken dental crown among her injuries. The suit pleads false arrest and imprisonment, battery, intentional infliction of emotional distress and negligent denial of medical care. Democracy Forward, a progressive legal group, represents her, Newsmax reported.

The government’s version is the opposite. A DHS spokesperson told Newsweek the driver used her vehicle to “ram” the agents’ vehicle and “violently resisted.” Sen. Dick Durbin, D-Ill., quoted DHS in a November 2025 floor speech as saying she “crashed into an unmarked government vehicle and violently resisted arrest, injuring two officers”; Durbin called that false and said she was released with no charges. A Justice Department spokesperson said agents “are protected by long-established legal immunities and defenses” and that filing a claim “does not mean it has merit,” Newsmax reported.

Why the Federal Tort Claims Act carries the load

People injured by federal officers once could also sue the officers personally under Bivens. In Egbert v. Boule (2022), the Supreme Court refused to recognize such a claim against a Border Patrol agent, citing national security concerns at the border that it said belong to Congress. The practical effect is that the Federal Tort Claims Act, which makes the United States itself liable for certain wrongs of its employees, is now nearly the only damages route after an immigration enforcement encounter.

The act runs on a fixed sequence. Under 28 U.S.C. 2675, a claimant first presents a written claim to the agency, usually on Standard Form 95, and may sue only after a denial or six months of silence, which counts as a denial. Figueroa filed an administrative complaint with DHS and received no response within six months, according to Newsmax and other outlets. The same section generally caps recovery at the sum demanded in that claim, which is why these suits name a fixed ceiling. Claims must be presented within two years under 28 U.S.C. 2401(b), so people hurt in the fall 2025 Chicago operation have until roughly fall 2027.

Assault, battery and false arrest are normally excluded, but 28 U.S.C. 2680(h) restores them when the actor is a federal “investigative or law enforcement officer,” which covers CBP and ICE agents. Figueroa’s claims are the kind Congress expressly allowed.

Where the government is likely to fight

The main battleground is likely to be the discretionary function exception in Section 2680(a), which shields government choices involving judgment or policy. In Martin v. United States (June 2025), a suit over an FBI raid on the wrong house, a unanimous Supreme Court held that the law enforcement proviso overrides only the intentional-tort exception, not the discretionary function exception, and sent the case back for that analysis. That leaves the open question here: whether how agents box in a car and remove a driver is a protected judgment call. Many lower courts have refused to treat unconstitutional conduct as discretionary, so the probable cause allegation is likely to carry real weight.

Two other features shape the stakes. These cases are tried to a judge, not a jury, under 28 U.S.C. 2402, and liability turns on Illinois tort law. Punitive damages are barred, and any award is paid by the government, not the agents, who are not defendants.

More claims in the same pipeline

DHS has said its Illinois operation produced more than 4,500 arrests, Newsweek reported. No public dataset counts how many people stopped were U.S. citizens or how many administrative claims followed. What is visible is a steady run of related disputes, including a $25 million claim by a U.S. citizen shot in Ontario, Calif., the deportation of a Texas man whose citizenship DOJ later conceded, the arrest of U.S. citizens in Oakland and a CBP shooting in Portland.

Next comes the government’s answer, generally due 60 days after the United States is served, and a likely motion to dismiss on discretionary function grounds. How the Northern District of Illinois rules will tell other Midway Blitz claimants how much the act can deliver after Martin.

This article is for general information and is not legal advice.

Newsmax, report on the Figueroa lawsuit (Nov. 25, 2026)

Sen. Dick Durbin, floor remarks on the Figueroa arrest (Nov. 4, 2025)

Martin v. United States, No. 24-362 (June 12, 2025)

title: DOJ acknowledges deportation of U.S. citizen in legal proceedings - Yahoo
description:
That is what happened to Brian José Morales García, a 25-year-old man from Austin, Texas.
In a November 20, 2026, court filing, the Trump administration acknowledged that Morales García is a US citizen.
On April 3, 2026, Morales García was traveling to a job site near Fredericksburg, Texas.
However, authorities did not accept his explanation and contacted federal immigration agents.
Morales García was then taken into custody, setting off a chain of events that led to his removal from the United States.
text:
Depositphotos

A US citizen deported to Mexico

Imagine being stopped on your way to work and suddenly finding yourself in immigration custody, despite being an American citizen. That is what happened to Brian José Morales García, a 25-year-old man from Austin, Texas.

In a November 20, 2026, court filing, the Trump administration acknowledged that Morales García is a US citizen. Although the government previously maintained that he was in the country illegally, it continues to dispute his allegations surrounding his deportation to Mexico.

Depositphotos

Who is Brian Morales García?

Brian José Morales García was born in Denver, Colorado, and grew up in Mexico. Before his deportation, he was living in Austin, Texas, where he worked as an air-conditioning installation technician.

On April 3, 2026, Morales García was traveling to a job site near Fredericksburg, Texas. His journey was interrupted by a traffic stop that led to his detention and months of separation from his home and family.

Virrage Images/Depositphotos

A routine traffic stop

Morales García was riding as a passenger in his boss's vehicle when state and local officers pulled them over. He did not have identification with him at the time of the stop.

He reportedly told officers that his birth certificate and Social Security card were at home. However, authorities did not accept his explanation and contacted federal immigration agents. Morales García was then taken into custody, setting off a chain of events that led to his removal from the United States.

Matt Gush/Shutterstock.com

Why officers questioned him

According to court filings, a federal immigration agent noted that Morales García spoke only Spanish. The agent also examined records relating to his birthplace while investigating his citizenship status.

Customs and Border Protection agent Robert Gil Jr. reviewed Mexican records indicating that Morales García was born in Mexico. According to court filings, Gil also maintained that Morales García had identified Mexico as his birthplace. The circumstances surrounding his statements are disputed in the lawsuit.

Depositphotos

Deported within days

Four days after the traffic stop, on April 7, 2026, Morales García was deported to Mexico despite having claimed American citizenship. His attorneys later challenged the procedures authorities followed before his departure.

The Trump administration later described him in a public statement as someone who had been living in the country illegally. However, that description would later become a major issue in his legal battle, especially after officials reviewed additional information about his birthplace.

Depositphotos

His family tried to intervene

According to Morales García's lawsuit, his family and friends attempted to provide documents proving that he was a US citizen before his deportation. Those efforts allegedly included trying to deliver important records to authorities.

His attorneys argued that officials rejected or failed to properly consider the evidence. The lawsuit also claimed that Morales García signed paperwork agreeing to a quick deportation after agents threatened him with imprisonment. The government disputed his account, creating a legal disagreement over how the removal happened.

Little-known fact: US citizens are not legally required to carry identification or citizenship documents during everyday activities.

Depositphotos

A lawsuit seeks answers

On May 1, 2026, Morales García's attorneys filed a federal lawsuit seeking unspecified financial compensation and legal protections for his right to return to and remain in the United States.

The lawsuit also named unidentified state and local Texas law enforcement officers as defendants. His legal team argued that officials had wrongly treated him as an undocumented immigrant despite his American citizenship. The case put the actions of several law enforcement agencies under closer examination.

gints.ivuskans/Depositphotos

The government disputes his claims

The Trump administration has not accepted Morales García's version of events. In its court filing, the government argued that he went to Mexico voluntarily and therefore had no valid basis for seeking financial damages.

Justice Department attorneys asked the court to dismiss the claims against federal defendants, arguing that Morales García lacked a valid legal basis for seeking damages from the federal government.

Depositphotos

A major admission in court

The November 20, 2026, court filing marked a change from the government's earlier position. Federal authorities had previously questioned Morales García's American citizenship following his detention and deportation.

US Attorney Justin Simmons for the Western District of Texas also confirmed in the filing that Morales García holds dual citizenship in the United States and Mexico. The admission was significant because it confirmed that the man deported in April was, in fact, an American citizen.

Depositphotos

He returned to America

Morales García returned to the United States on August 30, 2026, nearly five months after his deportation. His return followed an agreement between his attorneys and federal authorities after additional citizenship evidence was presented.

Although he was back in the country, his legal dispute was far from over. His attorneys continued pursuing the lawsuit, seeking damages over the circumstances surrounding his removal. The government's request to dismiss the case also meant that a judge would have to consider the competing legal arguments.

morozzz/Depositphotos

The judge has a decision

US District Judge Robert Lee Pitman is overseeing Morales García's lawsuit in Austin. The judge did not immediately rule on the administration's November 20 motion, which specifically asked the court to dismiss the claims against federal officials.

The federal government's dismissal request does not automatically end the lawsuit. The court must determine whether the challenged claims can proceed, while allegations involving state and local officers remain separate from the federal defendants' request.

Little-known fact: The 287(g) provision was added to the Immigration and Nationality Act through a law passed in 1996.

Depositphotos

Other citizens faced detention

Morales García's case is not an isolated example. An updated ProPublica investigation identified 519 US citizens reportedly detained by immigration agents between January 2025 and October 21, 2026. Researchers noted that the actual number could be higher.

These cases have drawn attention to the importance of accurate identity checks. They also highlight why citizenship claims and supporting documents need careful review before immigration authorities take action against someone.

Why did Instacart agree to a $5 million settlement with the Department of Justice? Discover what prompted the hiring-related agreement and what it means for the company's employment practices.

Depositphotos

A wider enforcement debate

Texas is among the states where law enforcement agencies cooperate with federal immigration authorities. The Texas Department of Public Safety participates in the federal 287(g) program, which authorizes designated state and local officers to perform certain immigration enforcement duties.

Morales García's case has added another layer to the debate over these partnerships and deportation procedures. While his lawsuit continues, the government's admission raises an important question about how officials can prevent American citizens from being wrongly removed from their own country.
