text:
This editorial originally appeared in The Dallas Morning News:

In his interview with “60 Minutes,” President Donald Trump seemed to extend an olive branch to Democrats, acknowledging his deportation policies may have been “too rough” and floating the possibility of bipartisan immigration reform, calling it “doable.”

That gesture of goodwill was called into question the same day the interview aired, when Trump elevated Stephen Miller, the architect of his administration’s violent immigration crackdown, to White House chief of staff.

On the one hand, the Trump White House recognizes that most Americans are not on board with the aggressive removal of immigrant workers with strong community ties and no criminal history. But by promoting Miller, Trump is indulging his worst impulses and sending mixed signals to the incoming Congress.

There is still a chance for Trump to rise above a broken legacy on immigration that includes the killings of Americans and immigrants on his watch. He could be the president who not only fixed the crisis at the southern border but also found a bipartisan path forward for broader immigration reform.

As things stand today, however, he is the man who unleashed ill-trained immigration officers to brutalize undocumented immigrants and U.S. citizens alike.

A united Congress can bring momentum to this issue. Voters punished Republicans down the ballot for Trump’s immigration excesses. Republicans had said before that a secure border was necessary before they would entertain a comprehensive immigration bill. Well, we have a secure border now.

Meanwhile, it’s up to Democrats taking their seats in Congress to stand by their pro-border control stances from this midterm election season.

Americans’ broad support for stronger border control never equated to indiscriminate, unnecessarily cruel immigration enforcement. Republicans now face an important choice: continue a divisive approach that deepens public distrust, or work toward meaningful reforms that fix America’s broken immigration system.

Reforms should focus on temporary guest workers in industries where there is a shortage of labor, such as agriculture, as well as visa programs for skilled workers. Congress should also secure a permanent pathway for recipients of DACA, or Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals.

The Obama-era program offered temporary protection from deportation to undocumented immigrants who had been brought into the U.S. illegally as children. But DACA recipients have been stuck in limbo, caught between lawsuits challenging the program and Congress’ inaction. Yet 81% of Americans support a legal pathway for DACA holders as long as they meet certain requirements, according to a recent Gallup poll.

This editorial page has also raised concerns about the reshaping of immigration courts reviewing asylum cases. We’ve swung between a permissive asylum system to one that seems unfairly biased against immigrants. Congress should review these courts.

A comprehensive approach balances the needs of American businesses and employees while ensuring immigrants are treated fairly, with clear and predictable guidelines.

Congress should take advantage of the current public interest in immigration reform and find the balance we’ve been looking to establish for decades.

text:
The United Nations Special Rapporteur on counterterrorism & human rights and 10 other mandates of the United Nations Special Procedures have today expressed their ‘grave concern’ about the ‘transboundary abduction’ of Thuan Duc Nguyen and Hiep Tran.

Thuan and Hiep are pro-democracy activists who were attacked and kidnapped in Cambodia before resurfacing 10 days later in Vietnam, where they are now detained on terrorism charges relating to their exercise of freedom of association and assembly.

The signatories to the Special Procedures’ statement disclose that they have contacted the Government of Vietnam, calling upon it to disclose the circumstances of arrest and any involvement of its officials the ‘alleged abductions, transfers and enforced disappearances’. They have also called upon Cambodia to investigate what happened on its territory.

Alex Tinsley, of Doughty Street’s International team, acts for the families of Thuan and Hiep together with colleagues Maria Hessen-Jacobsen and Aleksander Hatlem (Norway), Alison Battisson (Australia), and Michael Polak (UK). The team have raised the case in international forums and in Norway and Australia, Thuan and Hiep’s states of nationality.

The legal team have today issued a statementwelcoming the Special Procedures’ action and calling upon Norway and Australia to escalate their responses in the face of this serious case of transnational repression (TNR).

TNR is an umbrella term for the methods by which states seek to silence, intimidate and harass their opponents beyond their borders (physical attacks, abuse of legal cooperation such as INTERPOL tools and extradition, surveillance etc.). TNR has been a major priority of the international community (via the United Nations, G7, Council of Europe, European Union).

States’ TNR policies have been tended to be focused how to combat TNR at home, e.g. by ensuring resilient asylum and extradition systems and prosecuting acts of TNR committed on their own territory. Thuan and Hiep’s case puts in focus the need for effective responses when citizens are subject to ‘overseas TNR’ when exercising freedom of assembly on their travels.

Karoline Leavitt is taking a jab at Ms. Rachel after the educator and popular content creator met with families and children facing deportation at a federal youth immigration court in New York City.

“If Ms. Rachel truly cares about all children, she should visit the Angel Family kids who lost their mom or dad to an illegal alien criminal,” Leavitt, the former White House press secretary, wrote in a post on X Nov. 24. “Or the innocent children the Trump Administration continues to rescue from human traffickers who exploited them during four years of the Democrats’ open border.”

“But she won’t,” Leavitt added.

Leavitt doubles down on Ms. Rachel on Fox News

In a later appearance on Fox News, Leavitt accused Ms. Rachel, whose full name is Rachel Accurso, of being a left-wing activist "in reality" while "masquerading as an innocent children's entertainer."

"Her stunt at the courthouse was reminiscent to me of that photo shoot that (Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez) did down at President Trump's border wall during his first term," Leavitt said. "You remember that, when she was pretending to cry? There were no tears from AOC or Ms. Rachel for four years under the Biden administration, when the Democrat Party opened our borders to violent illegal alien criminals who took the lives of innocents Americans across the country."

Leavitt said she felt compelled to speak out about this because during her time as the White House press secretary, she "had the honor and the privilege of getting to know so many of those Angel Families whose lives have been forever devastated and torn apart because of the vicious crimes committed against them."

"Their loved ones taken away in heinous acts of murder because of people who should never have been in this country in the first place," Leavitt said.

She added that one can have sympathies for unaccompanied minors and young children "entangled" in immigration courts because of the "irresponsibility of their parents, who should never illegally brought them into our country in the first place" but that "we must be a nation of laws."

USA TODAY has reached out to Accurso for a comment on Leavitt's remarks.

Ms. Rachel says child facing deportation 'stole my heart'

Accurso visited the court in Lower Manhattan with Rep.-elect Brad Lander, D-New York, to shine a light on "a growing crisis" of "immigrant children being forced to fight for their safety and futures without an attorney," according to a Nov. 24 post on Instagram from ICARE, a coalition of legal advocates working to expand access to legal representation for immigrant children facing deportation in New York City.

“I think about how that makes a child feel whether or not you are removable. … I don’t want any child to hear that word associated with them,” Accurso told ABC7NY. "I think our problems would really be a lot less if we all just focus on taking care of kids and centered kids (in) policies."

Accurso said a fourth grader facing deportation, Angel, was reunited with his mother but they do not have representation.

“He came and gave me this, and it says, the first thing he wants is an immigration lawyer,” she told Spectrum News, holding up a letter Angel, 9, wrote. “And then Nikes that are blue, and a TV. And he’ll be getting all of these things from me, don’t you worry. He just stole my heart.”

Lander told the outlet the "new Democratic majority is going to stand up for these kids."

Accurso, in a post on Instagram, said "seeing this precious child, not even able to reach the mic in immigration court, and hearing the word 'removable' over and over" made her "feel sick."

"Grown ups need to get it together and stop traumatizing kids," she wrote on Instagram. "The fact that children are expected to argue their immigration cases themselves is unconscionable. It’s traumatizing and absurd."

She added that while she's "getting this child a lawyer," she's "so scared for the other kids!"

Accurso has openly advocated for immigrant children, most recently calling for an end to Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s (ICE) practice of detaining families at Texas’ Dilley Immigration Processing Center during a meeting with Texas Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa on Nov. 19.

During the meeting, Accurso called the detention of children "a violation of human rights of kids" and praised Hinojosa for calling for an end to the controversial immigration practice.

In an interview with The Texas Tribune published Nov. 18, Hinojosa, a Democrat, said she had a positive conversation with President Donald Trump and that they both want a secure border.

text:
At least two additional Justice Department civil rights leaders are departing after their Trump-appointed chief recently did the same, emptying the leadership ranks of an office in flux since the midterms.

Jeffrey Morrison and Eric Sell, two of the four deputy assistant attorneys general in the Civil Rights Division, will exit in the coming days, while more officials are expected to follow suit, according to people familiar with their plans. The newly appointed acting head of the division, Craig Trainor, is splitting his time between DOJ and his Senate-confirmed role at the Department of Housing and Urban Development, the individuals added.

Trainor inherited a chief of staff, Matthew Zandi, who has already been demoted to special counsel, leaving the key operational position vacant, one of the people said.

The thinning front office expands the uncertainty on the future vision for a civil rights unit that played a prominent role in President Donald Trump’s first two years — overhauling enforcement to advance causes important for conservatives and the White House. Civil Rights Division attrition is part of a wave of Trump DOJ political appointees who’ve been leaving or contemplating new employment since voters overwhelmingly rejected the Trump agenda in the midterms.

Morrison, for instance, is retiring at the end of November after 21 years at the division, said the individuals, who spoke anonymously about internal personnel matters. A longtime career attorney, he was elevated in the second Trump administration to oversee the division’s aggressive efforts targeting universities and other employers for their diversity policies and alleged antisemitism.

Harmeet Dhillon, the official who spearheaded the administration’s civil rights transformation away from its traditional mission protecting marginalized communities, resigned Nov. 5. Sell is following Dhillon out of DOJ, just as he’d joined her at the division upon her swearing in last year — after spending the prior three years working for Dhillon’s nonprofit, Center for American Liberty.

“Staff departures are a fact of life in every department and every administration,” Kiersten Pels, a DOJ spokesperson, said in a statement. “These moves were planned well in advance, and the Division remains staffed with experienced career and political leaders.”

The Nov. 10 announcement of Trainor as acting head was seen as the administration’s attempt to install a longer term director than his temporary title suggested, given the long odds of confirming an assistant attorney general when Democrats take control of the Senate next year. But his inability to shed responsibilities as HUD’s assistant secretary for fair housing and equal opportunity may call into question his bandwidth to run a sprawling DOJ office with jurisdiction over voting rights, immigration employment, and more.

“Acting Assistant Attorney General Trainor is leading the Civil Rights Division, and the Division will continue to ensure that every American’s civil rights are protected,” DOJ’s Pels said in her statement.

Dhillon had stocked her office with numerous Trump-appointed lawyers who were handed heavy caseloads as about three quarters of the 400 career attorneys left the division in this administration. Trainor would need to recruit a new batch of political aides to offset some of the losses.

text:
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement said Tuesday, Nov. 24, that San Mateo County Board of Supervisors President Noelia Corzo attempted to impede ICE operations and “verbally assaulted” several agents in a parking-related altercation over the weekend in Redwood City.

On Saturday afternoon, Nov. 21, Corzo confronted two cars with ICE agents, asking the agents not to park in spots designated for county employees near the Maguire Correctional Facility. Corzo posted videos of the encounter on social media.

“I was calmly asking him to move his vehicle to one of the public spots as our ordinance prohibits ICE from using county property to stage for immigration enforcement purposes,” Corzo wrote in one of the posts.

San Mateo County’s noncooperation ordinance bans federal immigration enforcement from using county property to stage or establish an operational base for enforcement action.

But ICE said it’s allowed to enforce federal immigration laws without permission from local authorities.

Corzo has accused one of the agents of assault, writing on one of the posts that he “pushed” her on her left shoulder. The alleged assault is not visible, but suddenly Corzo tells the officer not to touch her after he appears to say, “Do not touch the car.”

Corzo then yelled several profanities at the officers, telling them to leave, as seen in the videos.

A statement Tuesday from ICE, however, contends Corzo was “preventing ICE agents from driving their vehicle” and that a crowd gathered in the parking lot as she “verbally assaulted” the agents.

The Redwood City Police Department is investigating the altercation. Police officers contacted Corzo and completed a police report with her allegations.

The department is asking those with information regarding the case to contact its non-emergency number at 650-780-7100.

ICE operations would continue, the agency said.

“ICE will not be slowing down, regardless of the meaningless taunts or insults from pro-criminal illegal alien politicians like Noelia Corzo,” the agency said.

Arrests by ICE have risen in San Mateo County this month, detaining at least 37 people people since the start of November, according to Faith in Action Bay Area, which operates the Rapid Response Hotline for the county. Rapid Response is coalition of immigrant rights activists that connect people to resources who are impacted by immigration enforcement.

Faith in Action Bay Area urges the public to call the Rapid Response Hotline immediately at 203-666-4472 if anyone sees ICE activity. More resources can be found at smcgov.org/ceo/rapid-response-hotline.

This story was written by Alise Maripuu for Bay City News.

text:
Ariel Antonio Velásquez Morales’ smile was short-lived. Just a few days ago, he was happily posing for a camera with a symbolic check for the $1 million he had won in the lottery. Today, this Salvadoran immigrant is in the custody of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), which claims there is a deportation order against him and that, therefore, he should not have claimed the prize.

Velásquez Morales was arrested by ICE agents in Boston, Massachusetts, days after visiting a state lottery office to present a winning instant-win lottery scratch ticket and begin the process of claiming his prize.

The Salvadoran spent $10 on scratch-off tickets at a store in East Boston. He opted to receive the prize as a lump-sum cash payment, receiving $650,000 before taxes. “Looks like his luck ran out,” Micah Bock, ICE’s assistant director of public affairs, noted sarcastically in a press release.

On its X account, the federal agency maintained that the immigrant was not entitled to receive the money because he was in the country without legal authorization.

“The rights and privileges reserved for American citizens are for American citizens, NOT illegal aliens,” the agency posted. “The patriots of ICE continue to work around the clock to enforce our nation’s laws and serve the American people.”

According to ICE, Velásquez Morales entered the country illegally in 2013, and Border Patrol agents in the Rio Grande Valley, Texas, detained him, served him a summons to appear before an immigration judge, and released him. When he failed to appear in court, a final deportation order was issued in April 2014.

The Salvadoran immigrant was arrested early Tuesday morning following a brief foot chase in East Boston, according to Fox News.

ICE did not respond to a series of questions sent by this newspaper regarding Velásquez Morales’s whereabouts and the fate of the prize he won.

Until Wednesday, the Massachusetts Lottery’s Facebook page still displayed a photo of a smiling Velásquez Morales, posted last Saturday. In a brief statement sent to this newsroom, the agency emphasized that the official rules of the Massachusetts Lottery allow any adult to purchase tickets and claim prizes. “Anyone over the age of 18 who is physically present in Massachusetts can purchase lottery tickets at retail locations and win prizes,” its press office said.

On its website, the agency does not list U.S. citizenship or legal residency as requirements for participation. It emphasizes that “non-residents can collect their prizes at the same locations by the same methods available to all players.”

In a statement quoted by the Boston Herald, David Wesling, acting director of ICE’s local Enforcement and Removal Operations (ERO) office, also commented on the case: “For more than 12 years, Ariel Antonio Velasquez-Morales ignored a judge’s order to deport and remained in the United States illegally. Thanks to Massachusetts sanctuary laws, illegal aliens feel comfortable enough to win lotteries and take the payouts that lawful, tax-paying citizens should be collecting,” he said.

Wesling added: “In this case, the individual’s luck has run out: he will remain in ICE custody pending his removal from the United States. ICE in Boston will continue to prioritize public safety by arresting and removing illegal aliens who have broken the law, whether they are millionaires or not.”

title: ECHR finds fault with treatment of some border crossers from Belarus
description:
"The Court first considered the removal of the applicant children and their accompanying family members.
"Accordingly, the Latvian authorities should have taken proper account of that and assessed their need for protection prior to their removal to Belarus.
However, the Latvian authorities had disregarded the evident vulnerability of those applicants and had proceeded with their summary removal to Belarus," said the ECHR.
The Latvian authorities had not therefore fulfilled their obligation under Article 3 of the Convention on the occasions in question.
The ECHR produced a video about the whole set of rulings, which can be viewed above.
text:
The case of 'H.M.M. and Others versus Latvia' (case no. 42165/21) was part of a trio of cases that involved similar ones in Poland and Lithuania, all of whom have had to deal with Belarus' ovet weaponisation of illegal migration flows.

The judgments delivered by the ECHR have affirmed the need for the national authorities to ensure that even migrants crossing borders by illegal means "benefit from the essential protection of Article 3 against the risk of inhuman or degrading treatment."

At the outset, the Court reiterated that States have the right to control the entry of foreign

nationals into their territory including by fully closing their borders. It went on to find that in a context of instrumentalisation of migration, "the removal of a foreign national to the instrumentalising State would not, as such, constitute a violation of Article 3 (prohibition of torture and inhuman and degrading treatment)."

However, before removing an individual in such circumstances, the national authorities have an obligation "to detect those individuals who would be particularly at risk of suffering or enduring ill-treatment" such as minors or people disabilities.

Consequently, in the case of H.M.M. and Others v. Latvia, the Court held that the applicant children fell within the category of vulnerability and that their adequate protection could not be ensured without the presence and support of their close family members.

"The Court held, unanimously, that there had therefore been a violation of Article 3 in respect of the applicant children and their accompanying family members on account of their removal to Belarus on various dates. However, in respect of the adult applicants in that case, who did not fall into either category, the Court held, unanimously, that there had been no violation of Article 3."

So, in essence, the minors who were part of the application should have had their other family members with them, even though those same family members were not subject to the same protection and, arguably, were the ones who had placed them in such an extremely dangerous situation in the first place.

The ECHR explained: "The application was struck out for seven of the original 26 applicants. Of the 19 remaining applicants, 12 made up three family groups comprising two parents and two children. The question of whether and on which dates the applicants had actually been on Latvian territory and therefore within Latvia’s jurisdiction was examined in the light of all of the relevant evidence. The Court made detailed findings on that point.

"The Court first considered the removal of the applicant children and their accompanying family members. The Court reiterated that children, whether accompanied or unaccompanied, had to be treated as an extremely vulnerable group with specific needs that were related to their age, lack of independence and asylum‑seeker or migrant status. The exploitative nature of instrumentalisation of migration was particularly apparent where such young children were brought into it. Therefore, in accordance with its approach as set out above in such cases, the Court considered that the applicant children, four of whom had been infants or very young children, and one of whom had been nearly 11 years old, belonged to the group of people whose personal vulnerability was evident in view of their young age. Those five applicants should therefore have been detected, at the time of their interception by the Latvian border guards, as falling within the first category.

"Accordingly, the Latvian authorities should have taken proper account of that and assessed their need for protection prior to their removal to Belarus. However, the Latvian authorities had disregarded the evident vulnerability of those applicants and had proceeded with their summary removal to Belarus," said the ECHR.

In the specific context of instrumentalisation of migration, the Court emphasised "the importance of families being kept together given the complete dependence of the child applicants on their accompanying family members."

The Court considered that adequate protection of the child applicants in the case could not have been ensured without the presence and support of their close family members. That referred to the applicant parents, and also to applicant no. 25, as the adult sibling of applicant no. 26.

"That degree of dependence should have been recognised by the national authorities and included in the required assessment of the child applicants’ need for protection. The Latvian authorities had not therefore fulfilled their obligation under Article 3 of the Convention on the occasions in question. Furthermore, they had failed to demonstrate that they had put in place an effective procedure enabling the applicant children, who had been evidently personally vulnerable, and their close family members travelling with them, to benefit from the protection required by Article 3 of the Convention before their removal to Belarus."

The ECHR produced a video about the whole set of rulings, which can be viewed above.

text:
A federal judge in the District of Columbia Wednesday issued a classwide injunction to prevent the Trump administration from implementing its second attempt at redefining the constitutional right to birthright citizenship.

The order from Judge Christopher Reid Cooper will remain in effect while litigation continues. A classwide injunction blocks action affecting a defined group of individuals, as opposed to a nationwide injunction.

In a memorandum opinion, Cooper noted the Supreme Court earlier this year denied President Donald Trump’s executive order that would deny citizenship to babies born from immigrants either in the country unlawfully or on a temporary basis, in the case Barbara v. Trump.

“Yet Barbara’s ink had scarcely dried when the President issued a second executive order—Executive Order 14418, at issue here—directing federal agencies to withhold recognition of citizenship from additional categories of U.S.-born children with noncitizen parents,” he wrote. “As the Supreme Court has made clear, however, the President cannot carve out new exceptions to birthright citizenship for children born within the United States and subject to its laws.”

The American Civil Liberties Union, which led the first challenge against the Trump administration’s birthright citizenship order and is leading the second, welcomed the ruling.

“Enough is enough,” Cody Wofsy, deputy director of the ACLU’s Immigrants’ Rights Project, said in a statement. “The Supreme Court has twice rejected efforts to gut birthright citizenship, in 1898 and again earlier this year. Third time is not the charm, and the President needs to accept that birthright citizenship is the law of the land.”

The Department of Justice did not respond to States Newsroom’s request for comment.

Earlier this month, Cooper seemed skeptical of the legality of the Trump administration’s second attempt to redefine the constitutional right to birthright citizenship.

The president’s recent executive orders would deny citizenship to babies born in the United States to parents deemed part of a designated terrorist organization and to parents who purposefully came to the United States to gain citizenship in what critics call “birth tourism.”

The executive order also aimed to deny citizenship to children born to foreign diplomatic staff and children born in U.S. territories where Congress has not passed a law granting citizenship.

There is already a small carve out for birthright citizenship, extended to children born to foreign diplomats.

title: New report and lawsuit reveal the ordeal of 733 pregnant women in ICE custody
description:
In the first 16 months of the Republican’s second term, 733 pregnant women remained in the custody of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), most of them for extended periods.
Among those facing high-risk pregnancies, few had access to specialized medical care and were not released immediately.
From nine pregnant women in ICE custody in January 2025, the number rose to 128 last March, representing a 1,320% increase.
Through this tool, it gathered testimonies from women who suffered miscarriages, were malnourished, or did not receive specialized medical care.
“There, we heard testimonies from women with life-threatening conditions who were denied medical care,” the group notes.
text:
Even when it comes to pregnant immigrants, the Trump administration has proven itself indifferent. In the first 16 months of the Republican’s second term, 733 pregnant women remained in the custody of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), most of them for extended periods. One of them was detained for seven months. Among those facing high-risk pregnancies, few had access to specialized medical care and were not released immediately.

These revelations appear in a report published Tuesday by the Women’s Refugee Commission (WRC), which questions the federal administration’s lack of empathy toward a particularly vulnerable population — both in ICE detention centers, which have been repeatedly cited for mistreating immigrants — and in local jail facilities that held contracts with the government and where most of these women were held.

The report accompanies a lawsuit that the WRC and organizations such as the Venezuelan Association of Massachusetts and the Workers’ Center of Central New York filed in a District of Columbia court. In it, they demand that ICE and the Department of Homeland Security put an end to the ordeal suffered by these women, who are caught up in Trump’s immigration crackdown.

“Immigration detention has become a black box of impunity,” said Zain Lakhani, director of the WRC’s Migrant Rights and Justice Program, in a statement. This organization, Lakhani said, has documented “a substantial increase in the number of pregnant women in detention and brought to light grave concerns about their treatment and care.” “Now, this data shows that these abuses are happening at scale,” he added.

Among these abuses, it is notable that of some 128 women diagnosed with high-risk pregnancies, only four were transferred to a “higher level of care.” The report details at least 16 cases of miscarriages recorded between January 2025 and February 2026.

Malnourished and sleeping on the floor

During Joe Biden’s administration, between 2021 and 2024, ICE released most of the pregnant women it had detained — either on parole or under a promise to appear in court.

But at the start of Trump’s second term, the number of women in detention began to rise as the president’s immigration crackdown intensified. From nine pregnant women in ICE custody in January 2025, the number rose to 128 last March, representing a 1,320% increase. Most of them — about 75% — were held in state or local facilities under contract with the government, which, according to the WRC report, “have lower medical standards and higher taxpayer costs.”

The report estimates that ICE spent at least $4 million on the detention of 557 pregnant women, not including the costs of medical care.

The Department of Homeland Security has not commented on this report and lawsuit, but in the summer of 2025, in response to an investigation by the office of Georgia Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff — which documented 14 credible reports of mistreatment of pregnant women in ICE custody — the agency denied having neglected these migrants.

The reports compiled by Ossoff’s office point to deficiencies such as a lack of adequate medical care and timely checkups, the absence of emergency care when needed, the denial of adequate snacks and meals, and the requirement to sleep on the floor due to overcrowding.

In its response, DHS stated that these women received medical care and nutritional support, and maintained that “the detention of pregnant women is rare and subject to rigorous oversight and review.” It added that “no pregnant woman has been forced to sleep on the floor.”

Seven months in custody

Human rights advocates, Democratic members of Congress, and journalistic investigations have documented an alarming increase in the number of pregnant women detained by ICE during the current administration, which is determined to deport as many undocumented immigrants as possible.

“Advocates interviewed more than a dozen women, and in their letter, also describe disturbing accounts of shackling and use of restraint during transport, solitary confinement, denial of prenatal vitamins, inadequate food, delayed or substandard medical care, and lack of interpretation during medical visits. One woman experienced a dangerous infection after a miscarriage due to ICE’s medical neglect,” states a letter sent by the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) to ICE in October 2025.

The indiscriminate detention of these women demonstrates that ICE has failed to comply with its own directive, established in 2021, which stipulates that, except in exceptional circumstances or for other legally justified reasons, pregnant women, women in the postpartum period, or breastfeeding women should not remain in the agency’s custody.

In its recent report, the WRC places special emphasis on the length of time these women spend in detention. During the Biden administration, the average was about five days. Under the Trump administration, that figure skyrocketed to 43 days — a 750% increase.

At least 145 women were held in custody for 90 days or more. The report highlights the case of one woman who was detained for 219 days — nearly seven months into her pregnancy.

To collect reports from these migrants, the WRC launched a tool called the Detention Pregnancy Tracker in September 2025. Through this tool, it gathered testimonies from women who suffered miscarriages, were malnourished, or did not receive specialized medical care.

The organization even traveled to Honduras to interview recently deported individuals. “There, we heard testimonies from women with life-threatening conditions who were denied medical care,” the group notes.

title: State Department reports downplay the dangers in countries that asylum seekers are fleeing
description:
“Overall, Gracias a Dios is a low-crime, functioning department,” says a State Department background report obtained by The Associated Press.
In a statement, the State Department said that in line with US laws and regulations it “may provide information about conditions in foreign countries” to immigration courts and US Citizenship and Immigration Services.
The Justice Department, which oversees immigration courts, did not respond to a request for comment on what role the reports play in influencing asylum decisions.
Former officials and advocates say the six-page reports pale in comparison to traditional State Department human rights reports, lengthy dissections of more than 100 nations around the world, which under the second Trump administration have been truncated and delayed.
They are “especially problematic given that the country reports themselves for last year have yet to be issued,” he said.
text:
MINNEAPOLIS: In its travel adviseries, the US State Department warns Americans not to visit Honduras’ Gracias a Dios region, alerting them to violent crime, armed robbery, murder and active terrorist groups.

But for Hondurans, the message is less stark. “Overall, Gracias a Dios is a low-crime, functioning department,” says a State Department background report obtained by The Associated Press.

The report, and similar documents about Guatemala, Mexico and El Salvador, were prepared for use in immigration courts, where asylum denial rates have soared to 94 percent during President Donald Trump’s second term.

The reports use cherry-picked data, careful phrasing and, in some cases, facts that don’t stand up to scrutiny to create misleading depictions of countries that are, in fact, often plagued by violence, government corruption and police inaction.

They appear designed to make it easier for judges to deny asylum to people from those nations fleeing domestic violence and criminal gangs, painting pictures of life in their home countries that often clash with reality.

The reports have been “reverse-engineered,” said Elliott Young, a professor at Lewis & Clark College who analyzed the documents for the college’s Migration and Asylum Lab.

“They’re trying to hit the most frequent kinds of (asylum) cases that come up and provide counterevidence to the overwhelming evidence that these are dangerous places,” said Young, a scholar of Latin America and asylum law who has testified as an expert witness in more than 700 asylum cases.

In a statement, the State Department said that in line with US laws and regulations it “may provide information about conditions in foreign countries” to immigration courts and US Citizenship and Immigration Services. The Justice Department, which oversees immigration courts, did not respond to a request for comment on what role the reports play in influencing asylum decisions.

A system in turmoil — and targeted

Cutting back on asylum has been a centerpiece of Trump’s immigration crackdown dating to his first term, when he dismissed migrants waiting in Mexico to get into the US as “not legitimate asylum-seekers.”

Most asylum seekers, the Republican president said, were fleeing poverty.

“Asylum is a very special protection intended only for those fleeing government persecution based on race, religion and other protected status,” he said in a 2018 White House appearance.

Trump was years out of date. While asylum was largely seen after World War II as a way to protect people fleeing political persecution, the definition was expanded long ago, including to encompass some people fleeing domestic and criminal violence.

But he had a point about poverty.

Legal and illegal migration, particularly from Latin America, has exploded over the past two decades as people have sought more economic opportunity, with increasing asylum claims based on safety fears from domestic partners and criminal gangs.

Even during President Joe Biden’s years, most asylum claims were rejected.

But denials have jumped from roughly 72 percent at the end of that Democratic administration to 94 percent in June under Trump, according to the data research nonprofit Transactional Records Access Clearinghouse.

Trump was elected to a second term in part by focusing on frustrated voters who had seen illegal immigration soar under Biden, with border arrests from Mexico reaching a record 250,000 in December 2023. The asylum system, meanwhile, faced a backlog of millions of cases.

The Trump administration has reshaped immigration courts as part of its push to increase deportations, organizing mass hearings, authorizing military lawyers as immigration judges, and giving judges more leeway to summarily dismiss claims.

A sanitized view of troubled countries

Immigration judges must weigh whether people seeking asylum based on domestic violence or criminal threats have a reasonable fear of persecution because of their race, religion, nationality, political views or an often-debated catch-all category, “membership in a particular social group.” They also have to show that their government can’t or won’t protect them and that they can’t move elsewhere in their home country to escape persecution.

The reports offer what can sometimes seem like travel brochure descriptions of life in these countries.

They mention good schools, low crime, quality hospitals and constitutions that protect individual rights, with brief notes that “the availability of services” can vary across each country.

Take El Salvador, where the government of President Nayib Bukele has long faced accusations of widespread human rights abuses, including torture.

The State Department report takes a far more generous view of the situation, noting the government’s approach to rights abuses “is no different than that of developed countries in Europe and North America, including the United States itself,” and highlighting a handful of prosecutions tied to the civil war, which ended in 1992.

“In any country, a rogue official can mistreat those under their power,” it says.

For Honduras’ Gracias a Dios province, violent crime rates “compare favorably with rates of violent crime in many parts of the United States,” says the report.

Former officials and advocates say the six-page reports pale in comparison to traditional State Department human rights reports, lengthy dissections of more than 100 nations around the world, which under the second Trump administration have been truncated and delayed.

“These shorter reports clearly don’t address the full range of human rights issues that the country reports have traditionally addressed,” said Scott Busby, former deputy assistant secretary in the Bureau of Democracy, Human Rights and Labor at the State Department and now a senior adviser at the group Human Rights First.

They are “especially problematic given that the country reports themselves for last year have yet to be issued,” he said.

Looking at asylum-seekers’ ability to move elsewhere

In many ways, the reports appear aimed most directly at asylum regulations around a person’s ability to escape persecution by simply moving.

Those regulations are key for anyone seeking asylum based on domestic or criminal violence.

The reports highlight specific parts of each country, mentioning places like an off-the-beaten-track tourist destination in Guatemala and a province in El Salvador that has low crime and 24-hour emergency medical care.

But those mentions only tell part of the story.

“The fact that there may be pockets of a country that are relatively safe for some people doesn’t mean that everybody can just move to that part of the country,” said Neela Chakravartula, an asylum attorney with the Center for Gender & Refugee Studies at the University of California College of the Law, San Francisco.

If that were the case, Chakravartula said: “We’d all be living in Malibu.”

name: Human Rights
title: Under threat of deportation to Liberia, Kilmar Abrego Garcia leaves US for Spain
description:
Speaking from Spain, Abrego Garcia said, “The government did not decide where my story continues.
Abrego Garcia had lived in the United States since he was a teenager.
In court filings, Abrego Garcia described guards kicking him and striking him with wooden batons as they marched him to his cell.
What Abrego Garcia escaped can be seen in the fate of Diadie Camara, who fled hereditary slavery in Mauritania.
Abrego Garcia escaped a deportation flight to Liberia and chose his own destination on Tuesday.
text:
Kilmar Abrego Garcia, the Maryland sheet metal worker whom the Trump administration illegally deported to a Salvadoran torture prison in March 2025, arrived in Madrid Wednesday morning with his wife, Jennifer Vasquez Sura. Before he could board the commercial flight at Washington Dulles International Airport Tuesday night, federal authorities had to remove the GPS monitor strapped to his ankle. A federal judge had ordered them to do so.

The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) celebrated his “self-deportation.” For more than a year, Abrego Garcia had been willing to leave for Costa Rica, whose government had offered to receive him and protect him from being sent back to El Salvador. The Trump administration insisted on the power to choose where he would go. Its preferred destination was Liberia, a West African country where he had no ties.

Speaking from Spain, Abrego Garcia said, “The government did not decide where my story continues. My family and I decide our future.” His attorney, Simon Sandoval-Moshenberg, described the departure as “temporary.” In a statement reported by the BBC, he said the family expected that “the next administration will prioritise reunifying this family and bringing him back to Maryland.” Abrego Garcia has a US citizen wife and son. His lawyer said a return would require a waiver he does not expect the Trump administration to grant.

The November 20 order by US District Judge Paula Xinis, unsealed Wednesday, spells out what it took to get Abrego Garcia safely onto a plane. Officials had to lift any alert that might lead to his detention or prevent him from boarding. Xinis expressly forbade them to ask “any air carrier, common carrier, or person to detain, divert, or delay” his journey or to arrange for him to be sent elsewhere. The same order directed the government to record his departure as the execution of his removal order.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin declared Tuesday, “Now, this El Salvadoran man cannot terrorize innocent Americans.” His department branded Abrego Garcia a “Human Trafficker, Wife Beater, and MS-13 Gang Member” in the headline of its press release. Further down the page, DHS retreated to “suspected” and “accused.” It cited no criminal conviction for any of these claims. The one criminal case the administration brought against him ended in dismissal at the trial court.

Abrego Garcia had lived in the United States since he was a teenager. He was raising three children in Maryland with Vasquez Sura and working as a union sheet metal apprentice. On March 12, 2025, he finished a shift in Baltimore and picked up his five-year-old son from the boy’s grandmother. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents pulled him over with the child in the back seat. According to the family’s court filing, agents gave Vasquez Sura 10 minutes to collect her son before they would turn him over to child protective services.

Three days later, the government flew him to El Salvador in violation of a 2019 immigration court order barring his return because he faced persecution there. More than 250 men were delivered to President Nayib Bukele’s Terrorism Confinement Center (CECOT) that weekend. Trump had invoked the Alien Enemies Act of 1798 against Venezuelans he claimed belonged to a gang called Tren de Aragua. The flights went on to El Salvador despite District Judge James Boasberg’s instruction to turn back planes carrying men covered by his order. Abrego Garcia, a Salvadoran, had his own protective court order. Of the 238 Venezuelans sent to CECOT, 60 Minutes could find no criminal record for 179.

In court filings, Abrego Garcia described guards kicking him and striking him with wooden batons as they marched him to his cell. They forced prisoners to kneel from 9 at night until 6 in the morning and beat those who collapsed. Held without access to his lawyers and given so little food that he lost 30 pounds in two weeks, he was later transferred to another Salvadoran prison. Other prisoners later told Human Rights Watch that the water they had to drink was sometimes green and contained visible vermin.

As protests spread in Maryland and across the country, Trump circulated an altered photograph of Abrego Garcia’s hand where the letters and numerals “MS-13” had been superimposed above his finger tattoos. Trump presented them as proof of gang membership.

On April 10, 2025, the Supreme Court upheld the requirement that the government facilitate his release. The administration waited until June 6 to bring him back, by which time it had secured a bogus federal indictment in Tennessee. The human smuggling charges grew out of a 2022 traffic stop at which state troopers had let him go without so much as a ticket. In August 2025, his lawyers reported that prosecutors were offering removal to Costa Rica in exchange for a guilty plea. When he refused, ICE threatened to send him to Uganda and seized him at a Baltimore check-in. Xinis ordered him released in December. On May 22, 2026, Federal Judge Waverly Crenshaw dismissed the Tennessee indictment after prosecutors failed to rebut the claim of vindictive prosecution. The Justice Department has appealed.

Cornell University doctoral student Momodou Taal faced a similar choice in March 2025. After Taal challenged Trump’s executive orders targeting opponents of the Gaza genocide, the government directed him to surrender to ICE. When a judge declined to block his detention, the British-Gambian student left the United States. “I have lost faith I could walk the streets without being abducted,” he wrote. In January 2026, British police detained him at Heathrow Airport and interrogated him for six hours under anti-terrorism powers. In both cases the US government secured an immigrant’s departure through the threat of imprisonment without having to win a criminal conviction.

The administration’s insistence on deportation to Liberia also served a wider purpose. In a March 2026 memo, acting ICE Director Todd Lyons argued that sending Abrego Garcia to Costa Rica would be “prejudicial to the United States.” Washington had spent resources and political capital getting Liberia to accept other countries’ nationals, he reasoned. By early September, Human Rights First and Refugees International had documented transfers under such arrangements to at least 31 countries. An exact nationwide total through November remains unavailable. Human Rights Watch, analyzing ICE records, counted 27,943 third-country deportations between January 20, 2025 and August 5, 2026, including 536 to Africa.

What Abrego Garcia escaped can be seen in the fate of Diadie Camara, who fled hereditary slavery in Mauritania. A US immigration judge had granted him protection from deportation there. Washington sent him instead to Equatorial Guinea, where deportees were held under armed guard in a hotel near Malabo’s airport. Within weeks Camara was back in Mauritania, in hiding from the family that had enslaved him. By September, Equatorial Guinea had received about 65 third-country deportees from the US and sent at least two dozen on to their countries of origin. Many had obtained protective orders from American judges.

Since the Trump administration ended Temporary Protected Status for Haitian refugees, ICE has operated weekly deportation flights to Haiti, according to ICE Flight Monitor. On November 12 and again on November 19, the group tracked ICE Air flights from Alexandria, Louisiana, to Cap-Haïtien. A flight on September 3 carried 101 people to the port city on Haiti’s northern coast. At the time, gang violence had displaced nearly 1.5 million people across Haiti, and the main international airport in Port-au-Prince was considered too dangerous for the flights.

This past week the WSWS reported on the seizure of Princeton neuroscientist Eva Yi Xie at Reagan National Airport and of Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza and his daughter Sofia Hernandez Mejia as they boarded a domestic flight at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport. All three had federal work permits and pending asylum cases.

Video of masked agents dragging the father and daughter off the jet bridge prompted Seattle rock band Pearl Jam to condemn “the human toll of a system driven by cold cruelty.” Pearl Jam wrote that voters had seen what ICE was doing to their neighbors and said “no more.”

Ahead of Thanksgiving, singer Brandi Carlile asked listeners to consider what it meant to hear the family’s cries while making plans to see their own relatives. She urged them to turn their “distress into action” and raise money for organizations assisting immigrants in detention.

That opposition found expression in the midterm elections. Yet the airport kidnappings took place after the votes were counted. Abrego Garcia escaped a deportation flight to Liberia and chose his own destination on Tuesday. He still had to leave his home in Maryland. The defense of the workers and families now in ICE’s sights cannot wait two years on the slim hope that another administration will be more humane. It requires mobilizing the working class, immigrant and US-born alike, to stop the raids and deportations.

title: Temporary Protected Status to expire for Lebanese immigrants in the US | Big Country News
description:
WASHINGTON — Humanitarian protections for thousands of Lebanese immigrants living in the United States are set to expire by Nov. 27, and the Department of Homeland Security has not indicated if their Temporary Protected Status will be renewed.
“An announcement on Lebanon’s TPS will be made at the appropriate time,” a DHS spokesperson said in a statement.
The moves have resulted in more than 1 million immigrants having their TPS stripped, and opening them to the president’s mass deportation agenda.
The remaining TPS holders whose protections expired but who maintain deportation protections include roughly 200,000 Salvadorans, 100,000 Ukrainians and 2,000 Sudanese.
However, passage of any legal protections for immigrants will likely face a veto from President Donald Trump, and need a two-thirds majority to override.
text:
WASHINGTON — Humanitarian protections for thousands of Lebanese immigrants living in the United States are set to expire by Nov. 27, and the Department of Homeland Security has not indicated if their Temporary Protected Status will be renewed.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin in May renewed TPS for an estimated 11,000 nationals from Lebanon for six months, citing instability in the region due to the U.S.-Israel-backed war in Iran, which is still active.

Nationals who hail from a country deemed too dangerous for return, due to war, violence or other extreme instability, are granted anywhere from six-month to 18-month cycles of protections to remain and work in the U.S.

A DHS spokesperson did not answer State Newsroom’s questions about the renewal status for Lebanese immigrants with TPS.

“An announcement on Lebanon’s TPS will be made at the appropriate time,” a DHS spokesperson said in a statement. “Until such an announcement is made, Lebanese individuals present in the U.S. under TPS retain protection.”

DHS has made the same announcement for nationals with TPS from El Salvador, Sudan and Ukraine. TPS for people from all those countries expired this year, but DHS for now will allow those immigrants to also keep their work authorization and deportation protections.

Overall, the Trump administration has aimed to wind down the program created by Congress in the 1990s. At the start of the second Trump administration, 17 countries were designated under TPS, but now only Lebanon has the status, until Nov. 27.

The moves have resulted in more than 1 million immigrants having their TPS stripped, and opening them to the president’s mass deportation agenda.

The remaining TPS holders whose protections expired but who maintain deportation protections include roughly 200,000 Salvadorans, 100,000 Ukrainians and 2,000 Sudanese.

Congressional Democrats have tried to pass legislation to extend TPS broadly, and for certain nationals such as Haitians and Afghans, but have been unable to with Republicans controlling both chambers.

In January, Democrats will hold the majority in the House and Senate, and members of both chambers have expressed immigration reform as a top priority.

However, passage of any legal protections for immigrants will likely face a veto from President Donald Trump, and need a two-thirds majority to override.

text:
A change in judicial assignments at the Fort Snelling immigration court has introduced accelerated filing deadlines and concerns over in-person attendance requirements for children from Minnesota and the Dakotas. Federal officials describe interstate judicial assignments as a mechanism for reducing immigration court backlogs.

FORT SNELLING, MN (November 26, 2026).

Immigration attorneys representing children in Minnesota and neighboring states are raising concerns about changes in the administration of juvenile immigration proceedings following the assignment of cases to a Houston-based immigration judge. The development has introduced questions about access to legal representation, the time available to prepare applications for immigration relief and the transportation obligations imposed upon children residing considerable distances from the regional immigration court.

According to November 25 reporting by MPR News, Immigration Judge Jason Stern, who serves at the Houston Greenspoint Park immigration court, began overseeing a juvenile docket associated with Minnesota's immigration court earlier this month. Proceedings have continued at the Bishop Henry Whipple Federal Building at Fort Snelling, with Stern participating remotely from Texas.

Attorneys familiar with the regional court describe the assignment as a departure from previous arrangements under which juvenile cases were generally heard by a locally based immigration judge.

Accelerated Proceedings Raise Questions About Case Preparation

The concerns expressed by attorneys center partly on the time available to determine whether children qualify for immigration protections and to prepare the necessary supporting documentation. During proceedings Tuesday, November 24, Stern established December and January filing deadlines in several cases, according to MPR News.

Immigration attorney Meg Kaiser described the pace of those deadlines as comparatively rapid based upon her previous experience with immigration proceedings at Fort Snelling.

Legal preparation involving children can require particular care. An attorney evaluating a potential asylum claim may need to establish a client's personal history, circumstances in their country of origin and the nature of any harm or persecution they have experienced or fear experiencing.

For children who have endured traumatic circumstances, obtaining that information may require multiple conversations conducted at a pace appropriate to their age and emotional condition. Accelerated deadlines can make coordinating evidence, interpretation services and supporting documentation more difficult.

These considerations do not independently establish that any individual deadline violates immigration law. They do, however, illustrate the practical concerns attorneys have identified regarding their ability to prepare children's cases effectively.

Children With Existing Immigration Protections Face Continuing Proceedings

Attorneys have also expressed concern about the treatment of children who have obtained Special Immigrant Juvenile Status, a federal immigration classification available to qualifying young people who have experienced abuse, neglect, abandonment or similar circumstances recognized under applicable state law.

The classification can provide eligible individuals with a pathway toward lawful permanent residence. It does not automatically confer permanent residency, and obtaining that status may involve additional applications and waiting periods.

Madeline Lohman, advocacy director at The Advocates for Human Rights, told MPR News that Stern has continued proceedings involving children awaiting permanent residence through this classification. She also reported that one child possessing Special Immigrant Juvenile Status had received a removal order.

The specific circumstances of that case, including any outstanding applications, procedural history or subsequent legal challenges, were not independently available for examination. Its outcome should therefore not be generalized to every child possessing the same immigration classification.

Nevertheless, the account highlights the importance of distinguishing eligibility for immigration relief from the completion of the legal processes through which permanent status is obtained.

Transportation Requirements Affect Families Across Three States

The immigration court's regional jurisdiction includes Minnesota, North Dakota and South Dakota, meaning that some children must travel substantial distances to attend hearings.

Attorneys have identified concerns about Stern's approach to requests for remote participation. In one case reported by MPR News, an attorney representing a teenager residing approximately 220 miles from the court requested permission for a future video appearance. Stern requested a written application before making a decision.

In-person attendance can create transportation, scheduling and financial difficulties for children and the adults responsible for supporting them. Those difficulties may be particularly pronounced in rural communities, where public transportation and access to specialized immigration legal services can be limited.

The consequences of missing an immigration hearing may also be substantial. Under applicable circumstances, immigration judges can issue removal orders when individuals fail to appear for scheduled proceedings after receiving the required notice.

For attorneys representing minors, ensuring that clients understand their obligations and possess the practical means to attend hearings is therefore an important component of legal representation.

Federal Officials Cite Court Backlog Reduction

The United States Department of Justice, which administers the immigration court system through the Executive Office for Immigration Review, has defended the assignment of judges across geographical jurisdictions as a means of addressing pending caseloads.

In its response to MPR News, the department identified reducing the immigration court backlog as a continuing administrative priority.

The federal government's objective of resolving pending cases exists alongside the obligation to provide respondents with proceedings consistent with applicable immigration law. Questions concerning the appropriate balance between administrative efficiency and adequate opportunities to prepare individual cases remain central to the concerns raised by Minnesota attorneys.

The immigration courts operate within the Department of Justice rather than the independent federal judiciary established under Article III of the United States Constitution. Their administrative structure gives federal officials responsibilities involving judicial assignments, case scheduling and operational priorities.

It remains unclear whether Stern's assignment to the regional juvenile docket represents a temporary arrangement or a longer-term change.

For the children whose cases are presently before the court, the immediate concerns involve meeting application deadlines, securing any available immigration protections and ensuring attendance at future proceedings. For Minnesota's legal advocacy organizations, the development raises broader questions about how administrative changes affect access to justice for some of the immigration system's youngest participants.

text:
A 7-year-old girl from New Orleans named Charlotte is among dozens of children who will spend Thanksgiving locked up with their families at a for-profit detention center in Dilley, Texas.

Attorneys representing Charlotte and her mother, also held at Dilley, shared a plea the girl wrote to President Trump while locked up.

“I would like to visit my father and study at my school,” Charlotte wrote in Spanish. She also drew a picture of herself standing beside her mother and father.

Charlotte and her mother have been at Dilley for almost a month after ICE arrested the mother while she was working as a delivery driver.

The family came to the U.S. from Venezuela legally through a humanitarian parole program, but the Department of Homeland Security says they failed to leave the country when their authorization expired.

RELATED STORY | 'Mom, what did we do?' Parents recall weeks in ICE family detention

Charlotte’s mother and 31 other detainees have filed sworn declarations in a federal court case challenging their detention at Dilley.

The new declarations suggest ICE and the CoreCivic company, which owns and operates the facility, have not addressed complaints about conditions first exposed by Scripps News in March.

The affidavits claim children are losing weight, developing rashes, are offered foul-tasting water and are unable to sleep in bunk rooms where the lights stay on all night.

“The conditions that the families are exposed to once they get into this trailer prison are horrendous,” said Kristin Etter, director of policy and legal services at the Texas Immigration Law Council. “There's no incentive for this private prison industrial complex to improve conditions when that would cut into their bottom line.”

In a statement to Scripps News, CoreCivic says it “strongly rejects” claims of care being driven by profit and refutes the claims from detainees in the declarations.

“We would caution against treating allegations in those declarations as established facts,” the statement said. “Nothing matters more to CoreCivic than the health, safety and well-being of the families entrusted to our care.”

A CoreCivic spokesman said the staff are preparing a special meal and activities for families to celebrate Thanksgiving.

The declarations raise another question: Why are some of the children still there?

The longstanding Flores federal court ruling says children should not be detained longer than 20 days, yet 25 children at Dilley now have been held beyond that limit.

Detainees declared not being told about the 20-day maximum, also saying they did not have access to phone calls with their lawyers.

Some of the immigrants at Dilley said they have already agreed to leave the United States and return to their countries of origin, but they remain held in ICE custody.

One man and his 6-year-old daughter had been at Dilley 43 days despite the man saying he signed a voluntary departure agreement.

"Every time I ask ICE why we are still here, they say ‘next week you’ll leave,’” the man stated in his declaration.

ICE INC | ICE is detaining children with their families beyond limit set by federal judge

A family of four, including an 8-year-old boy and 10-year-old girl, had been kept in Dilley much longer —143 days.

“ICE officers have told us that they are detaining us for so many months because we are waiting here for travel documents,” the father said in an affidavit.

DHS has defended the level of care provided to Dilley detainees and said undocumented immigrants should leave the country rather than risk being held against their will.

“Most of the families in Dilley are doing exactly what the government has told them that they need to do, they are following the legal process,” Etter said. “There is really no point to this detention other than cruelty and corruption.”

Charlotte has lost 15 pounds in detention and only wants to eat corn flakes, her attorneys said.

title: Democrats face tests on cultural fights picked by Republicans - WCIV
authors: RAY LEWIS | The National News Desk, RAY LEWIS, The National News Desk
description:

Successful Democrats in this month's elections resisted the bait dangled by Republicans to focus on cultural issues tied to the public's top concerns.

text:
Democrats taking control of Congress in just a few weeks will have a chance to rebuild their reputation after years of Republican attacks on the party's brand.

They'll be better able to shape the narrative on the nation's top issues, including those which contributed to their fall into the minority. Republicans seized on Democratic failures during the Biden administration to communicate effectively on the economy, immigration and presidential missteps, but now, after the blue tsunami that was the midterms, the GOP is on its back foot on the very same issues.

Successful Democrats in this month's elections resisted the bait dangled by Republicans to focus on cultural issues tied to the public's top concerns. They'll likely face more of the same challenges when they take power, and they'd do well to avoid the wars the GOP's long tempted them to fight.

The sensitive issue of immigration will be an important test. Democrats must strike a balance between defending immigrants' rights and opposing the Trump administration's mass deportation policies without falling into traps set by Republicans and the conservative media that's ready to pounce.

Representative Jamie Raskin, the Maryland Democrat, showed the dangers of entertaining right-wing fights last year, when he went toe-to-toe in an argument with a conservative X user over Kilmar Ábrego García, the immigrant involved in an illegal deportation fight. The two yelled over each other on Capitol Hill, fueling Republican attacks against sympathetic Democrats.

Raskin and other Democrats appear to have learned from their mistakes as they prepare to take control of Congress. The party's largely united around the goal of lowering prices that have concerned Americans for the past several years, brushing off Republican attempts to stir up anger over sensitive topics.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries and his Senate counterpart, Chuck Schumer, pledged after their party's electoral triumph to address voters' most important issues, like the high cost of living that's risen under President Donald Trump.

"The American people have forcefully rejected MAGA extremism and are demanding dramatic change in their lives," the Democrats said in a statement. "House and Senate Democrats have been given a clear mandate to aggressively address the affordability crisis, stop the reckless war of choice in Iran, meaningfully expand access to affordable healthcare and hold the crooks accountable who have unleashed unprecedented corruption on the country.

“A new day is coming on January 3rd. Democrats are united and ready to lead.”

name: Litigation
title: New report and lawsuit reveal the ordeal of 733 pregnant women in ICE custody
description:
In the first 16 months of the Republican’s second term, 733 pregnant women remained in the custody of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), most of them for extended periods.
Among those facing high-risk pregnancies, few had access to specialized medical care and were not released immediately.
From nine pregnant women in ICE custody in January 2025, the number rose to 128 last March, representing a 1,320% increase.
Through this tool, it gathered testimonies from women who suffered miscarriages, were malnourished, or did not receive specialized medical care.
“There, we heard testimonies from women with life-threatening conditions who were denied medical care,” the group notes.
text:
Even when it comes to pregnant immigrants, the Trump administration has proven itself indifferent. In the first 16 months of the Republican’s second term, 733 pregnant women remained in the custody of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), most of them for extended periods. One of them was detained for seven months. Among those facing high-risk pregnancies, few had access to specialized medical care and were not released immediately.

These revelations appear in a report published Tuesday by the Women’s Refugee Commission (WRC), which questions the federal administration’s lack of empathy toward a particularly vulnerable population — both in ICE detention centers, which have been repeatedly cited for mistreating immigrants — and in local jail facilities that held contracts with the government and where most of these women were held.

The report accompanies a lawsuit that the WRC and organizations such as the Venezuelan Association of Massachusetts and the Workers’ Center of Central New York filed in a District of Columbia court. In it, they demand that ICE and the Department of Homeland Security put an end to the ordeal suffered by these women, who are caught up in Trump’s immigration crackdown.

“Immigration detention has become a black box of impunity,” said Zain Lakhani, director of the WRC’s Migrant Rights and Justice Program, in a statement. This organization, Lakhani said, has documented “a substantial increase in the number of pregnant women in detention and brought to light grave concerns about their treatment and care.” “Now, this data shows that these abuses are happening at scale,” he added.

Among these abuses, it is notable that of some 128 women diagnosed with high-risk pregnancies, only four were transferred to a “higher level of care.” The report details at least 16 cases of miscarriages recorded between January 2025 and February 2026.

Malnourished and sleeping on the floor

During Joe Biden’s administration, between 2021 and 2024, ICE released most of the pregnant women it had detained — either on parole or under a promise to appear in court.

But at the start of Trump’s second term, the number of women in detention began to rise as the president’s immigration crackdown intensified. From nine pregnant women in ICE custody in January 2025, the number rose to 128 last March, representing a 1,320% increase. Most of them — about 75% — were held in state or local facilities under contract with the government, which, according to the WRC report, “have lower medical standards and higher taxpayer costs.”

The report estimates that ICE spent at least $4 million on the detention of 557 pregnant women, not including the costs of medical care.

The Department of Homeland Security has not commented on this report and lawsuit, but in the summer of 2025, in response to an investigation by the office of Georgia Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff — which documented 14 credible reports of mistreatment of pregnant women in ICE custody — the agency denied having neglected these migrants.

The reports compiled by Ossoff’s office point to deficiencies such as a lack of adequate medical care and timely checkups, the absence of emergency care when needed, the denial of adequate snacks and meals, and the requirement to sleep on the floor due to overcrowding.

In its response, DHS stated that these women received medical care and nutritional support, and maintained that “the detention of pregnant women is rare and subject to rigorous oversight and review.” It added that “no pregnant woman has been forced to sleep on the floor.”

Seven months in custody

Human rights advocates, Democratic members of Congress, and journalistic investigations have documented an alarming increase in the number of pregnant women detained by ICE during the current administration, which is determined to deport as many undocumented immigrants as possible.

“Advocates interviewed more than a dozen women, and in their letter, also describe disturbing accounts of shackling and use of restraint during transport, solitary confinement, denial of prenatal vitamins, inadequate food, delayed or substandard medical care, and lack of interpretation during medical visits. One woman experienced a dangerous infection after a miscarriage due to ICE’s medical neglect,” states a letter sent by the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) to ICE in October 2025.

The indiscriminate detention of these women demonstrates that ICE has failed to comply with its own directive, established in 2021, which stipulates that, except in exceptional circumstances or for other legally justified reasons, pregnant women, women in the postpartum period, or breastfeeding women should not remain in the agency’s custody.

In its recent report, the WRC places special emphasis on the length of time these women spend in detention. During the Biden administration, the average was about five days. Under the Trump administration, that figure skyrocketed to 43 days — a 750% increase.

At least 145 women were held in custody for 90 days or more. The report highlights the case of one woman who was detained for 219 days — nearly seven months into her pregnancy.

To collect reports from these migrants, the WRC launched a tool called the Detention Pregnancy Tracker in September 2025. Through this tool, it gathered testimonies from women who suffered miscarriages, were malnourished, or did not receive specialized medical care.

The organization even traveled to Honduras to interview recently deported individuals. “There, we heard testimonies from women with life-threatening conditions who were denied medical care,” the group notes.

text:
Over the weekend, the Massachusetts Lottery shared a picture of Ariel Velasquez-Morales smiling gently as he gripped an oversized check for US$1 million in winnings. On social media, commenters congratulated him, with one person writing they hoped he would be able to “make any dreams come true.”

But Velasquez-Morales was arrested Tuesday by Immigration and Customs Enforcement in East Boston, the same neighborhood where he bought the $10 winning scratch-off ticket from a local market.

He now faces deportation as ICE says the Salvadoran national has been in the country illegally for more than a decade.

“Looks like his luck ran out,” said ICE Assistant Director of Public Affairs Micah Bock in a release announcing the arrest.

It is unclear whether the publication of his lottery winnings attracted ICE’s attention. ICE declined to answer questions from CNN about what led to the arrest or where Velasquez-Morales is being detained.

Velasquez-Morales illegally entered the United States in 2013, during the Obama administration, in the Rio Grande Valley in Texas. Border Patrol agents issued him a notice to appear before an immigration judge, and he was released into the country with a list of free legal service providers, the agency said.

“A Department of Justice immigration judge ordered Velasquez-Morales removed in 2014, but he illegally remained in the country,” the ICE release said.

He will remain in ICE custody pending his removal from the U.S.. CNN has been unable to determine whether he has legal representation.

U.S. President Donald Trump has overseen a massive immigration crackdown after promising to lead the largest deportation operation in U.S. history. In his second term, arrests have shifted away from the border and focused more on the interior of the country, where aggressive tactics have become a hallmark of ICE’s ramped-up detention efforts.

By July 2026, there were nearly 66,000 detainees in ICE custody, an increase of nearly 70 per cent from the total detained when Trump took office the year prior.

But after a Republican wipeout in the midterms, Trump has publicly questioned whether the tactics were too hard-line and unpopular. It remains to be seen, though, whether he is considering significant changes to his immigration policies.

“Criminal illegal aliens are not welcome in the United States and will be removed as quickly as possible,” ICE said in its release on Velasquez-Morales. “Under President Trump and Secretary Mullin’s leadership, ICE is delivering on its mission to enforce our nation’s immigration laws, restore accountability and protect American communities.”

Velasquez-Morales was playing the lottery’s “$2,000,000 50X Cashword,” in which players scratch cards resembling crossword puzzles to try to reveal complete words. It was the first puzzle he had scratched, the lottery said, and he matched 11 words.

He chose to accept his winnings in cash, which would give him a one-time lump sum of $650,000 before taxes, according to ICE. It is not clear what will happen to his winnings.

Massachusetts lottery participants do not need to be legal residents of the state to play, but they must be 21 or older and be located in the state at the time they purchase or play.

CNN has sought comment from the Massachusetts State Lottery Commission.
