title: ICE Habeas Petitions: How They Work as DOJ Adds Civil Lawyers - Immigration Analytics
description:
Trustee Program, to help U.S. Attorneys’ Offices answer habeas corpus petitions filed by people in ICE custody, CBS News reported.
It is a civil case in federal court, separate from the removal case in immigration court.
What the Supreme Court case could change On Oct. 1, the Supreme Court agreed to hear Rhoney v. Barbosa da Cunha, No.
Quick answers Does the DOJ memo change the law on ICE habeas petitions?
Can a family member file a habeas petition for someone in ICE detention?
text:
The Justice Department’s new staffing order changes who defends ICE in court, not the rules a detainee’s petition must follow. Here is how those petitions work.

Attorney General Todd Blanche’s Nov. 24 memo directs lawyers from the department’s Antitrust, Civil, Civil Rights and Environment and Natural Resources divisions, along with the U.S. Trustee Program, to help U.S. Attorneys’ Offices answer habeas corpus petitions filed by people in ICE custody, CBS News reported. The memo counts more than 97,000 detainees who have filed such petitions since January 2025, about 10,000 of them since October 2026.

As reported earlier, the memo is a sign that the government intends to contest more of these cases rather than let them go unanswered. For families and detainees, the practical questions are more basic: what a habeas petition is, who can file one, where it goes, how fast it moves and what a judge can actually order.

What is a habeas petition for an ICE detainee?

A petition for a writ of habeas corpus under 28 U.S.C. 2241 asks a federal district judge to decide whether a person’s detention is lawful. It is a civil case in federal court, separate from the removal case in immigration court. It does not decide whether the person can stay in the United States; it decides whether the government may keep holding them while that question is resolved.

Most of the recent petitions challenge the government’s position, adopted in July 2025 and endorsed by the Board of Immigration Appeals in Matter of Yajure Hurtado, that people who entered without inspection are “applicants for admission” subject to mandatory detention under 8 U.S.C. 1225(b)(2)(A), with no bond hearing before an immigration judge. Petitioners typically argue they fall under 8 U.S.C. 1226(a) instead, which allows bond, or that holding them without any hearing violates due process.

Who can file, where, and what does it cost?

Who signs it: Under 28 U.S.C. 2242, the petition must be signed and verified by the detained person or by someone acting on their behalf. Relatives sometimes file as a “next friend,” but courts examine whether that person qualifies, so most petitions are filed by an attorney.

Who is named: The petition must name the person who has custody of the detainee. In practice that usually means the warden of the facility and the ICE field office director, often with DHS officials added.

Where it goes: Petitions are generally filed in the federal district where the person is being held. That is why transfers matter: a move from one state to another can change which court, and which circuit’s law, applies.

The fee: Under 28 U.S.C. 1914(a), the court filing fee for a habeas application is $5, compared with $350 for most civil cases. Attorney’s fees are a separate matter and vary widely.

Finding the right facility first is often the hardest step. Our guide to locating someone missing from the ICE detainee locator covers what to do when the online system comes up empty.

How long does a habeas case take?

The statute is built for speed. Under 28 U.S.C. 2243, when a judge orders the government to show cause, the government’s response is due within three days unless the court allows more time for good cause, up to 20 days. A hearing is to follow within five days of that response, again subject to extensions for good cause.

Real timelines vary. Many judges grant extensions, some decide on the papers without a hearing, and busy districts move slower than the statute contemplates. The Blanche memo is aimed at precisely this pressure point: with more government lawyers available, fewer petitions should go unanswered or be resolved because the government could not respond in time.

What can a judge order?

In the mandatory-detention cases, the most common relief is an order requiring a bond hearing before an immigration judge within a set number of days, or release if no hearing is held. Some judges have ordered outright release. A habeas win does not end the removal case, and judges have recently had to address ICE re-arrests after release by writing conditions into their orders.

Does it matter which state the detainee is held in?

Yes, more than at any point in recent years. According to SCOTUSblog’s Nov. 17 summary, nine federal appeals courts (the 1st, 2nd, 3rd, 4th, 6th, 7th, 9th, 10th and 11th Circuits) have rejected the government’s reading of Section 1225(b)(2)(A), while the 5th and 8th Circuits have accepted it. The 5th Circuit, sitting en banc on Oct. 23 in Sosnava Rodriguez, also held there is no due process right to a bond hearing for people never admitted, which practitioners at the National Immigration Project say leaves no bond-hearing right for that group in Texas, Louisiana or Mississippi.

Habeas remains available in those states on other grounds, such as whether a person is properly classified under the mandatory-detention statute at all, according to CLINIC and the National Immigration Project. But a detainee held in Texas faces a very different legal landscape from one held in New Jersey or Washington.

What the Supreme Court case could change

On Oct. 1, the Supreme Court agreed to hear Rhoney v. Barbosa da Cunha, No. 26-104, a government appeal from a unanimous 2nd Circuit ruling for a Brazilian man who had lived in the U.S. for more than 20 years. No argument date has been set; SCOTUSblog expects argument in late winter or spring, which points to a decision by mid-2027. Our earlier coverage of the case heading to the Court explains the statutory dispute.

If the government wins, much of the current habeas volume could shrink, because the statutory argument behind most petitions would be foreclosed nationwide, leaving constitutional and individual classification claims. If the detainees win, bond hearings would be required in immigration court nationwide, and the 5th and 8th Circuit rulings on the statute would fall.

Quick answers

Does the DOJ memo change the law on ICE habeas petitions? No. It reassigns government lawyers. The legal standards and deadlines are the same.

Can a family member file a habeas petition for someone in ICE detention? The statute allows someone acting on the detainee’s behalf, but courts scrutinize next-friend filings, so an attorney is usually involved.

How much does it cost to file? The federal court filing fee is $5. Legal fees are separate.

How fast will a judge rule? The statute sets a three-day response deadline, extendable to 20 days, but actual timing varies by court.

Will winning stop deportation? No. Habeas addresses detention; the removal case continues in immigration court.

This article is for general information and is not legal advice.

description:
It is clear that this nation needs comprehensive immigration reform that works with our farmers, not against them,” said Governor Shapiro.
From poultry and dairy to specialty crops, livestock, and food processing, the industry’s success depends on the people who make the entire food system work.
Industry sectors like mushrooms and poultry production have seen the biggest disruptions across various parts of their supply chains as a result.
The Pennsylvania State Police and Commonwealth agencies do not conduct immigration enforcement.
"Disruptions to our agricultural workforce are costly for our farmers and for the entire Commonwealth.
text:
Marietta, PA – Today, Governor Josh Shapiro and Pennsylvania Department of Agriculture Secretary Russell Redding held a roundtable discussion led by PennAg Industries Association at Hershey Ag(opens in a new tab) with farmers, agricultural organizations, and industry leaders from across the Commonwealth to discuss increased U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) activity across Pennsylvania and the effects those enforcement actions are having on the industry and its workforce.

Pennsylvania’s food processing, meat, poultry, mushroom, dairy, and agricultural sectors rely heavily on experienced immigrant workers and as a coalition of agricultural leaders wrote this week(opens in a new tab), recent federal immigration actions have resulted in substantial workforce losses across the Commonwealth. These losses result in sudden workforce disruptions which can have immediate animal-welfare, operational, and economic consequences that extend well beyond an individual business, ultimately affecting consumers and the nation’s food supply.

“For months, I’ve heard directly from farmers all across the Commonwealth who have raised their concerns about the way that the federal government’s cruel, chaotic immigration policies are making it hard for their workers. It is clear that this nation needs comprehensive immigration reform that works with our farmers, not against them,” said Governor Shapiro. “My Administration has repeatedly called on members of our federal delegation and the Trump Administration, urging them to listen to our farmers and work with them to develop comprehensive immigration reform that shows respect for our neighbors and keeps our border secure while creating legal, reliable pathways for agricultural labor. We will continue to shine a light on this issue and advocate for our farms and the workers who keep them running smoothly and help families across Pennsylvania and our country put food on the table.”

Pennsylvania is home to nearly 48,800 farms, and its agriculture industry contributes $132.5 billion to the Commonwealth’s economy and supports nearly 600,000 jobs. From poultry and dairy to specialty crops, livestock, and food processing, the industry’s success depends on the people who make the entire food system work.

“Farmers are asking for a system that recognizes the realities of running a farm and respects the essential people who make it possible,” said Secretary Redding. “When workers are afraid to come to work, or employers don’t know whether they can count on the people caring for their animals, harvesting their crops, and processing their products, the consequences reach far beyond the farm. Today’s conversation is about listening to our industry, standing with our agriculture community and the workers who deserve our support, and making sure Pennsylvania agriculture is part of the national conversation about immigration reform.”

The roundtable was held at Hershey Ag where agribusinesses in the company’s surrounding region — and all across the Commonwealth — have been targeted by ICE and impacted by Temporary Protected Status (TPS) terminations.

“While we have wonderful, efficient systems — that are, today, more sustainable and more efficient than ever — they also are highly interconnected and highly dependent on what happens with the people who are here every day. They are tightly managed and time-sensitive,” said Brent Hershey, Owner and President, Hershey Ag. “We need common sense here [to avoid] the destruction of the food system… We’re happy with secure borders, but we need a program that we can follow, and that program needs to be honored. We're playing by the rules, we're hitting the target — so don't take it away in the middle.”

Among the companies represented at today’s roundtable, more than 1,000 of their employees have lost legal status protection due to sudden changes in TPS, visas, and other legal pathways to live and work in the United States. Industry sectors like mushrooms and poultry production have seen the biggest disruptions across various parts of their supply chains as a result.

“In September, we met with the Governor to talk about this issue. Rather than he make a statement, he asked to stand with us instead, so here we are today, a room full of folks from all different segments of agriculture,” said Chris Herr, President of PennAg Industries Association. “We want a secure border — mission accomplished — we're happy about that, but we also believe it's important that Congress and the Administration in Washington fix this problem.”

Throughout the conversation, participants emphasized the need for an immigration system that strengthens border security, respects the rule of law, and recognizes the essential role immigrant workers play in the nation’s food supply. This also follows a joint letter(opens in a new tab) signed by 32 agricultural organizations and employers to the U.S. Secretaries of Agriculture Brooke Rollins and Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin, expressing concern that employees with legal status have been detained during recent enforcement actions and that aggressive enforcement activity has caused other workers with legal status to miss work, out of fear.

“Our farm, along with several others, have had local workers detained and deported after traffic stops during their morning commute… And being here legally does not get you a get out of jail free card for harassment from ICE. We have H-2A workers, and they come on visas to pick seasonal fruit for us,” said Sarah Zost, President of the State Horticultural Association of Pennsylvania and fourth-generation fruit grower. “But there's a culture of fear and concern because you get targeted because of what you look like… and it causes lost time on all farms because workers, regardless of visa status, stay home. The immigrant workforce is a critical part of agriculture and we literally cannot grow and harvest fruit without them.”

While bipartisan solutions are pursued, industry leaders have continued urging local and federal officials to conduct enforcement actions that prioritize dangerous criminals rather than essential workers who provide much of the food Americans eat. Since taking office, the Shapiro Administration has worked to strengthen Pennsylvania’s agricultural workforce through investments in workforce development, agricultural education, and career pathways, while supporting an environment where agricultural businesses can grow and create opportunity.

This work has included additional steps to address critical workforce needs — and combat chaotic and cruel federal immigration policy:

In February 2025, Governor Shapiro signed legislation allowing permanent legal residents to become certified poultry technicians after completing a state-administered training course, helping expand the pool of qualified workers available to meet critical industry needs.

In July 2026, the Shapiro Administration confirmed(opens in a new tab) the federal government would not move forwardwith proposed ICE detention centers in Berks and Schuylkill counties, following administrative orders(opens in a new tab) issued by the PA Department of Environmental Protection.

In October 2026, the PA Department of Agriculture unveiled their Strategic Plan for Agriculture(opens in a new tab), recognizing that a robust and well-trained ag workforce is the backbone for a strong agricultural economy — prioritizing workforce development and recruitment as a key pillar of the Shapiro Administration’s work to ensure Pennsylvania agriculture remains profitable and globally competitive.

The Administration has also developed multilingual “Know Your Rights(opens in a new tab)” resources and regularly engages with immigrant advocates, service providers, and local officials to understand the impacts of changing federal immigration policies.

"Disruptions to our agricultural workforce are costly for our farmers and for the entire Commonwealth. Like every sector of our economy, agriculture depends on a reliable workforce. Farmers need workers to harvest crops, work in food processing plants and perform essential tasks that help put food on our tables,” said Senator Judith Schwank, Democratic Chair of the Agriculture & Rural Affairs Committee. “The indiscriminate and inhumane targeting of immigrant communities by the federal government is not only morally wrong, but it's also depriving Pennsylvania's agricultural industry of the hardworking individuals it relies on to sustain food production and support our economy."

description:
In a civil case in Maryland, Ábrego García challenged the Department of Homeland Security’s attempts to deport him to a series of African countries.
Here is a timeline of key events: Arrival: around 2011 Ábrego García flees El Salvador for the U.S. as a teenager.
Deportation: March 15, 2025 Ábrego García is mistakenly deported to El Salvador and held in a notoriously brutal prison.
In immigration custody: Aug. 25, 2025 Ábrego García reports to an immigration office in Baltimore and is taken into custody.
Self-deportation: Nov. 24, 2026 Ábrego García leaves the U.S. voluntarily for Spain, departing from Washington Dulles International Airport.
text:
Kilmar Ábrego García entered the news in March 2025 after he was deported to El Salvador despite a court ruling that should have prevented it. His complicated legal fight after that galvanized both sides of the debate over President Donald Trump’s immigration policies.

In a civil case in Maryland, Ábrego García challenged the Department of Homeland Security’s attempts to deport him to a series of African countries. A criminal case in Tennessee, where the government accused him of human smuggling, was dismissed after a judge found evidence of “vindictive prosecution” by the Justice Department. Months later, Ábrego García self-deported to Spain, potentially ending a defining saga of the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown.

Here is a timeline of key events:

Arrival: around 2011

Ábrego García flees El Salvador for the U.S. as a teenager.

Arrest: March 28, 2019

Ábrego García is arrested outside a Maryland hardware store. Police accuse him of being a gang member and turn him over to U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

Immigration court: Oct. 10, 2019

A Maryland immigration judge rules that Ábrego García cannot be deported to El Salvador, where a gang has threatened his family. He is given a work permit and placed under federal supervision.

Detained by ICE: March 12, 2025

Ábrego García is detained by ICE in Maryland while driving home with his 5-year-old son.

Deportation: March 15, 2025

Ábrego García is mistakenly deported to El Salvador and held in a notoriously brutal prison.

Supreme Court: April 10, 2025

The U.S. Supreme Court says the Trump administration must work to bring Ábrego García back.

Senator visits: April 17, 2025

In defiance of Trump, Democratic Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland meets with Ábrego García at a hotel in El Salvador, helping to establish hope and momentum for Ábrego García’s family.

Criminal charges: June 6, 2025

Ábrego García is returned to the U.S. and charged with human smuggling, based on a Tennessee traffic stop from 2022.

Attempts at second deportation: July 23, 2025

ICE announces plans to remove him to a series of African countries, but is blocked by an injunction from a Maryland federal judge.

Released from jail: Aug. 22, 2025

Ábrego García leaves the Tennessee jail, where he has been since June, to return to his family in Maryland and await trial. Within minutes of his release, ICE sends notice that they intend to deport him to Uganda.

In immigration custody: Aug. 25, 2025

Ábrego García reports to an immigration office in Baltimore and is taken into custody.

Judge orders release: Dec. 11, 2025

A federal judge in Maryland orders ICE to immediately release Ábrego García.

No immigration detention: Feb. 17, 2026

A Maryland federal judge rules ICE cannot re-detain Ábrego García.

Judge dismisses criminal case: May 22, 2026

A federal judge in Tennessee dismisses the human smuggling case against Ábrego García after finding evidence that the government engaged in “ vindictive prosecution."

Prosecutors argue for reinstating criminal charges: Aug. 17, 2026

The Justice Department tells a federal appeals court that the federal judge in Tennessee erred in his scathing May ruling in the criminal case against Ábrego García.

Self-deportation: Nov. 24, 2026

Ábrego García leaves the U.S. voluntarily for Spain, departing from Washington Dulles International Airport. According to an unsealed Nov. 20 order, a federal judge said the government informed her that Ábrego García was free to self-deport “to any country that is willing to accept him.” The judge, in turn, set Nov. 24 as the deadline for his departure and ordered the removal of his GPS ankle monitor before he boarded the flight.

Arrival in Spain: Nov. 25, 2026

text:
Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detained a Princeton University doctoral candidate on Nov. 19 at an airport in Arlington, Virginia. Her colleagues, classmates, and lawmakers are calling for her immediate release ahead of Thanksgiving Weekend.

Eva Yi Xie, a Chinese national, was detained at the Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport as she departed from an annual conference of the Society for Neuroscience. Xie’s lawyers say that she was not presented with a warrant.

She was later taken to the Caroline Detention Center in Virginia, a court filing says. U.S. District Judge Anthony Trenga ordered the federal government to respond to a petition challenging Xie’s detention by 5 p.m. E.T. on Wednesday. In the meantime, he ordered ICE not to transfer or remove Xie from the Eastern District of Virginia.

According to court documents, Xie, 24, came to New York on a travel visa with her family in March 2016. Four months later, Xie’s mother applied for asylum. The family’s case is still pending, with a hearing scheduled for January 2028. Xie was granted work authorization and does not have any criminal history.

Kerry Doyle, a lawyer who represents Xie, tells TIME that Xie has received “unprecedented” support from Princeton, as well as the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, where Xie earned her undergraduate degree in 2024. She says that there is an effort to collect letters of support in order to facilitate her release.

“We have this incredibly talented student—and by all accounts, an incredible person—who studies neuroscience. She has a very great future, and we're arresting her at the airport for no reason,” Doyle says.

In a statement shared with TIME, an ICE spokesperson says that a pending asylum application does not confer legal status and that Xie never held “valid authorization to study in the United States.”

“Xie was admitted to the United States on a temporary basis on March 16, 2016, but chose to violate our nation’s laws by refusing to depart by the required date of September 15, 2016,” the spokesperson says.

Democratic Senator Andy Kim of New Jersey, where Princeton is located, wrote on X on Monday that his office has been in touch with the school, Xie, and DHS in an effort to get more information and get her home.

“It's heartbreaking to see her detained and turned into another example of this administration's cruel immigration policies,” he said.

About 250 people showed up to a “Free Eva” rally at Princeton University on Monday in support of Xie. The organizers put together a phone bank to urge supporters to contact their federal representatives on Xie’s behalf.

Brody Lab, a neuroscience research group at Princeton, announced Xie’s arrest in a social media post last week and has since urged followers to contact congressional lawmakers to advocate for her prompt release. It says that Xie messaged the lab’s Slack channel for help when she got detained.

Rodney Priestley, the dean of the Graduate School at Princeton University, said last Friday that Xie’s detention was “distressing.” The university has provided legal counsel to Xie and remains in contact with Xie’s family.

Xie’s PhD adviser Carlos Brody told the Associated Press in an interview on Tuesday that Xie called into a weekly lab meeting to thank her coworkers for their support and is in “remarkable spirits.”

Adrian Bondy, a research scholar in the lab, told AP that even in detention, Xie “wants the science to continue and is thinking about scientific ideas.”

Xie is not the first researcher arrested by ICE. Science reported that Di Liu, a chemistry assistant professor at Arizona State University with a valid work visa, was detained by ICE in July at an airport on his way to a scientific conference in Nashville, Tennessee. A few days later, he was released without explanation. Last year, Tufts researcher Rumeysa Ozturk was detained by ICE in Cambridge, Massachusetts. She decided in April 2026 to voluntarily leave the U.S.

Two days after Xie’s arrest, ICE officers detained a father and daughter at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport as passengers boarded an Alaska Airlines flight to Los Angeles. A viral video captured the moment when Mexican immigrant Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza and his daughter, Sofia Hernandez Mejia, were arrested. It showed Hernandez Mejia pleading for help before being dragged out of the jet bridge.

The recent arrests continue a trend seen throughout the Trump Administration’s second term. Stateline reported that there was a nationwide goal of 2,000 ICE arrests a day; a senior Department of Homeland Security (DHS) official told NBC News that officers were averaging 20 to 40 arrests a day at U.S. airports as of August.

Since May 2025, ICE has been obtaining traveler information through the Transportation Security Administration (TSA) through a previously undisclosed data-sharing program, according to records obtained by the watchdog group American Oversight. The New York Times reported that the program gives ICE access to the names and birth dates of passengers whom the TSA believes may be subject to arrest.

On July 21, two plainclothes ICE agents arrested Chantal Morales Rojas, a 27-year-old from Ecuador, at the jet bridge at Denver International Airport. The next day, ICE arrested Ethiopian Berhanu Kibret, a University of Maryland School of Pharmacy instructor returning from a conference where he received a teaching award, at the University of Maryland at Dallas Fort Worth International Airport.

The Trump Administration has also broadened its use of administrative warrants. Previous Administrations used such warrants to arrest people who were already in deportation proceedings. More recently, they have also been used in cases involving immigrants who are actively applying to renew their immigration status.

“In the past, people like that have never been prioritized for deportation if they pose no other public safety threat, given that they're taking steps to get into compliance with the law,” Gupta says.

“Our policy right now is to go after the worst of the worst,” DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin said during a congressional hearing last week. “When we encounter someone here illegally, I am required to find out who they are.”

text:
Inundated by thousands of ICE detainee lawsuits, DOJ directs non-immigration attorneys to help with caseload

WASHINGTON, D.C. (CBS NEWS) — The Justice Department has directed attorneys from across its civil litigation divisions to help defend the Trump administration against a growing number of lawsuits filed by individuals in immigration detention.

More than 97,000 detainees have filed habeas corpus petitions challenging their detention since January 2025, including approximately 10,000 new petitions just since October 2026 alone, according to a Nov. 24 memo obtained by CBS News.

Habeas petitions are a legal mechanism through which individuals may challenge the lawfulness of their detention.

Prior to the second Trump administration, the federal caseload for habeas immigration detention petitions tended to be much lower — closer to a few hundred in an entire year.

It can take weeks or even months to resolve an immigration habeas petition.

The Justice Department says the litigation is straining resources at U.S. attorneys’ offices, which have been primarily responsible for handling the cases.

“Many of the Department’s U.S. Attorneys’ Offices have been overwhelmed by the influx of petitions and impracticable procedures set by the courts,” Attorney General Todd Blanche wrote in a three-page memo.

The memo directs attorneys from the department’s Antitrust, Civil, Civil Rights, and Environment and Natural Resources divisions and U.S. Trustees Program, to assist with the litigation — roughly 2,000 litigators across its civil components.

The memo doesn’t specify how many attorneys will be reassigned or how many cases they will be expected to handle.

Attorneys from the offices of the attorney general, deputy attorney general and associate attorney general will also take on additional cases.

Immigration-related habeas cases have skyrocketed since President Trump returned to office, as his administration has placed record numbers of individuals in ICE detention and narrowed the avenues for them to be released, including on bond.

Blanche characterized many of the habeas petitions as “frivolous” in his memo.

“The increase in habeas petitions resulted, in part, from the immigration bar’s attempt to thwart President Trump’s promise to the American people to prioritize their safety and security,” he wrote.

Last year, Stephen Miller, the architect of the Trump administration’s deportation policy and now the White House chief of staff, floated the idea of suspending the right of habeas corpus for those detained as part of Mr. Trump’s crackdown on illegal immigration.

The administration has not moved forward with the proposal, which would likely trigger swift legal challenges.

text:
Immigration and Customs Enforcement says it now has enough body cameras to equip all its officers and agents. The update comes after years of immigration officials telling lawmakers and advocates that they did not have enough devices for a body-worn camera program to be implemented agency-wide. "Training required to equip individual officers remains ongoing and we expect to complete this training soon," an unnamed spokesperson told NPR in a statement. Cameras could help alleviate some concerns about ICE transparency and accountability after federal immigration officers were involved in over two dozen shootings under the Trump administration's immigration crackdown. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said he predicts that by the end of September every officer in the field will have a body-worn camera. "We have the permanent cameras, but we also have Motorola [that] is working with us on the mics that we use," Mullin said during a press conference in New York on Tuesday, noting that the microphones could also act as a camera. He said he plans to meet with the CEO of Motorola this week to discuss how to use that technology. "It's for our safety and the public safety, too," he said. Federal immigration officers came under fire in July after the deadly shooting of two immigrants, Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in Texas and Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero in Maine. In both instances, neither the target of the arrest nor the officers involved were wearing body cameras, according to the agency. The incidents prompted renewed calls from lawmakers, including from GOP Sen. Susan Collins of Maine and dozens of Democrats, for the agency to roll out body-worn cameras to every officer. The demand also comes as ICE hit its highest monthly arrest totals so far this administration — some 50,000 people in July. The agency faces growing calls for body cameras as it's both hired more officers and ramped up arrests. But those who want body-worn cameras say they're still waiting to see if the program is fully implemented, and if footage from incidents is publicly released. Independent Sen. Angus King of Maine called ICE's remarks about enough devices a "hollow promise." "Unless and until there is a change of policy and leadership, today's news simply means that there is more expensively-equipped lawlessness on our streets rather than responsible, legitimate law enforcement," King said in a statement. ICE did not respond to questions regarding how long training will take or how many officers already have cameras. But some members of Congress, including Rep. Henry Cuellar (D-Texas), have been told that training is already completed. "The fact that ICE has now acquired enough cameras to equip officers and agents nationwide is important progress. We understand training has been completed across all ICE areas of responsibility," Cuellar said in a statement to NPR. "Body cameras protect the public and officers by providing a clear record of what happens during enforcement actions while strengthening transparency and accountability." Multi-year effort to push for cameras Money provided by congressional Republicans last year made ICE the highest-funded federal law enforcement agency. But none of the money was specifically earmarked for body-worn cameras. At the start of the year, top DHS officials, including Mullin, urged lawmakers to provide funding specifically for purchasing more body cameras and training officers on how to use them. Congress, across two different funding measures, responded by providing $31 billion for technology, including for body cameras, and $20 million specifically for body cameras — though lawmakers were unable to negotiate a mandate for ICE to purchase or use the cameras. It is still unclear how many body cameras the agency owns. Officials in February told lawmakers that ICE had 3,000 cameras for 13,000 officers. In some instances, entire field offices were not equipped with any cameras. During "Operation Metro Surge" in Minneapolis last winter, for example, there were no body-worn cameras "physically located" at the St. Paul field office, according to court records. However, immigration officers in Minneapolis were wearing cameras when they shot and killed two U.S. citizens in January. Footage from the cameras worn by CBP officers involved in the death of 37-year-old Alex Pretti contradicted the administration's initial narrative of his death, and renewed calls for broader use of the cameras. This summer, DHS awarded two contracts to Axon Enterprise totaling more than $30 million for cameras. ICE has been looking at how to equip its officers with body-worn cameras for at least five years. Congress mandated in 2021 that the agency work with the Homeland Security Office for Civil Rights and Civil Liberties to design a pilot program for body-worn cameras. A DHS report from 2024 says ICE expected body cameras to be implemented agency-wide by September 2025; it's now been a year since that prediction. The initial effort was part of a broader Biden administration executive order to expand federal law enforcement use of body cameras. But President Trump rescinded that Biden executive order when he returned to the White House last year. And DHS shrunk the office tasked with helping to oversee the ICE camera pilot program.

The Allied Forces News Desk #TheAlliedForces *********************** "The Trump administration proposed massive cuts to Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s body camera program for this fiscal year as officers surged into U.S. cities to arrest immigrants, calling into question the agency’s commitment to deploying cameras. In its initial budget proposal, the Department of Homeland Security said it planned to slash the body camera program’s 22-person staff to three employees and reduce spending on the initiative from about $20.5 million to $5.5 million. Officials instead proposed “sustaining” the cameras ICE had last year to devote more resources to “frontline operations.” A string of violent incidents involving federal immigration officers — including the fatal shooting of Minneapolis resident Renée Good in her SUV this month — has added fresh urgency to calls from congressional Democrats and some Republicans for more body-worn cameras. In several use-of-force incidents, witnesses and Homeland Security officials have given wildly differing accounts of the confrontations. Yet the government has voluntarily released little officer-worn footage. To address these concerns, House appropriators this week said they would allocate about $20 million for cameras for DHS, which oversees ICE and its sibling agency, Customs and Border Protection, and require the agency to report back on its progress in 30 days. But the House plan stops short of requiring officers to wear cameras, and some congressional aides and analysts said this week that the extra money is meaningless if the cameras are not mandatory. Rep. Rosa DeLauro of Connecticut, the top Democrat on the House Appropriations Committee, said Republicans would not agree on requiring agents to wear the cameras. “Body cameras only enhance transparency and accountability which is required to build public trust — which ICE has totally lost under the leadership of [Homeland Security] Secretary Kristi Noem and Stephen Miller,” DeLauro said in a statement. Top Republicans on the committee did not respond to questions about that assertion. But a Trump administration official confirmed Friday that the White House opposed mandating body-cameras as one of “many unserious poison pill demands” from Democrats in the budget bill. The official, in an unsigned email from the Office of Management and Budget, did not explain the administration’s reasoning. The latest figures, which were compiled in June, showed that ICE had 4,400 cameras, though its workforce has since swelled to 22,000, while CBP had 13,400 cameras for a workforce of at least 45,000 armed officers, according to the House Homeland Security Committee. It is unclear how many of those cameras are in use. Homeland Security officials have said they have been working to expand officers’ access to body cameras. But the agency did not ensure that every ICE officer had a camera last year after receiving a massive infusion of cash, and it has not responded to multiple questions from The Washington Post and lawmakers about why so many officers and agents don’t have them. According to a 2024 DHS report, ICE’s cameras were supposed to have been fully operational by September after years of testing. Congressional Republicans nearly tripled ICE’s annual budget for the previous fiscal year, but Trump officials did not appear to prioritize cameras. ICE officer Jonathan Ross and other officers at the scene of Good’s killing did not appear to be wearing body cameras and DHS has not released any corresponding footage. DHS has not explained why Ross and his colleagues weren’t equipped with cameras, but Ross testified last month that he and other ICE officers in his five-state region were not allowed to wear body cameras because their field office did not have a written policy for it. Ross was filming Good with his cellphone shortly before shooting her, raising additional questions about why he was handling a phone and a gun at the same time. “They’ve gotten so much money, they have more than enough money to do the [camera] program,” Claire Trickler-McNulty, a Biden administration ICE official, said. “It seems more like a policy and operational choice not to use body-worn cameras.” Homeland Security spokeswoman Tricia McLaughlin told CNN this month that the agency “of course” allowed officers to wear cameras and said the agency was working on expanding the program. McLaughlin told The Post the same thing in September, and officials have not provided data on how many officers and agents are equipped with cameras. President Joe Biden ordered federal law enforcement to wear body cameras and make other reforms in a 2022 executive order. Trump rescinded that directive after starting his second term. Nevertheless, a month after Trump began his second term, then-acting ICE director Caleb Vitello issued a directive that said cameras can build trust and transparency and wrote that officers should activate them “as soon as practicable at the beginning of an enforcement activity.” Vitello was soon demoted for reasons that were never disclosed, and did not respond to requests for comment. Since Trump took office, ICE has released only one body-camera video, of a confrontation outside a New Jersey detention center. CBP has issued three videos, all of shootings on the southern border. Body-worn cameras were broadly accessible to law enforcement as far back as 2016, when Justice Department figures show that roughly half of police agencies had them. Usage spread after a Minneapolis police officer killed George Floyd in 2020, igniting the largest anti-racism protests in U.S. history. At first, police said Floyd suffered a medical incident, but witness video — and, later, police body-camera footage — showed the officer had used excessive force. Officer Derek Chauvin was convicted of murder and manslaughter, and sentenced to 22 and a half years in prison. At least eight states mandate that law enforcement officers use body-worn cameras: Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Illinois, Maryland, New Jersey, New Mexico and South Carolina, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures. Proponents of cameras say they provide an independent accounting of law enforcement’s interactions with the public that benefit officers and residents. Footage can gather evidence of crimes, dispel false accusations, and de-escalate tensions between police and the public. “It protects both the law enforcement officers and the people they interact with,” said Deborah Fleischaker, a former top DHS official and an acting ICE chief of staff under Biden. “If an agent did something wrong, you want to know about it so you can handle it, so you can fix it. But it’s also protective of the agents because, look, the reality is that not every claim of use of force or bad language or abuse is true.”

Attorney General Todd Blanche is mobilizing civil litigators across the Justice Department in an all-hands-on-deck push to fight tens of thousands of legal filings by detained migrants asking federal courts to review whether their imprisonment is lawful.

The pre-Thanksgiving memo comes as the Justice Department has been hit with 97, 000 habeas corpus petition filings since January 2025, including close to 10,000 new petitions filed since October. Typically, the Justice Department faces only a few hundred habeas corpus cases a year.

DHS TOUTS HIGHEST ICE DEPORTATIONS IN HISTORY, AS MULLIN SAYS AGENCY HAS BEEN ‘UNLEASHED’

The surge in lawsuits comes after the Trump administration changed its detention policy to deny bond hearings to migrants arrested inside the U.S. — even those who have lived in the country for years. SUPREME COURT TO SCRUTINIZE KEY PILLAR OF TRUMP DEPORTATION MACHINE IN BLOCKBUSTER CASE

description:

text:
WASHINGTON — A federal district court today blocked President Trump’s new executive order targeting birthright citizenship.

The ruling stems from a lawsuit, Nathan v. Trump, brought by the American Civil Liberties Union, ACLU of New Hampshire, ACLU of Maine, ACLU of Massachusetts, ACLU of the District of Columbia, Legal Defense Fund, Asian Law Caucus, and Democracy Defenders Fund on behalf of people subjected to the new executive order.

The groups already secured a major Supreme Court victory concerning birthright citizenship in Trump v. Barbara in June. That decision affirmed protections for babies who would have been denied citizenship under President Trump’s first failed birthright citizenship executive order.

In its ruling this summer, the Supreme Court confirmed that the Constitution’s Citizenship Clause puts “the question of citizenship ‘once and forever [to] rest.’” Despite that, the administration is again trying to restrict birthright citizenship.

In today’s ruling, the district court explained that “Barbara’s ink had scarcely dried when the President issued [the] second executive order,” but emphasized that “the President cannot carve out new exceptions to birthright citizenship for children born within the United States and subject to its laws.”

The following is reaction to today’s ruling:

“Enough is enough,” said Cody Wofsy, Deputy Director of the ACLU’s Immigrants’ Rights Project. “The Supreme Court has twice rejected efforts to gut birthright citizenship, in 1898 and again earlier this year. Third time is not the charm, and the President needs to accept that birthright citizenship is the law of the land.”

“This should put to rest all attempts to limit the citizenship protections owed to any child born in the United States,” said Brittany Carter, assistant counsel at the Legal Defense Fund. “This ruling affirms that the Administration’s continued efforts to circumvent the Constitution will not stand, and upholds the rule of law rather than the vengeful whims of the executive.”

“The president keeps trying to rewrite the Constitution by executive fiat. Today’s ruling reinforces, yet again, that he cannot,” said Winnie Kao, senior counsel at Asian Law Caucus. “Instead of addressing the real problems Americans face, the Trump administration is wasting taxpayer dollars on yet another attempt to strip birthright citizenship from US-born babies, threatening to throw government agencies and families into chaos. Birthright citizenship has allowed generations of immigrants to build, contribute, and make this country what it is. We will continue to defend it.”

“Today’s ruling is a victory for families across the country,” said Tianna Mays, legal director at Democracy Defenders Fund. “The court correctly stopped this unlawful order before it could inflict irreversible harm on America’s youngest citizens. We will continue protecting these guaranteed rights from these lawless attacks.”

“Birthright citizenship is the law of the land — period. Cruel attacks on this core constitutional right must not be allowed to stand, which the court reaffirmed once again today,” said SangYeob Kim, director of the ACLU of New Hampshire’s Immigrants’ Rights Project.

“The courts have yet again reaffirmed that babies born in the United States are citizens,” said ACLU of Maine Legal Director Carol Garvan. “The president may keep signing unlawful executive orders, but the Supreme Court was clear when it ruled that neither the president nor Congress can end birthright citizenship.”

“This ruling affirms that birthright citizenship is here to stay — and there is nothing President Trump can do about that,” said Carol Rose, executive director at the ACLU of Massachusetts. “The Trump administration must follow the law, acknowledge the constitutional rights of our clients, and abandon this futile effort to rewrite the Fourteenth Amendment.”

“The court yet again affirmed that the government cannot concoct new exceptions to the constitutional principle of birthright citizenship,” said Scott Michelman, legal director of the ACLU of the District of Columbia. “This ruling will hopefully put an end to President Trump’s cruel crusade against the country’s youngest citizens.”

What does the Executive Order require?

text:
With Democrats taking control of both houses of Congress in the new year, the Trump administration is seeking to limit the range of executive branch information available to Congressional investigators. To that end, President Trump issued Executive Order 14439, Protecting the Executive’s Privileges and Enhancing Efficiencies in Government Contracts (the EO). On its face, the EO would require a government contractor to receive permission from the executive branch prior to providing information to Congress related to their contracts. This could put contractors (and their subcontractors) in the position of risking noncompliance with a contractual requirement, being suspended or debarred by a contracting agency, or being held in contempt of Congress.

The Office of Management and Budget was also tasked with issuing guidance that should offer additional details, expectations, and instructions.

What does the Executive Order require?

At its core, the EO requires that contractors and subcontractors notify the contracting agency and the White House of any Congressional inquiries and “abide by any instructions received from the White House and contracting agency related to the withholding of communications that the White House or the agency has determined are protected by executive privilege.”

Notwithstanding this, Congress will likely assert that it is entitled to information no matter what the EO (or a contract) requires. This, of course, will put contractors in the difficult position of having to choose between noncompliance with executive branch and legislative branch directives.

When will the requirements under the EO attach?

Traditionally, executive orders impacting government contractors require rulemaking and, once rulemaking is complete, insertion of those regulations into government contracts.

This implementation method has been short-circuited a number of times by the Trump administrations. For instance, on September 22, 2020, the first Trump administration issued an executive order, Combating Race and Sex Stereotyping. In that executive order, compliance was required within 60 days after the issuance of the executive order irrespective of any rulemaking. Other executive orders during the second administration have followed suit, including this one. Here, compliance could conceivably be required almost immediately under the plain language of the EO: “[e]ach agency shall promptly inform all contractors and subcontractors of the obligations in this order and shall require such contractors and subcontractors to comply with the requirements set forth in section 2 of this order.” Obligations under federal contracts, however, usually do not take effect until they are inserted into contracts, and bilateral modifications (as would be required here) could give contractors leverage to receive other concessions from agencies.

What happens if contractors fail to comply with the EO?

Under the terms of the EO, contractors who fail to comply could have their contracts canceled (though not specified, presumably for default), or face suspension or debarment. Suspension and debarment are usually reserved for when contractors do not have the requisite responsibility under FAR Part 9 to receive or perform contracts.

What happens if contractors fail to comply with Congressional inquiries?

Courts have long held that Congressional investigations are “inherent in the legislative process” and Congress generally has broad powers to receive documents or testimony. Failure to comply could result in contempt of Congress and potential jail time. In 2024, two former Trump administration officials were jailed for failing to respond to Congressional subpoenas. Besides that, Members of Congress and Senators could use their bully pulpit to highlight contractors that fail to comply with Congressional inquiries.

What is the legal basis for the EO?

The EO was issued under the Federal Property and Administrative Services Act (FPASA), which allows for new regulatory requirements for better efficiency under the government contracting process. This has been used by both administrations to effect policies. For instance, during the Biden administration, this statute was used as a basis for the executive order requiring vaccination of certain federal contractor workers. A number of courts found that the Biden administration overstepped its bounds, and it would not be surprising to see cases challenging the EO filed by Congress, contractors, or other interested parties.

Further, the EO takes a potentially expansive view of privilege that can be asserted by the executive branch. Typically, in government contracting, contract documents and documents related to performance are available during protests at the Court of Federal Claims or the Government Accountability Office and in response to Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) requests (with potential redactions). Congress typically does not recognize confidentiality or attorney-client privilege assertions (though those can potentially be negotiated).

What steps should contractors take?

Contractors and their subcontractors should begin preparing for Congressional inquiries and potential conflicts with this EO where contractors may have to choose between (1) complying with this EO/contractual directives and risk being in contempt of Congress or (2) complying with a Congressional inquiry and having their contract be terminated or the company be suspended or debarred. Contractors should:

Develop a strategic and comprehensive approach led by counsel on next steps and consideration of potentially competing directives;

Involve inside or external counsel now to develop a written policy on how to handle attempts by contracting officers to modify contracts or give directives consistent with the EO;

In advance, understand the implications of noncompliance with Congressional inquiries versus the EO, forthcoming guidance, and any newly inserted contract clauses; and

Monitor and analyze the expected legal battle to understand what will be required.

Feel free to reach out to us if you have any questions.

text:
We, the Sonoma County Commission on Human Rights, state our belief that Flock Cameras and similar ALPR technology are not worth their risk factor in our community, and have been misrepresented to both the public and our elected officials. The technology itself, as well as the way in which it was rolled out in Sonoma County, represents a breach of the public trust and urgently needs to be re-evaluated in a thoughtful, public, and transparent manner.

Based on our review of available information, and informed by our Flock Camera & ALPR Community Forum on October 19th, 2026, we find the following to be true:

Flock was sold to the public on false and outdated premises. ALPRs in Sonoma County were allegedly originally rolled out in response to a COVID-era wave of “smash-and-grab” retail thefts and other crimes. That is not our current reality, and it is unclear exactly how ALPRs are benefitting our communities now.

Law enforcement officials themselves are unable to confidently state that ALPRs help them solve crimes or catch criminals. Indeed, available data from the CA Department of Justice suggests that Sonoma County’s crime clearance rates have barely changed since 2023 when the Flock rollout began. Rates have even decreased in several categories.

Law enforcement officials frequently reiterate that they have “strong policies” that prevent any wrongdoing related to ALPRs. But policy can change at the drop of a hat, meaning that today’s ‘guardrails’ are tomorrow’s mere suggestions. Furthermore, as revealed time and time again by the widespread wrongdoing around the country by law enforcement officers with access to ALPR databases, policy can be bypassed.

Even if ALPRs are responsive to actual crime in our communities, even if they do help solve crimes or catch criminals, and even if no Sonoma County law enforcement officer ever violates any law or policy on ALPR data, these cameras and the technology supporting them do nothing to change the socioeconomic conditions that lead people to commit crimes in the first place.

The public of Sonoma County is resolutely opposed to the use of this technology in their communities. Their opposition is based on a wide range of reasoning and reasonable fears, including racial profiling, collaboration with federal law or immigration enforcement, corporate monitoring of people’s movements, high incarceration rates, centralization and misuse of personal data, and many more.

text:
MINNEAPOLIS – In its travel advisories, the U.S. State Department warns Americans not to visit Honduras' Gracias a Dios region, alerting them to violent crime, armed robbery, murder and active terrorist groups.

But for Hondurans, the message is less stark. “Overall, Gracias a Dios is a low-crime, functioning department,” says a State Department background report obtained by The Associated Press.

The report, and similar documents about Guatemala, Mexico and El Salvador, were prepared for use in immigration courts, where asylum denial rates have soared to 94% during President Donald Trump’s second term.

The reports use cherry-picked data, careful phrasing and, in some cases, facts that don’t stand up to scrutiny to create misleading depictions of countries that are, in fact, often plagued by violence, government corruption and police inaction.

They appear designed to make it easier for judges to deny asylum to people from those nations fleeing domestic violence and criminal gangs, painting pictures of life in their home countries that often clash with reality.

The reports have been “reverse-engineered,” said Elliott Young, a professor at Lewis & Clark College who analyzed the documents for the college’s Migration and Asylum Lab.

“They’re trying to hit the most frequent kinds of (asylum) cases that come up and provide counterevidence to the overwhelming evidence that these are dangerous places,” said Young, a scholar of Latin America and asylum law who has testified as an expert witness in more than 700 asylum cases.

In a statement, the State Department said that in line with U.S. laws and regulations it “may provide information about conditions in foreign countries” to immigration courts and U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services. The Justice Department, which oversees immigration courts, did not respond to a request for comment on what role the reports play in influencing asylum decisions.

A system in turmoil — and targeted

Cutting back on asylum has been a centerpiece of Trump’s immigration crackdown dating to his first term, when he dismissed migrants waiting in Mexico to get into the U.S. as “not legitimate asylum-seekers.”

Most asylum seekers, the Republican president said, were fleeing poverty.

“Asylum is a very special protection intended only for those fleeing government persecution based on race, religion and other protected status,” he said in a 2018 White House appearance.

Trump was years out of date. While asylum was largely seen after World War II as a way to protect people fleeing political persecution, the definition was expanded long ago, including to encompass some people fleeing domestic and criminal violence.

But he had a point about poverty.

Legal and illegal migration, particularly from Latin America, has exploded over the past two decades as people have sought more economic opportunity, with increasing asylum claims based on safety fears from domestic partners and criminal gangs.

Even during President Joe Biden's years, most asylum claims were rejected.

But denials have jumped from roughly 72% at the end of that Democratic administration to 94% in June under Trump, according to the data research nonprofit Transactional Records Access Clearinghouse.

Trump was elected to a second term in part by focusing on frustrated voters who had seen illegal immigration soar under Biden, with border arrests from Mexico reaching a record 250,000 in December 2023. The asylum system, meanwhile, faced a backlog of millions of cases.

The Trump administration has reshaped immigration courts as part of its push to increase deportations, organizing mass hearings, authorizing military lawyers as immigration judges, and giving judges more leeway to summarily dismiss claims.

A sanitized view of troubled countries

Immigration judges must weigh whether people seeking asylum based on domestic violence or criminal threats have a reasonable fear of persecution because of their race, religion, nationality, political views or an often-debated catch-all category, “membership in a particular social group.” They also have to show that their government can't or won't protect them and that they can't move elsewhere in their home country to escape persecution.

The reports offer what can sometimes seem like travel brochure descriptions of life in these countries.

They mention good schools, low crime, quality hospitals and constitutions that protect individual rights, with brief notes that “the availability of services” can vary across each country.

Take El Salvador, where the government of President Nayib Bukele has long faced accusations of widespread human rights abuses, including torture.

The State Department report takes a far more generous view of the situation, noting the government’s approach to rights abuses “is no different than that of developed countries in Europe and North America, including the United States itself,” and highlighting a handful of prosecutions tied to the civil war, which ended in 1992.

“In any country, a rogue official can mistreat those under their power,” it says.

For Honduras’ Gracias a Dios province, violent crime rates “compare favorably with rates of violent crime in many parts of the United States,” says the report.

Former officials and advocates say the six-page reports pale in comparison to traditional State Department human rights reports, lengthy dissections of more than 100 nations around the world, which under the second Trump administration have been truncated and delayed.

“These shorter reports clearly don’t address the full range of human rights issues that the country reports have traditionally addressed,” said Scott Busby, former deputy assistant secretary in the Bureau of Democracy, Human Rights and Labor at the State Department and now a senior adviser at the group Human Rights First.

They are “especially problematic given that the country reports themselves for last year have yet to be issued,” he said.

Looking at asylum-seekers’ ability to move elsewhere

In many ways, the reports appear aimed most directly at asylum regulations around a person's ability to escape persecution by simply moving.

Those regulations are key for anyone seeking asylum based on domestic or criminal violence.

The reports highlight specific parts of each country, mentioning places like an off-the-beaten-track tourist destination in Guatemala and a province in El Salvador that has low crime and 24-hour emergency medical care.

But those mentions only tell part of the story.

“The fact that there may be pockets of a country that are relatively safe for some people doesn’t mean that everybody can just move to that part of the country,” said Neela Chakravartula, an asylum attorney with the Center for Gender & Refugee Studies at the University of California College of the Law, San Francisco.

If that were the case, Chakravartula said: “We’d all be living in Malibu.”

___

Associated Press reporter Joshua Goodman in Miami contributed to this report.

___

This story has been updated to correct the spelling of the first name of the professor at Lewis & Clark College. It is Elliott, not Elliot.

text:
MADRID (AP) — Kilmar Ábrego García, a Salvadoran national who fought his mistaken deportation from the United States, arrived in Spain on Wednesday after voluntarily leaving the U.S., potentially ending a defining saga of President Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown.

Ábrego García, who has an American wife and child and had lived in Maryland for years, was arrested in Baltimore in March 2025 and was deported to a Salvadoran prison in what an official later called an “administrative error.” His departure to Spain follows months of legal wrangling as he battled the Trump administration’s drive to deport him to Africa.

“The U.S. government may be the most powerful government in the world, but justice can still prevail,” Ábrego García said in a statement released Wednesday. “In this case, despite everything they tried to say, every obstacle they put in my way, and every attempt to shame me, justice prevailed under this administration in a way that many people never thought was possible.”

Ábrego García, who’s in his 30s, migrated to the U.S. illegally as a teenager. In 2019, an immigration judge ruled that he could not be deported to El Salvador because he faced danger there from a gang that had threatened his family. The judge allowed him to live and work in the U.S. under Immigration and Customs Enforcement supervision, but he was not given residency status.

He didn’t speak to reporters after landing at Madrid’s international airport and raised a fist as he entered a van. But at a virtual news conference later, he thanked his supporters and said, “I’m happy, and I’m celebrating my freedom.”

Simon Sandoval-Moshenberg, a Virginia-based attorney representing Ábrego García, called the move “a temporary departure.”

“Mr. Ábrego García has many options to return to the United States as the husband of a U.S. citizen spouse and the father of a U.S. citizen child. We don’t expect that to happen under this administration, which we know will never give him a fair shake, but we expect that the next administration will prioritize reunifying this family and bringing him back to Maryland,” Sandoval-Moshenberg said.

Sandoval-Moshenberg thanked Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen, who met with Ábrego García when he was sent back to El Salvador, for his advocacy and said that visit was a turning point in the case. “Without that," Sandoval-Moshenberg said, “I have no doubt that El Salvador would have continued to stonewall.”

Van Hollen said he spoke to Ábrego García and his wife before they departed the U.S. He reflected on his visit to see Ábrego García in El Salvador, saying, “We had no idea whether Kilmar Ábrego García was alive or dead.”

He said he was glad the Trump administration didn’t succeed in carrying out its vendetta against Ábrego García because he stood up for his rights. “They wanted to leave him to rot there, to rot there for the rest of his life," he said.

Ábrego García would decide where to settle for the next two years to wait out the remainder of the Trump administration, Sandoval-Moshenberg said. Ábrego García’s immigration status in Spain wasn’t immediately clear.

U.S. District Judge Paula Xinis, who presided over Ábrego García’s long-running immigration proceedings in Maryland, ordered the case’s dismissal on Wednesday after receiving confirmation that he had left the U.S.

The court also unsealed an order that Xinis signed last Friday to spell out the terms of his “unimpeded” departure. In the order, Xinis said the government informed her that Ábrego García was free to self-deport “to any country that is willing to accept him.”

The judge, in turn, set Tuesday as the deadline for his departure and ordered the removal of his GPS ankle monitor before he boarded the flight.

The order didn’t address why the government had changed its position on him leaving the U.S. to a country of his choice.

The U.S. Department of Homeland Security said Tuesday night that he self-deported to Spain as part of a removal order and that he didn’t receive any incentives and won’t be allowed back into the U.S.

U.S. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said in a post on X that he was “delighted” about Ábrego García’s departure, listing a familiar litany of allegations for why he should be deported, including that he was a gang member, an accusation that Ábrego García has repeatedly denied.

Ábrego García’s deportation in early 2025 came as Trump, a Republican, was ramping up his immigration crackdown, promising to deport 1 million people annually.

Through an infusion of billions of dollars approved by the U.S. Congress, the Trump administration later supercharged its immigration enforcement capabilities, growing its cadre of immigration officers, expanding detention capabilities and pushing to deport an increasing number of people.

They are "especially problematic given that the country reports themselves for last year have yet to be issued," he said.

Looking at asylum-seekers' ability to move elsewhere

In many ways, the reports appear aimed most directly at asylum regulations around a person's ability to escape persecution by simply moving.

Those regulations are key for anyone seeking asylum based on domestic or criminal violence.

The reports highlight specific parts of each country, mentioning places like an off-the-beaten track tourist destination in Guatemala and a province in El Salvador that has low crime and 24-hour emergency medical care.

But those mentions only tell part of the story.

"The fact that there may be pockets of a country that are relatively safe for some people doesn't mean that everybody can just move to that part of the country," said Neela Chakravartula, an asylum attorney with the Center for Gender & Refugee Studies at the University of California College of the Law, San Francisco.

If that were the case, Chakravartula said: "We'd all be living in Malibu."

Associated Press reporter Joshua Goodman in Miami contributed to this report.

text:
Kilmar Ábrego García, whose deportation last year to an El Salvador jail became a flashpoint in President Donald Trump's immigration crackdown, has left the US for Spain.

He took a commercial flight to the country on Tuesday. His lawyer said the relocation was temporary while Ábrego García sought eventually to return to the US.

After the US government admitted it had wrongfully sent Ábrego García to his home country, he was returned to face human trafficking charges that were later dropped.

The Trump administration had continued its attempts to deport him to other countries, including Uganda and Ghana.

Ábrego García, who is married to a US citizen and lived in Maryland, came to the US illegally from El Salvador as a teenager.

Senator Chris Van Hollen, a Democrat from Maryland, visited Ábrego García while he was in the notorious Cecot prison in El Salvador in 2025 and advocated for his release.

"A year and a half ago, the Trump administration wanted to leave Kilmar Ábrego García to rot in a Salvadoran gulag," Van Hollen said in a statement on Tuesday.

"Today, Kilmar is travelling to a country of his choice, a free man - unharmed and with dignity."

Footage shared with the BBC's US partner CBS shows an ICE ankle monitor being removed from Ábrego García upon his arrival in Spain. He told the outlet that he was leaving the US "happy" and "with his freedom".

Ábrego García's lawyer said in a statement his departure was "temporary" as he had "many options to return to the United States".

"We don't expect that to happen under this administration, which we know will never give him a fair shake, but we expect that the next administration will prioritise reunifying this family and bringing him back to Maryland," the statement said.

"Where he goes from here, where he chooses to settle for the next two years while he waits out the end of this administration, will be his choice, not the administration's choice."

Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin confirmed to the BBC that Ábrego García had left the country, decrying him as a criminal.

"We are delighted to announce that Kilmar Ábrego García has self-deported from the United States to Spain," Mullin said in a statement, adding "now this El Salvadoran man cannot terrorise innocent Americans".

The Trump administration claims Ábrego García is a member of the MS-13 gang, which he has denied.

In a post on social media, the Department of Homeland Security wrote that Ábrego García had left the country "pursuant to a removal order".

"He paid for his own flight and received no incentives," the DHS said on X. "He will NEVER be allowed back inside the United States."

Ábrego García was arrested in 2019 alongside three other men and detained by federal immigration authorities.

A judge granted him protection from deportation to El Salvador at the time, citing the risk of persecution by one of the country's criminal gangs.

In March 2025, the Trump administration deported him to El Salvador, where he was held in Cecot, a prison known for its harsh conditions. The US Supreme Court then ordered the government to facilitate his return.

The administration acknowledged that he had been wrongly deported and brought him back to the US, where he was set to face human trafficking charges.

A federal judge dismissed the case, saying Ábrego García had been charged for political reasons.

For months, he was locked in a battle with the government over further efforts to deport him.

Ábrego García had repeatedly said he would be willing to be deported to Costa Rica, while the Costa Rican government had agreed to accept him as a refugee and offer him legal status.

On Oct. 17, a team of ICE agents detained Guerrero Romo, a truck driver, outside his Oakland home as part of the Trump administration’s ongoing efforts to remove immigrants without permanent legal status — even those with legal protection from deportation, like Guerrero Romo — from the U.S.
