The Chronicle obtained and reviewed almost eight hours of footage from body-worn cameras on seven ICE agents as they smashed Guerrero Romo's car window and forcibly removed and cuffed him on the street. The videos provide a rare firsthand look at ICE tactics during the agency’s mass arrests in the Bay Area, including their interactions with Guerrero Romo and with passersby.

The altercation caused cuts and bruises that landed Guerrero Romo in the hospital, part of what several Bay Area attorneys say is a rise in injuries during immigration arrests.

Immigration attorneys said they have seen more clients injured or threatened with force from ICE agents in the past two months, incidents documented in court filings reviewed by the Chronicle.

“At that moment, I was scared, I was broken, angry,” Guerrero Romo said in an interview on Monday. “I thought I was doing everything right, and I never imagined that could have happened to me.”

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

The use of violence during immigration arrests is at “an unprecedented level,” said Nikolas De Braemaker, managing attorney for the immigrants’ rights practice at Centro Legal de la Raza, who said ICE agents are increasingly causing injuries.

Since President Donald Trump took office in January 2025, ICE has hired more deportation officers, increasing the total from about 6,900 in the 2024 fiscal year to 11,400 in the 2026 fiscal year, according to federal workforce data. The New York Times reported last week that the hiring spree involved loosening training standards, including allowing thousands of recruits with law enforcement backgrounds to complete training virtually and letting applicants who failed a training test retake it an unlimited number of times.

“For me, one of the main causes is just the lack of training and the lack of proper vetting when hiring new agents that we’re seeing play out on the ground,” De Braemaker said.

A Department of Homeland Security spokesperson did not respond to specific questions from the Chronicle about the Oakland incident, citing ICE policy not to discuss law enforcement operations for “operational security and safety of our officers.”

“ICE law enforcement officers are trained to use the minimum amount of force necessary to resolve dangerous situations to prioritize the safety of the public and our officers,” the spokesperson said. “Officers are highly trained in de-escalation tactics and regularly receive ongoing use of force training, and they are entrusted with upholding the rule of law and are held to the highest standards of professionalism, integrity, and ethical conduct.”

DHS’ spokesperson also said there was “a highly coordinated campaign of violence against our law enforcement” and alleged an increase in assaults against officers, without providing evidence.

ICE activity has continued in Oakland, where two U.S. citizens were detained by agents Sunday and smoke bombs, pepper spray and physical force were used against community members who had shown up at a targeted enforcement operation, Oakland Mayor Barbara Lee said in a public statement.

The Chronicle reviewed court filings from the past two months detailing allegations by five Bay Area residents that they were injured by ICE agents during arrests, including three who were hospitalized from their injuries. The review also found three instances where agents are accused of smashing someone’s car window, five people who accused agents of forcibly removing them from their vehicle and two incidents where agents are accused of threatening to use force during arrests.

One man was on his way to a pizza shop near his Emeryville home on Oct. 16 when he was arrested by an ICE officer who allegedly sat on his chest, fracturing six of his ribs. An ICE agent in Sonoma County allegedly pointed guns “like a rifle” at a U.S. citizen on Oct. 13. She was driving a car registered to her partner, who was targeted for arrest, according to a court filing. She was not injured and was released after showing her identification. Her partner was detained later that day.

Felix Medina, a San Jose resident of 23 years whose wife and seven children are all U.S. citizens, was driving to work on Oct. 30 when ICE agents stopped his car. The construction company owner told the Chronicle that an agent grabbed his arm with such force that it left a bruise, which took several days to heal.

“They twisted my arm,” he said. “He said I shouldn’t resist the arrest or it would be worse.”

He complied because his 17-year-old nephew was with him and afraid of the guns the agents were carrying. The agents handcuffed Medina so tightly it cut him, according to court filings, and chained him by his legs and waist for 11 hours, he said. A judge ordered his release that night, through a habeas corpus petition. Medina still has no feeling in his thumb due to the handcuffs, he said.

Sen. Alex Padilla said in an emailed statement that he was tracking “the latest surge in violent ICE operations, which are causing chaos in communities throughout California.”

“These operations are fueled by ICE’s loosened hiring and training standards as they onboarded thousands of new officers, along with an administration doubling down on Donald Trump’s and Stephen Miller’s mass detention and deportation agenda,” Padilla said. When Democrats assume the majority of Congress in January, he said, “we will do everything we can to put an end to ICE’s out-of-control tactics and hold anyone who violates the law accountable.”

There is little to no legal recourse for injuries caused by ICE agents making arrests, said Lorraine Van Kirk, an attorney representing Guerrero Romo.

“ICE is violently arresting people on our streets, often while wearing masks, and people are ending up in the hospital,” she said. “All too often, these arrests violate the Fourth Amendment and the right to due process. That’s what we contend occurred in Mr. Guerrero Romo’s case.”

The video footage of Guerrero Romo’s arrest was provided to the Chronicle upon request by the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California, which is hearing Guerrero Romo’s habeas corpus petition, challenging the legality of his arrest and detention by the federal government.

He was released on a temporary restraining order on Oct. 20 after Judge Noel Wise ruled that Guerrero Romo's continued detention likely violated his constitutional due process rights and that the government had no justification for arresting him, since it had already determined him not to be a “flight risk nor a danger to the community” when he was granted a form of protection from deportation in 2018.

A hearing for his case is set for December.

Guerrero Romo was on his way home on Oct. 17 when he realized he was being followed by an unmarked black SUV, according to his court declaration.

Born in Mexico, he came to the U.S. in 2002 as a teenager. Following a DUI arrest in 2012, for which he completed DUI classes and had his license eventually restored, he was placed in removal proceedings. Guerrero Romo applied for asylum and, in 2018, an immigration judge granted him withholding from removal.

He had appeared for required ICE check-ins for more than a decade, court records show, and is authorized to work legally in the U.S. through 2029.

The ICE agents who arrived to arrest him in October were not interested in those details.

“I’m not sure if you’re aware, a lot of illegal aliens can still get a work permit,” an agent responded to Guerrero Romo's explanations.

Guerrero Romo asked to see a warrant for his arrest, saying he was on private property. The agent pressed the screen of his phone against the car window, showing what the agent said was an administrative warrant, which is an internal ICE document authorizing civil arrests in public spaces of people suspected of immigration violations.

After about 10 minutes of verbal back-and-forth, Guerrero Romo refused to exit the car.

“This guy is basically asking for physical extraction,” an agent could be heard telling his colleagues on the footage.

“If you get out of the car, we can preserve your vehicle, give you your keys, you’ll be able to have your phone calls,” the agent says, attempting to convince Guerrero Romo to surrender. “Otherwise, if you don’t open the door, I’m going to break the window and I’m going to take you out.”

He told Guerrero Romo to look away because “I don’t want to hurt your eyes,” then smashed the window with a hammer.

Glass shattered over Guerrero Romo .

“People are trying to kidnap me! People trying to kidnap me!” Guerrero Romo shouted into his phone. He had called 911. An agent grabbed his upper arm, and another started wrestling with his upper body, trying to pull him out.

“Get out of the vehicle, you’re making it harder for yourself,” an agent said. “We just showed you the warrant.”

“No you didn’t,” Guerrero Romo responded. “Show me the paper one.”

Over the next 30 minutes, at least five ICE agents pulled on Guerrero Romo's arms and legs trying to drag him from the car. One pulled out pepper spray and pointed it at Guerrero Romo but did not use it.

Guerrero Romo asked the agents if they were not immigrants too.

“My family did paperwork,” an agent responded.

“My family did paperwork for immigration,” Guerrero Romo said.

At one point, agents take turns trying to use their hands to force Guerrero Romo to bend his leg, which he had braced against the front of his car.

“Now you’re hurting me,” Guerrero Romo said as two agents twisted his arms in an “x” shape. “You increasing the level of pain? Is that what you guys do?”

“No, you’re being noncompliant,” an agent said.

Midway through the melee, a passerby in a white pickup truck stopped on the street, got out of his car and asked an agent whether they were allowed to be driving unmarked vehicles.

“I think you’re not supposed to be here,” the man said. “We have a lot of people scared of you guys.”

“Well, we’re federal law enforcement,” an agent responded. “Nothing is happening with you.”

“No, I’m just concerned about him as well,” the man said. “Is he fine with that?”

“He will be fine,” the agent said. The man asked him for his name. The agent refused. “Why do you need to know my name? … I got to protect myself.”

“Protect from what?” the man said.

“There’s a lot of people out there doing things they’re not supposed to be doing,” the agent said.

“You guys are doing what you’re not supposed to be doing,” the man said. “You’re breaking the law.”

“How am I breaking the law?” the agent responded.

“You don’t want to take your mask off, you don’t want to say your name,” the man said.

“I’m a federal law enforcement officer,” the agent said. “I don’t listen to California. I listen to the USA.” The man drove off, telling the officer he was only doing this because he couldn’t be “FBI or CIA.”

After half an hour of struggling, several agents dragged Guerrero Romo out by his four limbs and pinned him on the ground, face down.

“In the moment, I felt like it broke my leg,” Guerrero Romo told the Chronicle later.

A woman heard in the background shouted, “He’s a f—ing American, you asshole.”

Guerrero Romo said he could not walk. An agent half-carried him into the black SUV and drove him to the San Francisco ICE field office in the Financial District, where he was pushed in a wheelchair to a cell. His forehead could be seen cut and bleeding on body camera footage.

According to Guerrero Romo's court declaration, within 30 minutes of his arrival, he was taken to a hospital because he still could not walk. He was hospitalized for three days until a judge ruled his detention was illegal.

“The doctor told me the muscle had broken down from so much force,” he wrote in his court declaration. “The diagnosis is for rhabdomyolysis and traumatic neuropraxia/neuralgia,” using the terms for conditions resulting from muscle breakdown and nerve damage. “They expect it will need months to heal.”

After returning home, Guerrero Romo said he could not put full weight on his leg for three to four days. He took a week off before returning to work. But he is still in pain and his knee sometimes starts trembling, like when he goes up the stairs too quickly.

“Mentally, I am still afraid,” he wrote in a court declaration. “I do not leave the house much now, as I worry that they could arrest me again.”

His biggest hope now, he told the Chronicle, is “to get justice.”

title: The Supreme Court is about to take a closer look at Trump's immigration agenda - CBS 58
description:

And the court limited his ability to use the 1798 Alien Enemies Act to quickly remove certain migrants from the country.

text:
By John Fritze

(CNN) — Democrats want to sideline President Donald Trump’s immigration agenda when they take control of Congress next year, but the real fight may take place across the street where the conservative Supreme Court is poised to uphold several of his most controversial policies.

The court will soon consider blockbuster appeals on the president’s asylum ban, his vast expansion of mandatory detention of migrants and his push to send certain people in the US illegally to countries other than their homeland — including some with dubious human rights records.

Decisions in those cases are expected by late June.

Though those three cases and several others are less flashy than this past summer’s blockbuster decision upholding birthright citizenship, the outcomes in the nuts-and-bolts disputes will have profound implications for policies the administration says are “indispensable” to its overall immigration crackdown.

“In all three of these cases, the Trump administration is trying to rewrite laws enacted by Congress, in service of a radical anti-immigrant agenda that has hurt not only immigrants, but the rule of law,” said Cecillia Wang with the American Civil Liberties Union, which is opposing the administration in two of those cases. “These Trump policies are not only illegal but also unpopular.”

Trump has had a mixed record on immigration at the 6-3 conservative court since returning to power last year. His unprecedented push to upend birthright citizenship was rejected. And the court limited his ability to use the 1798 Alien Enemies Act to quickly remove certain migrants from the country.

On the other hand, six-justice majorities in June allowed Trump to end a form of humanitarian relief known as Temporary Protected Status and to limit asylum claims made at the border.

White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis dismissed Wang’s assertion that the court will find Trump’s immigration policies illegal.

“If the American Civil Liberties Union cares more about criminal illegal aliens than they do about American citizens, then they should change their name,” she said.

Some Democrats have framed the recapture of Congress as a rejection by voters of the administration’s immigration policies. Minnesota Sen.-elect Peggy Flanagan vowed to “rip ICE apart.” New York Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, who is all but certain to become the next House speaker, told CBS that Democrats would “put an end to Donald Trump’s violent mass deportation machine.”

But Republicans have already frontloaded funding for ICE for years. And Trump this month named Stephen Miller, the architect of his immigration crackdown, as White House chief of staff — a sign that the administration has no intention of slowing its immigration agenda.

“It stands to reason that hyper-aggressive immigration enforcement will continue to be one of the hallmarks of the Trump administration even as it faces Democratic majorities in both chambers of the legislature,” said Steve Vladeck, CNN Supreme Court analyst and professor at Georgetown University Law Center. “Whether the extremism of these policies will be allowed to continue is therefore going to be up to the Supreme Court.”

Conservatives who support the policies see a court that is prepared to back the president’s program.

“Over and over, judges in the district courts and the courts of appeals have interpreted the law contrary to clear congressional intent as evidenced by the text. And as a result, those decisions keep getting overturned,” Iowa Solicitor General Eric Wessan, whose state led briefs supporting the administration in two of the biggest cases, told CNN.

Wessan predicted that the justices will view lower court decisions on immigration against the administration with similar skepticism.

“Looking at the immigration cases the Supreme Court has taken this term,” he predicted, “I think it’s doing the same kind of cleanup.”

Human rights and arrests

The showdown will begin on December 9, when the justices will hear arguments in a case challenging Trump’s push to remove certain migrants to countries other than their homeland. In many cases, those removals are carried out without giving the migrant an opportunity to raise human rights concerns.

Federal law allows such “third country” removals in cases when a migrant’s home country refuses to accept them. The administration has used that provision to remove an Iranian national to Nicaragua, for instance, and Venezuelans to El Salvador, according to immigrants’ rights groups.

In some of those cases, immigrant rights groups say, migrants were sent back to their homeland from the “third country,” even when an immigration judge ordered that the administration not return to them to their native country.

Congress has also required the administration to ensure migrants won’t be tortured or persecuted once they land in a third country. That determination was previously made on a case-by-case basis. Under the second Trump administration, the government now accepts blanket assurances from a foreign country that no torture will take place, and migrants are often removed to that country without notice.

The Supreme Court, on its emergency docket, three times allowed the administration to pursue the policy while the case remained pending. It has not explained its reasoning.

Increase in arrests of migrants

Next year, the court will turn to the Trump administration’s decision to funnel not only recent border crossers into mandatory detention but also people who have been living within the United States for years.

That shift has permitted the Department of Homeland Security to dramatically increase the number of migrants arrested. And so if the court rejects that change, it will almost certainly jeopardize the administration’s ability to carry out massive sweeps for migrants that have played out in cities like Chicago and Minneapolis.

Immigrant rights groups say no prior administration, including Trump’s first, has interpreted federal law to require mandatory detention of so many migrants. But Justice Department officials told the Supreme Court that it is simply following the law that Congress enacted.

Asylum ban

And in the spring, the court will hear a challenge to Trump’s asylum ban. The president argues people crossing the border are making false asylum claims as a way to enter the country then stall the deportation process, since it can take years to resolve them.

US Solicitor General D. John Sauer, the administration’s top appellate attorney, warned the court of a “vicious cycle” that encouraged “illegal entry by millions of aliens, who (quite justifiably) inferred that even if they lacked meritorious asylum claims, they would ‘be released to live and work in the United States during their removal proceedings.’”

But the Immigration and Nationality Act specifically allows migrants to claim asylum, even as it leaves the decision about whether to grant safe harbor up to administration officials.

In stark language, the Justice Department has described its asylum policy as one of the “most important and effective” policies for stemming illegal immigration. A lower court order against the policy, the administration said, “threatens to revive the chaos along the southwest border that the proclamation has fended off for the past year and a half.”

The ACLU, representing 13 individuals and three immigrant rights groups that challenged the policy, said that if Trump wants to change the way asylum works, he should have passed a bill in Congress during the two years the chambers were in Republican hands.

Richard Caldarone, a senior litigation attorney at the National Immigrant Justice Center, said that the policies at issue in the cases had already put tens of thousands of people in harm’s way.

“These policies have been overwhelmingly rejected by lower courts across the country, and they flatly violate US immigration law as it has been understood for decades,” said Caldarone, whose group is fighting the administration in the asylum case.

“If the court validates the policies,” he said, “it will enshrine a new generation of internment camps, all but end the US asylum system as we have known it for almost half a century, and shatter our nation’s commitment to upholding human rights and democratic norms.”

The story headline has been updated.

text:
Kilmar Ábrego García, a Salvadoran national who fought his mistaken deportation from the United States, arrived in Spain on Wednesday after voluntarily leaving the U.S., potentially ending a defining saga of President Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown.

Ábrego García, who has an American wife and child and had lived in Maryland for years, was arrested in Baltimore in March 2025 and was deported to a Salvadoran prison in what an official later called an “administrative error.” His departure to Spain follows months of legal wrangling as he battled the Trump administration’s drive to deport him to Africa.

“The U.S. government may be the most powerful government in the world, but justice can still prevail,” Ábrego García said in a statement released Wednesday. “In this case, despite everything they tried to say, every obstacle they put in my way and every attempt to shame me, justice prevailed under this administration in a way that many people never thought was possible.”

Ábrego García, who's in his 30s, migrated to the U.S. illegally as a teenager. In 2019, an immigration judge ruled that he could not be deported to El Salvador because he faced danger there from a gang that had threatened his family. The judge allowed him to live and work in the U.S. under Immigration and Customs Enforcement supervision, but he was not given residency status.

He didn't speak to reporters after landing at Madrid’s international airport and raised a fist as he entered a van.

Simon Sandoval-Moshenberg, a Virginia-based attorney representing Ábrego García, called the move “a temporary departure.”

“Mr. Ábrego García has many options to return to the United States as the husband of a U.S. citizen spouse and the father of a U.S. citizen child. We don’t expect that to happen under this administration, which we know will never give him a fair shake, but we expect that the next administration will prioritize reunifying this family and bringing him back to Maryland,” Sandoval-Moshenberg said.

Ábrego García would decide where to settle for the next two years to wait out the remainder of the Trump administration, the attorney said. Ábrego García's immigration status in Spain wasn’t immediately clear.

U.S. District Judge Paula Xinis, who presided over Ábrego García’s long-running immigration proceedings in Maryland, ordered the case’s dismissal on Wednesday after receiving confirmation that he had left the U.S.

The court also unsealed an order that Xinis signed last Friday to spell out the terms of his “unimpeded” departure. In the order, Xinis said the government informed her that Ábrego García was free to self-deport “to any country that is willing to accept him.”

The judge, in turn, set Tuesday as the deadline for his departure and ordered the removal of his GPS ankle monitor before he boarded the flight.

The order didn’t address why the government had changed its position on him leaving the U.S. to a country of his choice.

The U.S. Department of Homeland Security said Tuesday night that he self-deported to Spain as part of a removal order and that he didn’t receive any incentives and won’t be allowed back into the U.S.

U.S. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said in a post on X that he was “delighted” about Ábrego García’s departure, listing a familiar litany of allegations for why he should be deported, including that he was a gang member, an accusation that Ábrego García has repeatedly denied.

Ábrego García's deportation in early 2025 came as Trump, a Republican, was ramping up his immigration crackdown, promising to deport 1 million people annually.

Through an infusion of billions of dollars approved by the U.S. Congress, the Trump administration later supercharged its immigration enforcement capabilities, growing its cadre of immigration officers, expanding detention capabilities and pushing to deport an increasing number of people.

Ábrego García was fighting against a second deportation to a series of African countries proposed by Department of Homeland Security officials.

Self-identified Latinos account for nearly half of Border Patrol agents and about 30 percent of ICE agents.
So why do so many Latinos join the immigration enforcement agencies that have targeted their own communities?
This episode traces the evolution of immigration enforcement agencies and their appeal to Latino recruits, to explain why so many ICE and Border Patrol agents are Latino.

text:
Under the second Trump administration, immigration enforcement agencies have undergone a significant expansion. President Donald Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill raised ICE’s budget from $10 billion to $85 billion, making it the most funded law enforcement agency in the United States. With that funding, they began offering economic incentives like signing bonuses and student loan forgiveness programs. The number of ICE agents and officers doubled in just one year, with another recruiting push underway through the end of 2026. Today, perhaps more than ever, the front lines of those federal immigration law enforcement agencies reflect the demographics of the populations they were created to police. Latinos are overrepresented in the Department of Homeland Security, which houses ICE and Border Patrol. Self-identified Latinos account for nearly half of Border Patrol agents and about 30 percent of ICE agents. So why do so many Latinos join the immigration enforcement agencies that have targeted their own communities? The answers reveal complexities about American Latino identity and the splintered points of view on immigration policy at the border. Hosted by Kahlil Greene, this video is part of our new series, Kahlil Explains, that unites Vox’s unique brand of explainer journalism with Greene’s expertise in how politics and culture shape society. This episode traces the evolution of immigration enforcement agencies and their appeal to Latino recruits, to explain why so many ICE and Border Patrol agents are Latino. text:
MINNEAPOLIS —

In its travel advisories, the U.S. State Department warns Americans not to visit Honduras' Gracias a Dios region, alerting them to violent crime, armed robbery, murder and active terrorist groups.

Video above: Why is the Trump administration changing the green card application process?

But for Hondurans, the message is less stark. “Overall, Gracias a Dios is a low-crime, functioning department,” says a State Department background report obtained by The Associated Press.

The report, and similar documents about Guatemala, Mexico and El Salvador, were prepared for use in immigration courts, where asylum denial rates have soared to 94% during President Donald Trump’s second term.

The reports use cherry-picked data, careful phrasing and in some cases facts that don’t stand up to scrutiny to create misleading depictions of countries that are in fact often plagued by violence, government corruption and police inaction.

They appear designed to make it easier for judges to deny asylum to people from those nations fleeing domestic violence and criminal gangs, painting pictures of life in their home countries that often clash with reality.

The reports have been "reverse-engineered,” said Elliot Young, a professor at Lewis & Clark College who analyzed the documents for the college’s Migration and Asylum Lab.

“They’re trying to hit the most frequent kinds of (asylum) cases that come up and provide counterevidence to the overwhelming evidence that these are dangerous places,” said Young, a scholar of Latin America and asylum law who has testified as an expert witness in more than 700 asylum cases.

The State Department did not respond to a request for comment on the reports. The Justice Department, which oversees immigration courts, did not respond to a request for comment on what role the reports play in influencing asylum decisions.

A system in turmoil – and targeted

Cutting back on asylum has been a centerpiece of Trump’s immigration crackdown dating to his first term, when he dismissed migrants waiting in Mexico to get into the U.S. as “not legitimate asylum-seekers.”

Most asylum seekers, the Republican president said, were fleeing poverty.

“Asylum is a very special protection intended only for those fleeing government persecution based on race, religion and other protected status,” he said in a 2018 White House appearance.

Trump was years out of date. While asylum was largely seen after World War II as a way to protect people fleeing political persecution, the definition was expanded long ago, including to encompass some people fleeing domestic and criminal violence.

But he had a point about poverty.

Legal and illegal migration, particularly from Latin America, has exploded over the past two decades as people have sought more economic opportunity, with increasing asylum claims based on safety fears from domestic partners and criminal gangs.

Even during President Joe Biden's years, most asylum claims were rejected.

But denials have jumped from roughly 72% at the end of that Democratic administration to 94% in June under Trump, according to the data research nonprofit Transactional Records Access Clearinghouse.

Trump was elected to a second term in part by focusing on frustrated voters who had seen illegal immigration soar under Biden, with border arrests from Mexico reaching a record 250,000 in December 2023. The asylum system, meanwhile, faced a backlog of millions of cases.

The Trump administration has reshaped immigration courts as part of its push to increase deportations, organizing mass hearings, authorizing military lawyers as immigration judges, and giving judges more leeway to summarily dismiss claims.

A sanitized view of troubled countries

Immigration judges must weigh whether people seeking asylum based on domestic violence or criminal threats have a reasonable fear of persecution because of their race, religion, nationality, political views or an often-debated catch-all category, “membership in a particular social group.” They also have to show that their government can't or won't protect them and that they can't move elsewhere in their home country to escape persecution.

The reports offer what can sometimes seem like travel brochure descriptions of life in these countries.

They mention good schools, low crime, quality hospitals and constitutions that protect individual rights, with brief notes that “the availability of services” can vary across each country.

Take El Salvador, where the government of President Nayib Bukele has long faced accusations of widespread human rights abuses, including torture.

The State Department report takes a far more generous view of the situation, noting the government approach to rights abuses “is no different than that of developed countries in Europe and North America, including the United States itself,” and highlighting a handful of prosecutions tied to the civil war, which ended in 1992.

“In any country, a rogue official can mistreat those under their power,” it says.

For Honduras’ Gracias a Dios province, violent crime rates “compare favorably with rates of violent crime in many parts of the United States,” says the report.

Former officials and advocates say the six-page reports pale in comparison to traditional State Department human rights reports, lengthy dissections of more than 100 nations around the world, which under the second Trump administration have been truncated and delayed.

“These shorter reports clearly don’t address the full range of human rights issues that the country reports have traditionally addressed,” said Scott Busby, former deputy assistant secretary in the Bureau of Democracy, Human Rights and Labor at the State Department and now a senior adviser at the group Human Rights First.

They are “especially problematic given that the country reports themselves for last year have yet to be issued,” he said.

Looking at asylum-seekers’ ability to move elsewhere

In many ways, the reports appear aimed most directly at asylum regulations around a person's ability to escape persecution by simply moving.

Those regulations are key for anyone seeking asylum based on domestic or criminal violence.

The reports highlight specific parts of each country, mentioning places like an off-the-beaten track tourist destination in Guatemala and a province in El Salvador that has low crime and 24-hour emergency medical care.

But those mentions only tell part of the story.

“The fact that there may be pockets of a country that are relatively safe for some people doesn’t mean that everybody can just move to that part of the country,” said Neela Chakravartula, an asylum attorney with the Center for Gender & Refugee Studies at the University of California College of the Law, San Francisco.

If that were the case, Chakravartula said: “We’d all be living in Malibu.”

title: A timeline of key events in Kilmar Ábrego García's fight with the Trump administration
description:
Kilmar Ábrego García entered the news in March 2025 after he was deported to El Salvador despite a court ruling that should have prevented it.
In a civil case in Maryland, Ábrego García challenged the Department of Homeland Security’s attempts to deport him to a series of African countries.
Months later, Ábrego García self-deported to Spain, potentially ending a defining saga of the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown.
Here is a timeline of key events: Ábrego García flees El Salvador for the U.S. as a teenager.
A Maryland immigration judge rules that Ábrego García cannot be deported to El Salvador, where a gang has threatened his family.
text:
Kilmar Ábrego García entered the news in March 2025 after he was deported to El Salvador despite a court ruling that should have prevented it. His complicated legal fight after that galvanized both sides of the debate over President Donald Trump’s immigration policies.

In a civil case in Maryland, Ábrego García challenged the Department of Homeland Security’s attempts to deport him to a series of African countries. A criminal case in Tennessee, where the government accused him of human smuggling, was dismissed after a judge found evidence of “vindictive prosecution” by the Justice Department. Months later, Ábrego García self-deported to Spain, potentially ending a defining saga of the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown.

Here is a timeline of key events:

Ábrego García flees El Salvador for the U.S. as a teenager.

Ábrego García is arrested outside a Maryland hardware store. Police accuse him of being a gang member and turn him over to U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

A Maryland immigration judge rules that Ábrego García cannot be deported to El Salvador, where a gang has threatened his family. He is given a work permit and placed under federal supervision.

Ábrego García is detained by ICE in Maryland while driving home with his 5-year-old son.

Ábrego García is mistakenly deported to El Salvador and held in a notoriously brutal prison.

The U.S. Supreme Court says the Trump administration must work to bring Ábrego García back.

In defiance of Trump, Democratic Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland meets with Ábrego García at a hotel in El Salvador, helping to establish hope and momentum for Ábrego García’s family.

Ábrego García is returned to the U.S. and charged with human smuggling, based on a Tennessee traffic stop from 2022.

ICE announces plans to remove him to a series of African countries, but is blocked by an injunction from a Maryland federal judge.

Ábrego García leaves the Tennessee jail, where he has been since June, to return to his family in Maryland and await trial. Within minutes of his release, ICE sends notice that they intend to deport him to Uganda.

Ábrego García reports to an immigration office in Baltimore and is taken into custody.

A federal judge in Maryland orders ICE to immediately release Ábrego García.

A Maryland federal judge rules ICE cannot re-detain Ábrego García.

A federal judge in Tennessee dismisses the human smuggling case against Ábrego García after finding evidence that the government engaged in “ vindictive prosecution."

The Justice Department tells a federal appeals court that the federal judge in Tennessee erred in his scathing May ruling in the criminal case against Ábrego García.

Ábrego García leaves the U.S. voluntarily for Spain, departing from Washington Dulles International Airport. According to an unsealed Nov. 20 order, a federal judge said the government informed her that Ábrego García was free to self-deport “to any country that is willing to accept him.” The judge, in turn, set Nov. 24 as the deadline for his departure and ordered the removal of his GPS ankle monitor before he boarded the flight.

text:
Democrats want to sideline President Donald Trump's immigration agenda when they take control of Congress next year, but the real fight may take place across the street where the conservative Supreme Court is poised to uphold several of his most controversial policies.

Video above: Kilmar Ábrego García self-deports out of the U.S.

The court will soon consider blockbuster appeals on the president's asylum ban, his vast expansion of mandatory detention of migrants and his push to send certain people in the U.S. illegally to countries other than their homeland — including some with poor human rights records.

Decisions in those cases are expected by late June.

Though those three cases and several others are less flashy than this past summer's blockbuster decision upholding birthright citizenship, the outcomes in the nuts-and-bolts disputes will have profound implications for policies the administration says are "indispensable" to its overall immigration crackdown.

"In all three of these cases, the Trump administration is trying to rewrite laws enacted by Congress, in service of a radical anti-immigrant agenda that has hurt not only immigrants, but the rule of law," said Cecillia Wang with the American Civil Liberties Union, which is opposing the administration in two of those cases. "These Trump policies are not only illegal but also unpopular."

Trump has had a mixed record on immigration at the 6-3 conservative court since returning to power last year. His unprecedented push to upend birthright citizenship was rejected. And the court limited his ability to use the 1798 Alien Enemies Act to quickly remove certain migrants from the country.

On the other hand, six-justice majorities in June allowed Trump to end a form of humanitarian relief known as Temporary Protected Status and to limit asylum claims made at the border.

White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis dismissed Wang's assertion that the court will find Trump's immigration policies illegal.

"If the American Civil Liberties Union cares more about criminal illegal aliens than they do about American citizens, then they should change their name," she said.

Some Democrats have framed the recapture of Congress as a rejection by voters of the administration's immigration policies. Minnesota Sen.-elect Peggy Flanagan vowed to "rip ICE apart." New York Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, who is all but certain to become the next House speaker, told CBS that Democrats would "put an end to Donald Trump's violent mass deportation machine."

But Republicans have already frontloaded funding for ICE for years. And Trump this month named Stephen Miller, the architect of his immigration crackdown, as White House chief of staff — a sign that the administration has no intention of slowing its immigration agenda.

"It stands to reason that hyper-aggressive immigration enforcement will continue to be one of the hallmarks of the Trump administration even as it faces Democratic majorities in both chambers of the legislature," said Steve Vladeck, CNN Supreme Court analyst and professor at Georgetown University Law Center. "Whether the extremism of these policies will be allowed to continue is therefore going to be up to the Supreme Court."

Conservatives who support the policies see a court that is prepared to back the president's program.

"Over and over, judges in the district courts and the courts of appeals have interpreted the law contrary to clear congressional intent as evidenced by the text. And as a result, those decisions keep getting overturned," Iowa Solicitor General Eric Wessan, whose state led briefs supporting the administration in two of the biggest cases, told CNN.

Wessan predicted that the justices will view lower court decisions on immigration against the administration with similar skepticism.

"Looking at the immigration cases the Supreme Court has taken this term," he predicted, "I think it's doing the same kind of cleanup."

Human rights and arrests

The showdown will begin on Dec. 9, when the justices will hear arguments in a case challenging Trump's push to remove certain migrants to countries other than their homeland. In many cases, those removals are carried out without giving the migrant an opportunity to raise human rights concerns.

Federal law allows such "third country" removals in cases when a migrant's home country refuses to accept them. The administration has used that provision to remove an Iranian national to Nicaragua, for instance, and Venezuelans to El Salvador, according to immigrants' rights groups.

In some of those cases, immigrant rights groups say, migrants were sent back to their homeland from the "third country," even when an immigration judge ordered that the administration not return to them to their native country.

Congress has also required the administration to ensure migrants won't be tortured or persecuted once they land in a third country. That determination was previously made on a case-by-case basis. Under the second Trump administration, the government now accepts blanket assurances from a foreign country that no torture will take place, and migrants are often removed to that country without notice.

The Supreme Court, on its emergency docket, three times allowed the administration to pursue the policy while the case remained pending. It has not explained its reasoning.

Increase in arrests of migrants

Next year, the court will turn to the Trump administration's decision to funnel not only recent border crossers into mandatory detention but also people who have been living within the United States for years.

That shift has permitted the Department of Homeland Security to dramatically increase the number of migrants arrested. And so if the court rejects that change, it will almost certainly jeopardize the administration's ability to carry out massive sweeps for migrants that have played out in cities like Chicago and Minneapolis.

Immigrant rights groups say no prior administration, including Trump's first, has interpreted federal law to require mandatory detention of so many migrants. But Justice Department officials told the Supreme Court that it is simply following the law that Congress enacted.

Asylum ban

And in the spring, the court will hear a challenge to Trump's asylum ban. The president argues people crossing the border are making false asylum claims as a way to enter the country then stall the deportation process, since it can take years to resolve them.

U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer, the administration's top appellate attorney, warned the court of a "vicious cycle" that encouraged "illegal entry by millions of aliens, who (quite justifiably) inferred that even if they lacked meritorious asylum claims, they would 'be released to live and work in the United States during their removal proceedings.'"

But the Immigration and Nationality Act specifically allows migrants to claim asylum, even as it leaves the decision about whether to grant safe harbor up to administration officials.

In stark language, the Justice Department has described its asylum policy as one of the "most important and effective" policies for stemming illegal immigration. A lower court order against the policy, the administration said, "threatens to revive the chaos along the southwest border that the proclamation has fended off for the past year and a half."

The ACLU, representing 13 individuals and three immigrant rights groups that challenged the policy, said that if Trump wants to change the way asylum works, he should have passed a bill in Congress during the two years the chambers were in Republican hands.

Richard Caldarone, a senior litigation attorney at the National Immigrant Justice Center, said that the policies at issue in the cases had already put tens of thousands of people in harm's way.

"These policies have been overwhelmingly rejected by lower courts across the country, and they flatly violate U.S. immigration law as it has been understood for decades," said Caldarone, whose group is fighting the administration in the asylum case.

"If the court validates the policies," he said, "it will enshrine a new generation of internment camps, all but end the U.S. asylum system as we have known it for almost half a century, and shatter our nation's commitment to upholding human rights and democratic norms."

name: Litigation
title: ICE arrests mount in Massachusetts courthouses despite law - Muslim Network TV
description:
The arrests occurred despite new restrictions introduced under Massachusetts’ PROTECT Act, which generally prohibits civil immigration arrests at courthouses without a judicial warrant or court order.
According to Massachusetts Trial Court records cited by WBUR, ICE agents carried out more than 36 courthouse arrests after the restrictions took effect.
Signed by Governor Maura Healey in early August, the PROTECT Act prohibits most civil immigration arrests at courthouses without judicial authorization.
Massachusetts court records further indicate that courthouse immigration arrests more than doubled during the first year of President Donald Trump’s second term, reaching an average of 2.5 arrests per day.
Importantly, the reported arrests do not establish that every detention violated the PROTECT Act, which distinguishes civil immigration enforcement from federal criminal arrests.
text:
BOSTON (MNTV) — U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents have arrested more than 36 people at courthouses across Massachusetts since Nov. 3, raising serious concerns about due process, immigrant rights and the federal government’s willingness to respect state-level safeguards against warrantless immigration enforcement.

The arrests occurred despite new restrictions introduced under Massachusetts’ PROTECT Act, which generally prohibits civil immigration arrests at courthouses without a judicial warrant or court order.

The legislation was designed to protect immigrants accessing the justice system from being detained by federal immigration authorities while attending court proceedings.

According to Massachusetts Trial Court records cited by WBUR, ICE agents carried out more than 36 courthouse arrests after the restrictions took effect.

Five arrests were recorded on the law’s first day, Nov. 3, twice the daily average reported in 2025. The figures have intensified concerns among defense attorneys and immigrant rights advocates, who argue that federal enforcement practices may be undermining access to justice and violating protections established by state law.

Signed by Governor Maura Healey in early August, the PROTECT Act prohibits most civil immigration arrests at courthouses without judicial authorization. It also extends restrictions to schools, childcare facilities and certain healthcare locations, limits cooperation between state and local authorities and ICE, and provides avenues for legal action against government officials involved in specified violations.

Under the legislation, unlawful courthouse detentions may constitute false imprisonment, potentially exposing those responsible to legal consequences. Massachusetts Attorney General Andrea Campbell’s office has confirmed receiving complaints about ICE conduct and encouraged individuals with relevant information to come forward.

One particularly concerning case involves 24-year-old Brazilian national Rhyan Oliveira, who was arrested by ICE agents at Framingham District Court on Nov. 17, shortly after Judge Sarah Kennedy ordered his release under conditions in a state criminal case.

Oliveira faced three felony charges arising from an alleged domestic violence incident. His public defender disputed the allegations and said he had no prior criminal record. Despite the judge’s release order, ICE agents detained him in the courthouse lobby while his mother and sister were waiting to take him home.

WBUR reported finding no federal criminal charges against Oliveira and no judicial warrant in his state court file. ICE did not respond to questions about the circumstances or legal basis of his arrest.

The incident has raised fundamental questions about the relationship between immigration enforcement and the state judicial system, particularly when individuals are detained immediately after receiving court-authorized release.

Experts argue that such practices risk undermining judicial authority and discouraging immigrants from appearing in court, cooperating with legal proceedings or seeking protection from abuse.

Another case illustrates how the threat of immigration detention is influencing decisions within the criminal justice system. In Marlborough, defense attorney Trevor Clement said one of his clients chose to remain in state custody rather than pay $5,000 in bail out of fear that release would expose him to an ICE arrest.

Federal agents subsequently arrested a Brazilian woman facing a misdemeanor shoplifting charge.

For immigrant communities, the consequences extend beyond individual arrests.

The possibility of being detained at a courthouse can discourage people from reporting crimes, attending hearings, seeking legal assistance or complying with court orders.

Such fears could disproportionately affect vulnerable individuals, including victims of domestic violence and people with limited access to legal representation.

ICE has defended its courthouse operations, arguing that such locations provide a safer environment for enforcement because visitors must pass through security screening.

An agency spokesperson also invoked the Constitution’s Supremacy Clause, arguing that state and local officials cannot restrict federal immigration enforcement and declaring that sanctuary policies do not control federal law enforcement.

However, the constitutional dispute does not automatically resolve whether individual arrests comply with applicable legal requirements. While federal immigration law generally operates under federal authority, the scope of federal enforcement powers, the validity of state restrictions and the circumstances surrounding specific arrests remain subject to legal scrutiny.

The Supremacy Clause does not eliminate the need for federal agencies to comply with constitutional protections and applicable legal procedures.

Massachusetts court records further indicate that courthouse immigration arrests more than doubled during the first year of President Donald Trump’s second term, reaching an average of 2.5 arrests per day.

The figures point to an intensification of immigration enforcement within judicial spaces, raising broader questions about the administration’s approach to immigration, federalism and civil liberties.

Importantly, the reported arrests do not establish that every detention violated the PROTECT Act, which distinguishes civil immigration enforcement from federal criminal arrests.

Determining whether individual operations breached the law requires examining the legal authority, warrants and circumstances involved in each case.

Nevertheless, the growing number of courthouse arrests presents a serious challenge to the principle that access to justice should not expose individuals to arbitrary detention.

Courthouses are essential institutions where people must be able to defend themselves, seek protection and comply with judicial orders without fearing that their presence will trigger unrelated immigration enforcement.

As Massachusetts officials investigate complaints and immigrant advocates demand accountability, the central legal and humanitarian question remains whether federal immigration enforcement is respecting the rights of individuals and the boundaries of lawful authority.

Protecting public safety cannot come at the expense of due process, judicial independence and equal access to justice.

text:
By TIM SULLIVAN

MINNEAPOLIS (AP) — In its travel advisories, the U.S. State Department warns Americans not to visit Honduras’ Gracias a Dios region, alerting them to violent crime, armed robbery, murder and active terrorist groups.

But for Hondurans, the message is less stark. “Overall, Gracias a Dios is a low-crime, functioning department,” says a State Department background report obtained by The Associated Press.

The report, and similar documents about Guatemala, Mexico and El Salvador, were prepared for use in immigration courts, where asylum denial rates have soared to 94% during President Donald Trump’s second term.

The reports use cherry-picked data, careful phrasing and in some cases facts that don’t stand up to scrutiny to create misleading depictions of countries that are in fact often plagued by violence, government corruption and police inaction.

They appear designed to make it easier for judges to deny asylum to people from those nations fleeing domestic violence and criminal gangs, painting pictures of life in their home countries that often clash with reality.

The reports have been “reverse-engineered,” said Elliot Young, a professor at Lewis & Clark College who analyzed the documents for the college’s Migration and Asylum Lab.

“They’re trying to hit the most frequent kinds of (asylum) cases that come up and provide counterevidence to the overwhelming evidence that these are dangerous places,” said Young, a scholar of Latin America and asylum law who has testified as an expert witness in more than 700 asylum cases.

In a statement, the State Department said that in line with U.S. laws and regulations it “may provide information about conditions in foreign countries” to immigration courts and U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services. The Justice Department, which oversees immigration courts, did not respond to a request for comment on what role the reports play in influencing asylum decisions.

A system in turmoil – and targeted

Cutting back on asylum has been a centerpiece of Trump’s immigration crackdown dating to his first term, when he dismissed migrants waiting in Mexico to get into the U.S. as “not legitimate asylum-seekers.”

Most asylum seekers, the Republican president said, were fleeing poverty.

“Asylum is a very special protection intended only for those fleeing government persecution based on race, religion and other protected status,” he said in a 2018 White House appearance.

Trump was years out of date. While asylum was largely seen after World War II as a way to protect people fleeing political persecution, the definition was expanded long ago, including to encompass some people fleeing domestic and criminal violence.

But he had a point about poverty.

Legal and illegal migration, particularly from Latin America, has exploded over the past two decades as people have sought more economic opportunity, with increasing asylum claims based on safety fears from domestic partners and criminal gangs.

Even during President Joe Biden’s years, most asylum claims were rejected.

But denials have jumped from roughly 72% at the end of that Democratic administration to 94% in June under Trump, according to the data research nonprofit Transactional Records Access Clearinghouse.

Trump was elected to a second term in part by focusing on frustrated voters who had seen illegal immigration soar under Biden, with border arrests from Mexico reaching a record 250,000 in December 2023. The asylum system, meanwhile, faced a backlog of millions of cases.

The Trump administration has reshaped immigration courts as part of its push to increase deportations, organizing mass hearings, authorizing military lawyers as immigration judges, and giving judges more leeway to summarily dismiss claims.

A sanitized view of troubled countries

Immigration judges must weigh whether people seeking asylum based on domestic violence or criminal threats have a reasonable fear of persecution because of their race, religion, nationality, political views or an often-debated catch-all category, “membership in a particular social group.” They also have to show that their government can’t or won’t protect them and that they can’t move elsewhere in their home country to escape persecution.

The reports offer what can sometimes seem like travel brochure descriptions of life in these countries.

They mention good schools, low crime, quality hospitals and constitutions that protect individual rights, with brief notes that “the availability of services” can vary across each country.

Take El Salvador, where the government of President Nayib Bukele has long faced accusations of widespread human rights abuses, including torture.

The State Department report takes a far more generous view of the situation, noting the government approach to rights abuses “is no different than that of developed countries in Europe and North America, including the United States itself,” and highlighting a handful of prosecutions tied to the civil war, which ended in 1992.

“In any country, a rogue official can mistreat those under their power,” it says.

For Honduras’ Gracias a Dios province, violent crime rates “compare favorably with rates of violent crime in many parts of the United States,” says the report.

Former officials and advocates say the six-page reports pale in comparison to traditional State Department human rights reports, lengthy dissections of more than 100 nations around the world, which under the second Trump administration have been truncated and delayed.

“These shorter reports clearly don’t address the full range of human rights issues that the country reports have traditionally addressed,” said Scott Busby, former deputy assistant secretary in the Bureau of Democracy, Human Rights and Labor at the State Department and now a senior adviser at the group Human Rights First.

They are “especially problematic given that the country reports themselves for last year have yet to be issued,” he said.

Looking at asylum-seekers’ ability to move elsewhere

In many ways, the reports appear aimed most directly at asylum regulations around a person’s ability to escape persecution by simply moving.

Those regulations are key for anyone seeking asylum based on domestic or criminal violence.

The reports highlight specific parts of each country, mentioning places like an off-the-beaten track tourist destination in Guatemala and a province in El Salvador that has low crime and 24-hour emergency medical care.

But those mentions only tell part of the story.

“The fact that there may be pockets of a country that are relatively safe for some people doesn’t mean that everybody can just move to that part of the country,” said Neela Chakravartula, an asylum attorney with the Center for Gender & Refugee Studies at the University of California College of the Law, San Francisco.

If that were the case, Chakravartula said: “We’d all be living in Malibu.”

Associated Press reporter Joshua Goodman in Miami contributed to this report.

title: Quiet Deportation to Spain Ends Abrego Garcia Saga - National Review
description:
Kilmar Abrego Garcia has arrived in Madrid after the Trump administration finally acceded to his request to be deported to Spain, a country agreeable to him — which is what federal immigration law calls for when such an accommodation is practicable.
Thus ends, for now, a nearly two-year saga that we’ve covered extensively (see, e.g., here).
We have to qualify with “for now” because, after all the twists and turns, there’s a very good chance that Abrego (whose wife and child are American citizens) will be triumphantly readmitted to the United States — this time, lawfully — if a Democrat is elected president in 2028.
For immigration hawks (such as moi), his case is a cautionary tale in how benighted execution of a popular enforcement policy can turn a political asset into a liability.

title: Trump Administration Is Hiking Immigration Bond Costs to Keep Migrants Locked Up
authors: Marianne Dhenin, Mike Ludwig, Jamila Osman
description:

Even when a bond is granted, freedom remains out of reach for many caught in the Trump administration’s deportation machine because median bond amounts have also increased.
“It’s a lot harder to fight your immigration case when you’re in a jail cell,” Tan told Truthout.
The Trump administration has also purged dozens of immigration judges and recruited replacements that it now calls “deportation judges,” rather than immigration judges.

text:
When Donald Trump returned to the White House in January 2025 after campaigning on mass deportation, his administration got to work expanding immigration detention and reshaping the nation’s immigration courts to make it more difficult for jailed migrants to seek release. Almost two years later, data show just how successful those policies have been.

The number of people jailed in Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detention nationwide is up roughly 80 percent since President Joe Biden left office. The Trump administration has foreclosed most avenues through which jailed migrants have historically sought release. For the shrinking share of the jailed population that does access an immigration bond hearing, the average bond denial rate has jumped. It rose to about 60 percent in the first year of Trump 2.0, up from about 53 percent in the last year of Biden’s tenure. The denial rate has continued to rise this year.

Even when a bond is granted, freedom remains out of reach for many caught in the Trump administration’s deportation machine because median bond amounts have also increased. Those amounts have even doubled from 2024 to the first months of 2026 in some of the federal circuit court jurisdictions with the most immigration bond cases, according to data compiled and analyzed by Bklg.org.

“This is a linchpin in the administration’s deportation strategy,” Michael Tan, deputy director of the Immigrants’ Rights Project at the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU), told Truthout. “The primary reason they’re subjecting people to detention with no avenue for release is to coerce them into giving up their immigration cases, their claims to legal status, to remaining in the country, and to acquiesce to a deportation because they can’t stand being locked up for so long.”

Even for those who do not agree to so-called self-deportation, outcomes tend to be worse for those who fight their immigration cases while detained. Those who are released are more likely to have their immigration cases resolved with permission to remain in the U.S. than with deportation orders. Once freed, a person tends to have more resources and more time to participate in their case, gather evidence, and access other needed support. “It’s a lot harder to fight your immigration case when you’re in a jail cell,” Tan told Truthout. Especially, he added, “when ICE moves people all over the place, and so it’s not the case that you’ll be detained often in your community or near your family [and] your lawyer. Instead, ICE is routinely shipping people to far-flung locations.”

Fisayo Okare, digital communications manager at Envision Freedom Fund, told Truthout that migrant community members with whom her organization works regularly face these pressures. “Families are thinking of whether it’s worth it or not to even remain in the country or just choosing to voluntarily deport,” she said. The nonprofit Envision Freedom Fund is the largest immigration bond fund in the nation; it helps cover bonds for individuals jailed in New York or New Jersey and those who will return home to the area on release. Since the fund launched in 2018, it has provided over $15 million in bond support to help secure the release of over 1,600 people from immigration jails.

An October report from Envision Freedom Fund shows how the increase in the number of migrants jailed and struggling to access release is affecting communities in New York and New Jersey. The volume of requests for support that the bond fund receives has risen so much that it projects it will cover nine times as many bonds in 2026 as in 2024, if it can raise the funds needed to meet demand through the end of the calendar year.

“The fact is that we’re forced to bond so many more people out now because the sheer volume of the system — everything is increasing,” Ben McCoubrey, Envision Freedom Fund’s data and advocacy manager, told Truthout.

It has never been easy for those in ICE jails to access bond, a process that entails securing a bond hearing in immigration court, finding a lawyer to present the case, then convincing the immigration judge to grant a bond, and ultimately finding someone outside with U.S. citizenship or a green card and the funds needed to post the bond. But the obstacles to accessing bond are now greater than ever before thanks to what Tan characterized to Truthout as the Trump administration’s “takeover of the immigration courts.”

Since Trump returned to office, he has signed executive orders to expand detention and restrict release. Based on those directives, ICE’s lawyers have made legal arguments and issued guidance meant to subject as many immigrants as possible to mandatory detention and limit their access to bond. Those directives have become standard practice following administration-friendly decisions from the Board of Immigration Appeals, which governs the immigration courts and judges from within the Department of Justice.

The Trump administration has also purged dozens of immigration judges and recruited replacements that it now calls “deportation judges,” rather than immigration judges. Many of these new judges come from the ranks of former military lawyers, ICE lawyers, and prosecutors with little or no experience or training in immigration law.

“They’ve fired immigration judges that they think, in their view, are too friendly to immigrants and replaced them with so-called deportation judges [and] for the judges who remain, who didn’t get fired, we know that the administration is exerting pressure on them to deny relief, and to really crack down, and serve as foot soldiers in a mass deportation campaign,” Tan told Truthout. “They’ve taken an immigration court system that is supposed to be neutral and fair and made it into an arm of the immigration enforcement system.”

The ACLU has litigated the Trump administration’s mandatory detention scheme in every circuit court where it could be heard, a total of 11 of the nation’s 13. Only two circuits have concurred with the administration’s interpretation of the law. Nine have rejected it, opening the door for more individuals to access bond hearings in the 40 states covered by those circuits. The Supreme Court will hear the issue in a case arising from the Second Circuit, Rhoney v. Barbosa da Cunha, next year; Tan told Truthout a decision is expected by the end of June. The outcome will affect access to bond hearings for those in ICE jails nationwide.

While the legal fight continues, the humanitarian crisis created by the Trump administration’s policy changes is deepening. Envision Freedom Fund’s recent report helps put a human face on the issue. “We paint a picture of what’s happening in the context of detention and deportation, how things are growing, and go beyond what we see when it’s just [the number of] people getting released on bonds,” McCoubrey told Truthout about the report’s aims.

The report includes stories of immigrants who have suffered medical neglect and other traumas in ICE jails and are navigating the lasting effects after being bonded out with Envision Freedom Fund’s support.

One man for whom the fund helped cover a $50,000 bond to secure his release in July 2026 shared that he “felt unmeasurably happy when [he] got released from the jail.” He had been jailed for over two months, and after release, said, “I believed that now everything will be okay. Because when I was in there, I was stressing a lot. I didn’t know what would happen because nowadays it’s really tough.” Just two weeks after the man’s release, his asylum case was granted — ending a more than four-year wait that began in 2022.

More recently, Okare told Truthout that Envision Freedom Fund secured release for a man in his mid-thirties who had been transferred from Delaney Hall in New Jersey to an ICE jail in Georgia. The fund then coordinated with partners to arrange transportation to bring him home in time to be with his wife and witness the birth of his child. “His wife was actually in the hospital when we got the bond request, and he got out right in time,” she said.

Okare told Truthout that stories like these are common in the work of Envision Freedom Fund and other immigration bond funds operating nationwide. For each of the tens of thousands of people jailed in the country’s ICE detention facilities, there are families missing a parent or a sibling and communities missing a neighbor.

As the Trump administration continues pulling these communities apart, Okare told Truthout that organizations like hers will keep fighting to make them whole again: “[We’re] not just paying their bond but ensuring that they get out and make it back to their community.”

Based off the story gathered through city workers and video footage of the instance, Galvan told reporters an unmarked vehicle had followed a father and son onto the public driveway at the waste collection center around 9 a.m. Nov. 19.

>> ICE arrest man at city bulk waste drop-off; San Antonio councilman asks family to contact him

Jones said the location was open to the public at the time and that the man who was detained drove onto the property himself after being pulled over.

“It wasn’t like there was any cooperation between city staff or certainly (the San Antonio Police Department),” Jones said, adding that the immigration enforcement had “no city association” other than the arrest happening on the city’s property.

Jones said the city is working on its federal and state legislative agendas and met with Congressman-elect Johnny Garcia, who formerly worked with the Bexar County Sheriff’s Department before running to represent Texas’ newly drawn 35th Congressional District.

Jones said there are 100,000 undocumented people in the community and noted a “chilling effect” on people reporting crimes or abuse to law enforcement.

Asked about the coming change in Austin, Jones said she has shared the city’s priorities with newly elected state leaders. She listed Medicaid expansion and the repeal of both versions of Senate Bill 4 — which looks to prohibit “sanctuary city” policies — among the top items.

Some related bills have already been filed, according to Jones.

“We look forward to the change that our neighbors clearly said they want as a result of the recent election,” she said.

Jones, who is an Air Force veteran, also discussed the city’s push to expand housing protections for veterans.

title: Can Democrats in Congress stop Trump's deportations? - Latinoamérica 21
description:
Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress and key governorships, partly thanks to Latino voters who had supported him in 2024.
